records.title: Human Saliva Induces Acetoin-Dependent Metabolic Adaptation that Promotes Stress Tolerance in  Streptococcus mutans
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Oral microbes are continually exposed to host-derived saliva, yet its effects on bacterial metabolism and stress adaptation remain incompletely defined. We investigated how saliva supplementation alters the physiology of the caries-associated bacterium  Streptococcus mutans using transcriptomics (RNA-Seq), targeted metabolite measurements, specific gene deletions, and transposon sequencing (Tn-Seq). Growth in a chemically defined medium supplemented with pooled saliva altered expression of genes involved in carbohydrate transport, purine biosynthesis, and pyruvate-associated metabolism, including induction of the acetoin dehydrogenase operon. Saliva significantly increased extracellular acetoin accumulation across all  S. mutans isolates tested, whereas little accumulation occurred in two commensal streptococcal species examined. Deletion of acetolactate synthase/decarboxylase (  alsSaldB ) abolished the saliva-associated increase, while deletion of individual acetoin dehydrogenase components (  adhC /  lplA ) enhanced accumulation, supporting the predicted roles of genes in acetoin synthesis and catabolism. Increasing the available carbohydrate concentrations within the media further increased acetoin accumulation, alongside declining terminal culture pH that was significantly lower in cultures supplemented with saliva. Following growth with saliva,  S. mutans exhibited approximately 10,000-fold greater survival during a hydrogen peroxide challenge than cells grown without saliva. Mutants within the acetoin pathway retained saliva-associated protection but showed approximately 100-fold lower survival than the wild type. Serial passage of a pooled transposon library identified previously unrecognized saliva-associated fitness determinants, including depletion of mutants carrying insertions in the acetoin dehydrogenase operon. Together, these findings identify acetoin metabolism as a contributor to saliva-associated metabolic remodeling and oxidative stress tolerance in  S. mutans and establish saliva as a critical modulator of  S. mutans physiology.
records.authors: Harris JS, Deever AN, Lee K, Kaspar JR.

records.title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury.
records.abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3-5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

records.title: Bacteriophages versus priority pathogens: resistance mechanisms, therapeutic challenges, and opportunities for novel combinations.
records.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a critical global health threat, and renewed interest in bacteriophage (phage) therapy highlights its potential as a targeted alternative to antibiotic monotherapy. However, phage resistance in bacteria remains a key limiting factor in phage therapy, driven by evolutionary adaptations to phage exposure. Antibacterial modalities (antibiotics, adjuvants, antimicrobial peptides, and RNA-based therapeutics) could help overcome these barriers and represent untapped potential for synergistic, precision antimicrobial interventions when combined with phage therapy. Importantly, bacterial physiology and environmental context could strongly influence treatment outcomes, underscoring the need for clinically relevant models for testing combinations. Integration of multi-omics and artificial intelligence-driven approaches could help predict patterns for the development of precision therapies and support the development of novel antimicrobial interventions.
records.authors: Byrne S, Collins ACZ, Nolan AC, Wigneshweraraj S, Zeden MS.

records.title: Multi-omics insights into rare earth element recovery by microalgae under salinity gradients.
records.abstract: Conventional rare earth element (REE) extraction methods are resource-intensive and generate secondary pollutants, whereas biomining using microorganisms such as microalgae offers a more sustainable alternative. Microalgal growth and metal recovery are strongly influenced by environmental factors, especially salinity; however, the molecular mechanisms driving REE recovery in microalgae exposed to saline conditions remain largely unexplored. The overarching aim of this study is to elucidate the effects of salinity on REE recovery by microalgae using a multi-omics framework. Specifically, nine microalgal strains were screened across salinities of 0-5 %, followed by integrated metabolomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic characterization of Limnospira maxima under control, REE-only, 3.5 % salinity, and combined REE-salinity conditions. Among the tested species, L. maxima exhibited the highest REE recovery efficiency, outperforming other microalgae by a factor of 2-10. In L. maxima, heavy REE (Sc, Y, Tb, and Dy) were recovered 10-15 % more efficiently than light REE (La, Pr, Nd), particularly under salinities between 0.5 % and 5 %. The selective recovery of REE by L. maxima was most pronounced at elevated salinities. Global metabolomic profiles of the combined treatment were primarily associated with salinity, suggesting that salinity establishes the dominant physiological state within which REE-associated responses occur. Multi-omics analysis showed distinct responses to REE and salinity stress, including changes in carbon fixation, photosynthesis, and amino acid and lipid metabolism, with both transcript-protein convergence and pathway-level discordance indicating complex cross-layer regulation. Overall, the results identify L. maxima as a promising candidate for REE recovery under saline conditions while defining molecular responses and knowledge gaps relevant to future development of microalgae-based REE separation.
records.authors: Vo PHN, Songsomboon K, Kim M, Strezov V, Clark S, Kuzhiumparambil U, Pernice M, Ralph PJ.

records.title: Adaptive evolution identifies candidate genetic routes associated with oxalate utilization in probiotic and gut-derived E.coli.
records.abstract: Functional probiotics offer a therapeutic modality for degrading disease-associated compounds in the gut. In hyperoxaluria, therapeutic strategies based on natural oxalate degraders such as Oxalobacter formigenes have shown variable efficacy, motivating methods to expand the repertoire of oxalate-utilizing bacterial chassis and explore native genetic routes by which this function can evolve. Here, we used adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) under microaerobic conditions to enable oxalate utilization in probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 and three gut-derived E. coli isolates. Within ∼400 generations, all lines evolved robust growth on minimal medium with oxalate as the sole carbon and energy source. Recurrent mutations identify native aldehyde-dehydrogenase-associated modules, including AdhE and the Eut system, as candidate genetic routes associated with evolved oxalate utilization. We propose ALE as a scalable framework to uncover latent metabolic potential in probiotic and gut-associated bacteria and generate mechanistically tractable candidates for downstream functional validation.
records.authors: Yona AH, Joshua Liu CW, Ben-Moshe Z, Nichols TM, Bodhankar GA, Key FM, Rao CV, Lieberman T, Tullman-Ercek D, Gore J.

records.title: TEDEdb: A multicohort analysis and resource for transposable element differential expression in cancer.
records.abstract: The human genome consists of nearly 50% repetitive DNA, referred to for decades as "junk DNA." These repetitive sequences, usually under the strict control of epigenetic silencing, can become aberrantly expressed in cancer. Some of these expressed sequences, e.g., transposable elements (TEs), can induce innate immune responses when derepressed following treatment with epigenetic therapies. As a result, epigenetic therapy has been suggested to augment cancer therapies. TEs are traditionally ignored in most RNA-seq studies and their expression is often excluded from publicly available data sources. Thus, the vast amount of publicly available RNA-seq data is an untapped resource for exploring the role of TE expression in cancer and cancer treatment. Here, we present a uniform reanalysis of over 7,000 RNA-seq samples, encompassing more than 2,000 differential expression experiments across 220 cancer cell lines and 700 drug treatments. We observed that TE expression is more prone to batch effects than gene expression alone, necessitating the use of meta-analysis techniques to probe the dataset for global trends. We confirm that DNMTi and HDACis are powerful inducers of TE expression. We also show that nonepigenetic compounds such as cyclin-dependent kinase and topoisomerase inhibitors can also induce robust up-regulation of TE-derived repetitive DNA elements and confirm that this induction is consistent with transcriptional signatures of viral mimicry response. We made all data available through a publicly available database called the Transposable Element Differential Expression Database, or TEDEdb, and created an interactive web application for its exploration located at https://dataexplorer.coriell.org/TEDEdb/.
records.authors: Calendo G, Chaunzwa M, Dehzangi I, Madzo J, Issa JJ.

records.title: Evolutionarily diverged on-switch for actin assembly in fungal endocytosis.
records.abstract: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is a conserved eukaryotic trafficking process where an Arp2/3 complex-nucleated branched actin network provides force for vesicle formation. The mechanisms that initiate endocytic actin assembly are incompletely understood. In the fission yeast, Schizosaccharomyces pombe, actin assembly is initiated by Dip1, an Arp2/3 complex activator. In the budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the initiation of actin assembly has remained a mystery. Here, we show that S. cerevisiae Ldb17, the homolog of Dip1, functions as an on-switch for endocytic actin assembly. Unexpectedly, the regulation of Ldb17 is more complicated than that of constitutively active Dip1. Ldb17 is controlled by a coat protein, Sla1, via separate recruitment and activation steps. This regulation was likely lost in the S. pombe lineage, and this simplification may be related to other changes in actin assembly between these species. Our findings add a key missing piece in the understanding of endocytosis in S. cerevisiae and reveal an intriguing evolutionary tinkering of the actin on-switch.
records.authors: Sebellin J, Kandiyoth FB, Bagyashree VT, Picco A, Carvalho N, Hakala M, Rivier-Cordey AS, Michelot A, Toret CP, Kaksonen M.

records.title: Temporal phosphoproteomic programmes set a redox-gated rheostat on neutrophil phagocytosis
records.abstract: Neutrophils are essential frontline immune cells in the defence against bacterial pathogens such as  Staphylococcus aureus , but their killing machinery also causes host tissue damage. How neutrophils regulate these processes remains incompletely understood. Here, we profiled the proteome and phosphoproteome of human neutrophils across a two-hour exposure to  S. aureus , alongside five simultaneous functional readouts, before investigating how an initial encounter modulates the response to a second. The phosphoproteomic response resolved into qualitatively distinct early and late windows: the early landscape drives particle uptake, while by the late window this machinery is deactivated, with a broadly supressed kinome, and cells geared towards inflammatory output. Correlating protein phosphorylation and functional kinetics — an approach we term KINETIC — implicates putative mediators of key neutrophil antimicrobial functions. A genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen in neutrophil-like PLB-985 cells, sorted on phagocytic load, recovered canonical engulfment machinery among the strongest facilitators of phagocytosis, additionally identifying the lysosomal Ragulator-mTORC1 nutrient sensing pathway and HOPS complex corresponding to the KINETIC-identified pathways. Conversely, the NRF2 repressor KEAP1 was the strongest phagocytic brake, positioning oxidative burden as a regulator of phagocytic appetite. Neutrophils in the late window exhibited impaired phagocytosis and phagosomal acidification on  S.aureus re-challenge. Underlying these functional deficits, cells in the late window were refractory across multiomic layers: a second  S. aureus meal altered no phosphoprotein, protein, or transcript, whereas the chemoattractants PAF and fMLP evoked a largely consistent phosphoproteomic programme, delineating the phenotype as receptor-specific rather than a global loss of signalling capacity. Consistent with de-repressing the antioxidant response via genetic loss of KEAP1 increasing phagocytosis, reducing ROS production via inhibition of the NADPH oxidase resulted in a partial rescue of phagocytosis of the re-exposed  S.aureus . Together, these findings describe a ROS-gated phagocytic rheostat, enabling neutrophils to meter their phagocytic appetite according to their exposure history, likely limiting uptake of pathogens they lack the capacity to effectively digest. Inappropriate activation of this rheostat under conditions of physiological stress or severe illness may underpin the defects in phagocytosis identified in such patients.

records.title: A novel lineage of  Chilomastix mesnili  in wild Moroccan Barbary macaques (  Macaca sylvanus  )
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Chilomastix spp. are flagellated protists found in the intestines of a broad range of hosts. They are generally non-pathogenic and have been little studied, especially using molecular techniques, and significant taxonomic uncertainty regarding the host specificity of lineages remains. As part of a study of intestinal microbial communities of wild Barbary macaques (  Macaca sylvanus ) from Morocco, we mined 50 faecal metagenomic sequence libraries and found 11 rRNA sequences matching  Chilomastix . Compared to published 18S rRNA sequences, the Barbary macaque  Chilomastix sequences formed a well-supported clade distinct from human-derived  C. mesnili ST1 from Indonesia. The macaque  Chilomastix sequences cluster with a single pig-derived isolate and two sequences from Japanese macaques (  Macaca fuscata ). This indicates that  M. sylvanus harbours a lineage of  Chilomastix distinct from the common human strain of  C. mesnili and geographically widespread. We were also able to reconstruct the complete rDNA operon from this lineage.

records.title: Sequence-structured fitness landscapes predict influenza evolution
records.abstract: Seasonal influenza viruses continually evolve to evade host immunity. Vaccines must be regularly updated to protect against new circulating strains, motivating efforts to forecast viral evolution. Recent experimental and computational methods have made progress on this problem, but learning the fitness landscape driving viral evolution remains challenging because genomic surveillance samples only a small fraction of the possible sequence space. Here, we developed a generative framework that shares information across genetically related variants, inferring effective mutation-level contributions to viral fitness from temporal sequence data. Applied to hemagglutinin and neuraminidase from A/H3N2 and A/H1N1 viruses, the inferred fitness landscapes recovers known determinants of antigenicity and reveals convergent spatial organization across subtypes consistent with common antibody-mediated selection. Forward simulations from these landscapes predicted both the fixation or loss of circulating mutations and the future composition of viral populations, outperforming models based on neutral evolution or multinomial-logistic growth. Collectively, our results show that interpretable representations of pathogen fitness landscapes can reveal biologically important features and improve prospective evolutionary forecasting.
records.authors: Rodríguez-Horta E, Barton JP.

records.title: Transcriptomic and metabolomic profiling reveals early responses of tomato plants elicited by compost-derived bacteria
records.abstract: Compost produced from biowaste has a defined microbiota, and some bacterial species may represent promising resources for low-input crop systems. However, their effects on plant physiology are poorly investigated and remain difficult to predict from standard bacterial traits alone. We isolated several bacterial strains (  Bacillus sonorensis, Glutamicibacter arilaitensis, and  Kocuria rhizophila ) from biowaste compost and examined their early effects on tomato seedlings under controlled in vitro conditions. Responses were assessed by root phenotyping, root and shoot transcriptomics, and mass spectrometry-based profiling of primary metabolites in plant tissues, root exudates and bacterial culture filtrates.  B. sonorensis induces the broadest response, reducing primary root length and lateral root number and density and triggering broad transcriptional changes related to metabolism, redox balance, hormone signalling and defence-associated pathways.  G. arilaitensis elicits a more selective, tissue-dependent response, whereas  K. rhizophila has limited phenotypic and transcriptional effects at this stage. All isolates reshape primary metabolism, with recurrent effects on amino acid-, carbohydrate- and lipid-related pathways, together with isolate-specific changes in root exudate composition. This study characterises the early molecular and metabolic responses of tomato to compost-derived bacteria and identifies common and strain-specific physiological signatures that provide a foundation for future studies under biotic and abiotic stress.
records.authors: Ghirardello G, Araniti F, Cipriani R, Zanardi W, Bonato T, Baldan B, Nigris S.

records.title: Selection through soft and incomplete sweeps underlies postglacial ecotype differentiation in an Arctic wide-ranging ungulate
records.abstract: Abstract  Ecotypes offer a window into the earliest stages of adaptive divergence, before reproductive isolation is complete. In eastern Canada, migratory and boreal caribou (Rangifer tarandus caribou) represent a striking example of recent ecological divergence, differing primarily in movement strategy despite ongoing gene flow. We used low- and high-coverage whole-genome sequencing from migratory and boreal populations in Quebec and Labrador to characterize the timing, demographic history, and genomic signatures of this divergence. Demographic modeling supported a secondary contact scenario, with an estimated divergence time roughly 7,000–11,700 years ago, coinciding with the last deglaciation period. Despite weak overall population structure (genome-wide FST = 0.02) and evidence of continued gene flow, we identified distinct genomic peaks of differentiation, nearly half of which coincided with divergent haplotype length (XP-nSL), a pattern consistent with recent, incomplete soft selective sweeps rather than classic hard sweeps. Combining differentiation-, diversity-, and haplotype-based statistics proved essential for detecting this subtle selection signature. Candidate genes under selection point to a polygenic architecture spanning bone and connective tissue development (including antler-related pathways), mitochondrial energy metabolism, and other traits plausibly linked to the ecological differences between ecotypes. Together, our results suggest that caribou ecotypes are not fixed evolutionary endpoints but a dichotomy that can re-emerge from standing genetic variation as opportunity arises.
records.authors: Dallaire X, Yannic G, Taillon J, St-Laurent M, Robert C, Côté S, Shafer A.

records.title: Infection-Induced SRSF2 Downregulation Drives VEGF-A Isoform Switching to Impair Angiogenesis in Diabetic Foot Ulcers
records.abstract: Abstract    Background:  Impaired vascular repair and infection contribute to delayed healing in diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs). Whether infection-associated inflammatory stress affects endothelial function through altered RNA processing remains incompletely understood. We investigated SRSF2 and VEGFA isoform regulation in this setting. Human DFU tissues and microbiota were assessed across Wagner grades, and bacterial inoculation was examined in a diabetic mouse wound model. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) were exposed to high glucose (HG) with or without lipopolysaccharide (LPS). SRSF2 was manipulated to assess scratch closure, EdU incorporation, and tube formation. Knockdown RNA sequencing was performed separately in HMEC-1 cells. Isoform-directed RT-qPCR, RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP)-qPCR, and a dual-fluorescence VEGFA minigene reporter were used to examine RNA regulation in HUVECs.  Results:  Higher Wagner grades were associated with lower granulation tissue and CD31-positive areas and differences in microbial composition. In diabetic mice, bacterial inoculation delayed wound closure and was accompanied by reduced vascularization and endothelial SRSF2 staining. HG+LPS reduced SRSF2 expression and impaired endothelial functional readouts. SRSF2 knockdown reproduced these defects, whereas overexpression partially improved them under HG+LPS. Transcriptomic analysis identified widespread splicing changes after SRSF2 depletion. Under HG+LPS, RT-qPCR showed lower VEGFA-165a and higher VEGFA-165b signals; SRSF2 overexpression partially reversed these changes. The minigene reporter shifted toward VEGF-A165b-associated output under HG+LPS or SRSF2 knockdown and toward VEGF-A165a-associated output following SRSF2 overexpression. VEGFA pre-mRNA was enriched in SRSF2 immunoprecipitates.  Conclusions:  SRSF2 contributes to endothelial angiogenic function under hyperglycemic and LPS stress, and its manipulation alters VEGFA isoform-associated readouts. These findings support a potential role for SRSF2-associated RNA processing in diabetic wound vascular dysfunction. They do not establish that VEGFA isoform switching mediates the functional effects of SRSF2 or that the same mechanism operates in human DFUs.
records.authors: Zeng Z, An J, Mo Z, Luo G, Liu C, Cai Y.

records.title: Rhizobacterial genetic diversity associated with Paspalum atratum and Paspalum notatum by metagenomic analysis
records.abstract: Abstract    The genus  Paspalum  belongs to the Poaceae family and encompasses several species native to South America. The  Paspalum  Germplasm Bank of Embrapa Pecuária Sudeste has about 450 accessions of 50 species. Among the conserved accessions,  Paspalum notatum  BGP 26 and  Paspalum atratum  BGP 308 were selected for their importance as turfgrass and forage, respectively. The rhizospheric bacterial community of  P. atratum  and  P. notatum  was analyzed via 16S (V3-V4 region) metabarcoding sequencing. The statistical difference found for the Chao ecological index indicates that the bacterial composition and diversity were associated with each species. Thirty-one operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were identified with a predominance higher than 1% from 9 phyla (Proteobacteria n = 11, Acidobacteria n = 8, Actinobacteria n = 3, Planctomycetes n = 2, Nitrospirae n = 2, Verrucomicrobia n = 2, Chloroflexi n = 1, Gemmatimonadetes n = 1, and Bacteroidetes n = 1). Among these, 19 OTUs significantly differed between the species studied. Soil hydrogen-ionic potential (pH) was one of the most important factors influencing the species-specific difference of bacterial populations among accessions. Acidobacteriaceae (Subgroup 1), from the phylum Acidobacteria, was the most abundant family in  P. atratum  . The main group found in  P. notatum  was related to the family Nitrosomonadaceae from the phylum Proteobacteria. Our findings highlight a significant distinction in the rhizospheric bacterial community among the examined  Paspalum  accessions and underscore the existence of a species-specific association. These results can aid soil management practices, particularly in relation to vital economic aspects. Further research could help optimize agricultural strategies and promote sustainable soil health.
records.authors: de Paula AF, de Andrade PHM, Matheucci E, Carazzolle MF, de Carvalho LM, Vigna BBZ, Bernardi ACdC, Fávero AP, Cunha AFd, Lacava PT.

records.title: Bacterial supplementation during black soldier fly rearing improves frass plant growth-promoting properties
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Black soldier fly (BSF,  Hermetia illucens  ) frass is increasingly valued as an organic fertilizer, yet how the rearing substrate and its microbial supplementation shape the frass bacterial community and its agronomic quality remains poorly understood. Aims  We assessed whether microbial supplementation of an olive pomace substrate affects black soldier fly larval performance and the agronomic and microbial quality of the resulting frass. Methods  The substrate was supplemented with two commercial  Bacillus velezensis  formulations (CAL, LAL) and two gut-derived strains selected for broad enzymatic capabilities (LG, closest match  Paenibacillus cookii  ; PD, closest match  Shouchella clausii  ), each supplied live or heat-inactivated. Larval performance was recorded, the heat-treated frass (70°C, 60 min) was evaluated on cherry tomato, and the frass bacterial community was characterized by 16S rRNA sequencing. Results  Effects on larval performance were modest and preparation-dependent: inactivated PD increased larval weight, inactivated LG increased harvest weight, and frass production increased with live CAL, LAL and LG. All supplemented frass types increased root dry weight relative to non-supplemented frass, with LG-F performing best, and frass generally promoted greater plant biomass than mineral and organic fertilizers while maintaining germination. Despite similar chemical profiles, treatment explained 79.1% of the variation in frass community structure;  Bacillus  was enriched in LAL-F and  Oceanobacillus  , a genus with plant growth-promoting traits, in three of the four supplemented treatments. Conclusions  Although strain viability was not confirmed, microbial supplementation during rearing altered the bacterial composition and agronomic value of BSF frass, supporting its potential as a tailored biofertilizer.
records.authors: Fagua DC, Savio C, Fantatto RR, Souza CSe, Garcia-Fraile P.

records.title: Identification and applicability of azg1 as counter-selectable marker in Trichoderma species
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  The widespread use of pesticides and antibiotics in agriculture and clinical settings has accelerated the emergence of antimicrobial resistance across diverse organisms. Although this phenomenon is widely recognized in pathogenic microorganisms, much less is known about the effect on beneficial fungi that are playing a role in sustainable agriculture, such as  Trichoderma  . Many  Trichoderma  isolates, especially those originating from intensively treated soils, exhibit low sensitivity to commonly used laboratory antifungals, complicating their genetic manipulation. Results  In this study, we developed new genetic tools to facilitate the characterization and engineering of  Trichoderma  species, exploiting endogenous counter-selectable markers. Using  Trichoderma atroviride  as a model species, we first assessed fungal susceptibility to the nucleobase analogs 8-azaguanine, 5-fluorouracil and 5-fluorocytosine. While the fungus was sensitive to the first two compounds, 5-fluorocytosine showed no inhibitory effect. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated protoplast transformation, we generated mutants lacking a putative nucleobase analog transporter and identified the gene responsible for 8-azaguanine uptake. Deletion of this gene conferred resistance to 8-azaguanine without affecting the overall phenotype or growth behavior of  T. atroviride  under a range of tested conditions. This locus was subsequently employed as a counter-selectable marker for targeted integration events in  T. atroviride  and additional  Trichoderma  species. Furthermore, heterologous expression of the  Penicillium chrysogenum  cytidine deaminase gene, which catalyzes the intracellular metabolization of 5-fluorocytosine to 5-fluorouracil, rendered  T. atroviride  sensitive to this compound. Conclusion  Together, our findings establish  azg1  as a multifunctional genomic platform and expand the genetic toolkit available for  Trichoderma  research, providing the foundation for advanced strain engineering in agricultural and biotechnological applications.
records.authors: Baldin C, Oberdanner A, Schark L, Nagler J, Schreiner U, Huymann L, Gsaller F, Zeilinger S.

records.title: Exploring the causal role of the human gut microbiome in breast cancer risk
records.abstract: Background The relationship between the human gut microbiome and breast cancer (BC) risk is uncertain. Methods We used Mendelian randomization (MR) and multivariable linear regression to investigate the causal relationship between the human gut microbiome and BC risk (overall and subtype-specific) and interrogate the role of circulating metabolites as potential mediators. Summary-level data from genome-wide association studies of gut microbial traits (N = 3,890), circulating metabolites (N = 7,824), overall (N = 247,175) and subtype-specific (N = 200,898) BC risk, including triple negative BC (TNBC; N = 120,493), alongside individual-level data from the Flemish Gut Flora Project (N = 2,242). Sensitivity analyses were applied to examine the robustness of causal estimates. Results Initial two-sample MR analyses suggested that the presence of bacteria within the  Ruminococcus genus increased overall BC risk, that higher abundances of bacteria within the  Parabacteroides genus decreased and presence of unclassified bacteria within the  Bacteroidales order increased TNBC risk, and that several circulating metabolites altered BC risk (e.g., homostachydrine with overall BC and Luminal A BC, and betaine with TNBC). Whilst, in multivariable linear regression analyses, several of these metabolites were also associated with the microbial traits that influenced BC risk, given directional inconsistency of associations across analyses of microbial traits, metabolites and BC coupled with sensitivity analyses implying violations of MR assumptions, associations were unlikely to reflect causality nor a causal pathway between the gut microbiome, metabolites, and BC risk. Conclusions In conclusion, whilst our initial analyses suggested that the gut microbiome and certain circulating metabolites may be associated with BC risk, importantly, sensitivity analyses demonstrated that these relationships are complex and, certainly for the case of the gut microbiome, unlikely to reflect causality.
records.authors: Edmunds G, Robinson T, Yarmolinsky J, Lee M, Hayes B, Hughes D, Gibbs L, Braybrooke J, Raes J, Timpson N, Wade K.

records.title: Comparative analysis of various infection models to provide methodological insights for the characterization of new antivirulence drugs to fight antibioresistance.
records.abstract: Bacterial infections remain a major global health burden, amplified by the rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Among priority pathogens, the ESKAPEE group represents a critical threat due to their high prevalence in healthcare-associated infections, and their capacity to acquire multidrug resistance. Antivirulence strategies, aiming at disarming pathogens rather than inhibiting their growth, constitute a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics. Their development, however, is hindered by the lack of suitable experimental models to evaluate virulence and antivirulence efficacy. Here, we establish complementary in vitro and in vivo infection models to characterize pathogenicity and assess antivirulence activity against clinically relevant ESKAPEE bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli). We developed a robust nitric oxide (NO)-based in vitro assay that mimics host immune nitrosative stress and enables quantitative evaluation of bacterial resistance to innate immune defenses. In parallel, we established comparative insect infection models using Galleria mellonella and Bombyx species, allowing reproducible assessment of bacterial virulence across multiple hosts and pathogens. These models highlighted marked differences in pathogenic potential depending on both bacterial species and host background. As a proof of concept, we applied these systems to characterize NM102, a first-in-class antivirulence compound targeting the DNA repair protein Mfd. NM102 significantly reduced bacterial survival under NO stress in vitro and decreased bacterial burden in vivo in insect infection models. Together, our results demonstrate that combining immune-mimicking in vitro assays with complementary insect models provides a powerful and ethically acceptable platform to study bacterial pathogenicity and to accelerate the development of innovative antivirulence therapeutics to combat AMR.IMPORTANCEBacterial infections remain a major public health challenge, worsened by the rapid rise of antimicrobial resistance. Among the most concerning pathogens are the ESKAPEE bacteria, which frequently cause hospital-acquired infections and are often resistant to multiple antibiotics. Antivirulence strategies offer promising alternatives to traditional treatments by disarming bacteria rather than killing them, potentially reducing the risk of resistance. However, progress in this field has been limited by the lack of reliable models to measure bacterial virulence and evaluate antivirulence compounds. In this study, we developed complementary models to better assess bacterial pathogenicity and treatment efficacy. We created an in vitro assay that mimics immune defenses and established insect infection models to compare virulence across pathogens and hosts. Using these systems, we tested NM102, a first-in-class antivirulence compound targeting bacterial DNA repair. NM102 reduced bacterial survival and infection severity, highlighting the potential of antivirulence approaches as innovative therapies against drug-resistant infections.
records.authors: Cormontagne D, Lebreuilly L, Porrini C, Tran S-L, Ramarao N.

records.title: Satellite DNA content and distribution along the mitotic and meiotic chromosomes of Coleonyx mitratus (Eublepharidae, Gekkota).
records.abstract: Satellite DNAs (satDNAs) are repetitive sequences that play important structural and functional roles in vertebrate genomes; however, their genomic composition and behavior during meiosis remain poorly understood in geckos. Here, we investigated the satellitome of the Central American banded gecko (Coleonyx mitratus) using bioinformatic and cytogenetic approaches. We identified fifteen candidate satDNA sequences representing at least fourteen satDNA families and mapped their distribution on mitotic and meiotic chromosomes. Most satellites were concentrated in constitutive heterochromatin regions. One of the satDNA families, CmitSat-10-58, showed compact signals associated with the core of the synaptonemal complex on most chromosomes and co-localized with anti-centromere antibodies, suggesting a possible role in centromeric function. A heterochromatin region on chromosome 6 containing two satDNA families showed delayed synapsis and excessive stretching during the pachytene stage. Differences in satDNA composition between the X and Y chromosomes may be associated with their delayed synapsis. Our results provide new insight into the organization, chromosomal distribution, and potential functional significance of satellite DNA in gecko genomes, and support further investigation of the relationship between repetitive DNA, heterochromatin organization, and chromosome dynamics during meiosis.

records.title: Comparative RT-qPCR and qPCR Reveal 'Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus' Early and Low-Titer Infection and Relative Cell Activity in Citrus and Psyllids.
records.abstract: Citrus huanglongbing (HLB) is recognized as the most destructive bacterial disease affecting citrus. Among the causal agents, 'Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus' (Las) is the predominant species causing HLB epidemics worldwide. Detecting this phloem-limited bacterium at early or low-titer stages and assessing its cellular activity remain major challenges for HLB research and management. To address these limitations, we developed a one-step reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) assay for highly sensitive Las detection using total nucleic acids and the established Li 16S rRNA/rDNA primer-probe set. This method simultaneously amplifies both Las 16S rRNA and rDNA in a single reaction, increasing sensitivity by up to 500-fold compared with qPCR, which targets only 16S rDNA. The improved sensitivity reduced false negatives, expanded sampling capacity, and enabled detection of low-titer infections previously undetectable. In addition, the higher abundance of 16S rRNA generated a consistent Ct gap between RT-qPCR and qPCR, which we used to estimate relative Las cell activity in vivo in host insects and plants and to identify the most effective inoculum sources. This comparative detection strategy was further applied to evaluate inoculum potential, to monitor changes in relative cell activity during in vitro cultures, and to assess antimicrobial treatments targeting Las. The persistent detection of long-lasting, low-titer Las infections underscores the complex biology of the HLB causal agents and highlights ongoing challenges for effective disease management.
records.authors: Patterson R, Zheng D, Luo W, Deng Z, Bock C, Li R, Duan Y.

records.title: Autophagy and intratumoral bacteria abundance influence the prognosis of patients with pancreatic carcinoma.
records.abstract: The biological and clinical significance of the intratumoral microbiota in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains poorly defined. Using oncogenic Kras-driven mouse models of pancreatic tumorigenesis and human pancreatic tissue from patients with non-metastatic PDAC treated with neoadjuvant (n = 62) or adjuvant therapy (n = 101), along with samples from intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMN, n = 24), chronic pancreatitis (CP, n = 33), and healthy donors (n = 9), we determined tissue lipopolysaccharide (LPS), 16S rRNA sequencing, high-resolution quantitative multiplex immunofluorescence of autophagy markers (LAMP2, LC3B) and LPS, 16S rRNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) staining, and TLR4 signaling. In KrasCre mice, we identified significant bacterial accumulation in the pancreas, indicated by elevated LPS, increased FISH signals, enhanced TLR4 signaling, and activation of autophagy. Administration of exogenous LPS further amplified autophagy and TLR4 signaling, supporting a mechanistic link between microbial sensing and autophagy. In human tissue, both adjuvant and neoadjuvant PDAC samples showed significantly increased bacterial alpha- and beta diversity compared with controls, while CP showed a similar enrichment pattern that IPMN lacks; the underlying microbial diversity differs fundamentally across these conditions. Increased LPS levels, along with elevated autophagy markers and abundant FISH-positive bacteria, support the presence of intratumoral bacteria. Across four independent transcriptomic datasets, PDAC samples showed elevated expression of bacteria-associated pathways (including TLR4) and autophagy-related genes. Clinically, higher autophagy-associated LAMP2-LC3B colocalization and increased densities of FISH-positive cells were independently associated with prolonged survival in both adjuvant and neoadjuvant or combined PDAC patients. Collectively, these findings link intratumoral microbial enrichment to increased autophagy-associated signaling and improved patient outcomes, suggesting that microbial signals within the tumor microenvironment were associated with favorable survival.
records.authors: Zhang Y, Gobin TL, Huang Z, Miao B, Kurilov R, Sun H, Tjaden C, Heger U, Hackert T, Hinz U, Schaefer M, Bergmann F, Springfeld C, Mughal SS, Brors B, Schaal P, Cheaib B, Licastro D, Iebba V, Fortunato F.

records.title: Genome-Wide Characterization of BMP/GDF Genes in Sika Deer: Spatiotemporal Expression During Antler Regeneration and Computational Analysis of the BMP2–BMPR1A Complex
records.abstract: Antler regeneration involves rapid chondrogenesis and ossification, yet the bone morphogenetic protein/growth differentiation factor (BMP/GDF) genes associated with skeletal development remain poorly characterized in sika deer. We identified 16 BMP genes and two GDF genes belonging to seven phylogenetic subfamilies. Synteny analysis identified segmental and putative tandem duplications; two duplicated pairs had Ka/Ks ratios below 1. RNA-seq data showed differences across regenerative stages, with BMP3B and BMP5 expressed during early regeneration, BMP2, BMP4, and BMP6 during rapid growth, and BMP7 and BMP3 during terminal ossification. RT-qPCR supported distinct spatial expression patterns for five genes in rapidly growing antler tips. AlphaFold 3 modeling and molecular dynamics simulations indicated that the predicted BMP2–BMPR1A complex remained stable over the simulated trajectories. Free-energy decomposition and alanine scanning identified candidate interface residues. Sequence comparisons showed that these residues are conserved across the mammalian species examined. The results describe BMP/GDF family organization and expression during antler regeneration and identify candidate contacts for experimental analysis of BMP2–BMPR1A binding.
records.authors: Jian L, Lin Y, Cheng X, Zhang H, Liu Q, Xu J, Lu T, Wang Y, Wang Y.

records.title: Persistent Pediatric Cervical Lymphadenopathy: A Case Report of Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease Mimicking Infection and Malignancy.
records.abstract: Case presentationA 10-year-old female presented with 2 months of unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy despite several courses of oral antibiotics. She presented to the emergency department due to persistent pain and swelling along with new fever. On presentation, she was febrile to 39.0°C. Physical examination revealed significant left-sided cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy with tenderness, warmth, and overlying erythema. Initial labs were notable for leukopenia (2.6 × 103/μL), thrombocytopenia (135,000/μL), and elevated liver enzymes. Computed tomography (CT) of the neck demonstrated necrotic left cervical lymphadenopathy with prominent right cervical lymph nodes. An infectious workup, including testing for Epstein-Barr virus, Cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, coccidioidomycosis, tuberculosis, and microbial cell-free DNA sequencing, was negative. Initial fine-needle aspiration (FNA) and core needle biopsy showed predominantly necrotic tissue. Cultures obtained during the biopsy showed no growth, and flow cytometry was negative for leukemia/lymphoma markers. Intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone administration resulted in improvement in neck swelling and fever resolution. Histopathologic examination from excisional biopsy revealed histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis consistent with Kikuchi-Fujimoto (KFD) lymphadenitis. Comprehensive autoimmune serologies were negative. Naproxen was prescribed to help with residual inflammation.DiscussionKFD should be considered in children presenting with prolonged cervical lymphadenopathy refractory to antibiotics. This case illustrates several diagnostic challenges inherent in making this diagnosis. The patient's prolonged unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, necrotic imaging findings, and transient improvement with antibiotics strongly suggested bacterial lymphadenitis or malignancy. However, the persistence of symptoms despite multiple appropriate antibiotic courses, the development of cytopenias and elevated liver enzymes, and ultimately nondiagnostic cultures represented key findings prompting reconsideration of the initial differential diagnoses. This case also highlights the importance of considering excisional biopsy when core biopsy is nondiagnostic.
records.authors: Thomas M, Stevens D, Davis C, Money NM.

records.title: The miR-176-DcFoxO axis links CLas infection to juvenile hormone signaling and enhanced fecundity in Diaphorina citri.
records.abstract: BackgroundThe phloem-limited bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (CLas), associated with huanglongbing (HLB) disease, is transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid, Diaphorina citri. CLas-positive females display enhanced fecundity and increased metabolic demands, a phenotype that may promote both vector population growth and bacterial proliferation. Although recent studies have revealed that CLas-associated reproductive enhancement involves neuroendocrine and neurotransmitter pathways, the transcriptional regulators linking persistent bacterial infection, energy metabolism, juvenile hormone (JH) signaling, and ovarian development remain poorly understood.ResultsHere, we identify the forkhead transcription factor DcFoxO as a previously unrecognized regulatory node associated with CLas-induced fecundity enhancement in D. citri. DcFoxO expression was significantly elevated in the ovaries of CLas-positive females during reproductive maturation. RNA interference-mediated silencing of DcFoxO reduced triacylglycerol and glycogen reserves, decreased lipid droplet accumulation, impaired ovarian development, reduced fecundity, and lowered CLas titers in the ovaries. Using dual-luciferase reporter assays, RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), and microRNA (miRNA) gain-of-function experiments, we demonstrated that miR-176 directly targets the 3' untranslated region of DcFoxO and negatively regulates its expression. Overexpression of miR-176 phenocopied DcFoxO knockdown, suppressing energy reserves, ovarian development, fecundity, and CLas proliferation. Mechanistically, DcFoxO silencing or miR-176 overexpression reduced JH titers and down-regulated core JH-responsive reproductive genes, including DcMet, DcKr-h1, DcVg, and DcVgR.ConclusionThese findings reveal a miR-176-DcFoxO-JH regulatory axis that links CLas infection to metabolic reprogramming, ovarian maturation, and enhanced vector fecundity. This study adds a transcriptional layer to the emerging model of CLas-mediated manipulation of D. citri reproduction and identifies potential molecular targets for disrupting vector performance and HLB transmission. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

records.title: Empirical substitution models of evolution for protein phylogenetics of the Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus.
records.abstract: Probabilistic methods for phylogenetic inference rely on substitution models of molecular evolution. However, at the protein level, the availability of empirical substitution models remains limited, particularly for viruses. Here, we present empirical substitution models of protein evolution for several Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) proteins, including the nucleoprotein, glycoprotein precursor, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. For each protein, we estimated the exchangeability matrix and amino acid frequencies at equilibrium from hundreds of sequences using maximum likelihood, and we evaluated the models using independent data. The inferred CCHFV models revealed distinct evolutionary patterns among viral proteins, including patterns in polar and glycosylation-associated regions, while generally preserving common physicochemical features such as amino acid charge, polarity, and hydrophobic packing shaped by selective pressures. Remarkably, the CCHFV protein substitution models consistently outperformed all currently available empirical substitution models, including those inferred from other viral proteins, in terms of phylogenetic likelihood with independent CCHFV protein sequences. These findings support the use of these substitution models to improve the accuracy of phylogenetic reconstructions of CCHFV proteins, thereby enabling more reliable inference of evolutionary trajectories that may be useful for therapeutic design.
records.authors: Iglesias-Rivas P, Arenas M.

records.title: Multilevel metabolic engineering of Bacillus amyloliquefaciens for enhanced L-tyrosine production.
records.abstract: L-Tyrosine is a valuable aromatic amino acid with diverse applications. Although plasmid-based overexpression has markedly improved L-tyrosine production, the dependence on antibiotic selection and genetic instability under nonselective conditions limits its industrial applicability. To address these issues, this study employed a multi-level metabolic engineering strategy to enhance the L-tyrosine biosynthetic pathway at the genomic level in Bacillus amyloliquefaciens. First, an expression cassette containing the mutant prephenate dehydrogenase (TyrAI309A/E330V) was inserted into the genome of the wild-type strain Z1. When the copy number reached three (strain Z4), L-tyrosine production reached 437.43 mg/L. Subsequently, the mutant DAHP synthase (AroAR27A/K38A) was integrated, and the resulting two-copy strain Z7 increased L-tyrosine production to 591.29 mg/L. Systematic identification of rate-limiting steps showed that most pathway genes enhanced production to varying extents. A promoter in situ replacement strategy was then applied to construct strain Z21, which further increased the titer to 813.01 mg/L. Finally, by optimizing precursor supply, the engineered strain Z32 reached an L-tyrosine titer of 1079.94 mg/L. Overall, this plasmid-free and antibiotic-independent platform offers a promising strategy for stable biosynthesis of L-tyrosine and other aromatic amino acids in microbial cell factories.
records.authors: Zhang D, Jiang P, Wang L, Gu J, Ji A, Feng N.

records.title: Clinical utility of plasma microbial cell-free DNA sequencing in adult immunocompromised patients: A real-world cohort study.
records.abstract: BackgroundPlasma metagenomic next generation sequencing (mNGS) enables noninvasive pathogen detection independent of organism viability. Although analytic performance has been described, the real-world clinical impact in immunocompromised hosts remains incompletely defined.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study of immunocompromised adults undergoing plasma mNGS testing from January 2022 through November 2024 at the Medical University of South Carolina. Immunocompromised conditions included solid organ transplantation, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, active hematologic malignancy, HIV, or biologic immunosuppressants. Clinical impact was adjudicated by infectious disease physicians as positive, negative, or neutral. Positive results were classified as definite, probable, possible, or unlikely infectious based on clinical correlation and concordance with conventional microbiologic testing (CMT).ResultsNinety-eight patients were included (median age 60 years [range 18-76]; 63% male), including solid organ transplant (31%), hematopoietic stem cell transplant (8%), HIV (13%), active malignancy (42%), corticosteroids (3%), and biologic therapy (10%). At testing, 85% were receiving antimicrobials and 88% were hospitalized. Plasma mNGS was positive in 62% of cases, with CMT concordance in 30%. Thirty-two percent of tests had positive clinical impact, identifying unrecognized infection or antimicrobial optimization. Sixty-six percent had no treatment impact and 2% had potential negative impact. More than half of discordant positives were deemed possible or unlikely infections. False-negative cases included invasive mold and nontuberculous mycobacterial infections.ConclusionsIn this antimicrobial-exposed immunocompromised cohort, plasma mNGS frequently detected organisms but less often influenced clinical management. Discordant positives were common, and false negatives occurred in selected syndromes, supporting cautious interpretation and stewardship-guided use.

records.title: KmerSignificance score: A discriminative and biologically informed framework for viral k-mer prioritization.
records.abstract: Distinguishing closely related viral strains requires identifying genomic regions where subtle sequence differences carry biological significance. While k-mer-based approaches offer computational efficiency for genome analysis, existing methods lack standardized frameworks for evaluating which k-mers are most informative. Current selection strategies focus primarily on statistical discriminative power without integrating biological context. We introduce KmerSignificance Score (KSS), a k-mer prioritization framework combining three components: an information-theoretic method measuring strain-distinguishing capacity, an optimized amino acid substitution matrix (MIYATA_EVO) for mutation impact assessment, and a protein characterization score derived from annotations and database cross-references retrieved through UniProt. All three component scores and the integrated KSS are bounded in [0,1] by construction, providing a common numerical scale for ranking positions within a dataset. The discriminative component achieved a mean F1 of 0.881, not significantly different from chi-squared (0.876), the strongest of eight baselines. Top-ranked selections from the discriminative component nonetheless differed from those produced by chi-squared, especially for SARS-CoV-2 and HIV-1. The MIYATA_EVO matrix, optimized using a genetic algorithm, increased the composite agreement score across eight amino acid characteristics by 28.4% over the original MIYATA matrix. Across 17,471 viral proteins, the protein characterization score tracked UniProt's five-level annotation score closely (Kendall's τ=0.775), as expected for measures drawing on overlapping annotation content. Within each level, the continuous score provided finer numerical resolution among proteins. Literature cross-referencing on SARS-CoV-2 (278,738 sequences, 19 Pango-derived lineage labels), HIV-1 (12,223 sequences, 15 subtype labels), and human cytomegalovirus (HCMV; 399-646 sequences, 4-8 locus-specific genotypes) found that the top-ranked k-mers reported here map to established variant-defining mutations, subtype-specific polymorphisms, and genotype markers. KSS provides a standardized framework for viral k-mer prioritization with potential applications in variant surveillance, molecular epidemiology, and functional annotation. The tool is available at https://github.com/bioinfoUQAM/KmerSignificanceScore.
records.authors: Lebatteux D, Corso F, Soudeyns H, Boucoiran I, Gantt S, Baniré Diallo A.

records.title: Hepatitis C viral variants bear signatures of de novo CD8+ T cell and antibody pressure after spontaneous postpartum viral suppression.
records.abstract: Progression to chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection entails loss of HCV-specific CD4+ T cell help, emergence of viral variants that escape recognition by CD8+ T cells and neutralizing antibodies, and exhaustion of CD8+ T cells targeting remaining intact epitopes. Once chronic infection has been established, it is generally lifelong without treatment. However, in some chronically infected women, a surprising postpartum viral load decline has been linked to resurgent functional HCV-specific CD4+ helper T cells. A minority of women even spontaneously clear long-standing chronic infection postpartum. To test whether restored T cell help boosts HCV-specific CD8+ T cell or antibody responses in women with postpartum viral control, we performed serial near-full-length deep sequencing of HCV genomes to assess evolution of viral MHC class I epitopes and antibody epitopes in nine women with significant postpartum viral declines (≥ 1 log10 at 3 mo postpartum, "controllers") and 12 with more stable levels ("noncontrollers"). Although not associated with mutations arising early postpartum, at 12 to 24 mo postpartum, viral control was strongly associated with amino acid mutations in epitopes predicted to be targeted by CD8+ T cells and neutralizing antibodies. Plasma from controllers also demonstrated a postpartum increase in neutralization of multiple HCV strains. Together, these findings support the hypothesis that postpartum viral control is mediated by CD8+ T cell and antibody pressure.

records.title: OMICs-based Characterization of Probiotic or Psychobiotic Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB) from Philippine Fermented Foods: A Scoping Review.
records.abstract: Fermented foods are rich sources of diverse lactic acid bacteria (LAB) with promising functional potential. OMICs approaches enable comprehensive characterization. In the Philippines, many regions produce unique fermented foods that may contain potentially beneficial LAB. However, the extent of OMICs' application in studying these microorganisms remains unclear. This scoping review aims to determine the extent and availability of OMICs-based research investigating the probiotic or psychobiotic potential of LAB isolated from Philippine fermented foods. It also seeks to identify whether such studies are abundant or remain limited. Multiple databases were utilized to identify eligible studies. Studies were defined as peer-reviewed, English-language research articles (2000-2026) that applied OMICs approaches to characterize LAB isolated from Philippine fermented food sources. These studies also had accessible datasets and original analyses. Only five eligible studies were identified, comprising three publications from 2024 and two from 2025, with most consisting of genome announcements and only two full research articles. The reviewed studies showed limited taxonomic, food-source, and geographic coverage, representing only three LAB genera, three Philippine fermented foods, and samples originating exclusively from Central Luzon (Region III). OMICs-based studies on probiotic and psychobiotic LAB from Philippine fermented foods are markedly lacking. The identified studies were few and predominantly employed genomics, with only one study incorporating metabolomics. They are also limited to a single region and a narrow range of fermented foods. Expanding OMICs-driven research is essential to address these gaps, enable deeper characterization, and strengthen the scientific and cultural value of Philippine fermented foods.
records.authors: Veluz J, Buenavista CA, Gloria PC, Luague MJ, Austria K, Relucio-San Diego MAC, Siringan MA.

records.title: Hubei virga-like virus 2 in Aedes aegypti: Identification of a conserved 216-bp sequence missing from the RefSeq standard.
records.abstract: We report two near-complete genome sequences of Hubei virga-like virus 2 (HVLV-2) from Aedes aegypti in Oaxaca, Mexico. Both genomes contain a 216-bp insertion region absent from the reference sequence but present in all other reported isolates. Split-read analysis and de novo assembly of our samples, along with a reanalysis of raw reads from the reference sequencing project, confirm that this region is present in the original genetic material from which the assemblies were built. Altogether, these findings confirm that A. aegypti is a putative host of HVLV-2 and demonstrate that the insertion is conserved but missing from the RefSeq standard.
records.authors: Guerrero-Martínez LE, Solís-Vidal S, Yocupicio-Monroy M, Castelán-Sánchez HG, Zárate S.

records.title: Conjugative Transfer Potential of Antibiotic Resistance from Wastewater-derived Coliforms to riverine Escherichia coli.
records.abstract: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) discharged into rivers from wastewater treatment plants disseminate antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) through conjugative transfer, suggesting that aquatic environments serve as reservoirs for spreading antibiotic resistance. However, the actual extent of such dissemination of antibiotic resistance is unclear. This study investigated changes in the microbiota and antibiotic resistance profiles of other coliforms during the wastewater treatment process and evaluated whether other antibiotic-resistant coliforms persisting in treated wastewater could potentially transfer antibiotic resistance to Escherichia coli in receiving waters. The treatment process substantially reduced, but did not eliminate, E. coli and other coliforms (most probable number [MPN]/100 mL = 5 for E. coli and 4.3 × 10² for other coliforms), which were subsequently discharged into rivers. The resistance rates of other coliforms tended to increase throughout the treatment process, and the proportion of multidrug-resistant bacteria increased (influent: 4.9%, biologically treated water: 4.3%, effluent: 15.8%). Conjugation experiments using the filter mating method revealed the transfer of ARGs from Klebsiella species to E. coli (conjugation frequency: 10- 6-10- 3), suggesting the potential for antibiotic resistance transfer within biofilms. Experiments under simplified riverbed biofilm conditions confirmed the transfer of rifampicin resistance genes introduced into E. coli to antibiotic-resistant other coliforms (conjugation frequency: 9.7 × 10- 5-5.3 × 10- 4). The abundance of antibiotic-resistant other coliforms in the biofilm was 5.08 × 10² MPN/mL, which was lower than the observed conjugation frequencies, suggesting that the discharge area of treated wastewater is unlikely to function as a significant hotspot for ARB dissemination.
records.authors: Tamai S, Tsuda K, Suzuki Y.

records.title: U6  promoters in  Ulva prolifera  enable dual small-RNA/mRNA transcription and vector-based CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing
records.abstract: For establishing vector-based gene editing in the green-tide-forming alga  Ulva prolifera , development of endogenous RNA polymerase III (Pol III) promoters is a prerequisite to drive single-guide RNA (sgRNA) transcription. To meet the need, the promoters of  U6 snRNA genes in  U. prolifera (  UpU6 ) were identified, cloned, and functionally characterized. Results showed that three  UpU6 copies shared identical sequences, with divergent 5’ upstream sequences containing a positionally conserved TATA box but lacking the USE element typical of seed plants. All three  UpU6 promoters were shown to be capable of driving not only small RNA transcription but also protein-coding gene expression in  U. prolifera , exhibiting the dual transcriptional activity. Unexpectedly, all three  UpU6 promoters also supported  GUS reporter gene expression in  Agrobacterium , representing the first demonstration of  U6 promoter activity in a prokaryotic system. The results of the gene-editing experiment showed that, all three  UpU6 promoters supported vector-based CRISPR-Cas9 targeting of the  APT gene, yielding mutant strains. The mutation-positive fraction among resistant thalli was 92.3% (48/52), and the editing frequency calculated from the estimated starting cell number averaged 3.26 × 10⁻⁶ across the three  UpU6 promoters and did not differ significantly among them. In the mutants, high-frequency occurrences of base substitutions (45.5%) and insertions of long Mutator-like element (MULE) (18.2%) were detected, highlighting a potential association between endogenous DNA transposon insertion and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing. These findings expanded understanding of eukaryotic  U6 promoter functionality and enrich the toolkit for vector-based CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing in  U. prolifera .
records.authors: Hou Q, Wang Z, Zhao J, Jiang P.

records.title: From chromosome-scale assembly to the mappable genome of rubber dandelion: chromosome reorganization, rubber-pathway coordination, and domestication traits
records.abstract: Natural rubber supply depends almost entirely on one tropical tree, motivating development of temperate alternatives. Rubber dandelion (  Taraxacum kok-saghyz Rodin) is the leading candidate, with comparatively well characterized rubber biosynthesis pathways, but its large, repeat-rich genome has left breeding genomics far behind pathway biology. In response, we assembled OSU TarKok 3.0, a 1.19-Gb nuclear reference in which eight chromosome-scale scaffolds contain 98% of the sequence. Continuity within chromosomes improved markedly, with contig N50 rising from 1.3 to 37.8 Mb, and conserved gene-space recovery improved accordingly. Macrosynteny showed strong chromosome conservation within Taraxacum and, when compared to lettuce, displayed four nearly intact and four composite chromosomes, a signature compatible with descending dysploidy accompanied by rearrangement rather than a single end-to-end fusion. Across nine Cichorieae genomes, none of six surveyed rubber-related gene families was uniquely enlarged in rubber dandelion. Instead, a  cis -prenyltransferase locus, a rubber transferase activator, and three small rubber particle protein genes were enriched in underground tissues and grouped with rubber elongation factor in a latex-associated co-expression module, favoring coordinated pathway deployment over species-specific family expansion. Intersecting uniquely mappable and nonrepetitive sequence defined the mappable genome, approximately 210 Mb or 18% of the assembly, within which markers can be interpreted allelically. Mapping in an independent F₂ family of 83 plants identified a chromosome 1 locus for filled-seed production under restricted cross-pollination, whereas herbicide response yielded no significant locus in this design. OSU TarKok 3.0 links chromosome reorganization, pathway deployment, and domestication traits into one framework for improving an outcrossing crop.  Core Ideas  OSU TarKok 3.0 markedly improves within-chromosome continuity and conserved gene-space recovery. Repeat-aware defines a ∼210 Mb short-read mappable space (18% of the assembly), enabling reliable marker analysis. Four chromosomes retain conserved relationships, supporting dysploidy with rearrangement beyond simple fusion. No rubber-related gene family is uniquely expanded; rubber production reflects pathway coordination, not dosage. A chromosome 1 QTL for selfing-related filled-seed production overlaps the positional candidate  g7174 .  Plain Language Summary  As the global supply of natural rubber is dependent on one tropical tree, rubber dandelion has been proposed as a temperate alternative. Although scientists already understand many of the genes involved in its rubber production, breeding has been slowed by its large, highly repetitive genome. In response, we built OSU TarKok 3.0, a much more continuous genome that places 98% of the sequence on eight chromosomes. Comparison with related dandelions revealed broad chromosome conservation, while comparison with lettuce was consistent with rearrangements during the reduction from nine to eight chromosomes. Across nine members of the sunflower family, none of six rubber-related gene families were uniquely enlarged in rubber dandelion. Instead, genes involved in building rubber chains and particles were active together in underground tissues and latex-associated samples, suggesting that coordinated gene activity matters more than extra gene copies. We also identified ∼210 million base pairs, 18% of the genome, where short-read genetic markers can be interpreted reliably. Within that space, we mapped a chromosome 1 region associated with producing filled seed when cross-pollination was restricted. This region overlaps a candidate gene from a protein family involved in reproductive development in other plants, providing a testable target for improving seed production.
records.authors: Vargas-Mejía P, Gutierrez-Manriquez C, Anderson ES, Williams DR, Vega-Arreguín J, Fresnedo-Ramírez J.

records.title: Scaling a context-aware genomic model for condition-specific edit design in plants
records.abstract: Engineering agronomically relevant traits in crops often requires changing a gene’s activity in a specific tissue, developmental stage or environmental condition while preserving its roles in other contexts. Designing such selective changes requires predicting how cis-regulatory sequences are interpreted in different biological states, as the same edit can have different effects across contexts. Genomic models have made substantial progress in predicting gene expression from DNA sequence, yet sequence-only predictors do not receive an explicit description of biological states. We introduce CROP-1 (  C ontext-aware  R egulatory  O utput  P rediction model), which combines DNA sequence with transcription factor binding motifs and measured expression to predict gene activity as a function of both sequence and regulatory state. On a held-out test set spanning six plant species, CROP-1 achieves a median per-gene Pearson correlation across contexts of 0.831, compared with 0.486 for its parameter-matched sequence-only counterpart, and 57–246% higher median correlations than three genomic foundation models fully fine-tuned on the same task. Prediction accuracy also improves with scale: increasing model capacity reduces validation error by 48%, while expanding training data to include more diverse biological contexts reduces it by 58%. We then use gradient-based sequence optimisation to translate a desired gene expression pattern into candidate edits of its cis-regulatory sequence, targeting up- or down-regulation in one context while preserving expression in others. In soybean and tomato, edit designs with 1–20 nucleotide substitutions produce strong predicted target responses and much smaller average changes across non-target contexts. By connecting scalable learning of sequence–state relationships to selective edit design, CROP-1 provides a computational foundation for controlling where, when and under which conditions endogenous crop genes are active.
records.authors: Antinucci P, Wang L, Moss JD, Schwartz D, Hall D.

records.title: FluxSprout: Single-cell metabolic modeling of vascular sprouting in zebrafish
records.abstract: Genome-scale metabolic modeling offers a powerful framework for identifying cell-state-specific metabolic vulnerabilities, yet its application to heterogeneous biological systems remains limited by uncertainty in network annotations, thermodynamic feasibility, transcriptome-to-flux inference, and target specificity. Here, we introduce FluxSprout, a single-cell transcriptomics-informed genome-scale metabolic modeling framework to resolve metabolic heterogeneity during zebrafish sprouting angiogenesis. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing of 10,090 quality-controlled cells with Zebrafish-GEM, we reconstructed network ensembles for 14 endothelial and hemogenic states. We established four safeguards: stoichiometric auditing, loop auditing, cell-cycle-controlled testing, and ensemble specificity screening. First, we identified four inorganic pyrophosphatase reactions misannotated as oxidative phosphorylation, showing that apparent pathway essentiality arose only with unbounded exchange fluxes. Second, 19.5% of reactions could carry thermodynamically infeasible loop flux, including every candidate of a conventional screen. Third, tip-like and stalk-like cells differed mainly in cell-cycle phase, and elevated glycolysis separated sprouting from established vessels only in gene expression. In contrast, sprouting vessels had higher predicted growth capacity at both constraint strengths, with serine and nucleotide synthesis following in fixed proportion. Fourth, screening 825 genes across four network-extraction settings and 13 non-endothelial lineages left no candidate called by more than one setting. Notably, SLC25A20, that screen’s lead candidate, had no predicted effect in any FASTCORE network. Although the data derive from a single pooled clutch and require experimental validation, FluxSprout provides a transferable, uncertainty-aware framework for distinguishing genuine metabolic dependencies from artifacts of network reconstruction, model assumptions, and cellular heterogeneity, and identifies biosynthetic capacity as a testable feature of sprouting vessels.

records.title: Assessment of  in vivo  epithelial disruption to model anorectal  Chlamydia  infection in mice
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Chlamydia trachomatis (Ct) causes the most commonly diagnosed bacterial sexually transmitted infection. Ct can infect mucosal epithelial cells throughout the human body and is frequently found at the anorectal tract. However, there are currently few models of anorectal  Chlamydia infection, limiting our ability to investigate vaccines, identify therapeutics, and understand infection dynamics. Since epithelial disruption prior to infection has been used in other STI animal models to increase permissibility and improve reproducibility of infection, we evaluated the impact of different methods of epithelial disruption prior to inoculation on the bacterial burden of anorectal  Chlamydia muridarum (Cm). Mice were treated anorectally with physical (calcium alginate swab) and/or chemical (nonoxynal-9) disruption 24 hours prior to anorectal inoculation with 1 x 10  4 IFUs of a luciferase-expressing Cm (Luc-Cm). Infection progression was monitored in real time using an  in vivo imaging system (IVIS) and the shedding of Luc-Cm DNA in the stool was quantified by qPCR. Cm was detected in all infected treatment groups by both IVIS and qPCR, irrespective of treatment. However, N-9 treatment prior to inoculation with Luc-Cm increased infection reproducibility and persistence when monitored using IVIS imaging, while having minimal adverse reactions. Therefore, chemical disruption prior to Luc-Cm infection was utilized to examine the efficacy of a bacteriophage virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine against Luc-Cm (Qβ-VD4-Cm) in the anorectal tract. We found that immunization with Qβ-VD4-Cm did not reduce Luc-Cm infection in the anorectal tract, despite this vaccine previously being shown to reduce Luc-Cm infection in the female reproductive tract. This highlights the unique nature of vaccine-mediated protection that can occur at distinct anatomical sites of infection with the same pathogen.

records.title: Early tuberculosis treatment remodels blood mRNA and small RNA, and a baseline host signature is associated with early culture conversion
records.abstract: Background  Tuberculosis (TB) treatment monitoring relies on sputum-based microbiological assays, which are slow and provide limited insight into the host response. Blood-based biomarkers could offer rapid and minimally invasive treatment monitoring. Methods  We performed an integrative multi-omics analysis of paired whole-blood samples collected at baseline and four weeks after treatment initiation across three South African cohorts. A meta-analysis combined RNA sequencing data from GSE89403 (86 pairs) and a prospective cohort (11 pairs), with directional concordance assessed in an independent microarray cohort, GSE31348 (27 pairs). In the prospective cohort, small RNA sequencing profiled microRNAs (miRNAs) and tRNA-derived fragments (tRFs). In GSE89403 (n = 76), a k-top scoring pairs signature (EARLY5) was developed using leave-one-out cross-validation to predict week-4 sputum culture conversion from baseline samples. Findings  The meta-analysis identified 63 concordantly regulated genes. These changes reflected attenuation of neutrophil, inflammatory and complement programs, and deconvolution showed decreased neutrophils with increased T-cell and NK-cell populations. Seven miRNAs and eight nuclear-encoded tRFs changed during treatment, including erythroid-associated miR-144, with computationally identified candidate interactions involving complement genes. EARLY5 identified participants who converted by week 4 with a cross-validated AUC of 0.76 and remained associated with conversion after adjustment for baseline bacterial burden in logistic regression and performed comparably to existing TB signatures. Interpretation  Early TB treatment induces coordinated remodeling of blood mRNA and small RNA profiles. Baseline host transcriptional profiles were associated with early culture conversion after accounting for bacterial burden, supporting further evaluation in independent cohorts. Funding  CRDF Global/CFAR/RePORT and the National Institutes of Health (P30AI168436).
records.authors: Chinmayi GVA, Quijada D, Queiroz ATL, Martinson N, Andrade BB, Halushka MK, Bader JS, Karakousis PC.
