records.title: Multi-Environment Genomic Analysis Reveals Limited Concordance Between Sorghum Leaf Blight Incidence and Severity.
records.abstract: Leaf blight caused by Exserohilum turcicum constrains sorghum production in semi-arid environments. Disease incidence and severity are related, but their relationship need not imply shared resistance loci. Records from five locations in Niger and Senegal comprised 1339 paired plot observations. Field-stratum-adjusted accession values were estimated before rank-based inverse-normal transformation. The primary population contained 100 accessions evaluated in at least four locations; all 102 genotype-matched accessions were included in a sensitivity analysis. Genome-wide efficient mixed-model association (GEMMA) score tests used leave-one-chromosome-out kinship matrices, and trait-level p-values were combined with the aggregated Cauchy association test (ACAT) and the Simes procedure. Adjusted incidence and standard severity were moderately correlated (Pearson r = 0.429); the correlation was lower after conditioning severity on incidence (r = 0.066). Across 567,758 single-nucleotide polymorphisms, ACAT had a genomic inflation factor of 1.014 and a minimum p-value of 2.64 × 10-5. No marker passed the Benjamini-Hochberg 10% false-discovery-rate criterion for either trait or either combination; likelihood-ratio analyses also produced no discoveries at this threshold. Incidence-severity association-profile concordance was weak (Pearson r = 0.127; Spearman ρ = 0.094). Top-ranked overlap was 5.65-fold at 1% and 2.24-fold at 5% relative to the marker-count expectation, a descriptive comparison that does not account for linkage disequilibrium. ACAT and Simes rankings were similar (ρ = 0.895). Ten top-ranked, genotype-equivalence-aware, linkage-disequilibrium-clumped regions are presented as exploratory candidates. Phenotypic association was therefore stronger than detectable sharing of marker-association evidence. Limited sample size and sensitivity to phenotype definition, field composition and test choice constrain locus-level conclusions.
records.authors: Ahn E, Baek I, Prom LK, Kim MS, Meinhardt LW, Magill C.

records.title: Transcriptomic profiling of goats' systemic immune response to Haemonchus contortus infection during primary and secondary infection.
records.abstract: Haemonchus contortus is an economically important gastrointestinal nematode affecting small ruminants globally. Understanding immune responses during primary and secondary exposure may inform improved control strategies. This study investigated systemic immune transcriptional responses in Boer goat buffy-coat samples during early (D5) and late (D21) primary and secondary infections using RNA sequencing (N = 6; 3 animals/pool). Data were analysed using CLC Genomics Workbench, with functional enrichment assessed using STRING and immune pathways examined using KEGG. Differential gene expression analysis (p-value ≤0.05) identified 252 and 330 upregulated genes during primary infection and 373 and 269 during secondary infection at D5 and D21, respectively. Primary infection was characterised by a neutrophil-associated, pro-inflammatory signature involving CXCL8-CXCR1/2, CSF3R/CSF2R, IL-6-STAT3/5, and MYD88-MAPK signalling. Secondary infection showed early Th2-associated signatures at D5, including STAT6, IL4, and IL13 upregulation. However, canonical Th2-associated genes were not upregulated at D21, GATA3 and STAT4 were downregulated in both infections, indicating time-dependent responses. Additional changes involved IL-10/IL-10R, IL-4R/IL-13RA1, SOCS, and DUSP signalling. Functional enrichment identified Th2-associated immunity, complement activation, and leukocyte migration, antigen processing and presentation, B-cell receptor, and T-cell receptor signalling. These findings indicate temporally distinct systemic responses to primary and secondary exposure, rather than sustained helper-T-cell polarization. These signatures may be reflective of altered leukocyte composition, cell-specific transcriptional regulation, or both. Overall, these findings identify candidate immune pathways and signatures associated with immune responses to H. contortus in both naïve and previously exposed hosts, and may lay a foundation for future vaccine and genetic-resistance studies.

records.title: Recombinant depolymerase DP21 from Klebsiella phage GADU21 exerts Dual-Antibiofilm and biofilm-disrupting activity against multiple bacterial species.
records.abstract: Phage-derived depolymerases are promising antibiofilm enzymes. In this study, intact and disintegrated GADU21 phage were first tested for their ability to disrupt mature biofilm using the crystal violet assay. Disintegrated phage was more active on biofilms than intact phage. The dp21 gene encoding the depolymerase was then amplified from GADU21, cloned into pET30a, and expressed in E. coli BL21. Purified rDP21 (∼105 kDa) was characterized for antibiofilm activity at different pH values, residual activity following thermal pre-incubation, and Mg2+ dependence, with biofilm degradation and prevention capacity also shown by SEM and CLSM. rDP21 exhibited antibiofilm activity at pH 4-10 and retained partial activity after pre-incubation at temperatures up to 70 °C. Importantly, rDP21 did not affect planktonic growth of the tested bacteria, supporting a matrix-targeting rather than bactericidal mode of action, while significantly reducing preformed biofilm biomass and inhibiting biofilm formation by P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae, E. coli, P. mirabilis, S. epidermidis, S. aureus and E. faecalis by 58-59%, 49-50%, 46-47%, 30-34%, 33-31%, 30-24%, and 26-33%, respectively. SEM and CLSM images confirmed pronounced disruption of biofilm. These properties support its potential use as an effective antibiofilm agent.
records.authors: Salih Doğan H, Orbayoğlu GA, Karaynir A, Ali S, Doğan Y, Yalçin M, Hoşbul T, Bozdoğan B.

records.title: Disentangling the Genetic Relationship Between Sleep and Epilepsy.
records.abstract: ObjectiveA bidirectional relationship between sleep and epilepsy is well recognised, yet the biological mechanisms linking them remain poorly understood. Both have a genetic basis, with genome-wide association studies (GWAS) capturing polygenic contributions. By leveraging GWAS summary statistics, we aimed to investigate their shared genetic architecture.MethodsWe analysed seven sleep traits (morningness chronotype, sleep duration, habitual short/long sleep, insomnia, daytime napping/sleepiness) with common epilepsy types (focal epilepsy and genetic generalised epilepsy [GGE]). For each trait pair, we estimated genome-wide genetic correlation, tested bidirectional causality, quantified polygenic overlap, performed gene-trait associations to identify putative pleiotropic genes, estimated local genetic correlations and investigated whether regions of significance were driven by shared causal variants using colocalisation and fine-mapping.ResultsGenome-wide analyses supported a positive genetic correlation between higher GGE risk and habitual short sleep, with extensive polygenic overlap (75%-97%) across seven sleep traits. Gene-trait analyses identified RMI1 as a putative sleep-epilepsy candidate, with 13 additional sleep-associated genes linked to monogenic epilepsies (e.g., KANSL1, GRIN2A). Locus-specific analyses identified 16 genomic loci of interest (13 sleep-GGE, 3 sleep-focal epilepsy). Morningness-GGE shared the largest number of locus-specific associations. No significant causal relationships were identified, and causal variants did not colocalise.InterpretationOur findings support complex shared genetic contributions between sleep and epilepsy, with distinct patterns for focal compared to generalised epilepsy. These differences may help explain syndrome-specific sleep-wake associations, including seizure timing and predisposition. By localising shared loci and highlighting specific overlapping genes, we provide a foundation for future research into the mechanisms underlying epilepsy-sleep comorbidities.
records.journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology
records.authors: Le KN, Jackson VE, Stirling RE, Gerring ZF, Stevelink R, Berkovic SF, Scheffer IE, Karoly PJ, Bahlo M, Oliver KL.

records.title: The genetic basis of extra-lobed leaves in ivyleaf morning glory (  Ipomoea hederacea  )
records.abstract: Intraspecific leaf shape variation is common among angiosperms. Ivyleaf morning glory (  Ipomoea hederacea ) has become a useful system for studying the genetics and ecology of leaf shape variation as this species exhibits two leaf shapes: leaves with entire margins, and 3-lobed leaves. It is known that these phenotypes are controlled by a single locus, and differ in their ecophysiology, geographic distribution, ecology, and fitness. However, while lobed individuals producing leaves with 1-2 extra lobes have also been regularly observed, the genetic basis, if any, of these phenotypes has not been described. To investigate the genetic basis of extra-lobing, we compared phenotypic distributions of leaf shapes of an F2 generation to Mendelian ratios for a single locus trait and conducted a bulked segregant analysis to uncover quantitative trait loci. Our results suggest that producing extra-lobed leaves has a complex genetic basis and that there are multiple QTLs underlying this phenotype containing potential candidate genes involved with auxin distribution and leaf development. Whether these extra-lobed phenotypes also differ in terms of their physiology and ecology remains unexplored.  Article summary  Ivyleaf morning glory exhibits two main leaf shapes, heart-shaped entire leaves and 3-lobed, controlled by a single Mendelian locus. However, within the lobed genotypes, there are occasional individuals that produce leaves with extra lobes. We examined whether there was a simple genetic basis to producing extra lobes, and if so, does it have the same genetic basis as the other leaf shapes, or are different regions in the genome responsible? After planting 500 individuals in a greenhouse and collecting phenotypic and genomic data, we found that extra-lobing is heritable, does not have a simple Mendelian basis, but may be influenced by multiple QTLs.
records.authors: Henry MR, Hernandez DJ, Li MC, Glasgow E, Peake AL, Stinchcombe JR.

records.title: Revamped transposon-induced hepatocellular carcinoma model reveals deep similarities of cancer-driver landscapes across mice and humans
records.abstract: Genome-scale cancer-driver discovery is limited by statistical uncertainty in driver calling and by experimental constraints on mutations available for selection. We developed 3×fOnc3—a three-frame Sleeping Beauty (SB) mutagenesis system designed to broaden functional perturbations and reduce integration biases of traditional SB screens—and tested it in vivo in mouse liver. Within 12 months, 60% of mice developed heterogeneous hepatocellular tumors. Tumor-selected integrations were interpreted against an empirical reference from SB-based therapeutic gene delivery to hepatocytes, enabling correction for gene targetability. Background-aware filtering prioritized 315 driver candidates, including 243 protein-coding genes. Tumors were multiclonal, and identical integration-marked lineages expanded differently across lesions, supporting context-dependent clonal expansion. SB hits within young L1 subfamily members were selectively enriched in tumors. Human orthologues of candidate drivers were enriched for Cancer Gene Census genes and protein-altering pan-cancer mutations. Together, 3×fOnc3 reveals a background-corrected driver landscape linking driver selection to clonal tumor evolution and cross-species cancer relevance.

records.title: Structure of  Bacillus cereus  ZmaM, a peptidase-ABC transporter that secretes and activates zwittermicin A
records.abstract: Bacteria engage in microbial warfare by secreting toxic molecules. These toxins can serve as therapeutics or drug discovery starting points, motivating investigations of their production. Bacteria that produce these toxins must protect themselves, and a common strategy is to synthesize an inactive prodrug that is activated upon secretion. Some prodrugs are capped with  N -acyl-ᴅ-asparagine motifs, which are removed by two types of prodrug peptidases. Type I peptidases are membrane-bound S12 hydrolases; type II peptidases have an additional C-terminal half-ABC transporter module. Recent structures of a type I peptidase revealed how its transmembrane domain completes the substrate-binding site, but little is known about type II peptidases. Here, we show that the  B. cereus type II peptidase ZmaM is responsible for both the export of prezwittermicin and its activation into zwittermicin. The structure of homodimeric ZmaM reveals a central type IV ABC transporter flanked by peptidase modules. The periplasmic hydrolase domains interact over the transporter’s open outer vestibule. Mutations to intermodule interfaces impact both peptidase and ATP hydrolysis activities, indicating the peptidase and transporter modules are interdependent. Together, our findings reveal an evolutionary strategy to coordinate toxin activation with its export and inform future efforts to harness these systems in biotechnology.
records.authors: Zavala GE, Velilla JA, Walsh RM, Patel M, Mennes K, Rafat W, Aguilar Ramos MA, Daniel-Ivad M, Ramírez-Guadiana FH, Rudner DZ, Balskus EP, Gaudet R.

records.title: Genetic transformation and fluorescent protein expression in the biomaterial-producing fungus Fomes fomentarius.
records.abstract: BackgroundFungal-based materials are currently studied as renewable and sustainable alternatives to fossil-based materials used in construction, packaging, textile, and fashion industries. The polypore fungus Fomes fomentarius produces a range of lightweight, durable, and flexible materials from diverse plant residual streams. Genetic engineering of this fungus is an important technological objective, both from fundamental perspectives and to optimize performance characteristics of F. fomentarius materials.ResultsWe provide proof of principle that F. fomentarius can be genetically transformed. Hyphae produced high amounts of protoplasts using standard protocols. These protoplasts were transformed using nourseothricin selection and a nourseothricin N-acetyl transferase resistance marker (natR). Expression of natR was successful using a F. fomentarius translation elongation factor promoter. Stable, multicopy, and non-targeted integration of exogenous cassettes with recipient genome was confirmed by diagnostic PCR and Southern blotting. Preliminary attempts at genome editing based disruption of a putative ku70 encoding gene were, however, unsuccessful. We validated expression of two fluorescent proteins using a Schizophyllum commune H2B promoter using qRT-PCR and fluorescent microscopy. These data confirm functionality of mCherry and eGFP in F. fomentarius and suggest these proteins can be used for future protein localisation studies. Finally, we report DNase activity in F. fomentarius which we hypothesize may be a significant technical challenge for genetic transformation of this fungus.ConclusionF. fomentarius can be genetically transformed using the promoters, marker, and nourseothricin selection system developed in this study. Expression of both eGFP and mCherry is a significant step towards cell biological and gene functional analyses using fluorescent microscopy. We have laid the foundations for overexpression studies, and, additionally, identified several challenges which need to be overcome for targeted genetic engineering in this important material producing fungus.
records.authors: Regner C, Zillessen J, Hoberg F, Elsner S, Cairns TC, Freidank-Pohl C, Meyer V.

records.title: Roadmap for inferring metabolic regulation using multiomics, machine learning, and genome-scale modeling.
records.abstract: Machine learning and genome-scale metabolic modeling have accelerated the discovery of metabolic-regulatory relationships in model microbes and mammalian cells. This review provides a roadmap for integrating omics with computational methods for studying systems-level transcriptional, post-translational, and allosteric regulation. Developing methods to infer and integrate multiple regulatory mechanisms simultaneously is essential for discovering novel modes of metabolic regulation and precise engineering of metabolic networks.
records.authors: Schildcrout R, Rhoads N, Chandrasekaran S.

records.title: PrinTE: a forward simulation framework for studying the role of transposable elements in genome expansion and contraction.
records.abstract: Genome expansion and contraction are driven by transposable element activity, but the underlying dynamics remain enigmatic due to a lack of historical records tracing these changes. Here, we present PrinTE, a forward-time simulator of whole-genome sequences with customizable transposon dynamics for identifying the evolutionary parameters most consistent with an observed genome. Across simulations spanning four orders of magnitude, PrinTE recovers transposon insertion and deletion rates with less than 6% error. We demonstrate PrinTE on Arabidopsis and the fungal subdivision Pucciniomycotina, including myrtle rust (Austropuccinia psidii), which expanded its genome size to 1,018 Mb through transposon amplifications. Our simulations show that recombination-based removal of LTR retrotransposons alone cannot prevent genome obesity, and that preventing their invasion in the first place is more effective. We hypothesize that A. psidii might have experienced a prolonged expansion phase followed by a potent and ongoing period of contraction.
records.authors: Benson CW, Chen TH, Thomson SJ, Deng CH, Ou S.

records.title: Nanobody-Modified Outer Membrane Vesicles Attenuate Alzheimer's Disease-Like Neurodegeneration by Modulating Mitophagy-Associated Phenotypes and cGAS-STING-Related Inflammatory Signaling.
records.abstract: This study examined anti-transferrin receptor (TfR) nanobody-functionalized bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) as an engineered platform for improving Alzheimer's disease (AD)-like neuronal injury. Escherichia coli-derived OMVs were characterized for morphology, size distribution, surface charge, protein features, nanobody loading, residual endotoxin levels, endotoxin-associated inflammatory responses, and repeated-exposure immune-safety readouts, and were evaluated in neuronal-related cells and APP/PS1 mice. Engineered OMVs showed receptor-associated uptake and preferential brain-delivery signals, increased HT-22 cell viability, reduced apoptosis, and elevated mitophagy-associated markers including LC3-II, PINK1, and Parkin. OMV treatment also reduced cytosolic mtDNA abundance, DNA/cGAS colocalization, phosphorylation of STING/TBK1/IRF3, and inflammatory-marker expression. PINK1 or Parkin knockdown partially weakened OMV-associated mitochondrial and inflammatory readouts, whereas pharmacological autophagy modulation supported a contribution of autophagy-related processes without establishing selective PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy in vivo. In APP/PS1 mice, OMV administration improved Morris water maze and rotarod performance and alleviated neuroinflammatory and histological injury-related changes. Overall, anti-TfR nanobody-modified OMVs were associated with enhanced receptor-related delivery, mitophagy-linked phenotypes, reduced cytosolic mtDNA/cGAS-STING-related inflammatory signaling, and improved AD-like outcomes, supporting further delivery-system optimization and mechanistic validation.
records.authors: Xiao J, Yang Z, Li J, Xiong Q, Xia X, Hao L, Ling Z, Pang K, Zhou C, Wu H.

records.title: Multisensing photoreceptors: a cross-kingdom perspective.
records.abstract: Photoreceptors are classically depicted as monochromatic switches governed strictly by light. However, emerging biophysical and structural insights reveal that these proteins act as dynamic, multisensory hubs across kingdoms of life. Drawing primarily on plant and fungal systems, where mechanisms are most extensively characterized, this review synthesizes how photoreceptors integrate ambient temperature and cellular oxidative state alongside photon flux, with cross-kingdom examples extending this framework to bacteria. Thermal energy modulates dark reversion rates, quaternary assembly, and photobody phase separation, whereas reactive oxygen species alter the photocycle and trigger structural shifts through direct redox sensing. Under a 'stress-first' evolutionary model, ancestral stress-sensing scaffolds could be retrofitted with chromophores via exaptation, providing a unified biophysical rationale for how cells decode complex, fluctuating environments.
records.authors: Schuhmacher L, Landmark A, Fischer R.

records.title: Biochar-mediated N-Fe redox coupling for Cd immobilization and N<sub>2</sub>O mitigation in flooded paddy soil.
records.abstract: Coupled soil N and Fe redox processes influence heavy-metal mobility and greenhouse-gas emissions. As an electron shuttle, biochar can directly mediate N and Fe redox transformations. However, how this function regulates electron allocation within N-Fe redox processes and whether this regulation contributes to Cd immobilization and N2O mitigation remains unclear. Here, anaerobic incubation experiments combined with electrochemical characterization, electron allocation analysis and metagenomic analysis were conducted in Cd-contaminated paddy soils. Nitrate addition suppressed Fe(III) reduction and amorphous Fe oxide formation in the control treatments, indicating competition between nitrate and Fe(III) reduction. In contrast, biochar increased Fe(III) and nitrate reduction rates by 18-402% and 53-258%, respectively. Biochar also enhanced soil electron-transfer rate and capacity, enriched electroactive microorganisms and extracellular electron-transfer functional genes. The electron allocation analysis showed that biochar increased total quantified electron consumption and suggested that biochar may alleviate competition between nitrate and Fe(III) reduction. Enhanced Fe(III) reduction increased Fe(II) production and may have promoted nitrate-associated Fe(II) oxidation, with amorphous Fe oxide contents increasing by 9-63%. These Fe transformations redistributed Cd into Fe/Mn oxide-bound fractions and decreased CaCl2-extractable Cd by 29-55%. Within the nitrate reduction pathways, biochar increased absolute electron consumption by dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), while decreasing that by denitrification. These changes were accompanied by 10-49% higher NH4+ concentrations and 13-19% lower cumulative N2O emissions. These findings highlight the role of biochar-mediated electron transfer in regulating electron allocation within coupled N-Fe redox processes, providing novel insights into concurrent Cd immobilization and N2O mitigation in paddy soils.

records.title: Sulfur-iron-driven autotrophic constructed wetlands for coupled nitrogen removal and phosphorus transformation under low carbon-to-nitrogen ratio conditions.
records.abstract: Constructed wetlands are widely used for nitrogen removal, yet their performance in low carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) wastewater is often constrained by insufficient electron donors. Autotrophic denitrification provides a carbon-independent alternative, but systems relying on single inorganic substrates frequently exhibit limited electron supply and unstable nutrient transformation. Here, a sulfur-iron-slag-based constructed wetland (SCW) was developed to investigate nitrogen removal and its linkage with phosphorus dynamics under progressively decreasing C/N conditions. The system achieved consistently high nitrate removal (>93%) and a maximum total nitrogen removal efficiency of 79.22%, substantially outperforming a conventional sand-based wetland (53.58%) at a C/N ratio of 0.67. Enhanced nitrogen removal was associated with the sulfur-iron functional medium and sustained autotrophic denitrification. However, phosphorus showed a contrasting response: although aqueous P release decreased with continued operation, the SCW remained a net aqueous P source throughout the reported period, accompanied by redistribution of solid-phase P toward Fe/Al-associated and Ca-associated fractions. Microbial and metagenomic analyses revealed the enrichment of sulfur-oxidizing and autotrophic denitrifying taxa together with shifts in nitrogen- and sulfur-related functional-gene profiles, consistent with enhanced sulfur-associated autotrophic potential. Functional gene profiles further indicated that electron transfer processes governed the integration of multi-element biogeochemical cycles rather than isolated increases in individual pathways. Overall, this study elucidates process-level coupling between enhanced autotrophic nitrogen removal and dynamic phosphorus transformation, providing mechanistic insights and practical guidance for optimizing constructed wetlands treating low-C/N wastewater.
records.authors: Zhao L, Zhang Y, Tian T, Huang Y, Gu Y, He X, Tang J, He S.

records.title: Inarigivir exhibits RIG-I-independent antiviral activity against HBV DNA replication in vitro by inhibiting viral polymerase activity.
records.abstract: Inarigivir (SB 9200) is a linear dinucleotide antiviral drug designed to act as a RIG-I agonist, activating cellular innate immune responses. Clinical trials in hepatitis C virus (HCV) patients have confirmed the innate immune-activating antiviral activity of Inarigivir. In hepatitis B virus (HBV) patients, clinical trials using Inarigivir have demonstrated significant reductions in HBV DNA and RNA levels, although heterogeneous drug-induced liver injury has been observed at higher doses. To further explore Inarigivir's mechanism of action against HBV, we characterized its antiviral effect in various hepatocyte-derived cell lines, including transiently transfected HepG2 and Huh7 cells, inducible HBV stable cell lines HepAD38 and HepDES19, and HBV-infected human hepatocytes. Our results show that Inarigivir inhibits HBV DNA replication in a dose-dependent manner without affecting HBV RNA levels or pgRNA encapsidation. HBV RNA immunoprecipitation assays revealed that Inarigivir does not affect viral polymerase binding to pgRNA, while the in vitro endogenous polymerase reaction (EPR) assays demonstrated that Inarigivir inhibits HBV DNA synthesis catalyzed by polymerase within the capsid. Additionally, we provided several lines of evidence indicating that Inarigivir's antiviral effect is independent of the RIG-I signalling pathway in hepatocyte-derived cells. Taken together, our study demonstrates a RIG-I-independent antiviral mechanism of Inarigivir by inhibiting HBV DNA replication as a dinucleosidic non-chain-terminating reverse transcriptase inhibitor.
records.authors: Zhang JJ, Colledge D, Jurado A, Sun N, Zhang H, Jackson K, Sozzi V, Li X, Eyre NS, Beard MR, Iyer R, Afdhal N, Guo H.

records.title: Exploration of lymphoproliferative disease virus strains in wild turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo) in Iowa, USA.
records.abstract: Wild turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo) were nearly extirpated in the early 1900's and extensive restoration efforts utilizing translocated wild turkeys were employed to restore populations. Although these efforts were successful, populations have again been in decline due to unknown causes. Lymphoproliferative disease virus (LPDV) was first detected in the United States in 2009. The coinciding appearance of LDPV and declining populations have led to studies in several states and provinces in North America to characterize its prevalence and distribution due to concerns about its potential role in population declines. The spread of disease agents is a common outcome during translocation programs and could be related to the spread of LPDV. Prior studies have performed phylogenetic analyses to examine genetic variation across and geographic clustering among strains. In this study we aimed to identify the diversity of LPDV strains present in wild turkeys in Iowa and if there was geographic clustering within the state or with other locations where LPDV has been detected. We sequenced a subset (n = 77) of hunter-harvested samples covering eight of the nine agricultural regions in Iowa that tested PCR positive with the viral gag gene. We performed phylogenetic analysis on 73 unique Iowan strains as well as previously catalogued strains from other regions retrieved from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GenBank database. Overall, Iowa strains did not show geographic clustering within the state or with any other specific geographic regions. Our study demonstrated that there is a high level of genetic diversity among LPDV strains in Iowa and did not provide evidence of connection with a particular location external to Iowa as a source of introduction of LPDV to the state.
records.authors: Smith KC, Navarro D, Blanchong JA.

records.title: Recognition of the centromere-binding protein Ndc10 by Scm3  HJURP  directs Cse4  CENP-A  deposition at native centromeres
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Kinetochores connect centromeres to spindle microtubules, ensuring accurate chromosome segregation. Kinetochore assembly at centromeres depends on deposition of CENP-A, a histone H3 variant. Despite considerable progress, how CENP-A is specifically assembled on native centromeres remains an open question. Centromere-specific assembly of CENP-A occurs spontaneously in a cell-free extract system from the yeast  Saccharomyces cerevisiae , but with low efficiency, suggesting that one or more factors are limiting. Here, we show Scm3  HJURP , a specific chaperone for the centromeric histone Cse4  CENP-A , is one such limiting component. The addition of a complex of Scm3, Cse4 and histone H4 strongly stimulates Cse4 assembly in a centromeric DNA sequence- and dose-dependent manner; in addition, improvements in both Cse4 and kinetochore assembly were more prominent in mitotic versus interphase (G1) extracts. Using the complemented cell-free reconstitution system, we show that distinct Scm3 interfaces with Cse4 and with the Ndc10 subunit of the yeast centromere DNA sequence-recognizing CBF3 complex are essential for centromere-specific Cse4 assembly and cell viability. Thus, recognition of Ndc10 directs Scm3-dependent and locus-specific centromeric histone deposition.  SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT  Accurate chromosome segregation depends on the assembly of kinetochores at centromeres. In budding yeast, centromeres are specified by DNA sequence, but how sequence recognition is coupled to deposition of the centromeric histone Cse4 remains incompletely understood. Using a cell-free assembly system, we show that Scm3 promotes centromeric Cse4 assembly through distinct regions that bind Cse4/H4 and the centromere-binding protein Ndc10. Mutations that disrupt Ndc10 binding impair Cse4 assembly in extracts, reduce Scm3 association with centromeres in cells, and compromise viability. These findings support a mechanism in which a histone chaperone engages a sequence-specific centromere-binding complex to direct centromeric histone assembly.
records.authors: Cai J, Wang Z, Cheng L, Xu T, Zhang C, Hinshaw SM, Suhandynata RT, Desai A, Zhou H.

records.title: Single-probe, amplification-free multiplex mRNA PNA-FISH maps bacterial gene expression in intact three-dimensional biofilms
records.abstract: Biofilms are spatially structured communities in which local microenvironments drive physiological differentiation, yet mapping gene expression inside intact three-dimensional biofilms remains challenging. Bacterial spatial transcriptomics methods typically rely on tiled probe sets, sequential hybridization rounds, or signal amplification. Here, we show that a single short, directly labelled peptide nucleic acid (PNA) probe per target is sufficient to quantify bacterial mRNA  in situ without amplification. With all probes designed for a common hybridization condition, a transcript panel is resolved in one hybridization on a standard confocal microscope, in unmodified cells while preserving biofilm architecture. Benchmarked against the biphasic cycle of  Legionella pneumophila , multiplex mRNA PNA-FISH recovers the expected transcriptional switch and agrees quantitatively with RT-qPCR in planktonic and biofilm populations. In flow-cell biofilms, it shows that sessile populations do not recapitulate the planktonic program and that transcriptional differences follow cellular aggregation state rather than depth.

records.title: Machine learning guided design of strong transcriptional activation domains
records.abstract: Summary  Artificial intelligence has accelerated the design of structured proteins, but it remains difficult to design functional intrinsically disordered proteins because of weak structural constraints and poorly defined sequence-to-function relationships  1 . Activation domains (ADs), transcription factor regions that recruit coactivators, are an excellent test case for the  de novo design of intrinsically disordered sequences. ADs are one of the oldest groups of functional intrinsically disordered sequences  2 and designed ADs have applications in synthetic biology, biotechnology, and agriculture. We computationally generated 500,000 candidate sequences that resembled known ADs and predicted AD function with extant machine learning models, including three neural networks. From high-scoring sequences, we selected 18,750 for experimental validation in yeast. Surprisingly, >90% of the 16,770 well-measured sequences function as ADs. Sequences predicted to be active by multiple models were stronger, motivating development of a fast and accurate consensus AD predictor, MADRIGAL. A number of our designed ADs retain functionality across fungi, plants, and human cells. This work illustrates a generalizable paradigm for incorporating sequence-to-function models into the design loop to efficiently generate functional intrinsically disordered sequences.

records.title: Therapeutic vulnerabilities of the drug-resistant fungal meningitis pathogen  Cryptococcus neoformans
records.abstract: SUMMARY  Treatment options are limited for the priority fungal pathogen  Cryptococcus neoformans . We describe CRISPR-insert, a scalable gene inactivation method for global interrogation of drug targets. Genome-wide screens using this methodology combined with machine learning predict 1,297 essential genes under liberal criteria. Unexpectedly absent from this list is  FKS1 , encoding the target of echinocandin drugs to which  C. neoformans is resistant. Contrary to longstanding literature, targeted deletion shows that  FKS1 is not essential. Solid-state NMR reveals that  fks1 Δ mutants lack β-1,3-glucan, arguing against compensation by another synthase. We experimentally test essentiality predictions for genes lacking human orthologs, identifying high-priority drug target candidates. To uncover targets for combination therapies, we establish genome-scale quantitative genetic interaction mapping. We use this method to uncover synthetic lethal dependencies of echinocandin resistance determinants, including the druggable calcineurin and Cdc50-Apt1 pathways. CRISPR-insert illuminates therapeutic vulnerabilities of an invasive fungal pathogen.

records.title: Metagenomic insights into kapok-driven nitrogen-cycling hotspots enhancing soil biological resilience in tropical agroforestry systems
records.abstract: Abstract    Intensive rice monoculture in tropical regions is increasingly vulnerable to soil degradation, low nitrogen use efficiency (NUE), and amplified nutrient losses under climate change extremes, necessitating sustainable, biologically driven management strategies. This study evaluated the role of traditional kapok–rice agroforestry, integrating the native red silk-cotton tree (  Bombax ceiba  ), in regulating soil nutrient dynamics, nitrogen (N) mineralization, microbial biomass, extracellular enzyme activities, and microbial community composition across five rice growth stages (tillering, booting, heading, maturity, and fallow) compared to rice monoculture systems in Changjiang County, Hainan, China. Using a paired-plot design with three independent replicate fields per system, we compared kapok-integrated soils against adjacent rice monoculture controls. Kapok-integrated soils exhibited markedly enhanced fertility relative to monoculture, with soil organic matter increasing by up to 42%, total N by 44–49%, and available N, P, and K by 63%, 133%, and 93%, respectively, at the maturity stage, compared to monoculture controls. Microbial biomass carbon and nitrogen peaked at 397.17 and 362.40 mg kg  − 1  , accompanied by significantly higher N-acquiring enzyme activities (N-acetylglucosaminidase and leucine aminopeptidase), indicating intensified microbial functioning. Nitrogen mineralization potential (N  o  ) and cumulative mineralized N were substantially greater (63.42 and 67.46 mg kg  − 1  over 90 days), reflecting improved N retention and cycling capacity under agroforestry management. These enhancements were linked to distinct microbial community shifts dominated by Pseudomonadota, Actinomycetota, Ascomycota, and Bacillariophyta, suggesting increased functional stability and adaptive capacity under climate-sensitive conditions. Overall, kapok–rice agroforestry strengthens soil biological processes, enhances nitrogen cycling, and improves ecosystem resilience, demonstrating its potential as a nature-based, low-input management strategy to mitigate soil degradation and sustain productivity in tropical rice systems under climate change extremes.
records.authors: ALI S, Xiang W, Ren M, AHMED W.

records.title: A Candidate Genomic DNA Reference Material for PCR-Based Detection of Brucella spp.: Intralaboratory Characterization and Preliminary Application in LAMP Assays
records.abstract: Analytical standardization of Brucella molecular assays requires reference materials with assigned values and defined uncertainty. We produced and characterized intralaboratory a candidate genomic DNA reference material from Brucella abortus RB51 for PCR-based detection of Brucella spp., and evaluated its preliminary use in fluorescence-based and colorimetric LAMP assays. DNA was extracted, assessed by qPCR and dPCR, and diluted to two levels. Homogeneity and stability were evaluated by duplex qPCR targeting ctrA and nikR, whereas property values were assigned by duplex dPCR. qPCR efficiencies were 95.3% for ctrA and 92.1% for nikR. The material fulfilled the homogeneity criterion, with relative homogeneity uncertainties between 0.37% and 1.41%. Assigned values (levels 1 and 2) were 32 989 ± 5 475 and 285 ± 47 copies/µL for ctrA, and 29 722 ± 3 263 and 286 ± 42 copies/µL for nikR. Short-term stability at 4 °C was supported for 8 weeks and was included in the uncertainty budget. ctrA-based LAMP assays were optimized at 67 °C for 45 min and amplified reproducibly in both formats. Amplification was consistent from 2411 to 6.34 copies/µL. This material provides a metrologically characterized tool for quality control, method verification, and optimization of PCR- and LAMP-based assays for Brucella spp.
records.authors: Jaimes MP, Dávila SL, Leguizamón JE, Soto CY.

records.title: Extended DNA damage-induced G2/M arrests lead to aberrant mitoses through accumulation of securin.
records.abstract: The stochastic nature of DNA damage dictates various scenarios of stress survival among different cells. We used time-lapse microscopy to perform single-cell level analyses of yeast populations with double-stranded DNA breaks and nonfunctional telomeres. Activation of the DNA damage signalling resulted in a broad distribution in the duration of G2/M arrests. Strikingly, the longer arrests correlated with aberrant mitoses caused by miscoordination of nuclear division and cytokinesis, leading to cell death. Chk1-dependent phosphorylation of Pds1 (securin), an inhibitor of sister chromatid separation in mitosis, was responsible for this phenomenon. Securin progressively accumulated during G2/M arrests, leading to grossly delayed or missed nuclear divisions. This phenotype could be suppressed by slowing down the progression of mitotic exit via LTE1 deletion or by lowering securin levels. Our results demonstrate that in cells taking too long to complete DNA repair, the DNA damage checkpoint promotes aberrant mitoses and cell death, thereby eliminating cells with a higher chance of genomic instability.

records.title: NRF2 plays a significant role in the suppression of genotoxicity during aging whereas its protective role for acute UVB genotoxicity is limited to MIS response in mouse skin epidermis.
records.abstract: Our body is continuously exposed to endogenous and exogenous sources of oxidative stress arising from physiological metabolism and environmental factors such as ultraviolet (UV) radiation. These stresses generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) that can induce genotoxicity through oxidative DNA damage. To evaluate the contribution of NRF2, which is a master transcription factor regulating cellular antioxidant responses, to the suppression of oxidative stress-induced genotoxicity in the skin, we examined Nrf2-deficient mice regarding mutagenic responses to two separate biological situations: acute UVB exposures and the chronic process of aging. Analyses were performed using transgenic mice carrying the bacterial lacZ gene as a mutational reporter. No significant differences were detected between Nrf2-deficient and wild-type mice in mutagenicity, induced mutation spectrum, and mutation distribution within the reporter gene after acute UVB exposure, whereas the dose-response kinetics of UVB-induced mutation in the phase called "mutation induction suppression" (MIS) differed significantly between genotypes, with a more pronounced MIS response observed in the Nrf2-/- epidermis. Little contribution of ROS to genotoxicity was observed after the acute exposure. Notably, however, the age-dependent accumulation of mutations was significantly elevated in the Nrf2-deficient epidermis compared to the wild-type. These findings indicate that NRF2 plays a protective role for the skin, not by directly preventing genotoxicity, but by promoting tissue recovery after acute UVB damage and, more importantly, by suppressing the genotoxic effects of physiologically produced ROS in a chronic aging process.

records.title: iTB-DRS: a multi-stage feature selection framework to identify Mycobacterium tuberculosis drug-resistance using single-nucleotide polymorphisms.
records.abstract: Rapid and accurate prediction of Mycobacterium tuberculosis drug resistance is crucial for effective tuberculosis control. However, data from genome-wide association studies are often characterized by high dimensionality and many redundant features, posing significant challenges to prediction models. To address these challenges, we propose a novel computational framework called iTB-DRS, which employs a hierarchical multi-stage feature selection strategy. The workflow begins with data encoding followed by a four-step selection mechanism, including (i) filtering noise using a Mean Decrease Accuracy based on Random Forest; (ii) ranking features by Maximum Information Coefficient to capture nonlinear association; (iii) performing pairwise predictive evaluation to identify SNP-SNP combinations with increased joint predictive value; and (iv) optimizing feature subsets through backward feature elimination. Finally, a set of Random Forest classifiers is trained to predict drug resistance to different drugs. When using an independent data set, iTB-DRS generally outperformed RF, LASSO + RF, and mRMR + RF baselines across multiple drug metric combinations. Simultaneously, the developed framework achieved good predictive accuracy on the training data set close to that of the computational pipeline TB-Profiler frequently used to predict Mycobacterium tuberculosis lineage and drug resistance. However, a performance gap between these two predictive tools emerged on the independent data set for several second-line drugs, which is mainly due to the catalog-based prior knowledge used by TB-Profiler. Taken together, the data obtained showed that iTB-DRS provides a low-complexity and interpretable solution that balances predictive accuracy and computational feasibility, offering a complementary research tool for genomic surveillance and candidate-marker discovery.IMPORTANCEDrug-resistant tuberculosis poses a significant threat to global health, narrowing the range of effective treatment options and increasing mortality rates. Rapid identification of drug resistance is crucial for selecting appropriate treatments during therapy. However, existing genomic tools often rely on predefined mutation catalogs, which may not fully capture complex or emerging resistance patterns. Therefore, studies on the development of novel effective methods for prediction of drug-resistant tuberculosis are of great importance. Here, we introduce a data-driven computational framework abbreviated as iTB-DRS that predicts Mycobacterium tuberculosis drug resistance using whole-genome sequencing data and a multi-stage feature selection strategy. Unlike catalog-based tools that use embedded prior knowledge, the proposed framework can be retrained on newly accumulated data to evaluate mutations and drugs not represented in existing catalogs. This flexibility positions iTB-DRS as a complementary, hypothesis-generating tool for genomic surveillance rather than a stand-alone replacement for validated catalog-based clinical software.
records.authors: Chen Y-X, Andrianov AM, Gabrielian A, Rosenthal A, Tuzikov AV.

records.title: Activity of omadacycline and comparator agents against rapidly growing mycobacteria by broth microdilution and whole genome sequencing.
records.abstract: Pulmonary infections caused by rapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM), such as Mycobacteroides abscessus, are challenging to treat, highlighting the need for new therapeutic options. This study evaluated the in vitro activity of omadacycline against RGM and investigated the influence of tetracycline resistance mechanisms on its in vitro activity. In vitro susceptibility to omadacycline and comparator antimicrobials was assessed by broth microdilution against 476 geographically diverse RGM isolates from the United States. Omadacycline minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) distributions were compared between cystic fibrosis (CF) and non-CF RGM isolates. Variation in the TetR-TetX operon and the rrl, rrs, and erm(41) genes was evaluated by whole genome sequencing. Omadacycline exhibited low MIC values across all RGM species (MIC50/MIC90: 0.25/0.5 µg/mL). CF isolates showed a modest shift toward higher omadacycline MIC values (P = 0.001). The activity of comparator antimicrobials varied by species, whereas omadacycline was consistent and comparable to tigecycline. The TetR-TetX operon was present in all sequenced isolates, with variable amino acid sequences across species. These variations did not significantly affect omadacycline or tigecycline activity, whereas doxycycline and minocycline remained largely inactive regardless of TetR-TetX variation. The rrs A1408G mutation was identified in 6% of M. abscessus isolates, and rrl mutations were identified in 4% of isolates. The T28C erm(41) sequevar was present in 80% of M. abscessus subsp. abscessus and 100% of M. abscessus subsp. bolletii, whereas 100% of M. abscessus subsp. massiliense exhibited a truncated erm(41). Omadacycline consistently demonstrated potent in vitro activity across RGM species regardless of TetR-TetX operon variation, supporting its potential role in treating RGM infections.ImportanceRapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM) are a group of bacteria that often resist common antibiotics, making the infections they cause hard to treat. In this study, we tested omadacycline, a newer antibiotic in the tetracycline class, against a large collection of these bacteria collected from patients across the United States. We found that omadacycline showed consistent activity against different RGM species, requiring low concentrations to inhibit bacterial growth in laboratory testing. These findings support further evaluation of omadacycline as a potential treatment option for patients with RGM infections, which can be challenging to manage.
records.authors: Calado Nogueira de Moura V, Gillaspie JJ, Anastasiou DM, Serio AW, Strong M, Khare R, Daley CL.

records.title: Genome sequence of the endophyte Bacillus halotolerans Adn01R isolated from Agropyron desertorum roots.
records.abstract: We report the draft genome of endophytic Bacillus halotolerans Adn01R isolated from roots of Agropyron desertorum. Sequencing on Illumina NextSeq (1.4 M paired-end reads) and assembly with SPAdes yielded a 4.15-Mb genome (43.71% guanine-cytosine [GC], N50 4.14 Mb, 98× coverage). The assembly shows 99.8% BUSCO completeness and 4,298 genes.

records.title: Ineffectiveness of permethrin in human scabies treatment: A multicenter study of kdr gene mutations.
records.abstract: BackgroundScabies remains a widespread parasitic skin disease with increasing reports of treatment failure associated with permethrin, the first-line therapy. Emerging evidence suggests that genetic variation in the voltage-gated sodium channel (VGSC) may be associated with reduced susceptibility to pyrethroids, although its contribution to clinical treatment failure in human scabies remains incompletely characterized.ObjectivesTo investigate the presence and frequency of knockdown resistance (kdr) gene mutations associated with permethrin treatment failure in S. scabiei collected from patients in multiple centres across Europe and Africa.MethodsMite samples were obtained from patients with clinically diagnosed scabies in France, Belgium, Tunisia and Madagascar between 2023 and 2025. Genomic DNA was extracted and PCR amplification of the voltage-sensitive sodium channel (VSSC) gene was performed, followed by bidirectional sequencing to identify single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Detected mutations were analysed and correlated with clinical treatment outcomes.ResultsOut of 61 suspected cases, 45 were confirmed as scabies infestations. Molecular analysis identified three mutations-M918L, G733D and S916S-in 25 (55.5%) specimens, which were detected in patients with documented permethrin treatment failure. In contrast, 20 out of 45 patients without these mutations experienced successful treatment outcomes. M918L was the most frequent and widely distributed mutation. These genetic findings were consistent with the observed treatment ineffectiveness. This study is the first to report these mutations in Belgium, Tunisia and Madagascar.ConclusionsThis pilot multicentre study identified an association between specific VGSC polymorphisms and documented permethrin treatment failure in human scabies. M918L, G733D and S916S represent candidate resistance-associated variants, whereas the functional significance of the synonymous S916S substitution requires further investigation. Regarding the multifactorial nature of scabies treatment, the increasing occurrence of VGSC nucleotide substitutions highlights an emerging challenge in scabies management and underscores the urgent need for ongoing resistance monitoring, molecular surveillance and the development of alternative therapeutic strategies.

records.title: Structural characterization of a pseudaminic acid-modified lateral flagellar filament from Vibrio alginolyticus.
records.abstract: Bacterial flagellar filaments are often modified by glycans, but the structural basis and physiological significance of flagellin glycosylation remain poorly understood in many species. Vibrio alginolyticus produces lateral flagella for surface-associated motility in viscous environments, with LafA forming its filament as flagellin. A maf homolog encoding a putative flagellin glycosylation factor is located immediately downstream of lafA, suggesting that the lateral filament is glycosylated. To investigate this possibility, we purified the lateral flagellar filament from V. alginolyticus and determined the structure at 2.4 Å resolution by electron cryomicroscopy. Upon model building of LafA in the map, we identified additional densities connected to five serine residues, possibly corresponding to O-linked pseudaminic acid modifications. Mass spectrometric analyses identified these modifications as pseudaminic acid attached to Ser148, Ser173, Ser183, Ser189, and Ser197. Deletion of maf abolished lateral flagella formation and motility, and these defects were restored by complementation with maf. These results demonstrate that the Vibrio lateral flagellar filament is extensively modified by pseudaminic acid and that Maf is required for filament formation. Our findings provide the first structural insight into the glycosylation of the Vibrio lateral flagellar filament and establish a framework for understanding the role of flagellin glycosylation in surface-associated motility.IMPORTANCEA gene encoding a putative flagellin glycosylation factor (Maf) is located immediately downstream of lafA, the gene encoding lateral flagellin of Vibrio alginolyticus, suggesting that the lateral flagellar filament is glycosylated. Guided by this assumption, we determined the structure of the lateral flagellar filament by electron cryomicroscopy with mass spectrometry and identified five pseudaminic acid modifications on the filament surface. Genetic analyses further demonstrated that Maf is required for lateral flagellar formation and motility. These results provide the first structural characterization of a glycosylated Vibrio lateral flagellar filament and reveal a close link between flagellin glycosylation and motility organelle assembly.

records.title: ADAR-mediated RNA editing of Influenza A virus genomes may be age-dependent and inversely correlates with viral load.
records.abstract: BackgroundSeasonal influenza epidemics cause significant mortality, especially among the elderly. Influenza A virus triggers the host innate immune system through various mechanisms. Human enzymes belonging to the group of RNA-acting adenosine deaminases (ADARs) play a role in the innate antiviral immune response, partly by inducing mutations in viral RNA. The effect of this mechanismin influenza A virus infection remains unexplained in humans.ObjectiveThe aim of this study was to assess the clinical impact of ADAR-induced mutations on influenza A virus in hospitalised patients.MethodsFull-genome deep sequencing of Influenza A virus was performed on respiratory samples from 75 hospitalised, Influenza A(H3N2) virus infected patients, aged 41 to 95 years. ADAR-associated mutations in minor viral subpopulations were analysed in relation to demographic and clinical factors.ResultsADAR-associated mutations showed a significant inverse correlation with viral load (p p = 0.0051), especially in patients older than 75 years. The association between ADAR-associated mutations and viral load was independent of age, inflammation, and disease severity (p ConclusionsWe found an association between ADAR-induced mutations and viral load, which may indicate an antiviral function of ADAR on influenza A virus. The lower mutation rate and associated higher viral load in the elderly suggest an age-dependent reduced ADAR activity, which may contribute to increased disease severity.

records.title: CircaVal: a gene-centric multi-omics platform for exploring circadian regulatory features.
records.abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates daily physiological processes through coordinated regulation of clock-controlled gene expression across multiple molecular layers. However, systematic characterization of this multilayered rhythmic regulation remains challenging because relevant information is distributed across independent datasets and rhythmicity is evaluated using diverse analytical approaches. Here, we developed CircaVal, a gene-centric multi-omics platform for the integrated exploration and interpretation of circadian regulatory features in humans, mice, and baboons. To support this framework, CircaVal processes public datasets using standardized, data-type-specific pipelines, and gene rhythmicity is integrated with tissue-specific expression, cross-species orthology, functional annotations, and multi-omics regulatory features. CircaVal further introduces an integrated rhythmicity score (IRS), which combines concordance across multiple rhythm-detection methods with reproducibility across independent datasets to provide a quantitative basis for prioritizing candidate rhythmic genes. The platform enables users to examine gene rhythmicity across datasets, identify tissue-enriched rhythmic genes, compare rhythmicity across species, and explore associated regulatory features. Additional functions include interactive gene-centric exploration, genome-browser visualization, rhythmicity analysis of user-uploaded time-series data, and programmatic data access. Together, these capabilities provide an integrated framework for rhythmic gene prioritization and gene-level interpretation of circadian regulatory features across tissues, species, datasets, and omics data types. CircaVal is freely available at https://CircaVal.com.
records.authors: Han G, Wu X, Li Q, Shi R, Xiao X, Liu J, Zhang H, Gao D, Li C, Wang A, Jin Y, Chuang TJ, Chao HW, Chen H.

records.title: Decoding anterior-posterior patterning cues into embryo-wide binary fate decisions through recruitment-mediated targeting.
records.abstract: Developmental pattern formation requires patterning cues to be converted into discrete, gene- and cell-specific regulatory outputs, but how this conversion is achieved remains unclear. We address this problem in Caenorhabditis elegans anterior-posterior patterning, where quantitatively asymmetric Wnt/β-catenin cues, namely anterior-enriched POP-1/TCF and posterior-enriched SYS-1/β-catenin, are decoded into binary, switch-like fate decisions. We show that these cues are resolved into embryo-wide binary regulatory outputs through ZIP-7/DBP, a transcription factor with stage-specific, lineage-wide posterior-exclusive expression that is essential for multiple posterior fate decisions. We define a model for this cue-to-decision decoding. At the zip-7 promoter, the transcription factor ZIP-8/NFIL3, which begins to be expressed during mid-embryogenesis prior to ZIP-7 onset, provides an activating input while recruiting POP-1 and SYS-1. POP-1 restrains this activity anteriorly, whereas the POP-1-SYS-1 complex promotes it posteriorly, thereby generating a binary pattern of zip-7 transcription. This recruitment-mediated promoter control couples Wnt/β-catenin cues to gene-specific transcriptional regulation and enables flexible spatiotemporal control of cue-dependent transcription. Genome-wide analyses further suggest that recruitment-mediated cotargeting may extend beyond zip-7 and point to additional candidate factors with similar recruitment functions, supporting a scalable framework for decoding patterning cues into context-specific regulatory decisions.
records.authors: Xiao L, Cong Y, Qi H, Bai Y, Ma X, Zhou Z, Huang X, Wang Y, Du Z.

records.title: Food-derived resveratrol confers multigenerational host defense against PA14 via p38 MAPK and DAF-16 signaling in C. elegans.
records.abstract: Food-derived bioactive compounds are promising candidates for enhancing host immune defense. Here, we established an integrated screening strategy combining immunodeficiency-related gene mining, compound-target mapping, food-derived component annotation, and drug-likeness evaluation to identify candidate immunomodulators. Highly relevant immunodeficiency-associated genes were screened from GeneCards, and active compounds targeting these genes were retrieved from ChEMBL (pChEMBL ≥ 6). These compounds were cross-referenced with the food-derived components from FooDB, followed by network-based target analysis and rule-based drug-likeness filtering. Using this pipeline, resveratrol was prioritized as a representative candidate. In the Caenorhabditis elegans-Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 infection model, resveratrol significantly improved host survival, with 0.5 mM showing the strongest protective effect. This concentration also enhanced body length, locomotion, and lifespan without causing developmental delay. Fluorescence analysis suggested that resveratrol improved lysosomal and mitochondrial homeostasis and reduced infection-associated cellular damage. Integrated transcriptomic analysis and genetic validation demonstrated that resveratrol-mediated protection required intact p38 MAPK signaling and DAF-16 activity, and resveratrol promoted DAF-16 nuclear localization. Moreover, parental resveratrol treatment enhanced PA14 resistance in untreated offspring through both maternal and paternal lineages, with the heritable effect persisting for at least three generations. These findings identify resveratrol as a food-derived candidate with host-protective activity that promotes pathogen resistance and induces heritable host defense through p38 MAPK- and DAF-16-dependent mechanisms, highlighting the potential of dietary interventions for immune modulation and transgenerational health benefits.
records.authors: Wen Y, Shan S, Fu J, Yao J, Zhao C.

records.title: Designing sustainable systems: sustainability assessment of bio-based products and processes
records.abstract: In this webinar, we will introduce the EU’s Safe and Sustainable by Design (SSbD) framework and its application through NORCE biotechnology case studies, alongside an eco-design framework combining process simulation and evolutionary multi-objective optimization for sustainable decision-making. We will also explore CO₂ emissions from (bio)chemical processes, focusing on wastewater treatment, solvent incineration and energy consumption, as well as bacterial communities in microalgal production systems and their relationship with microalgal strains, growth conditions and scale-up.

records.title: Symbiont-Derived Key Innovations Across the Diversity and Diets of Herbivorous Insects.
records.abstract: With prodigious biomass and diversity, herbivorous insects are among the world's most successful animals. It is widely believed, however, that some plant-based diets do not meet the needs of insect metabolism. Microbial symbionts may balance such deficits through diverse biochemistry. Here, we consider whether obligate nutritional symbioses between insects and microbes support large portions of insect herbivore diversity. In doing so, we assess the evidence that these highly integrated relationships are key innovations, circumventing nutritive shortfalls within particular plant tissues. Toward these ends, we compile nutrient data for 20 plant- and non-plant foods, plus data on diet and symbiosis across 874 families of insects-both herbivorous and non-herbivorous. Our results reinforce widely believed, but often uncited evidence that several insect taxa have long-consumed plant tissues with low concentrations of B-vitamins, nitrogen, or accessible carbon. Emerging as symbiont-enriched are seed-feeders, which face insufficient quantities of several B-vitamins in their food. Experimental and genome assessments show how symbionts surmount these B-vitamin shortcomings, showing also where this same challenge, and those of high fibre or low amino acid content are surmounted through symbiosis on other diets. We thus show where symbiont services are key innovations. Over half of the world's insect herbivores persist without nutritive assistance from obligate symbionts. This is largely because many consume leaves, which are reasonably good sources of amino acids and B-vitamins. Lateral transfer of microbial genes encoding plant cell-wall degrading enzymes has helped to overcome high fibre content, defusing the most challenging nutritive aspect of leaf-chewing diets.
records.authors: Russell JA, Smith HM, Bechade B, Cabuslay C, Carpenter M, Freeman D, Hansen A, Higashi C, Hu Y, Peng L, Williams A, Abbot P.

records.title: Nucleotide metabolism and cervical cancer: A comprehensive study of molecular subtypes and therapeutic targets.
records.abstract: Cervical cancer (CC) is among the most prevalent malignancies in women worldwide. Tumor progression involves profound metabolic reprogramming, in which nucleotide metabolism sustains deoxyribonucleic acid/ribonucleic acid synthesis and proliferation; however, its role in CC remains unclear. Transcriptomic and clinical data of CC patients were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas. Nonnegative matrix factorization classified patients into molecular subtypes based on nucleotide metabolism-related genes and compared their survival, immune infiltration, somatic mutations, and drug sensitivity. Mfuzz soft clustering identified subtype-associated expression patterns. Gene set variation analysis scoring, differential expression analysis, and Gene Ontology/Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment of differentially expressed genes were then performed. Prognostic models were constructed using multiple machine learning algorithms, and the model with the highest concordance index (C-index) was selected. Patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups and assessed using multivariate Cox regression, Kaplan-Meier, and time-dependent receiver operating characteristic analyses. Immune checkpoint inhibitor response was predicted using the tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion algorithm, and molecular docking was performed between core genes and candidate compounds. Nonnegative matrix factorization revealed 5 subtypes with distinct outcomes: cluster 2 showed the worst prognosis, whereas clusters 3 and 4 had favorable survival. TTN, KMT2C, HUWE1, and PIK3CA were frequently mutated across subtypes. B cells, regulatory T cells, CD8+ T cells, and M2 macrophages were enriched in clusters 3 and 4. VX-680, CIL70, and BRD-K01737880 exhibited significantly lower IC50 values in the poor-prognosis group. Seven key genes (SERPINE1, CAV1, SOD2, SLC16A1, XDH, CYP27B1, and NAGS) were identified by Mfuzz clustering. Forty-two differentially expressed genes between the high- and low-score groups were predominantly enriched in xenobiotic response, nutrient sensing, small-molecule catabolism, inflammatory response, tumor necrosis factor signaling, apoptosis, and hypoxia. The generalized boosted regression model achieved the highest C-index, with 1-, 3-, and 5-year area under the curves of 0.62, 0.67, and 0.61, indicating modest discrimination. Tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion analysis indicated reduced immune checkpoint inhibitor responsiveness in the high-risk group. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding between core genes and candidate compounds, providing hypotheses for experimental validation. This study delineates the associations of nucleotide metabolism-related genes with molecular classification and prognosis in CC and identifies potential biomarkers, candidate therapeutic agents, and a prognostic model providing complementary assessment value.
records.authors: Li F, Bao C, Liu Y, Liu B, Zhai F.

records.title: Integrated Multi-Omics Profiling of Thymoma Identifies Subtype-Specific Remodeling and Myasthenia Gravis-Associated Targets.
records.abstract: Thymoma is a rare thymic epithelial tumor strongly associated with myasthenia gravis (MG), yet the tumor intrinsic molecular states underlying this link remain unclear. Here, we profiled paired thymoma and distant nontumorous thymic tissues using untargeted metabolomics, lipidomics, and label-free quantitative proteomics, integrating these layers with MG status, clinicopathologic data, immunohistochemistry, and external transcriptomic validation from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohort. Thymomas exhibited a reproducible metabolic and lipidomic signature characterized by coordinated alterations in amino acid and nucleotide metabolism alongside structured changes in lipid subclasses that support membrane remodeling. Proteomic profiling distinguished tumors from distant nontumorous thymic tissue and identified three exploratory proteomic groups with distinct pathway patterns tightly coupled to lipid metabolic shifts. Integrated analyses identified HMGCS1 and SCP2 as subtype-enriched, lipid-linked hubs and uncovered an MG-associated molecular module comprising creatine, MePC(37:4), ACP5, AP1S1, NECTIN4, and fatty acid pathways. AP1S1 showed an independent association with the overall survival in the TCGA thymoma cohort. A derived 13-lipid panel showed high discrimination in an internal evaluation, supporting its potential as a candidate signature for further validation. This tissue-based multi-omics study systematically maps coordinated molecular remodeling in thymoma, highlighting HMGCS1, SCP2, and AP1S1 as prioritized candidates for future mechanistic and translational research.
records.authors: Sun Y, Mao J, Sun X, Cao W, Liu J, Zhang G, Xu X, Wang R, Huo W, Zuo J.

records.title: Bison grazing and prairie fire shape soil microbial community diversity and assembly.
records.abstract: Soil microbes mediate ecosystem function in grasslands, but the impacts of megaherbivore grazing and fire on microbial community assembly are poorly understood, despite widespread changes in these drivers following bison extermination and fire suppression across North America in the 19th century. To better understand how grazing and fire influence microbial metacommunity assembly processes such as dispersal and environmental filtering, we analyzed five years of soil microbial community and soil chemistry data from a long-term, landscape-scale grazing and fire frequency field experiment. Bison grazing reduced soil microbial alpha diversity, while both drivers altered microbial composition. Grazing and fire interactively increased microbial community dissimilarity over distance, with the strongest distance-dissimilarity patterns in grazed, 20-year burn interval treatments, suggesting complex controls over microbial community assembly across large spatial scales. Increases in soil nitrogen and pH as a result of bison reintroduction, along with significant relationships between these factors and microbial composition, highlight environmental filtering as an important assembly process. Temporal patterns showed that grazing and fire effects on microbial composition did not covary with interannual differences in precipitation, but instead with soil environment differences, pointing again to the influence of the abiotic habitat on microbial community assembly. However, geographic distance and the soil environment independently influenced microbial composition, suggesting fire and grazing drive community assembly by influencing both local-scale environmental filtering and regional-scale dispersal processes. Notably, because bison grazing increases plant diversity at this experimental site while decreasing soil microbial diversity, our study reinforces how microbial communities can respond to the same drivers as plant communities, but with different patterns that reflect common ecological mechanisms operating at smaller spatial scales. Overall, this study shows that grazing and fire can shape soil microbiomes through multiple mechanisms, suggesting that soil microbial communities across the Great Plains shifted dramatically following bison extermination and fire suppression.

records.title: Cyanobacteria-Composite Biocrusts for Potential Source Regulation of Heavy Metal Migration From Tailings.
records.abstract: Heavy metals from copper tailings can be released into water bodies through weathering and rainfall, threatening regional water quality. Bioremediation is sustainable, but single microbial treatments often show poor adaptability and unstable performance. This 150-day microcosm experiment compared combined cyanobacteria plus nitrogen-fixing bacteria, each alone, and a control on Dexing copper tailings (China). The combined treatment significantly improved biocrust development and physicochemical properties, including crust thickness, chlorophyll, organic carbon, nitrogen, moisture, and available phosphorus. For metal stabilization, Cd, As, and Cu showed increased surface-layer concentrations due to biocrust enrichment, whereas Zn and Mn exhibited slower declines in surface concentrations relative to the control, suggesting potential retardation of downward leaching. Microbial analysis revealed Pseudomonadota (formerly Proteobacteria) as the dominant phylum under combined treatment, with Arenimonas, Gemmatimonas, and Hydrogenophaga continuously enriched, driving carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus accumulation in the tailings. Mantel tests identified heavy metals and nutrients as key community drivers. This study reveals synergistic mechanisms for reducing the potential for heavy metal mobilization from copper tailings into aquatic environments.

records.title: Comparative transcriptome analysis reveals candidate genes and defence pathways associated with resistance to potato cyst nematodes in potato (Solanum tuberosum).
records.abstract: Globodera rostochiensis and Globodera pallida are two nematode species responsible for are potato cyst nematode (PCN) that significantly reduce potato (Solanum tuberosum) productivity worldwide. To elucidate the molecular basis of PCN resistance, we compared transcriptomic responses of the highly resistant potato breeding clone SM/11-120 with the susceptible cultivar Kufri Jyoti following simultaneous infection with both PCN species. Nematode penetration assays showed that SM/11-120 completely restricted nematode invasion up to 7 days post-inoculation (dpi), whereas Kufri Jyoti was susceptible to nematode penetration within 24 h post-inoculation (hpi) and supported juvenile development at 72 hpi and 7 dpi. RNA-sequencing (RNA-Seq) generated 18-27 million high-quality paired-end reads per library, of which 51.6-68.3% mapped uniquely to the potato reference genome. Comparative transcriptome analysis identified 724, 795, 694, and 899 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between SM/11-120 and Kufri Jyoti at 0 hpi, 24 hpi, 72 hpi, and 7 dpi, respectively. The resistant genotype exhibited enhanced expression of genes involved in immune signalling (NRC1, NBS-LRR), transcriptional regulation (WRKY, MYB), calcium signalling, pathogenesis-related proteins (PR1), hormone and defence metabolism (ACO1, geraniol 10-hydroxylase), and cell wall reinforcement (HRGP, XTH3, pectinesterase, β-expansin). Gene Ontology analysis revealed stronger enrichment of stress response, biological regulation, nitrogen compound metabolism, and response to biotic stimulus in SM/11-120 than in Kufri Jyoti. Expression patterns of selected defence-related genes were validated by quantitative reverse transcription (qRT)-PCR, confirming their rapid and sustained induction in the resistant genotype.

records.title: A VIPR that wraps: A triplex biochemistry for next-gen biotechnology.
records.abstract: A putative ancestor to CRISPR systems, VIPR, was recently discovered.1,2 VIPR adopts a distinct non-contiguous code for PAM-free RNA-guided DNA recognition and is ultracompact and reprogrammable, making it a promising candidate for various genome-manipulation applications. Many open questions remain and their answers will foster exciting opportunities for next-generation biotechnology.

records.title: The small protein PhrS-P, encoded by the dual-function small RNA PhrS, augments fitness of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the presence of aminoglycosides.
records.abstract: PhrS (Pseudomonas Hfq-binding RNA S) is a dual-function small RNA of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The base-pairing small regulatory RNA PhrS-R positively regulates pyocyanin biosynthesis. PhrS-R stimulates the production of the Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) by indirectly activating the translation of pqsR mRNA, encoding the quorum sensing regulator PqsR (MvfR), and by inhibiting the synthesis of the anthranilate degradation regulator AntR. Furthermore, PhrS-R was shown to promote biofilm formation, swarming motility and CRISPR-Cas immunity. In addition, PhrS encodes a 37 amino acid long and conserved small protein (PhrS-P), the function of which remained unknown. Here, we provide evidence that PhrS-P is an inner membrane protein which does not contribute to the known physiological roles of its RNA counterpart. RNA-Seq-based transcriptome analyses revealed that multiple aminoglycoside resistance genes, including those of the AmgR regulon, are differentially expressed depending on PhrS-P. AmgR is the response regulator of the AmgRS two-component system (TCS), which affects aminoglycoside and zinc resistance in P. aeruginosa. A PhrS-P-deficient mutant strain exhibited reduced fitness when exposed to sub-inhibitory concentrations of the aminoglycosides tobramycin and amikacin as well as zinc. Based on our findings, we present a working model wherein PhrS-P positively regulates the AmgRS TCS activity through an unknown mechanism, leading to increased bacterial fitness in the presence of aminoglycosides.
records.authors: Lilić B, Cianciulli Sesso A, Berghoff B, Moll I, Sonnleitner E, Bläsi U.

records.title: Human Pegivirus Type 1 Coinfections: Epidemiology, Heterogeneity and Clinical Implications.
records.abstract: This narrative review explores the complex landscape of coinfections involving Human Pegivirus Type 1 (HPgV), a member of the Hepaciviridae family previously known as GB virus type C or hepatitis G virus. Structurally similar to hepatitis C virus (HCV), HPgV is lymphotropic and while viraemia in healthy donors is asymptomatic, it has been associated with the onset of several non-Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes. We begin with an overview of HPgV's genomic features, classification, transmission routes and natural history, including spontaneous clearance and post-infection anti-E2 antibody development. As of 03 February 2026, a PubMed search yielded 346 relevant studies from which data were synthesized, reporting HPgV coinfection across human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), HCV, hepatitis B virus and other viral diseases - highlighting genotype distributions, geographic variability and population-specific patterns. In summary, HPgV shows a reproducible signal in HIV coinfections, suggesting potential therapeutic benefits, while its impact on chronic hepatitis, acute infections and lymphoma risk remains preliminary and requires further investigation. This review highlights the need for rigorous prospective studies with standardized protocols to clarify HPgV's true impact on human health and its potential for therapeutic application.
records.authors: Garand M, Zhang CC, Guo G, Zhong T, Stapleton JT, Eghtesady P.
