records.title: The assembly pathway for human papillomavirus L1 capsid protein is encoded in electrostatic interactions.
records.abstract: Human papillomavirus L1 protein spontaneously folds and assembles into 60 nm virus-like particles (VLP), with T = 7d icosahedral symmetry at high salt concentrations but not in low salt. Rapid increase from low to high salt during the assembly process gives poor-quality VLPs, while slowly increasing salt, over as many as 48 h, gives rise to high-quality VLPs. Insight into this behavior is drawn from a computational model based on the cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the human papillomavirus Type 16 VLP. Electrostatic potential energy barriers were calculated using the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann equation. After initial, rapid oligomerization of monomers into symmetrical pentamers (capsomeres), these units form pairwise interactions in energetic order, lowest barrier first. But at high salt concentrations, the energetic barriers are more or less equal and irregular particles form, both in simulation and in experiments. The interaction interfaces were modified by mutation to favor the smaller, 30 nm T = 1 icosahedral symmetry and disfavor T = 7d symmetry. The results were smaller particles. By carefully controlling ionic strength, and/or by mutating interface residues by design, it is possible to make high quality, highly immunogenic VLPs directly from unpurified bacterial lysate, without requiring the use of a disassembly/reassembly step.
records.journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
records.authors: Yuan X, Nand KN, Patel JC, Jin A, Bystroff C.

records.title: Sources, Transmission, and Control of Salmonella in Vertically Integrated Broiler Chicken Production: Farm, Hatchery, and Processing Plant.
records.abstract: Salmonella remains one of the most important foodborne pathogens associated with poultry products, despite substantial progress in processing hygiene and antimicrobial interventions. This review critically examines the sources, transmission routes, and control strategies for Salmonella in vertically integrated broiler production systems. Attention is given to contamination originating from breeder flocks, hatcheries, feed, water, litter, grow-out farms, transport, processing environments, and finished products. Preharvest interventions, including biosecurity, breeder and hatchery control, vaccination, litter and water management, feed hygiene, probiotics, prebiotics, organic acids, essential oils, bacteriophages, and bacteriocins, are evaluated according to mechanism, evidence strength, and commercial relevance. Postharvest interventions, including scalding, picking, evisceration control, chilling, peroxyacetic acid application, carcass rinses, post-chill treatments, and finished-product verification, are reviewed in relation to microbial reduction and process control. The review also discusses quantitative bio-mapping, surveillance design, whole-genome sequencing, predictive modeling, and quantitative microbial risk assessment as tools for identifying contamination hotspots, persistent strains, and high-risk control points. Overall, effective Salmonella control requires coordinated preharvest and postharvest strategies supported by routine verification, stronger flock-to-product traceability, and field validation of interventions under commercial conditions.
records.journal: Comprehensive reviews in food science and food safety
records.authors: Subedi D, Mallavarapu B, Patil P, Niraula A, Kandel M, Kumar S, Singh AK.

records.title: Non-Canonical Function of ORC1: Regulating Notch-VEGFR2-Mediated Angiogenesis in Melanoma Progression.
records.abstract: Melanoma is an aggressive skin cancer characterized by high metastatic potential and substantial genetic heterogeneity. Although genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified numerous susceptibility loci, the functional roles of risk variants, most of which reside in non-coding regions, remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify genetic susceptibility genes involved in melanoma progression and investigate their non-canonical roles in the tumor microenvironment. GWAS summary statistics from the GWAS Catalog, FinnGen, and UK Biobank were integrated using MAGMA and FUSION to prioritize candidate genes, which were subsequently evaluated using TCGA-SKCM transcriptomic and survival data. ORC1 emerged as a key susceptibility gene that was significantly upregulated in metastatic melanoma and associated with poor overall survival. Bioinformatic analyses further showed that ORC1 expression was positively correlated with Notch signaling activity and alterations in the immune microenvironment. The functional effects of ORC1 were examined using in vitro co-culture systems in which human umbilical vein endothelial cells were exposed to melanoma-derived conditioned medium. ORC1 overexpression in melanoma cells promoted endothelial prol iferation, migration, tube formation, and vascular permeability in a paracrine manner. Dual-luciferase reporter assays, quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction, and Western blotting indicated that ORC1 was associated with enhanced NOTCH1 promoter-reporter activity, activation of Notch-related signaling, and induction of downstream angiogenic programs. In xenograft models, ORC1 overexpression was associated with increased tumor growth and microvascular density, whereas pharmacological inhibition of Notch pathway activity with the γ-secretase inhibitor DAPT attenuated ORC1-overexpression-associated tumor growth and vascular changes. Collectively, these findings identify a non-canonical pro-angiogenic role for ORC1 in melanoma progression that is mediated, at least in part, through Notch-VEGFR2 signaling. The ORC1-Notch-VEGFR2 axis may therefore represent a potential therapeutic target for modulating the melanoma microenvironment and limiting disease progression.

records.title: Genetic analysis of bone morphometry and ivory vertebrae in threespine stickleback.
records.abstract: Previous genetic studies of skeletal variation in threespine stickleback fish (Gasterosteus aculeatus) have focused primarily on striking morphological differences. Here, we examine the largely unexplored genetic architecture of internal bone microstructural variation between marine and freshwater stickleback. Micro-computed tomography X-ray analysis revealed differences in the porosity, bone thickness, and bone volume fraction within armor plates and vertebrae from a marine and freshwater stickleback. Quantitative trait locus mapping in F2 progeny from a marine × freshwater stickleback cross identified a significant locus on chromosome 4 influencing multiple aspects of armor plate internal microstructure. This locus overlaps the well-characterized Eda region previously known to control armor plate number and size. Co-mapping of bone microstructure could be due to pleiotropic effects of Eda on multiple aspects of plate development or to changes in closely linked genes including Itm2a, which also plays a role in bone formation. Most bone microstructure traits in vertebrae showed weak or no genetic signal, consistent with a polygenic architecture. However, we identified a highly significant locus on chromosome 17 that is strongly associated with abnormally thickened "ivory vertebrae" that occurred in 8.4% of F2 offspring. This phenotype resembles Paget's disease in humans, and the major locus region contains Tnfrsf1b, the stickleback ortholog of a human Paget's disease susceptibility gene TNFRSF11A. Together, our findings identify genetic loci underlying natural variation in bone microstructure in wild fish and reveal a candidate gene associated with a disease-like skeletal phenotype, highlighting stickleback as a model for studying both evolutionary and pathological bone biology.
records.authors: Behrens VC, Lee D, Wucherpfennig JI, Kingsley DM.

records.title: Drug resistance reversal: an overview of real world success stories.
records.abstract: This perspective provides an overview of what we know from real-world data on reversal of drug resistance evolution. An important question for those who study drug resistance is whether it is possible to reverse the evolution of resistance, for example by halting the use of specific drugs for a patient or even a community or country. Evidence for successful reversal of resistance levels is spread out in many different subfields of infectious disease. I use examples from P. falciparum malaria, several bacterial species including E. coli, M. tuberculosis, and S. aureus, and the viral pathogen HIV, to show that it is possible to reverse the evolution of resistance.
records.authors: Pennings PS.

records.title: Ancient truncated FtsZ paralogs likely tune cell division in Hyphomicrobiales.
records.abstract: Bacterial cell division is a well-conserved, tightly regulated process that allows the separation of 2 viable daughter cells. In most bacteria, the proteins that drive division, termed the divisome, are recruited to mid-cell by FtsZ after it polymerizes to form the Z-ring. Interestingly, FtsZ has undergone several independent duplication events across the bacterial kingdom. In this work, we searched for FtsZ GTPase protein sequences within Alphaproteobacterial genomes and observed numerous ftsZ duplications in the order Hyphomicrobiales. Hidden Markov Modeling (HMM) supported the maintenance of 2 distinct lineages of FtsZ GTPase duplications among 3 families. The Nitrobacteraceae duplication, occurring in only the genus Bradyrhizobium, exhibits a different substitution pattern from that shared by the Phyllobacteriaceae and Rhizobiaceae families. Within the Rhizobiaceae lineage, Agrobacterium tumefaciens contains 3 paralogs of FtsZ including the essential FtsZAT and paralogs FtsZ1 and FtsZ3. We show that FtsZ1, but not FtsZ3, inhibits cell division when expressed continuously. A hyperactive allele of ftsW partially protected against continuous expression of ftsZ1, suggesting that FtsZ1 may function to negatively regulate septal peptidoglycan biosynthesis during cell division. Overall, these observations suggest that maintenance of FtsZ paralogs in some bacteria may help control the division process.
records.authors: Aubry B, Randich AM, Hudson B, Horton E, Brown PJB.

records.title: Exploring the Mechanism of Zhigancao Decoction in the Treatment of Chronic Heart Failure via Modulation of Oxidative Stress.
records.abstract: BackgroundZhigancao decoction has shown therapeutic potential in the management of chronic heart failure (CHF); however, the molecular mechanisms underlying its pharmacological effects remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to investigate its potential mechanisms, with a particular focus on oxidative stress-related pathways.MethodsThe chemical profile of Zhigancao decoction was characterized by LC-MS/MS, and putative targets were predicted using SwissTargetPrediction. A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was established using the STRING database and Cytoscape software, followed by Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses. Differentially expressed genes from two GEO datasets (GSE9128 and GSE84796) were integrated with reactive oxygen species (ROS)-related genes to identify candidate targets. Network pharmacology and molecular docking were subsequently performed to investigate compound-target interactions.ResultsA total of 66 chemical constituents and 818 putative targets were characterized and collected, respectively. Among these targets, MMP9 emerged as a central candidate associated with the therapeutic effects of Zhigancao decoction. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses demonstrated that the core targets were significantly enriched in oxidative stress-related pathways, inflammatory signaling cascades, and cell fate regulatory pathways. Computational deconvolution of bulk transcriptomic data suggested marked alterations in the estimated immune cell composition of the CHF microenvironment. Network pharmacology analysis further indicated that multiple chemical constituents of Zhigancao decoction converge on MMP9 and its associated pathways. Molecular docking analysis demonstrated favorable binding affinities between 10 representative compounds and MMP9, with binding energies below -7.0 kcal/mol.ConclusionsIn silico predictions suggest that Zhigancao decoction may exert potential therapeutic effects against CHF through computationally predicted targeting of MMP9 and associated oxidative stress- and immune-related pathways. These computational findings provide a theoretical foundation for future experimental investigations into the mechanisms of Zhigancao decoction in CHF, though clinical application would require confirmation through rigorous in vivo and clinical studies.

records.title: STRATUM-structured framework for reporting, assessment, and translational utility of metagenomics.
records.abstract: BackgroundMetagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) enables broad, untargeted detection of pathogens and microbial signals across complex sample types. However, the diversity of operational contexts, from regulatory enforcement to exploratory discovery, challenges the defining of analytical or interpretive standards appropriate across all applications. Variability in laboratory practices, bioinformatic methods, and reporting conventions continues to limit consistency and decision-maker confidence in mNGS results.ObjectivesWe introduce Structured Framework for Reporting, Assessment, and Translational Utility of Metagenomics (STRATUM), a use-case-stratified framework that aligns QA, metadata reporting, and interpretive standards with the consequence and intended use of metagenomic sequencing outputs.MethodsSTRATUM is organized around five representative biosurveillance use cases spanning public health, food safety, environmental monitoring, synthetic biology detection, and national security. A three-tier interpretive model calibrates analytical rigor, validation expectations, and reporting requirements to decision consequence; from high-consequence regulatory and clinical determinations (Tier 1), through operational surveillance (Tier 2), to exploratory and hypothesis-generating contexts (Tier 3).ResultsThe framework provides graduated guidance across key domains including sample preparation, sequencing design, controls and contamination governance, reference database curation, bioinformatics reproducibility, and multi-factor signal validation. Cross-cutting principles include explicit documentation of evidentiary bases, transparency in database and pipeline provenance, and defined escalation pathways when results transition between interpretive tiers.ConclusionRealizing the operational potential of mNGS requires evidentiary standards responsive to decision context rather than fixed across applications. STRATUM offers a consequence-tiered model for quality and reporting in applied metagenomics, supporting reproducible, transparent, and defensible sequencing-based surveillance across public health and biodefense domains.HighlightsIntroduction of STRATUM, a consequence-tiered evidentiary framework for applied metagenomics. Structured calibration of analytical rigor and reporting standards to decision context. Cross-use-case guidance spanning surveillance, regulatory, and national security applications.

records.title: Sex-specific associations of the plasma proteome with incident coronary artery disease.
records.abstract: AimsThe aetiology of coronary artery disease (CAD) appears different for men and women, yet insights into underlying sex-specific biological mechanisms are limited. We integrated genomic and proteomic analyses to investigate sex-specific associations of the plasma proteome with CAD.Methods and resultsIn 40 829 UK Biobank participants (free-of-CAD, baseline 365 days thereafter; 55% women; mean age 56.9 ± 8.1 years), we examined associations between 2922 plasma proteins and incident CAD over a median follow-up of 13.7 years (IQR 13.1-14.4) using multivariable-adjusted Cox proportional hazards models. Sex-specific analyses identified 440 female exclusive and 32 male exclusive proteins associated with incident CAD (FDR-corrected P ConclusionWe identified sex-specific associations of proteins and biological pathways with incident CAD. Whereas the majority of proteins had consistent associations in both men and women, our findings suggest a degree of sex-specific pathogenesis with evidence for potential causality, opening new alleys for tailored prevention strategies and clinical cardiovascular risk management.

records.title: The serine protease homolog Skanda modulates Toll-phenoloxidase-mediated immunity in Drosophila.
records.abstract: Extracellular serine protease (SP) cascades are central regulators of insect innate immunity. These cascades are negatively controlled by serine protease inhibitors (serpins) and fine-tuned by serine protease homologs (SPHs), which resemble SPs but lack catalytic activity. In Drosophila, a key SP cascade-the Toll-phenoloxidase (Toll-PO) pathway-governs both the melanization response and Toll-dependent antimicrobial peptide production. This cascade is triggered by secreted pattern-recognition receptors or microbial proteases and converges on 2 clip-domain SPs, Persephone and Hayan, which activate the Toll ligand Spätzle via the Spätzle-Processing Enzyme (SPE) and process prophenoloxidases. Here, we characterize the SPH Skanda and uncover its role in the Toll-PO cascade. skanda is genomically clustered with hayan and persephone and is transcriptionally induced upon infection. Skanda is unusual among SPHs, containing a long serine/threonine-rich region, 2 clip domains, and atypical disulfide bonds. Skanda is unstable and subject to cleavage by Grass. Functional assays show that Skanda dampens activation of Hayan, and to a lesser extent Persephone, within the Toll-PO cascade. Notably, skanda-deficient flies are highly susceptible to Staphylococcus aureus despite displaying normal Toll signaling and cuticular melanization. Moreover, compound mutants lacking 2 members of the hayan-psh-skanda cluster reveal a hidden contribution of Skanda to Toll activation in the absence of Persephone. Together, our results identify Skanda as a modulatory SPH that fine-tunes Toll pathway activity in concert with Persephone and Hayan.

records.title: Molecular profiling and disease tracking of posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders using cell-free DNA.
records.abstract: AbstractPosttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) is a life-threatening complication of hematopoietic stem cell or solid organ transplantation. Current prognostic tools for PTLD lack sufficient precision in predicting treatment response. This prospective feasibility study evaluates circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for risk stratification and treatment monitoring in PTLD. Plasma samples (n = 86) from 27 patients (13 positive for Epstein-Barr virus [EBV] positive and 14 EBV negative) were analyzed using targeted 115-gene sequencing and low-coverage whole-genome sequencing at diagnosis, after rituximab treatment and/or chemotherapy, and at end of treatment (EOT). At baseline, somatic single-nucleotide variants were detected in all patients. Multinucleotide variants were mostly detected in the B-cell lymphoma 6 superenhancer hypermutation region, especially in EBV-negative patients. Copy number variants were detected in 13 of 27 patients. An elevated ctDNA level at baseline indicated a poor outcome of rituximab monotherapy, and an undetectable ctDNA level at interim was correlated with better response. Seven patients showed completely undetectable ctDNA levels, whereas positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET/CT) scan indicated active disease at interim; all 7 patients reached complete metabolic response by EOT. We demonstrate that ctDNA could potentially be used for prognostication and disease monitoring in PTLD, outperforming PET/CT in 8 patients. This indicates that ctDNA monitoring can complement PET/CT to guide early escalation to chemotherapy in high-risk patients, although larger cohorts are needed to validate these findings. This trial was registered at the Dutch Trial Register as NTR7402.

records.title: TMAO Correlates with Transcriptomic Signatures of Leukocyte Activation and Systemic Inflammation Following Burn Injury.
records.abstract: BackgroundSevere burn injury induces gastrointestinal dysfunction and bacterial dysbiosis, yet the systemic impact of altered bacterial metabolites remains poorly understood. We assessed whether changes in plasma levels of trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a gut-derived metabolite, have a relationship with changes in the whole blood transcriptomic profile following burn injury.MethodsUsing previously harvested plasma from 67 burn patients, we quantified circulatory levels of TMAO via ELISA. To assess TMAO's impact on the blood transcriptome, we applied a linear model to previously published whole blood microarray data from a subset of these patients (n = 22) with paired TMAO measurements.ResultsWhile initial TMAO levels were comparable across small and larger burns, concentrations significantly increased 24-36 h post-admission in patients with >10% total body surface area (TBSA) burns, independent of age or sex. Elevated TMAO positively correlated with both burn size and Baux score. Furthermore, transcriptomic analysis revealed that high TMAO levels were strongly associated with the enrichment of inflammatory and leukocyte activation pathways, despite a lack of association between TMAO levels and imputed fractions of immune cells.ConclusionBurn injury is associated with a delayed, severity-dependent elevation in circulating TMAO. This increase in TMAO correlates with transcriptomic signatures of robust immune activation and systemic inflammation, suggesting that targeting the gut microbiome and its metabolites may offer a novel therapeutic avenue to address post-burn inflammatory complications.

records.title: Whole-Genome HPV Liquid Biopsy for HPV-Associated Cancer Detection and Viral Physical State Classification.
records.abstract: PurposeHuman papillomavirus (HPV)-associated carcinomas (HPV+ cancers) account for 5% of all cancers. Circulating tumor HPV DNA (ctHPVDNA) assays for HPV+ cancer surveillance have limited prognostic utility at the time of cancer diagnosis. Although HPV integration into the host genome is a proven tissue-based biomarker predicting poor clinical outcomes, existing clinically utilized ctHPVDNA assays cannot classify the viral physical state.Experimental designWe previously developed HPV-DeepSeek, a multifeature HPV whole-genome sequencing liquid biopsy with 99% diagnostic accuracy at the time of HPV+ oropharyngeal cancer diagnosis. We tested the diagnostic accuracy of HPV-DeepSeek in a cohort of 235 HPV+ cancers across 9 anatomic sites and used a novel blood-based computational classifier to infer the HPV genome physical state from plasma, termed HPV sequencing-based integration analysis (HPV-SIGNAL), to assess its prognostic potential.ResultsHPV-DeepSeek achieved 99% sensitivity and specificity. In 189 eligible samples, HPV-SIGNAL identified 4 viral physical states: episomal-only (n = 71), episomal-rearranged (n = 52), integrated-mixed (n = 57), and integrated-clonal (n = 9), which were confirmed and further elucidated via 3 orthogonal tissue and blood approaches. Patients harboring integrated viral states in blood exhibited significantly worse age-adjusted and American Joint Committee on Cancer stage-adjusted progression-free survival [PFS; HR, 2.78; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.30-5.99; P = 0.009] and overall survival (OS; HR, 2.95; 95% CI, 1.01-8.61; P = 0.048) compared with patients with episomal states.ConclusionsHPV whole-genome sequencing liquid biopsy has high diagnostic accuracy across HPV+ cancer types and can be used to identify and classify HPV physical states from blood. Patients with integrated viral states detected in blood demonstrated worse PFS and OS, suggesting that blood-based HPV physical state classification could be used as a prognostic tool at the time of cancer diagnosis.

records.title: Deubiquitinase USP-14 regulates intestinal distension-induced immunity via Wnt/β-catenin signaling in C. elegans.
records.abstract: Pathogen infections disrupt multiple host cellular processes, and hosts have consequently evolved mechanisms to detect these perturbations and initiate appropriate immune responses. In Caenorhabditis elegans, gut distension caused by bacterial colonization is known to activate innate immunity, yet the molecular mechanisms linking intestinal distension to immune activation remain poorly understood. Here, we perform a forward genetic screen to identify suppressors of intestinal distension-induced immune activation in C. elegans. This screen identifies a loss-of-function mutation in the gene encoding the deubiquitinase (DUB) USP-14 as a potent suppressor of immune activation triggered by gut distension. We show that usp-14 knockout mutants exhibit increased sensitivity to the bacterial pathogens Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Global transcriptomic profiling further demonstrates that USP-14 modulates innate immune responses induced by intestinal distension. Epistasis analyses establish that USP-14 functions through the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway to regulate these immune responses. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for the conserved DUB USP-14 in host immunity, providing a foundation for future studies investigating how USP-14 modulates immune signaling.
records.authors: Ghosh A, Singh J.

records.title: Differences in genetic diversity between early isolates of yellow fever virus genotypes.
records.abstract: Yellow fever virus (YFV) is the prototypical member of the genus Orthoflavivirus and is responsible for the disease yellow fever. Phylogenetic studies show YFV can be characterized into seven genotypes (East Africa [EA], East and Central Africa [ECA], West Africa I [WAI], West Africa II [WAII], South America I [SAI], South America II [SAII], and Angola [ANG]). We used Next Generation Sequencing to investigate and compare the genetic diversity of the seven genotypes of YFV using early isolated strains of known passage history from a variety of collection years. Genetic diversity varied between the seven genotypes, with the ECA genotype being more diverse than EA and WAI genotypes, but not the WAII genotype. Genotype-specific amino acids (GSaas) were identified that occurred in all viral proteins but varied by genotype, with most being found in the non-structural proteins, which make up the viral replication complex. Interestingly, the fewest GSaas were found in the EA and ECA genotypes despite the ECA genotype having greater genetic diversity than either the EA or WAI genotypes. Overall, based on examination of early strains, we show that genetic diversity and GSaas varied between the seven genotypes of YFV and are not random but likely caused by selection pressure(s) such as different primate and mosquito hosts in different geographic areas. Examination of genetic diversity and GSaas in recent strains will enable genetic diversity to be investigated over time, and those involved in outbreaks may enable a better understanding of how outbreaks develop and help identify interventions to their spread.
records.authors: Lee ME, Hansen CA, Thompson JK, Hao H, Bourne N, Barrett ADT.

records.title: Wavelength-dependent effects of curcumin photodynamic inactivation at low light doses on Pseudomonas aeruginosa quorum sensing, virulence, and healing of infected wounds (405 nm vs. 425 nm).
records.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is a formidable public health threat due to its drug resistance and complex pathogenicity. Curcumin-mediated photodynamic inactivation (PDI) is a potential non-antibiotic treatment strategy. While blue light (e.g., 425 nm) is often used for curcumin PDI, the effects of different wavelengths at low light doses, especially on bacterial virulence, are not well understood. Here, we systematically compared the efficacy of 405 nm and 425 nm light-mediated curcumin PDI against PAO1 at an identical low light dose (12 J/cm2), evaluating bactericidal effects, intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, global gene expression (RNA-seq), regulation of key quorum sensing (QS) genes (lasR, rhlR, pqsA), and subsequent biofilm formation and pyocyanin production. We found that 405 nm-PDI induced higher ROS levels in PAO1 cells than 425 nm-PDI (4.97-fold vs. 2.23-fold increase over control). Transcriptomic analysis identified 190 differentially expressed genes between the 405 nm-PDI and 425 nm-PDI groups, indicating wavelength-associated transcriptional differences involving quorum sensing (QS)- and biofilm-related processes. RT-qPCR analysis further showed lower expression of selected QS-related genes, particularly rhlR and pqsA, following 405 nm-PDI. Consistent with these molecular observations, 405 nm-PDI pretreatment was associated with reduced subsequent biofilm formation (approximately 79% lower mean thickness) and normalized pyocyanin production (approximately 64% lower) relative to the untreated group. Furthermore, in a mouse full-thickness wound infection model, curcumin-mediated photodynamic treatment was associated with greater wound closure, lower IL-6 and TNF-α levels, and favorable histological features, particularly in the 405 nm-PDI group. Our findings indicate that 405 nm light may be more effective for optimizing the anti-virulence efficacy of curcumin PDI against PA at low light doses, warranting further evaluation in infection-related applications.

records.title: Detection and functional evaluation of novel MYF5 and MYF6 polymorphisms in relation to growth-related traits in Awassi and Awassi-Sakiz crossbred sheep.
records.abstract: Growth-related traits in sheep are economically important for meat production and breeding efficiency. Candidate genes involved in skeletal muscle development, such as MYF5 and MYF6, may contribute to phenotypic variation in growth performance; however, their polymorphisms remain insufficiently characterized in Awassi and Awassi-Sakiz crossbred sheep. This study aimed to identify novel polymorphisms in the MYF5 and MYF6 genes and evaluate their associations with growth-related traits in Awassi and Awassi-Sakiz crossbred sheep using genetic and in silico approaches. A total of 400 animals were included, consisting of 200 Awassi sheep and 200 Awassi-Sakiz crossbreds. Growth and morphometric traits were recorded, and polymorphisms in MYF5 and MYF6 were identified using PCR and Sanger sequencing. Genotype and allele frequencies were calculated, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium was tested, and associations between genotypes and growth traits were evaluated. In silico analyses were performed to assess the potential functional effects of the detected variants. Based on Ensembl genome browser database, two novel variants were identified: an intronic MYF5 NC_056056.1:g.116775493G > A polymorphism and a missense MYF6 NC_056056.1:g.116765792G > C polymorphism resulting in an R310T amino acid substitution. Both loci conformed to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in both populations. In Awassi sheep, MYF5 NC_056056.1:g.116775493G > A was significantly associated with live weight (p = 0.038) and chest circumference (p = 0.018), while MYF6 NC_056056.1:g.116765792G > C was significantly associated with live weight (p = 0.034) and chest circumference (p = 0.006). In Awassi-Sakiz crossbred sheep, MYF5 NC_056056.1:g.116775493G > A was significantly associated with live weight (p = 0.031), whereas MYF6 NC_056056.1:g.116765792G > C was significantly associated with body length (p = 0.026). In silico analyses suggested that MYF5 NC_056056.1:g.116775493G > A may affect splicing-related motifs, while the MYF6 R310T substitution may influence protein stability and DNA-binding interactions. The findings suggest that MYF5 and MYF6 are promising candidate loci for selected growth traits in Awassi and Awassi-Sakiz sheep. However, validation in larger independent populations is required before these variants can be recommended for marker-assisted selection.

records.title: Dairy cattle movement networks govern the spread and persistence of H5N1 B3.13 in the United States
records.abstract: Avian influenza virus H5N1 is predominantly found in wild and domestic birds. H5N1 genotype B3.13 was first detected in United States dairy cattle in March 2024 and spread through much of the country during 2024 and 2025, resulting in the largest known H5N1 outbreak in domestic mammals. By analysing viral genomic data jointly with historical cattle movement patterns, we find that live cattle movement is the predominant contributor to H5N1 spatial spread, rather than wild or domestic birds. Using phylogeographic methods we estimate that >40% of interstate viral transmissions occurred before B3.13’s first detection and >70% occurred before interstate dairy cattle movement restrictions were implemented in April 2024. After this implementation, interstate transmission slowed but within-state spread persisted, driven by local cattle network density and movement volume. Our epidemic simulations demonstrate that the connectivity of counties within and around the Texas Panhandle—where the earliest cases were documented—predisposed the region to become an outbreak epicentre. Counterfactual simulations indicate that interstate restrictions needed to have begun 2–3 months earlier in order to limit the epizootic substantively, given the extent of cryptic spread before detection. Network-informed interventions outperformed geographically-defined containment, but response speed (rather than intervention strength) was the limiting factor in our epidemic models, underscoring the need for surveillance systems capable of detecting pathogen emergence before widespread dissemination.

records.title: Natural habitats are reservoirs of  Fusarium  lineages highly pathogenic on  Triticum aestivum
records.abstract: Summary  Fungal plant diseases are a major cause of crop loss worldwide. Understanding the processes driving these diseases is therefore crucial to anticipate and control epidemics while improving crop yield production. Moreover, the new European « Green Deal » aims to reduce the use of pesticides, while, few alternatives are currently available on the market. There is therefore an urgent need to better track and anticipate fungal crop epidemics in the current context of fungicide reduction. In light of this, our study aims to understand  Fusarium spill overs from non-agricultural habitats in order to better characterise potential non-host  Fusarium reservoirs that may be implicated in the emergence of  Fusarium diseases. To address this question, we isolated  Fusarium lineages from natural populations of  Brassica rapa . We characterised their phylogenomic affiliation and found that they display high diversity, with a population structure related to the locality of isolation. By inoculation assays, we identified  Fusarium strains from non-agricultural habitats that were highly aggressive on wheat. In addition, we observed a strong effect of wheat variety on disease development. We monitored the  Fusarium colonisation through a microscopy approach in both wheat and  Brassica plants. We observed that while the fungus is mostly on root surface in  Brassica plants, it spreads inter-cellularly in wheat roots with vascular colonisation in the wheat shoots. Finally, we showed that most aggressive  Fusarium strains were isolated from Brittany, a French region where wheat is vastly cultivated.
records.authors: Mauriat J, Lefebvre B, Bonhomme L, Martinez Y, Le Ru A, Vailleau F, Bartoli C.

records.title: H5N5 virus transmission is driven by repeated cross-Atlantic introductions and transmission among high latitude seabirds
records.abstract: In November 2025, the first global H5N5 infection was reported in a person in Washington State. Previously, these viruses had only been detected in seabirds and shorebirds near the Atlantic Ocean, suggesting potentially distinct ecology from dominant H5N1 strains. Using 354 global H5N5 genomes, we show that H5N5 viruses have been carried by high latitude seabirds and shorebirds across the Atlantic at least 9 times, with introductions more frequent in the fall and spring. We reconstruct a plausible path of cross-continental movement via Arctic or sub-Arctic regions, followed by a year of cryptic circulation prior to human spillover. These data show that H5N5 viruses have undergone far more intercontinental movements than previously recognized, and exhibit host and geographic patterns that are fundamentally distinct from dominant H5N1 lineages. The distinct host ecology, geography, and movement, paired with the capacity to infect a person, suggest that enhanced surveillance may be warranted.

records.title: Defective Viral Genomes Reveal History-dependent Self-regulation of Type I Interferon Dynamics
records.abstract: Type I interferons (IFN) help clear a viral infection, but IFN levels can then decline to reset the antiviral state and avoid innate immune dysregulation. Such dysregulation can occur following infection with highly pathogenic and pandemic RNA viruses, such as H5N1 influenza A viruses or SARS-CoV-2. In spite of the strong innate immune response that these viruses induce, pandemic viruses replicate and spread successfully, suggesting that they can circumvent the effects of IFN. Innate immune activation is triggered when host cells detect viral RNA, especially defective viral genomes (DVGs). A strong IFN response (e.g. to DVGs or a highly immunogenic wild-type infection) must then decline through negative feedback involving the IFN receptor. How DVGs modulate this feedback remains poorly understood. To quantify positive and negative IFN regulation, we first performed in vitro experiments combining different doses of viral RNA and exogenous IFN, and measured subsequent IFN expression. We next developed an in vivo Bayesian computational model that captures the impact of influenza virus DVGs on both positive and negative IFN feedback. Competition between DVGs and virus is also considered. Finally, we calibrated this model on published in vitro and in vivo influenza virus infection data. Our model suggests that the cumulative IFN exposure of a host cell, rather than the instantaneous IFN level, shapes further IFN induction; this gives DVGs a dual role: beyond triggering IFN induction, they can also lower it through negative feedback. Our model further predicts that these effects are important locally, shaping the spatial dynamics of the response, allowing suppression of innate immune responses in neighbouring, uninfected cells. Through this model, we can explain two important biological observations: i) IFN levels can decline while virus and DVG levels continue to rise in tissue culture and mouse infections; and ii) pandemic viruses that produce high levels of immunogenic RNA molecules can successfully replicate through local innate immune suppression. Overall, we propose that heterogeneity within viral populations (including DVGs and other noncanonical viral RNAs) can modulate positive and negative feedback loops and shape infection outcomes. More broadly, our work may support studies into the therapeutic use of these viral RNA populations.

records.title: Structure-resolved fold annotation of the medicinal-leech salivary-EV cargo: a Ly-6/uPAR three-finger scaffold and a structurally dark fraction
records.abstract: Many proteins that medicinal leeches package into salivary extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry no interpretable sequence annotation, so the least-characterised part of a pharmacologically important secretome lacks even a fold assignment. A companion Astral-DIA study of  Hirudinaria manillensis 1 nominated 17 ultra-enriched candidate EV cargo proteins. Here we ask whether structure prediction and structural search can assign folds where sequence methods fail, and which candidates remain unresolved under prespecified criteria. With an offline pipeline (ESMFold, TM-align, Foldseek against AFDB-SwissProt and PDB100, UniRef90 search, protein-to-genome alignment), the candidates separate into intracellular/membrane machinery and a secreted, cysteine-dense fraction of three proteins with no Pfam domain. The predicted structure of the leech Protein-sleepless homolog g21166 supports its assignment to the Ly-6/uPAR three-finger fold (TM 0.58 vs CD59; best significant PDB match Lynx1); no function is inferred. g436 and g20791 returned no match meeting the criterion (alnTM ≥ 0.5, E ≤ 0.05) in either database, g436 even after homolog-informed modelling. Gene structure and splice junctions support a conserved locus for the two-Trypsin-segment model g8114 (catalytic unit not established). A Boltz-2 thrombin pilot did not support target engagement, and a pre-registered nicotinic test was terminated as undecidable. The results yield a structure-informed shortlist for experimental follow-up.

records.title: Parasitism to mutualism shift during a viral infection in Drosophila under thermal stress
records.abstract: Host–parasite interactions exist along a continuum from parasitism to mutualism, yet the environmental drivers governing transitions along this spectrum remain underexplored. Here we show that chronic thermal stress systematically attenuates virulence across multiple natural RNA viruses in  Drosophila melanogaster and shifts persistent Nora virus infection into conditional mutualism, enhancing host lifespan, reproductive output, and behavioral performance without compromising viral persistence. Driven by host immunometabolic reprogramming and aging deceleration rather than viral genomic adaptation, this phenotypic switch demonstrates that thermal stress can invert the sign of biotic interactions. Our findings establish that persistent infections can expand host thermal reaction norms in animals, revealing how climate warming can fundamentally alter selection pressures and host–pathogen coevolutionary trajectories. records.title: Clinical proteomics of glioblastoma: Functional states and the question of plasticity.
records.abstract: Genomic and transcriptomic studies have refined our molecular understanding of glioblastoma (GBM), yet the disease remains incurable, marked by extensive cellular heterogeneity and adaptability. Integrated spatial studies associate cellular programmes, including hypoxia-associated, immune-engaged and stem-like, with tumour niches. Experimental perturbations in selected models support context-dependent changes in malignant-cell state, without establishing general interconversion among all GBM states. These findings support a model shaped by interplay between cell-intrinsic regulatory programmes and the tumour microenvironment. Clinical proteomics is beginning to identify state-associated vulnerabilities and candidate biomarkers relevant to patient stratification and treatment. Defining the mechanisms and limits of GBM plasticity remains a central challenge for the field.
records.journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Proteins and proteomics

records.title: TRAF2 regulates Vibrio harveyi-induced autophagy and inflammatory responses in monocytes/macrophages of spotted sea bass, Lateolabrax maculatus.
records.abstract: Tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 2 (TRAF2) is a vital intracellular adaptor that coordinates multiple innate immune signaling cascades in vertebrates. Although TRAF2 participates in antibacterial immune defense, the functional crosstalk between TRAF2-mediated inflammatory responses and autophagy remains poorly defined in teleost fish. In this study, a TRAF2 homolog, LmTRAF2, was cloned and characterized from spotted sea bass (Lateolabrax maculatus). Tissue expression profiling showed that LmTRAF2 transcripts were widely distributed across tissues, with relatively high transcript levels in the gill and blood. After Vibrio harveyi infection, both LmTRAF2 mRNA and protein levels showed marked temporal fluctuations in major immune-related tissues and head kidney-derived monocytes/macrophages (MO/MΦ). Under bacterial stimulation, siRNA-mediated knockdown of LmTRAF2 in MO/MΦ suppressed the conversion of LmLC3-I to LmLC3-II, lowered the Lmp-P62/LmP62 ratio, and reduced the abundance of autophagic vesicles. Moreover, LmTRAF2 knockdown reduced the transcript levels of selected pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines and impaired the intracellular killing of V. harveyi without affecting phagocytic uptake. Together, these findings suggest that LmTRAF2 acts as an upstream modulator coordinating inflammatory, bactericidal and autophagic programs during bacterial infection. This provides new insight into the innate immune regulatory network in bony fish.
records.authors: Wang YY, Dang YF, Miao L, Chen J.

records.title: Bridging CO<sub>2</sub> electroreduction and microbial chain elongation toward C4-C6 carboxylic acids using formate and ethanol.
records.abstract: High-value conversion of CO2 through staged electrochemical-biological processes remains challenging because direct electrochemical synthesis of long-chain products involves complex reaction pathways and competing reactions. Microbial chain elongation provides an alternative route for upgrading low-carbon intermediates, but suitable bridging substrates are needed to connect upstream CO2 conversion with downstream microbial metabolism. Here, we developed a staged electrochemical-biological platform using formate and ethanol as bridging substrates. A Cu-Ag gas-diffusion electrode integrated with a solid-state electrolyte reactor enabled electrolyte-free co-production of formate and ethanol from CO2. At 300 mA cm-2, the Faradaic efficiencies of formate and ethanol remained above 23 % and 17 %, respectively, over 30 h. A synthetic electrolyte-free formate-ethanol mixture was then used as a defined co-substrate for microbial upgrading. Compared with acetate-ethanol, formate-ethanol was associated with greater butyrate accumulation but lower caproate formation. Microbial community and metagenomic analyses revealed distinct community compositions and genetic potentials related to co-substrate conversion and chain-elongation functions. This study provides evidence that formate-derived carbon is incorporated during microbial chain elongation, linking CO2 electroreduction with C4-C6 carboxylic acid production and offering a potential framework for coupling electrochemical carbon conversion with microbial product upgrading.
records.authors: Tang J, Sun B, Wang Y, Chen H, Zheng W, Lin H, Luo Y, Zeng Z, Chu N, Zeng RJ, Shen R, Jiang Y.

records.title: Nasopharyngeal bacterial carriage in Indonesian children under three years of age in the early post-PCV13 period.
records.abstract: IntroductionData on bacterial carriage following the recent implementation of the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) in Indonesia's national immunization program remain limited. This study described nasopharyngeal carriage in healthy children under three years, focusing on pneumococcal serotypes, antimicrobial susceptibility patterns, genetic lineages, and colonization risk factors.MethodsA community-based cross-sectional study was conducted from November 2023 to September 2024. Nasopharyngeal swabs were collected from 408 healthy children attending 61 integrated community health posts. Bacteria were identified by MALDI-TOF MS; Streptococcus pneumoniae isolates underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing using VITEK® 2 and whole-genome sequencing (WGS).ResultsAmong 408 children, 1,221 bacterial isolates representing 84 species were identified. Overall, 41.4% had completed the three-dose PCV13 schedule. Carriage rates of S. pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Haemophilus influenzae tended to be lower among fully PCV13-vaccinated than PCV13-unvaccinated children, although only H. influenzae differed significantly (p = 0.014). Incomplete routine immunization (excluding PCV13) and younger age were independently associated with pneumococcal carriage. PCV13 serotypes accounted for 51.4% of isolates, with 6B predominating (13.5%). Pneumococcal benzylpenicillin resistance was 6.5%, erythromycin 18.2%; all isolates were resistant to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, and 32.5% were multidrug-resistant.ConclusionThe findings provide an early post-PCV13 baseline and support continued surveillance of serotype replacement and multidrug-resistant pneumococci.

records.title: MANF promotes cell fitness and attenuates bortezomib sensitivity in multiple myeloma.
records.abstract: BackgroundMultiple myeloma (MM) is a clonal plasma cell malignancy in which disease relapse and treatment resistance remain major clinical challenges. Identifying molecular dependencies that support myeloma cell fitness may reveal therapeutic vulnerabilities beyond recurrent genomic alterations. Mesencephalic astrocyte-derived neurotrophic factor (MANF) is an endoplasmic reticulum-resident, stress-responsive protein, but its clinical and biological significance in MM remains poorly defined.MethodsPublicly available DepMap CRISPR dependency data were analyzed to identify candidate MM-preferential dependencies. MANF expression and prognostic associations were examined in the MMRF CoMMpass cohort. Single-cell RNA sequencing and in silico perturbation analyses characterized its cellular distribution and predicted functional associations. MANF knockdown and genetic rescue using an siRNA-resistant MANF construct were performed in RPMI-8226 and OPM-2 cells to assess proliferation, cell-cycle distribution, and bortezomib sensitivity. Transcriptomic profiling characterized gene expression changes following MANF knockdown, while measurements at multiple time points assessed the temporal patterns of IRE1α-XBP1s-associated readouts.ResultsMANF was identified as a candidate MM-preferential dependency. Higher MANF expression was associated with advanced ISS stage and inferior overall survival, with the survival association retained after adjustment for established clinical and cytogenetic risk factors. Single-cell analysis localized MANF expression predominantly to plasma cells, while virtual knockout predicted changes involving ER protein processing, proteasome function, and metabolism. MANF knockdown inhibited proliferation, increased G0/G1 accumulation, and reduced MYC/E2F-associated transcriptional programs and cell-cycle regulatory proteins. Time-course analyses revealed early enhancement followed by later attenuation in selected IRE1α-XBP1s-associated readouts. MANF knockdown also increased bortezomib-induced apoptosis and reduced its IC₅₀. MANF re-expression partially reversed proliferation and cell-cycle phenotypes, restored IRE1α-XBP1s-associated protein abundance, and attenuated bortezomib sensitization.ConclusionThese findings identify MANF as a previously underexplored candidate myeloma-associated dependency that supports proliferative fitness and modulates bortezomib sensitivity in the tested MM models. MANF depletion is associated with dynamic changes in IRE1α-XBP1s-related readouts. These results support further investigation of MANF as a candidate therapeutic vulnerability in MM.
records.authors: Huang C, Yu WJ, Rao YX, Xu P, Ji YF, Wang YX, Hu YJ, Li ZY.

records.title: Agroforestry development drives a progressive shift from physicochemical to microbially mediated organic matter cycling in tropical soils.
records.abstract: Land-use change in tropical soils alters dissolved organic matter (DOM) chemistry and carbon cycling, however, linkages to microbial functions remain unresolved. We tested whether microbial carbon-degradation potential is associated with DOM composition along an Amazonian agroforestry chronosequence (10, 20, and 30 years), using adjacent pasture and primary forest as references. We integrated shotgun metagenomics with high-resolution mass spectrometry to couple carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZymes) profiles to DOM composition. Soil chemistry explained 41.6% of the variability in microbial composition, while land-use type accounted for 28.5% of DOM variability. Seasonality did not affect microbial composition but was a significant source of variation in DOM. Relative to pasture, agroforests showed higher potential for sucrose and α-glucan degradation and a greater abundance of aliphatic DOM, indicating enhanced microbial processing. Older agroforests were enriched in genes targeting lignin and microbial-derived substrates such as peptidoglycan, resembling primary forest, whereas younger agroforests had higher abundances of GH36, GH5, and CE3 genes linked to cellulose and hemicellulose degradation, resembling pasture. Soil pH and available P were marginally associated with microbial-derived compound degradation, while pH, P, and Ca showed a stronger association with plant-derived compound processing. These results suggest that as agroforestry develops, carbon cycling may shift from physicochemical to microbial regulation, while DOM remained related to vegetation inputs and seasonality. Soil management of pH and available P during early establishment could support this transition, but the recovery may take decades.
records.authors: Martins GL, de Freitas AS, Pellegrinetti TA, Alexandre LF, Lange DF, Finck J, Hanada RE, Mendes LW, Gleixner G, Tsai SM.

records.title: Arbitrium crosstalk enables shared signaling among phages.
records.abstract: The arbitrium system has transformed our understanding of phage biology by demonstrating that temperate phages communicate through extracellular peptides to coordinate lysis-lysogeny decisions. Initially considered a highly specific signaling pathway restricted to individual phage lineages, arbitrium communication has now been shown to extend beyond lineage boundaries in some phage systems. Recent studies have shown that non-cognate arbitrium peptides can interact with heterologous receptors, providing evidence of inter-phage crosstalk. Here, we synthesize current knowledge of the molecular basis of arbitrium signaling, the structural determinants of peptide-receptor specificity, and the potential ecological and evolutionary consequences of inter-phage communication. We suggest that arbitrium crosstalk may shape phage ecology by mediating competitive and potentially cooperative interactions within shared signaling environments. We also discuss its potential uses in engineered phage systems, synthetic biology, and microbiome engineering. Collectively, the available evidence broadens the concept of viral communication beyond lineage-specific signaling, while the ecological significance and practical applications of arbitrium crosstalk remain to be established.
records.authors: Lomeli-Ortega CO, Balcázar JL.

records.title: Antimicrobial peptides against bacterial pathogens in aquatic and livestock systems: mechanisms, rational design, and translational barriers.
records.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are being investigated for bacterial-pathogen control in aquatic and livestock systems, but their translational evidence is uneven. This narrative review links membrane disruption, intracellular targeting, biofilm inhibition, and host-directed effects to the experimental systems that support each mechanism. Representative piscidins, defensins, cecropins, bacteriocins, and synthetic peptides are compared by assay endpoint and evidence tier. Target-animal infection studies include both protective and unsuccessful interventions, whereas in vitro activity, toxin-injury mitigation, and mammalian-model protection cannot independently establish veterinary efficacy. AMP-antibiotic interactions include synergy, indifference, and context-dependent antagonism, and resistance or cross-resistance can arise. Translation requires route-specific exposure, relevant host-cell safety assessment, and manufacturing feasibility. Biodegradation may limit environmental persistence while shortening effective exposure. AI tools can prioritize candidates, but their predictions require validation in the intended pathogen, animal species, and administration context.
records.authors: Horng YB, Chen WJ.

records.title: Exploring the relationship among nutrition, gut microbiota and musculoskeletal health in children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy: a cross-sectional study.
records.abstract: AimsThis study was aimed to explore the nutritional risk standards and nutritional support strategies in Chinese children with DMD.MethodsThis cross-sectional study included 217 children with DMD. Nutritional status was determined by measuring body composition and clinical testing indicators. Three-day 24-h diet recalls were used to assess nutrient intake. Metagenomic sequencing was performed to detect gut microbiota.ResultsChildren with obesity or high body fat percentage (BF%) had higher levels of caloric intake and lower levels of bone mineral density (BMD) and osteocalcin. Age increased the risk of low muscle mass (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.053‒2.152). Overweight (95% CI 0.078‒0.658), obesity (95% CI 0.003‒0.139), low BF% (95% CI 0.015‒0.524) and high levels of calories from protein (95% CI 0.001‒0.001) were protective factors for low muscle mass. The GC exposure (95% CI 1.03‒1.53) increased the risk of low BMD, whereas low body fat percentage (95% CI 0.11‒0.71) decreased the risk of low BMD. Gut microbiota was closely associated with the BMD Z-score, body fat percentage (P ConclusionBF% rather than obesity was the risk factor for low muscle mass in DMD. SMI may be a more accurate index for muscle mass assessment than SMM. High level of calories from protein may be benefit to SMI. Treatments targeting gut microbiota may alleviate glucocorticoid-induced low BMD in DMD.

records.title: Simultaneous visual detection of norovirus, rotavirus, and adenovirus using multiplex reverse transcription recombinase polymerase amplification combined with lateral flow strip.
records.abstract: Viral gastroenteritis (VGE) poses a major threat to children's health globally, with human norovirus (NoV), rotavirus (RV), and adenovirus (AdV) as the most common causative agents. In this study, a multiplex reverse transcription recombinase polymerase amplification (mRT-RPA) detection platform combined with a lateral flow strip (LFS) enables the simultaneous detection of the RNA viruses NoV and RV and the DNA virus AdV within a single-tube reaction. The platform employs a dual-labeled primer design: forward primers are labeled with fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC), while reverse primers are conjugated with specific nucleic acid tags (NATs), enabling signal transduction and multiplex recognition via a "bridging" mechanism. The platform provides sample-to-result detection within 40 min without the need for complex instruments, making it well-suited for point-of-care testing (POCT). Using serially diluted plasmid standards, the limits of detection were determined to be 101 copies/µL for NoV and RV, and 102 copies/µL for AdV. Specificity testing demonstrated no cross-reactivity with 11 other common pathogens. In clinical validation using 64 stool samples, the platform showed complete agreement with quantitative PCR (qPCR) for all target pathogens. In conclusion, this platform provides a reliable technical tool for early diagnosis and outbreak control of VGE.
records.authors: Yuan L, Song L, Zhang Y, Fang Z, Ma Z, Jiang R, Shen J.

records.title: The Fecal DNA Metabarcoding and Feeding Photos Reveal Prey of Eden’s Whales (Balaenoptera edeni edeni) in China
records.abstract: A stable population of Eden’s whales (Balaenoptera edeni edeni) inhabits the Beibu Gulf, southern China, but its diet remains poorly understood. We integrated fecal DNA metabarcoding, photographic identification, and fishery-market surveys to investigate prey composition around Weizhou Island, China. Sixteen fecal samples collected between 2021 and 2026 were analyzed using COI, while eight were additionally analyzed using 12S MiFish and 18S V4 markers. The 12S marker detected 41 fish-associated taxa, including small nearshore schooling fishes such as Ilisha, Nematalosa, Thryssa, and Sardinella. Surface and underwater photographs of feeding events supported two candidate prey taxa, with individuals morphologically consistent with Sardinella albella and Alepes djedaba. Comparisons between whale fecal DNA and seawater eDNA showed that several taxa had higher relative representation in fecal libraries than in seawater controls. Fishery-market surveys recorded 19 fish taxa from Weizhou Island and supplementary surveys in Dapeng Bay, among which eight taxa were not detected in the fecal DNA dataset and treated as market-only records of potential prey availability rather than direct molecular evidence of whale consumption. COI and 18S markers also recovered copepods, hydrozoans, bivalves, gelatinous organisms, and microalgae, which were interpreted cautiously as potential co-ingested, environmental, or broader food-web-associated signals rather than necessarily direct prey. Overall, the molecular, photographic, and fishery-based evidence consistently indicated that small nearshore schooling fishes represent the most robust candidate prey group. Spatial analyses using AquaMaps-derived distribution probability grids showed that candidate prey-associated taxa are mainly concentrated in coastal and shelf-associated ecosystems. This study provides the first multi-evidence assessment of prey composition in Eden’s whales in Chinese waters and highlights the value of integrating fecal DNA metabarcoding with field-based visual evidence for studying the diet of coastal baleen whales.
records.authors: Chen B, Lu F, Jia T, Jiang Y, Zhang Y.

records.title: Epitope-guided optimization improves the protective efficacy of NA-based mRNA vaccines against seasonal influenza A(H3N2) virus.
records.abstract: Neuraminidase (NA) is increasingly recognized as a promising target antigen for improving the breadth and durability of influenza vaccines, yet NA-based mRNA vaccines remain comparatively unexplored relative to hemagglutinin-based approaches. Here, we applied a computationally guided NA antigen-design strategy to seasonal H3N2 influenza viruses and investigated whether epitope-guided optimization could improve the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of NA-based mRNA vaccines. NA-D3, an NA antigen designed based on the evolutionary characteristics of circulating H3N2 viruses, was first evaluated in an mRNA vaccine. This vaccine provided partial protection against H3N2 challenge and reduced viral replication in the lungs, although detectable neuraminidase inhibition (NAI) activity was not observed. To further improve NA antigen immunogenicity, predicted B- and T-cell epitopes were incorporated into the antigen design process, resulting in three sequentially optimized NA candidates, F0, F1, and F2. In a subsequent challenge experiment, F1 and F2 conferred complete protection, achieving 100% survival and significantly lower viral RNA levels and infectious viral titers in the lungs compared to controls. The optimized NA mRNA vaccines also induced detectable NAI activity against heterologous H3N2 viruses, albeit at relatively modest levels. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the protective potential of NA-based mRNA vaccination against H3N2 influenza viruses and establish iterative, epitope-guided strategy in NA antigen optimization - integrating computational prediction with experimental validation - as an effective approach for developing broadly protective NA-based mRNA vaccines.

records.title: Genetic characterization and molecular evolution of porcine parvovirus 1 from clinical samples in China, 2022-2024.
records.abstract: Porcine parvovirus 1 (PPV1) is an important viral pathogen that causes reproductive failure in swine globally. To characterize the current genetic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of PPV1 circulating in China, we screened 1,644 tissue specimens submitted for routine diagnostic testing during 2022-2024 using PCR. PPV1 nucleic acid was detected in 81 samples, with a positivity rate of 4.93%. Fourteen PPV1 strains were isolated from these positive samples, and their full-length sequences were acquired. Phylogenetic analysis classified PPV1 into four evolutionary groups designated Groups I-IV, with Group IV predominated among sequences in our dataset. Molecular clock analysis estimated a nucleotide substitution rate of 8.36 × 10-5 per site per year, with the time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) dated to 1891 (95% HPD: 1813-1943). Bayesian skyline plot analysis demonstrated that the effective population size of PPV1 has declined continuously since 2005, suggesting a contraction of viral population diversity in recent decades. Selection pressure analysis detected a small set of positively selected sites across the whole dataset. Notably, Group III harbored substantially more positively selected sites relative to the other three groups, revealing divergent adaptive evolutionary patterns among distinct PPV1 groups. Substantial amino acid sequence variation was also observed across evolutionary groups. In conclusion, this study provides evolutionary data to support future epidemiological surveillance and the development of improved vaccines against PPV1.
records.authors: Liu S, Liu S, Liu N, Shen J, Lei M, Chen Y, Xu X, Cai X.

records.title: [Fifty years of vaccination in Spain: evolution, achievements and challenges for Public Health].
records.abstract: Vaccination has been one of the most effective public health strategies in Spain, evolving from isolated campaigns to the implementation of a common vaccination schedule. Initiated in 1975 with seven basic vaccines, the schedule was progressively consolidated, culminating in the 2018 approval of a unified calendar agreed upon by the Ministry of Health and the autonomous communities. This model has maintained very high childhood vaccination coverage and has contributed to smallpox eradication, the elimination of polio and rubella, and the maintenance of measles elimination for several years. Its success relies on interterritorial governance, evidence-based and ethical decision-making, and robust epidemiological surveillance. Despite these achievements, important challenges remain: coverage gaps between doses and age groups; territorial and organizational variability; incomplete vaccination in part of the adult population; vaccine hesitancy; and the sustainability of the schedule as new interventions are introduced. The recent measles situation also reinforces the need to close immunity gaps and maintain sensitive epidemiological and microbiological surveillance. The current approach promotes lifelong immunization, including adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals. Technologies such as mRNA vaccines and genomic surveillance offer new possibilities. The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the need for strong international coordination and community engagement. Thus, the common vaccination schedule stands as a pillar of healthcare cohesion, and its future depends on political consensus, scientific innovation, and equity.
records.authors: Fagundo-Rivera J, Castillejo-Del Río A, Fernández-León P, Garrido-Bueno M, El Khoury-Moreno L, Gómez-Salgado J.

records.title: Targeting HTLV-1 Tax: Towards a Therapeutic Strategy for HTLV-1- Associated Diseases.
records.abstract: Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is a human retrovirus that belongs to the family Retroviridae and the genus Deltaretrovirus. HTLV-1 infection is linked to acute and chronic illnesses, including adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL), HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP), and other inflammatory disorders. This overview focuses on the molecular biology of HTLV-1, with particular emphasis on viral structure and genome organization, as well as the roles of key viral proteins in replication and pathogenesis. Special attention is given to the viral regulatory proteins Tax and HTLV-1 basic leucine zipper factor (HBZ), which drive cellular transformation, immune dysregulation, viral persistence, and disease progression. This review examines the oncogenic role of the Tax protein and its potential contribution to the immunopathogenesis of HAM/TSP. Furthermore, it summarizes current and novel therapeutic strategies against HTLV-1-associated diseases, focusing on antiretroviral therapy, immunomodulatory approaches, and Tax-targeted therapies. Challenges in clinical translation and limitations of current treatments are also discussed. This review covers most facets of HTLV-1 biology, pathogenesis, and treatment strategies, with the overall message that more studies are warranted for effective targeted therapies and disease management.
records.authors: Roy S, Sanyal S, Dwivedi M, Sanyal S.

records.title: Bacteria-derived particle-stabilized Pickering emulsions reinforce chitosan active films for salmon headspace preservation.
records.abstract: Integrating bioactive delivery with film functionality is important for developing effective non-contact packaging for perishable aquatic products. In this study, chitosan active films were prepared by incorporating emulsions formulated with bacteria-derived particles from ultrasonically disrupted Lactobacillus casei and kiwifruit pectin crude extract. The emulsions, loaded with curcumin and oregano essential oil (OEO), were dispersed as droplets within the chitosan matrix. Structural analyses suggested reduced ordering of chitosan chains following emulsion incorporation. Emulsion incorporation improved film flexibility, increasing the elongation at break from 24.04% to a maximum of 141.56%. The films also served as OEO carriers, exhibiting an initial rapid release followed by a slower stage in ethanolic media. In addition, the composite films exhibited excellent UV-blocking properties and significant antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus under both contact and non-contact conditions. Soil burial further demonstrated substantial mass loss and progressive film disintegration. In a non-contact salmon headspace preservation system, the film with 6% emulsion loading showed the best overall preservation performance, effectively retarding spoilage, maintaining total volatile basic nitrogen below 13 mg/100 g on day 6, and suppressing microbial growth during refrigerated storage. Overall, this work demonstrated an emulsion-based strategy for improving chitosan film functionality and enabling non-contact salmon preservation.
records.authors: Yan X, Guo Y, Zhu Y, Xie Y, Wang K, Liu B, Fu J, Tan M, Su W.

records.title: Isoquercetin Attenuates Graves' Disease-Related Thyroid Epithelial Inflammatory Responses: Exploratory Evidence from Network Pharmacology, Mendelian Randomization, and Cellular Validation.
records.abstract: BackgroundGraves' disease (GD) is initiated by thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor autoantibody signaling, whereas cytokine-mediated inflammation within the thyroid may amplify thyrocyte activation. The microbiota-related metabolites contributing to this inflammatory component remain incompletely defined.MethodsWe integrated reported gut microbiota-metabolite associations with GD-associated genes, constructed protein-protein interaction and enrichment networks, prioritized candidate metabolites, and evaluated predicted docking of isoquercetin (ISO) with inflammatory targets. Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) used MiBioGen microbiota and FinnGen autoimmune hyperthyroidism data. A separate four-group experiment compared control, M22 alone, interferon-γ (IFN-γ) alone, and combined M22/IFN-γ stimulation in Nthy-ori 3-1 thyroid follicular epithelial cells. ISO treatment was then evaluated under combined stimulation; inflammatory transcripts, NF-κB p65 phosphorylation, and cell viability were assessed.ResultsFifty-three shared targets were identified, and the highest-degree PPI nodes included IL6, TNF, AKT1, IL1B, JUN, NFKB1, TP53, and CASP3. The shared targets were enriched in TNF, NF-κB, MAPK, PI3K-Akt, and Th17-related pathways. After chemical-name standardization, ISO had a network degree of 8 and was connected with TNF and IL6; docking indicated predicted molecular compatibility rather than direct binding. Twelve taxa showed nominal IVW associations with GD, but none survived false discovery rate correction. In the four-group experiment, IFN-γ was the dominant stimulus for IL1B, IL6, and TNF expression; the combined M22/IFN-γ group had the highest mean expression, but no interaction term was significant. Under combined stimulation, ISO reduced inflammatory transcripts and the phospho-p65/total p65 ratio without markedly changing total p65.ConclusionThese exploratory, convergent findings identify ISO as a microbiota-related candidate modulator of thyroid epithelial inflammatory responses. They do not establish microbial production, direct target binding, or clinical efficacy, and require further mechanistic and in vivo validation.

records.title: Microbial, Metabolic, and Inflammatory Features Associated with Delayed Diabetic Wound Healing in Mice.
records.abstract: IntroductionDiabetic ulcers are characterized by delayed tissue repair, persistent inflammation, and wound microenvironment remodeling, yet the systemic and local molecular features associated with impaired diabetic wound healing remain incompletely defined.MethodsIn this exploratory pilot study, we profiled gut microbiota (16S rRNA sequencing), wound-tissue metabolites (liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, LC-MS), and local gene expression (reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction, RT-qPCR) in a mouse model of diabetic ulcers. Three biological replicates per group (n = 3 mice/group) were included in each analytical platform.ResultsCompared with non-diabetic wound controls, diabetic mice showed delayed healing alongside altered gut microbial structures, including enrichment of Clostridiales and Mucispirillum and depletion of Lactobacillus. Wound metabolomics tentatively identified candidate metabolic shifts involving molecules such as 16-oxopalmitate and indoleacetaldehyde. Locally, candidate pro-inflammatory genes (Il1b, Tnf, Nos2, Mmp9) were upregulated, whereas candidate repair-associated markers (Arg1, Vegfa) were decreased. Correlation analysis further connected selected diabetes-associated microbial changes with local wound metabolic remodeling, revealing exploratory associations among gut microbial features, wound metabolites, and local inflammatory/repair-related gene expression in delayed diabetic wound healing.DiscussionIn view of very small sample size (n = 3 per group), these findings provide hypothesis-generating preclinical evidence relevant to diabetic wound microenvironment remodeling, and indicates specific microbial, metabolic, and gene-expression targets for larger validation studies.
records.authors: Wei JL, Zhao YN, Liu M.

records.title: Cold Plasma-Mediated Seed Priming: Plant Stress Responses and Potential Ecological Implications.
records.abstract: Cold plasma (CP) is being investigated as a non-thermal seed treatment because studies have reported effects on germination, early seedling growth, plant responses to stress, and seed-borne microorganisms. These effects have been linked to the generation of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS and RNS), changes in seed-surface characteristics, and alterations in physiological and biochemical processes within the plant. However, the response to treatment is not always consistent. It depends on factors such as plant species, plasma source, exposure time, and treatment intensity, while excessive exposure may adversely affect seed performance. Research to date suggests that CP may help improve crop establishment and modify plant responses to biotic and abiotic stresses. However, whether these effects lead to broader ecological benefits remains unclear. Relatively little is known about how CP treatment affects plant-microbe interactions, soil microbial communities, plant community structure, or ecosystem functioning under field conditions. It is also uncertain whether treatment-induced responses persist across generations or involve stress memory and epigenetic regulation. These possibilities require direct experimental evidence rather than inference from short-term physiological responses. This review examines current findings on the effects of CP on seed germination, pathogen suppression, and plant responses to environmental stress. It considers the mechanisms proposed to explain these effects, the variation observed across experimental systems, and the extent to which existing evidence supports the conclusions drawn. Potential ecological implications and unresolved evolutionary questions are also discussed. An important limitation of the current literature is its reliance on laboratory and controlled-environment experiments, alongside a shortage of long-term field studies and multigenerational investigations. As a result, the wider ecological consequences of CP seed treatment cannot yet be established with confidence. Addressing this gap will require more consistent treatment protocols, validation under field conditions, and studies that examine whether physiological and molecular responses are accompanied by measurable changes in plant performance, biological interactions, and ecosystem processes. Such evidence will be essential for determining both the practical value of CP seed treatment and its longer-term environmental implications.

records.title: Arsenite-associated attenuation of daptomycin-induced inhibition in Clostridium butyricum under co-exposure conditions.
records.abstract: The metalloid arsenic may co-occur with antibiotics in anaerobic environments, yet microbial responses to their combined stress remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how arsenite (As(III)) alters the response of Clostridium butyricum CXL-1 using phenotypic, physiological, and transcriptomic analyses. Individually, As(III) and daptomycin inhibited bacterial growth and fermentative metabolism in a dose-dependent manner, with an As(III) IC50 of 120 mg/L and complete growth inhibition at 5 mg/L daptomycin. Under co-exposure, increasing daptomycin concentrations at fixed As(III) progressively inhibited fermentative metabolism, whereas increasing As(III) concentrations at fixed daptomycin increased final biomass despite slower substrate utilization. Relative to daptomycin alone, As(III) co-exposure produced a higher ATP index, lowered reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and the NADH/NAD+ ratio, and reduced lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) leakage. Transcriptomic analysis under co-exposure revealed upregulation of the arsenic resistance operon (ars), mepA_6, and genes for thiamine biosynthesis, sulfur transport, and glutathione biosynthesis, and downregulation of phosphotransferase system and pentose phosphate pathway genes. At the relatively high laboratory As(III) concentrations tested, co-exposure was associated with attenuated daptomycin-induced inhibition, slower carbon utilization, a higher ATP index, improved redox balance, and membrane integrity. This study reveals a previously underexplored influence of arsenic exposure on bacterial responses to antibiotics under anaerobic conditions.
records.authors: Zeng X, Liu R, Chen W, Li X, Li Y, Jin C, Wang S, Li W, Jia Y.
