records.title: Evolution-Informed Viroinformatics Identifies Conserved Immune Targets with Predicted Lower Mutational Vulnerability Across Betacoronaviruses.
records.abstract: The extensive evolutionary diversity and continuous mutational adaptation of betacoronaviruses represent a major challenge to the development of broadly protective countermeasures. This study applied an evolution-informed Viroinformatics framework to systematically identify conserved and immune targets with predicted lower mutational vulnerability across betacoronaviruses. The workflow integrated comparative sequence conservation and phylogenetic analysis with immunoinformatics-based epitope screening, HLA population coverage, mutational escape profiling, structural modeling, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. Conserved cytotoxic T-lymphocyte and helper T-lymphocyte epitopes were prioritized based on immunogenicity, antigenicity, safety, HLA binding potential, evolutionary conservation, and predicted resistance to mutational escape. Combined MHC class I and II analysis predicted a theoretical global population coverage of 99.92%, which requires experimental validation. The resulting 409-amino-acid multiepitope construct was predicted to be antigenic, non-allergenic, and physiochemically stable. Structural validation showed that 99.7% of the residues were located within favored or additionally allowed regions. Molecular docking demonstrated favorable interaction of the vaccine construct with TLR7, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation supported persistence of the predicted vaccine-receptor association. Overall, these findings provide a computational framework for prioritizing evolutionarily conserved immune targets and developing pre-emptive candidate epitopes showing predicted cross-betacoronavirus conservation within the analyzed dataset. Experimental studies evaluating HLA binding, cellular and humoral immunogenicity, recombinant expression, cross-reactivity, and in vivo protection are required to validate the predicted immunological potential and determine whether the proposed construct can provide broad protection against diverse betacoronaviruses.
records.authors: Alshammari J, Alqahtani HA, Alonaizan R, Rahman IU, Alzhrani K, Al-Hoshani N, Alwaili MA, Aziz T, Aziz T.

records.title: Interferon-Induced Protein 6 (IFI6): Biological Functions, Molecular Mechanisms and Pathological Roles in Human Diseases.
records.abstract: Interferon (IFN)-induced protein 6 (IFI6) is an important member of the IFN-stimulated gene (ISG) family. It plays significant roles in anti-apoptosis, immune regulation, maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis, antiviral defense, and tumor progression. At the molecular mechanism level, IFI6 inhibits mitochondrial membrane depolarization, cytochrome c release, and caspase activation. It also regulates the balance between B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2)/Bcl-2 interacting mediator of cell death (Bim), activates the Janus kinase (JAK)/signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase-protein kinase B (PI3K-AKT) pathways, and upregulates the ferroptosis-related proteins solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), thereby enhancing cell survival and proliferation through multiple pathways. In terms of immune regulation, IFI6 is associated with immune cells (such as T/B cells, etc.) and the tumor microenvironment. IFI6 regulates mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and mitochondrial calcium homeostasis, influencing respiratory chain assembly and metabolism. In terms of viral infection, IFI6 may inhibit the replication of multiple viruses (such as hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), SARS-CoV-2, etc.) by inhibiting flavivirus-induced endoplasmic reticulum (ER) invagination, interfering with retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptor signaling pathways, and inhibiting epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) kinase activity. In addition, IFI6 is highly expressed in autoimmune diseases and malignant tumors and is associated with proliferation, metastasis, and poor prognosis. In this review, we aim to highlight IFI6 as a potential key target in disease diagnosis and treatment.

records.title: Dietary BmKn2-7 Supplementation Modulates Intestinal Microbiota and Hepatopancreatic Responses and Enhances Resistance to Vibrio parahaemolyticus in Litopenaeus vannamei.
records.abstract: Background: Global expansion of Litopenaeus vannamei aquaculture has intensified the reliance on antibiotics for disease control, raising concerns about hepatotoxicity, microbiota dysbiosis and antimicrobial resistance. Synthesized scorpion venom-derived antimicrobial peptide BmKn2-7 is a promising alternative, but its efficacy and mechanisms as a dietary additive in shrimp remain unclear. Methods: A 56-day feeding trial was conducted with six diets: a basal diet (FM), four diets supplemented with BmKn2-7 (0.8, 1.6, 2.4 and 3.2 mg/kg), and a florfenicol diet (FL, 3.2 mg/kg). Results: Growth performance was unaffected by any treatment. However, FL group significantly reduced condition factor and hepatosomatic index and markedly increased serum ALT and AST. The A2.4 diet increased whole-body crude lipid contents and significantly elevated serum ACP, AKP, HDL-C, and TG. 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that intestinal microbial diversity indices were numerically highest in the A2.4 group, although pairwise differences were not statistically significant. A2.4 was also associated with reduced Vibrio abundance and enrichment of genera such as Acinetobacter, while FL induced pronounced community shifts. Hepatopancreatic transcriptomics and pathway analysis indicated that A2.4 was associated with shifts in amino acid, organic acid, and carbohydrate metabolism, together with enhanced endoplasmic reticulum protein processing, whereas FL was mainly associated with reduced V-ATPase-related proton transport. Key BmKn2-7 responsive genes were positively correlated with phosphatase activities and lipid parameters, and Hsp90b1 was negatively correlated with ALT and AST. Following V. parahaemolyticus challenge, A2.4 showed the lowest cumulative mortality, significantly outperforming FL and high-dose BmKn2-7. Conclusions: Dietary supplementation with BmKn2-7 at 2.4 mg/kg improves intestinal microbial homeostasis, metabolic and proteostatic functions, and resistance to V. parahaemolyticus. These findings support the further evaluation of BmKn2-7 as a potential feed additive for reducing antibiotic dependence in shrimp aquaculture.

records.title: Grazing Management Regimen Shapes Soil Carbon Stocks and Associated Bacterial Community Composition in a Semi-Arid Rangeland.
records.abstract: Semi-arid rangelands are highly vulnerable to climate change and overgrazing, yet the functional coupling between soil carbon stabilization and microbial recovery remains largely unquantified. This study was carried out in Northern Mexico (24°0'33″ N, 104°42'28″ W, 1990 m.a.s.l.) and evaluated associations between a grazing management gradient comprising continuous grazing (CG), closed non-selective intensive grazing (GE), and open non-selective intensive grazing (SG) on soil carbon stocks and different labile fractions, bacterial community structures, and functional metabolic pathways in semi-arid soils. The results show that SG showed the highest observed organic and inorganic carbon stocks (SOC and SIC stocks, respectively), along with the labile carbon (LC) fraction. Conversely, GE favors the accumulation of stable, non-labile carbon (NLC). Although alpha diversity remained unaffected, grazing management induced differences in beta diversity. Redundancy and LEfSe analyses revealed a strong coupling between carbon fractions and microbial assembly, characterized by the exclusive enrichment of copiotrophic biomarker families (Burkholderiaceae and Sphingobacteriaceae) under SG. Furthermore, predictive functional profiling (PICRUSt2 and ANCOM) showed that pathways such as tRNA charging and nicotinate degradation were enriched under SG and GE, reflecting potential metabolic capacities and inferred microbial adjustments to heterogeneous, excreta-derived nutrient microenvironments during intermediate recovery states. Ultimately, the findings suggest that targeted rotational grazing may contribute to improved soil carbon stocks and microbial community recovery in semi-arid rangelands.

records.title: Genome-Wide Association Study of Body Conformation and Carcass Composition Traits in Landrace Pigs.
records.abstract: Body conformation and carcass composition are economically important traits in pig production, yet their underlying genetic mechanisms remain incompletely characterized. To dissect the genetic bases of body length (BL), body height (BH), backfat thickness (BFT), and lean meat percentage (LMP), we estimated genetic parameters and performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) using 50 K SNP array genotypes from 1527 Landrace pigs. Phenotypic variance decomposition revealed moderate-to-high heritability for all four traits, ranging from 0.23 for BH to 0.43 for BL. Genetic correlation analysis uncovered a strong negative correlation (-0.80 ± 0.05) between BFT and LMP, as well as a moderate positive correlation (0.46 ± 0.03) between BL and BH. Our GWAS identified 14 SNP-trait associations involving 10 unique SNPs and two genomic regions with overlapping association signals. On Sus scrofa chromosome 1 (SSC1), overlapping signals for BFT and LMP occurred near ABL1 and QRFP, whereas signals for body conformation mapped to SSC17 near BMP2, PROKR2, SLC23A2, and PCNA. These genes are positional and biologically plausible candidates, and these candidate markers hold potential for genomic selection to simultaneously improve body size and meat-production performance.

records.title: Genome-Wide Association Mapping of Low-Nitrogen Tolerance in Hexaploid Oat Identifies a Suggestive Candidate Locus near P5CDH Associated with Root Dry Weight.
records.abstract: Background/objectivesOptimizing nitrogen fertilizer efficiency is crucial for sustainable agriculture, but the genetic basis of low-nitrogen (LN) tolerance in oat (Avena sativa L.), an important forage and grain crop, remains poorly characterized.MethodsThis study investigated eleven LN tolerance phenotypes across 103 oat accessions using high-density resequencing markers, mixed-model association mapping (MLM), a FarmCPU sensitivity analysis, and Bayesian genetic architecture inference (BSLMM).ResultsNo locus achieved genome-wide Bonferroni significance, and Bayesian estimates indicated a low-to-moderate model-based PVE (0.10-0.23) with no clearly identified major-effect locus, suggesting that genomic selection represents a plausible future direction for LN tolerance in oat. At a suggestive threshold (p -5), a cross-model intersection nominated a hypothesis-generating locus at 1D:349,799,042 associated with root dry weight. This locus showed haplotype-level phenotypic segregation (Wilcoxon p = 1.36 × 10-5) on the discovery panel and concordant signals between the two models (r = 0.92). The nearest nitrogen-metabolism-related gene, P5CDH (22.7 kb away), encodes Δ1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase, which catalyses the terminal step of proline catabolism, and its wheat ortholog was significantly down-regulated under nitrogen deficiency.ConclusionsThese findings provide a testable hypothesis linking proline catabolism to oat root plasticity under low nitrogen and a framework for validation in larger panels.
records.authors: Ling Y, Wang Z, Yu S, Zhang Z, Yang H, Zhang L.

records.title: Integrative Multi-Omics and Single-Cell Analysis Prioritizes YWHAB Within Ubiquitination-Related Transcriptional Programs in Endometrial Carcinoma.
records.abstract: BackgroundUbiquitination-related transcriptional programs may help characterize epithelial heterogeneity in endometrial carcinoma (EC). We aimed to identify candidates associated with these programs and epithelial plasticity.MethodsWe integrated a 43,613-cell atlas from five endometrioid EC samples and two normal endometrial samples with bulk transcriptomic, genetic-association and protein-expression data. Five scoring methods defined a consensus expression score, with HIGH and LOW quartiles defined within the Epithelial + EMT_like lineage. Differential expression and high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA) identified candidates for exploratory Mendelian randomization (MR) and survival-based prioritization among 541 patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas Uterine Corpus Endometrial Carcinoma (TCGA-UCEC) cohort. Repeated nested cross-validation and cross-model feature support were used to evaluate internal performance and candidate stability. Pseudobulk, independently curated ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) gene sets and scSurv input masking provided sensitivity analyses.ResultsThe lineage-restricted screen identified 444 candidates, including 412 detectable in TCGA. GeneCards and curated Reactome and KEGG UCell scores were positively correlated (ρ = 0.519 and 0.579). YWHAB ranked fourth among 412 genes in the top-10% workflow analysis and fifth in the top-20% sensitivity analysis. Among the 12 nominal MR-associated genes, it had the highest machine-learning priority. Its single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) MR estimate was nominal (odds ratio (OR) = 1.732, p = 0.0488) and did not survive multiple-testing correction. Higher bulk YWHAB expression was associated with poorer overall survival (HR = 2.188, 95% CI 1.559-3.072). Western blotting showed higher YWHAB protein expression in EC than controls (nine versus nine tissues, p = 0.0027), consistent with descriptive Human Protein Atlas (HPA) staining. Single-cell analyses associated YWHAB with RNA processing, proteostasis-related expression and epithelial-state heterogeneity.ConclusionsLineage-restricted discovery and cross-model prioritization identify YWHAB as an exploratory candidate associated with ubiquitination-related transcriptional programs in EC. Protein-expression evidence supports its further investigation, while causal function and clinical prognostic utility require independent validation.
records.authors: Wang J, Zhu H, Li Y, Yang Y, Wang W, Fan W, Zheng R, Xu X, Qin T.

records.title: Tropheryma whipplei Pneumonia with Myelofibrosis: A Rare Actinomycetia Case Report and Literature Review.
records.abstract: Tropheryma whipplei (T. whipplei) is an uncommon pathogen that infects multiple sites, predominantly the gastrointestinal tract. However, pulmonary involvement is uncommon, and its clinical manifestations and imaging features lack specificity, making it prone to misdiagnosis. However, with the development of metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), clinicians have a potent tool at their disposal for detecting T. whipplei infections. We report a case of an elderly woman with a history Myelofibrosis who presented with a dry cough, fever, fatigue and difficulty breathing. Routine microbiological tests were negative; mNGS of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) suggested T. whipplei infection. Following a definitive diagnosis, the patient was treated with a regimen of meropenem in combination with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for 16 days followed by 2 weeks of TMP-SMX maintenance, after which the patient improved and was discharged uneventfully.
records.authors: Liu J, Wang X, Xie P, Dong L, Bai P, Liu Y, Chen G, Hao D.

records.title: A small molecule utilizes both antivirulence and host-directed mechanisms to combat bacterial infection.
records.abstract: BackgroundAntimicrobial resistance is progressively undermining the efficacy of conventional antibiotics, and intracellular infections caused by Salmonella typhimurium (ST) remain difficult to eradicate, underscoring the need for alternative therapeutic strategies.PurposeTo identify natural small molecules possessing both antivirulence and host-directed activities against ST infection, and further characterize their mechanisms of action.MethodsA dual-screening strategy was employed to identify compounds that inhibit both ST invasion and intracellular replication. RNA sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, western blot analysis, β-galactosidase reporter assay, scanning electron microscopy, and flow cytometry were performed to investigate the mode of action of the active compound. A murine enterocolitis model was established to evaluate its therapeutic efficacy.ResultsFerulic acid (FA) emerged as a dual-acting inhibitor. FA suppressed SPI-4 promoter PsiiA activity, reduced SPI-4 transcription and SiiE secretion, and impaired SiiE-dependent adhesion, thereby limiting bacterial invasion. In parallel, FA suppressed macrophage STAT3 phosphorylation and enhanced NRF2 signaling, leading to reduced intracellular ferrous iron and ferroptosis, which in turn restricted intracellular bacterial replication. Furthermore, FA treatment alleviated ST-induced enterocolitis in mice.ConclusionsFA protects against ST infection by attenuating bacterial virulence and modulating host iron homeostasis. These findings support its potential as a combined antivirulence and host-directed therapeutic candidate.
records.journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology

records.title: Population Genomic Analysis in Wild Medaka Populations: Identifying Candidate Loci for Balancing Selection.
records.abstract: Sexual selection, defined as individual differences in reproductive success, can contribute to the maintenance of genetic polymorphisms through pleiotropic trade-offs between life history components. However, the extent to which sexual selection maintains genetic polymorphisms in wild populations remains unclear. Here, we explored genomic signatures of balancing selection and selective sweep in the northern medaka, Oryzias sakaizumii in Japan by performing whole-genome resequencing of wild individuals. In addition, we reevaluated the population genetic structure and admixture of Oryzias latipes and O. sakaizumii across the Japanese archipelago and identified genomic regions largely affected by introgression between the two species using F d statistics to distinguish signatures of balancing selection from patterns potentially caused by introgression. Based on multiple population genetic statistics, we identified 18 candidate genomic regions showing signatures of selection. In particular, a 100-kb region at 6.85-6.95 Mb on chromosome 18 showed high genetic diversity that did not show outlier for the F d statistics, indicating the extent of introgression in this region did not largely differ from the genome-wide average. This pattern suggests that balancing selection maintains genetic polymorphisms of the locus in O. sakaizumii. The overlap with a QTL for female mating behavior and the known molecular function of a gene within this candidate region for balancing selection suggest that sexual selection through female mate choice may contribute to the maintenance of polymorphism at this locus.
records.authors: Fujimoto S, Myosho T, Kobayashi H, Aoyama H, Murase I, Sumarto BKA, Yagi M, Kunishima T, Matsunami M, Kimura R.

records.title: Identification of Immuno-Diagnostic and Therapeutic Markers in Tumors and Inflammatory Diseases Based on Single-Cell and Machine Learning Methods.
records.abstract: BackgroundChemotherapy is the mainstay of systemic treatment for colorectal cancer (CRC), but drug resistance and tumor heterogeneity markedly limit survival. Mitochondrial metabolism is increasingly recognized as a regulator of tumor progression, immune contexture, and therapeutic response. However, the prognostic relevance of mitochondrial metabolism-related transcriptional patterns and their relationships with chemotherapy-response signatures and immune features in CRC remain incompletely understood.MethodsClinical and transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas colorectal cancer cohort (TCGA-CRC) and Gene Expression Omnibus cohorts GSE17537 and GSE104645 were analyzed. A curated set of mitochondrial metabolism-related genes (MMRGs) were used to calculate an MMRG score, whereas genes upregulated in chemotherapy-sensitive cases in GSE104645 were used to derive a drug-sensitivity gene-set score by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA). Weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA), differential expression analysis, univariate Cox regression, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression, and multivariate Cox regression were used to construct a five-gene RiskScore. Prognostic associations were assessed using Kaplan-Meier curves, time-dependent receiver operating characteristic curves, external validation, and subgroup analyses. Immune-cell enrichment and pRRophetic-predicted half-maximal inhibitory concentration values were evaluated, and CD36 was examined using in vitro phenotypic assays.ResultsTumors showed lower MMRG scores than normal tissues, and higher MMRG scores were associated with better overall survival (OS). The drug-sensitivity gene-set score was higher in tumors but was not significantly associated with OS. A five-gene signature (CD36, CPA3, FCRL2, POU2F2, and S100B) generated a RiskScore that separated OS outcomes in the TCGA training, testing, and overall cohorts, as well as GSE17537, although its time-dependent discrimination varied across cohorts and follow-up periods. Similar survival associations were observed within subgroups defined by stage, age, and sex; however, independent or incremental prognostic value was not evaluated. High-risk tumors exhibited altered immune-cell enrichment, and the RiskScore was correlated with pRRophetic-predicted drug IC50 values after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. CD36 expression was higher in SW1116 than in NCM460 cells, and its knockdown inhibited proliferation, migration, and invasion. Mitochondrial function was not directly measured in these experiments.ConclusionThe five-gene RiskScore was associated with OS, immune-cell enrichment, and in silico drug-sensitivity estimates in CRC. It may serve as a candidate tool for prognostic stratification, but its incremental clinical value and treatment-predictive utility require prospective validation. The CD36 knockdown experiments support a tumor-promoting phenotype in SW1116 cells but do not establish dependence on mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming.
records.authors: Tang J, Yuan D, Wu Z, Xie Y, Xu J.

records.title: Molecular control of bacterial immunity.
records.abstract: Phage infection places strong selective pressure on bacteria to mount a rapid immune response to ensure survival. Although recent studies have uncovered a wide diversity of bacterial immune systems, how these systems function under the tight time constraints of phage infection remains poorly understood. Here we summarize structural, biochemical and genetic insights into bacterial immunity, focusing on steps that link infection sensing to activation and effector function. We highlight how conformational change, protein assembly and spatial organization shape immune activation, and how phages employ counter-defense strategies that disrupt these processes.
records.authors: Getz LJ, Fairburn SR, Maxwell KL.

records.title: Community context redirects evolutionary trajectories under stress.
records.abstract: Adaptation to abiotic stress is typically studied in single-species cultures, yet bacteria inhabit and evolve in multispecies communities where neighboring organisms reshape, for example, nutrient availability, redox state, and cellular physiology. We recently demonstrated that interspecies interactions can alter the fitness effects of antibiotic resistance mutations, and we suggest that this reflects a broader principle. Stress-response networks are extensively cross-regulated and draw upon a shared, finite pool of proteomic and energetic resources. Consequently, activation of one pathway constrains others, creating physiological trade-offs. Because microbial interactions routinely perturb the physiological inputs to these networks, they can systematically redirect evolutionary trajectories under abiotic stress. We discuss the evidence, limitations, and implications of this framework for predicting evolution and understanding microbiome stability.
records.authors: Warsi OM, Andersson DI.

records.title: Friend or foe? Functional roles of Ixodes ricinus microbes.
records.abstract: The tick Ixodes ricinus is a major vector of multiple pathogens in Europe, yet the functional roles of its microbial communities and their impact on disease risk remain largely unexplored. Here, we propose a framework linking microbial transmission mode and microbial function to their effects on I. ricinus. We argue that transmission mode shapes the evolutionary pressures on microbes and, therefore, the nature and stability of their interactions with ticks. Building on the apparent absence of a single obligate nutritional symbiont in I. ricinus, we further propose that complementary and functionally redundant microbial traits may be more important than individual microbial taxa. This perspective provides a basis for understanding how microbiome function may influence tick adaptation, resilience, and ultimately disease risk.
records.authors: Krawczyk AI, Duron O, Hübschen JM.

records.title: Fate of artificial sweeteners in urban aquifers: Evaluation of natural attenuation using mixing models.
records.abstract: Groundwater represents a critical source of freshwater, yet shallow aquifers are increasingly threatened by anthropogenic contamination from urbanized river recharge. Due to their domestic origin, high mobility in water, resistance to conventional wastewater treatment, widespread consumption, and constant discharge loads, artificial sweeteners (ASs) may serve as good candidate tracers for wastewater inputs in aquatic systems. The occurrence, distribution, and natural attenuation of four ASs, namely acesulfame (ACE), cyclamate (CYC), saccharin (SAC), and sucralose (SUC), were evaluated across the river-groundwater interface of the Besòs River Delta aquifer (NE Spain) under contrasting hydrological regimes. The Besòs River was identified as the primary contamination source, with groundwater AS concentrations exhibiting a progressive downgradient decrease along the flow path. Mixing analysis demonstrated a distinct pattern from a dry-period recharge regime dominated by low-flow end-members (93% combined contribution) to a wet-period regime with a substantially higher contribution of rainfall-driven recharge (35% W1 end-member). Natural removal efficiencies (Rabs) and first-order attenuation kinetics revealed distinct seasonal and compound-specific behaviors. Wet conditions enhanced natural attenuation, yielding higher mean Rabs, lower spatial variability, and usually, shorter half-lives across the aquifer. SAC and CYC were the most naturally attenuated, achieving near-complete attenuation under wet conditions (average 99.5% and 98.0%). ACE showed high but transient attenuation (82.7% dry vs. 96.5% wet). In contrast, SUC shows marked persistence and potential aquifer apparent accumulation during low-flow periods (15.6% dry vs. 67.0% wet), maintaining the highest persistence across both seasons (apparent half-lives of 16.0-21.3 d). Depth-dependent contrasts were also observed during dry periods, with deeper groundwater exhibiting higher attenuation. The results demonstrate that hydrological variability is a key control on the natural attenuation of ASs and identify SUC as a conservative tracer of wastewater-derived recharge. This integrated approach improves the assessment of contaminant fate in urban aquifers and supports groundwater quality management.
records.authors: Castro L, Gómez S, Osorio V, Jurado A.

records.title: Characterization of NfnAB of Heliomicrobium modesticaldum, an Electron Bifurcating Enzyme Involved in Phototrophic Energy Conversion.
records.abstract: Analysis of the Heliomicrobium modesticaldum genome suggests that polypeptides encoded by the genes HM1_0289 and HM1_0290 correspond to the NfnA and NfnB subunits of an NAD-dependent ferredoxin:NADP+ oxidoreductase electron-bifurcating enzyme, NfnAB, similar to that found in archea and anaerobic bacteria. NfnA contains a flavin cofactor and a [2Fe-2S] cluster, whose potential has not been previously measured. It exists in two spectroscopically distinct populations: a major species with Em ≈ -364 mV and a minor species with Em ≈ -423 mV. NfnB contains two [4Fe-4S] clusters, one with Em ≈ -430 mV and the other with Em ≤ -650 mV. Individually, NfnA and NfnB were selective for oxidation of NADH and NADPH respectively. Together, the NfnAB holoenzyme catalyzes the electron bifurcation reaction (2 Fdox + NAD+ + 2 NADPH ⇆ 2 Fdred + NADH + 2 NADP+), where Fd corresponds to a heliobacterial dicluster ferredoxin. In the absence of a traditional FNR, heliobacteria may use NfnAB in electron confurcation to accomplish two functions: light-driven cyclic electron transport and transfer of reducing equivalents from NADH to NADP+. Deletion of the nfnAB genes resulted in mutants that were viable in all growth modes tested, but in vivo spectroscopic analysis indicated that light-driven electron transport was limited in the absence of NfnAB. As heliobacteria are considered descendants of a clostridial-type bacterium that received the genes for phototrophy via lateral gene transfer, NfnAB may be an archaic protein that was re-purposed for use in phototrophic energy conversion, a function not previously reported for this enzyme.
records.authors: Walters KA, Tomah KR, Pham V, Baker P, Golbeck JH, Redding KE.

records.title: Microbial community shifts accompany divergent soil carbon recovery after aquaculture-pond restoration across China's coastal wetlands.
records.abstract: Aquaculture-pond restoration may rebuild coastal soil carbon, but gains in soil organic carbon (SOC) do not necessarily indicate lower lability or uniform microbial responses. We compared aquaculture ponds and adjacent restored wetlands at 10 sites across temperate, subtropical, and tropical China. SOC, microbial biomass carbon (MBC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and easily oxidizable carbon (EOC) were measured at 0-15 and 15-30 cm in 160 samples, and carbon pool management index (CPMI) components were calculated. Surface-soil bacterial communities and FAPROTAX-inferred functions were characterized at three sites. Restoration increased SOC at most sites and surface MBC at five, but carbon-pool responses differed among regions. Operationally non-labile carbon (CSS = SOC - EOC), an operational estimate of less-labile carbon rather than a directly measured persistent carbon pool, increased at Yancheng, Minjiang River Estuary, Zhanjiang, and Dongzhai Port. Caofeidian, Hangzhou Bay, Zhangjiang River Estuary, and Beilun River Estuary had high carbon pool activity indices, producing CPMI values of 239.78-363.74% and indicating labile-carbon enrichment rather than uniform stabilization. Bacterial community structure was dominated by geographic separation: pond and restored samples remained close within sites, whereas alpha diversity decreased at Caofeidian, changed little at Minjiang River Estuary, and increased at Dongzhai Port. Restoration also altered dominant genera and inferred functions, including greater representation of plant-polymer degradation functions in some restored soils. DOC accounted for 46.25% of the fitted variation in the 10 dominant genera and was positively associated with Sulfurimonas, SOC, and CSS. Pond-to-wetland restoration therefore followed multiple carbon-recovery trajectories, ranging from labile-carbon pulses to accumulation of a less labile fraction. Assessments should integrate SOC quantity, carbon lability, and microbial associations.
records.authors: Zhong X, Ye T, Xia H, Zhang Y, Li J, Li Y, Zheng Y, Wang W.

records.title: A phage-encoded small RNA that mimics chimeric guide to inhibit CRISPR-Cas9.
records.abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 relies on a dual CRISPR RNA (crRNA)-trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) guide, yet whether RNA-based anti-CRISPRs exist for this system has remained unknown. Here, we identify a phage-encoded small non-coding RNA, rAcrIIA1, that adopts an unexpected chimeric crRNA-tracrRNA architecture, faithfully recapitulating the entire single-guide RNA (sgRNA) of Cas9. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the Cas9-rAcrIIA1 binary complex and the Cas9-rAcrIIA1-DNA ternary complex reveal that rAcrIIA1 engages Cas9 nearly identically to the native sgRNA, competitively blocking crRNA and tracrRNA loading and thereby abolishing DNA interference. Strikingly, beyond its natural inhibitory function, rAcrIIA1 is fully reprogrammable: with variable guide sequences, it directs Cas9 for sequence-specific DNA cleavage with efficiency comparable to the canonical sgRNA, and it activates trans-cleavage more potently. Thus, rAcrIIA1 provides an experimentally validated, mechanistically resolved RNA-based inhibitor of CRISPR-Cas9, reveals a distinct anti-CRISPR mechanism through complete sgRNA mimicry, and serves as a versatile bifunctional scaffold for genome editing and diagnostics.
records.authors: Chen Y, Zhao P, Guo C, Chen D, Yun C, Chen J, Liu L.

records.title: Occurrence of lipophilic marine algal toxins in surface sediments from representative polar seas and implications for toxigenic microalgae.
records.abstract: Phytotoxins produced by harmful algal blooms threaten marine organisms and human health, yet research on algal toxins in polar marine system remains extremely limited. In this study, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry was used to systematically characterize the composition, concentration, spatial distribution, and potential sources of lipophilic marine algal toxins (LMATs) in surface sediments from Antarctic Prydz Bay and the Arctic Bering-Chukchi Seas. Only low levels of pectenotoxin-2 (PTX2) were detected in Prydz Bay sediments (mean ± SD: 6.649 ± 3.669 ng/kg; n = 8), providing evidence of sedimentary PTX2 occurrence. In contrast, eleven LMATs were detected in sediments from the Bering-Chukchi Seas, reflecting markedly higher LMAT chemical diversity. Notably, azaspiracids, PTX2-SA, and gymnodimine were recorded for the first time in this Arctic region. The mean ± SD concentration of ΣLMATs was 6313 ± 2842 ng/kg (n = 10), dominated by yessotoxin (YTX) and okadaic acid. ΣLMATs displayed pronounced spatial heterogeneity, with elevated levels concentrated in the southwestern portion of the study region near the Chukchi Peninsula, whereas the Bering Strait region showed low concentrations. Considering the observed LMAT diversity, documented YTX-producing taxa in the northwestern Pacific, and high-latitude records of Dinophysis and Azadinium/Amphidoma, the sedimentary LMAT assemblage may reflect contributions from multiple toxigenic microalgal sources. Because the vastness and harsh environmental conditions of polar oceans make comprehensive mapping of toxigenic microalgae difficult, sediment-derived LMATs provide baseline evidence of LMAT occurrence in high-latitude polar environments.
records.authors: Zhang H, Chen J, Han T, Liu Y, Yin X, He X.

records.title: Characterization of hydrocarbons and associated bacterial communities in the Pacific WWII shipwreck oil.
records.abstract: This study investigates the hydrocarbon composition and bacterial communities present in fuel oil retrieved from World War II shipwrecks in the Pacific. We quantified Total Petroleum Hydrocarbons (TPH), Benzene, Toluene, Ethylbenzene, and Xylene (BTEX), as well as Polyaromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) using Gas Chromatography - Flame Ionization Detection and Mass Spectrometry (GC-FID/GC-MS). Additionally, we profiled the bacterial community using the V3/V4 regions of the 16S rRNA gene, identifying a diverse microbial assemblage comprising 42 phyla, 107 classes, 249 orders, 432 families, 1047 genera, and 1505 species. Dominant phyla included Proteobacteria (77.9%), Actinobacteriota (35.7%), Firmicutes (19%), and Bacteroidota (6.1%). While active hydrocarbon degradation was not directly assessed, the presence of known hydrocarbon-associated taxa highlights a community structured around long-term hydrocarbon exposure. The distribution of microbial communities appeared to be influenced by both hydrocarbon composition and sampling location. Fuel oil from one site was a blend of distillate and residual oils with higher concentrations of BTEX and PAHs, while the other was only, with higher overall PAH and TPH levels. These findings offer valuable insights into the microbial community structure in historically contaminated marine environments and establish a baseline for future research. This study contributes to broader efforts in pollution monitoring, ecosystem conservation, and establishes a taxonomic baseline to inform future functional bioremediation research.
records.authors: Bainivalu AT, Panneerselvan L, Larsen JS, Mills TJT, Timms VJ, Lockhart PJ, Megharaj M, Neilan BA.

records.title: Polystyrene nanoplastics alter cadmium toxicity outcomes in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii: Physiological responses and multi-omics insights.
records.abstract: Cadmium (Cd) and micro/nanoplastics frequently coexist in aquatic environments, yet how plastic particles modulate heavy metal toxicity in microalgae remains poorly understood. Here, the freshwater microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii was employed to investigate the interaction between polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPs) and Cd at physiological, biochemical, ultrastructural, and molecular levels. Among the tested particle sizes, 500 nm PS-NPs exhibited the strongest observed growth inhibition under Cd co-exposure and were therefore selected for subsequent mechanistic investigation. Cd-NPs co-exposure caused pronounced growth inhibition, pigment disturbance, oxidative damage, and chloroplast ultrastructural disruption. Notably, EDTA-resistant cellular Cd accumulation was lower under simultaneous Cd-NPs co-exposure than under Cd exposure alone, indicating that the greater biological impairment observed under co-exposure was not attributable to an increased EDTA-resistant cellular Cd burden. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses revealed coordinated disturbances in metal/redox homeostasis, membrane lipid remodeling, pigment metabolism, nitrogen redistribution, and central carbon metabolism. These findings support a model in which NPs modify Cd-associated biological responses without increasing EDTA-resistant cellular Cd retention. This study provides new insights into how nanoplastics may modify metal toxicity outcomes in freshwater microalgae and highlights the potential importance of incorporating organism-level stress responsiveness into ecological risk assessment of emerging aquatic contaminants.
records.authors: Yu S, Zhang J, Yu Y, Liao H, Yue Z, Feng L, Li C, Hu Z.

records.title: Chemically encoded pH-tunable covalent adhesion by a bacterial thioester domain.
records.abstract: Thioester domains (TEDs) represent a family of bacterial adhesin domains that mediate covalent anchoring to target ligands via an intramolecular thioester bond. Although the broad distribution of TEDs among Gram-positive bacteria suggests a critical functional role, the biological significance of this covalent mechanism remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrated that TED-mediated covalent anchoring is reversible and that its equilibrium is regulated by pH. Specifically, SfbI-TED from group A Streptococcus binds tightly to fibrinogen at physiological pH, whereas mild acidification to pH 6.0 induces rapid dissociation of the complex. Thermodynamic analyses indicated that this pH responsiveness is largely dictated by the intrinsic pH sensitivity of the thioester-mediated acyl transfer reaction conserved within TEDs, rather than by surface residues specific to individual TEDs. Similar pH-dependent behavior was observed in phylogenetically distinct TEDs, suggesting that pH-responsive adhesion is likely to be a broadly shared feature of TED-containing adhesins across Gram-positive bacteria.
records.authors: Tokunaga Y, Matsunaga R, Kozuka-Hata H, Oyama M, Tsumoto K.

records.title: Crystal structures of SARS-CoV-2 main protease and its complex with PBI-0451.
records.abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro) has a pivotal role in mediating viral genome replication and transcription of the coronavirus, making it a prime target for antiviral drug development. This study presents four high-resolution crystal structures of SARS-CoV-2 Mpro in the apo state. Among these structures, we identify a previously unobserved, stable inactive conformation, characterized by a major displacement of the oxyanion loop (especially Phe140, Leu141 and Asn142), the rotation of some important residues (including His163 and His172) and the loss of many key interactions around the active site, which provides new insights into the conformational dynamics of the enzyme. We also report structures of Mpro in complex with the covalent inhibitor pomotrelvir (PBI-0451) for the wild-type enzyme and three clinical variant-associated mutants (G15S, K90R and P132H). PBI-0451 adopts a virtually identical mode when bound to wild-type Mpro and the K90R and G15S Mpro mutants. However, the crystal structure of PBI-0451 bound to SARS-CoV-2 Mpro P132H reveals a discernible shift of the Gln189-bearing loop and incomplete electron density for the Gln189 side chain, which may be responsible for the subtle modest reduction in PBI-0451 susceptibility. These findings expand the conformational landscape of Mpro and offer structural guidance for the design of Mpro-targeted antiviral drugs.
records.journal: Acta crystallographica. Section D, Structural biology
records.authors: Jiang H, Li W, Zhang J, Li J.

records.title: Lysobacter halodurans sp. nov., a Bacterium Isolated from the Sludge of a Bioreactor Treating Aromatic Compounds.
records.abstract: A novel bacterium, strain e5T, was isolated from the sludge of a bioreactor treating aromatic compounds. Cells of strain e5T were Gram-stain-negative, rod-shaped, forming yellow and viscous colonies on Reasoner's 2 A agar plates. Phylogenetic analyses based on 16 S rRNA gene showed that strain e5T shared 97.3% sequence similarity with Luteimonas arsenica 26-35T and formed a distinct lineage in the genus Luteimonas with low bootstrap values. However, phylogenomic analyses indicated that strain e5ᵀ formed a distinct lineage in the genus Lysobacter with high bootstrap values, indicating that strain e5ᵀ is a novel species in this genus. In agreement with the phylogenomic results, the enzyme activities and fatty acid profiles of strain e5ᵀ were consistent with its placement in the genus Lysobacter. Nevertheless, strain e5ᵀ can be distinguished from closely related species by its salt tolerance, phenylacetate assimilation, urease activity, gelatin hydrolysis, and the relative proportions of fatty acids such as iso-C15:0, iso-C16:0, and iso-C11:0 3-OH. These phenotypic and chemotaxonomic data thus provide additional support for the recognition of strain e5ᵀ as a novel species within the genus Lysobacter. Therefore, the name Lysobacter halodurans sp. nov. is proposed. The type strain is e5T (= KCTC 92385T =GDMCC 1.3249T).
records.authors: Geng C, Ren K, Liu J, Wang H, Sun L, Song P, Chen L, Deng T, Xu M.

records.title: Dual colored phenotypic switching and interaction-driven heterogeneity in clonal Candida auris clinical isolates.
records.abstract: Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant pathogen designated by the World Health Organization as a critical priority due to its persistence, transmissibility, and association with healthcare outbreaks. Despite its clinical significance, the contribution of phenotypic heterogeneity to pathogenicity and treatment response remains poorly understood. In this study, we identified dual white (W) and pink (P) morphotypes in seven of 278 clinical isolates screened on CHROMagar™ Candida Plus and characterized their genetic relatedness, antifungal susceptibility, and phenotypic switching behavior. Whole-genome sequencing and internal transcribed spacer (ITS) analyses confirmed that paired morphotypes were clonally related (0-57 SNPs divergence) and belonged to Clade I, indicating within-host diversification rather than co-infection with distinct strains. All isolates carried identical ERG11 Y132F mutations and wild-type FKS1 sequences across both morphotypes, demonstrating that morphotype variation occurs independently of primary antifungal resistance determinants. Phenotypic profiling demonstrated comparable resistance profiles and aggregation capacity between paired morphotypes, with pseudohyphal formation as the principal differential trait. Systematic switching analysis across CHROMagar, yeast peptone dextrose (YPD), and sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) under multiple temperature and population conditions identified three principal patterns: interaction-dependent switching, in which mixed subpopulations generated enhanced or novel phenotypes not reproduced in pure cultures; morphotype-driven switching, dominated by a single subpopulation; and intrinsic switching capacity retained independently by both morphotypes. Switching dynamics were strongly modulated by temperature, growth medium, and incubation duration. These findings establish phenotypic switching in C. auris as a dynamic, environmentally modulated process driven in part by intercellular interactions within clonal populations. This plasticity may contribute to persistence and virulence without altering antifungal resistance profiles, underscoring the need to recognize and separately evaluate distinct C. auris morphotypes for antifungal susceptibility, particularly in persistent or treatment-refractory infections.
records.authors: Lazreg I, Ghazawi A, Dakalbab S, Ismail H, Aly MAA, Haddad O, Al Dhaheri F, Soliman SSM.

records.title: Sustainable bilge water treatment and bioelectricity generation in microbial fuel cells: impact of substrate complexity on microbial adaptation.
records.abstract: Marine pollution driven by industrial activities poses a significant threat to aquatic ecosystems and human health, with bilge water (BW) representing a complex and persistent waste stream due to its heterogeneous composition of hydrocarbons, surfactants, and heavy metals. Microbial fuel cells (MFCs) offer a promising approach for simultaneous wastewater treatment and energy recovery; however, the influence of substrate complexity on bioelectrochemical performance and microbial adaptation remains poorly understood. Single-chamber MFCs inoculated with mixed microbial consortia were sequentially operated using synthetic (SBW), low-strength raw (LBW), and raw high-strength BW (RBW) to assess increasing complexity. Among BW types, LBW exhibited the highest power density (77.3 mW/m2). Performance declined under RBW, consistent with reduced substrate bioavailability and constrained electron transfer. Nevertheless, electricity generation was sustained for 95 days under 20% RBW, indicating sustained electrochemical activity following prolonged exposure. Microbial community analysis revealed stage-dependent restructuring, including enrichment of Pseudomonas, while predicted functional profiling indicated shifts in central carbon metabolism and hydrocarbon degradation pathways during sequential BW treatment. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics analyses provided complementary support for the potential interaction of dodecanoate with quinohemoprotein alcohol dehydrogenase from Pseudomonas putida. Overall, the results suggest that increasing BW complexity drives microbial community and functional reorganization, while biodegradation potential, contaminant removal, and electrochemical performance respond in a partial and functionally heterogeneous manner.
records.authors: Akagunduz D, Sever Kaya D, Kurt H, Bermek H, Catal T.

records.title: Lower airway microbiome transcriptional and metabolic activities influence responsiveness to immunotherapy in NSCLC.
records.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet a large proportion of patients do not respond. The lung microbiome is a key modulator of antitumor immunity, however, the functional contribution of active microbial communities and their interaction with host transcriptional programs in shaping ICI outcomes remain poorly defined. Here, we prospectively analyzed bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) samples from 71 NSCLC patients prior to ICI initiation. We profiled the microbiome and host transcriptome in the BAL to look for microbial and host signatures in the lower airways associated with treatment response. We found that enrichment of the lower airway microbiome with oral commensals was associated with disease progression and worse prognosis of patients treated with ICI. Metatranscriptomics-derived microbial clustering revealed distinct functional profiles. The microbial cluster enriched with oral commensals, which was only present among patients with poor response to ICI, had differential regulation of pathways involved in the metabolism of short-chain fatty acids, methane, and pyruvate. This cluster also correlated with host immune pathways including upregulation of interferon signaling, neutrophil degranulation, and mitophagy, all of which could contribute to the poor response to immunotherapy. In a preclinical murine model of lung cancer with dysbiosis, inoculating lung tumor-bearing mice with oral commensals increased intratumoral neutrophils and Th17 responses and impaired ICI efficacy. Our findings support the concept that microbial communities in the lower airways influence tumor-immune interactions via defined metabolic-immune axes.

records.title: Immune-related Plasma Proteins Associated with Recurrent Aphthous Stomatitis Identified by Mendelian Randomization and Clinical Validation.
records.abstract: PurposeTo identify immune-related plasma proteins causally associated with susceptibility to recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) through two-sample Mendelian randomization, and to validate their biological and clinical relevance using integrative multi-omics analyses and clinical samples.Materials and methodsTwo-sample Mendelian randomization was performed using protein quantitative trait locus (pQTL) data for immune-related plasma proteins from the deCODE genetics database and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics for RAS to identify proteins with potential causal associations. Candidate proteins were further evaluated by Gene Ontology (GO)/Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network, summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), and colocalization analyses. Single-cell transcriptomic data from oral mucosa were integrated to characterize the cellular expression patterns of the corresponding genes. Finally, plasma levels of the candidate proteins were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) in 35 patients with RAS (sampled during both the ulcerative and healing phases) and 35 healthy controls to validate their clinical relevance.ResultsA total of 28 immune-related plasma proteins were identified as having potential causal associations with RAS through two-sample Mendelian randomization. Functional enrichment analysis indicated that these proteins were mainly involved in immune and inflammatory pathways, including natural killer (NK) cell-mediated cytotoxicity, Th1/Th2 cell differentiation, and the IL-17 signaling pathway. SMR and colocalization analyses highlighted IL17A, MMP1, and IL2RA as key candidate genes, with IL17A showing the strongest genetic evidence. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis further revealed distinct cell-type-specific expression patterns of these genes in the oral mucosa. Clinical validation confirmed statistically significant alterations in the plasma levels of IL17A, MMP1, and IL2RA across different stages of RAS.ConclusionsThis integrative study combining genetic analysis, single-cell transcriptomics, and clinical validation identified IL17A, MMP1, and IL2RA as key immune-related molecules associated with RAS. Among them, IL17A showed the strongest genetic evidence and may serve as a promising biomarker and potential therapeutic target for RAS.
records.authors: Wang Y, Che J, Guan C, Guo H.

records.title: Meeting gene expression demand during evolution of antibiotic resistance.
records.abstract: Regulated gene expression in bacteria accommodates demands imposed by different environments. In addition to ensuring the production of required metabolic and structural components, gene regulation protects bacteria against the adverse effects of misexpression. Upon encountering a novel environment, such as sustained exposure to antibiotics, transcriptional recalibration ensues to improve fitness. For antibiotics, this involves enhancing the expression of an existing repertoire of resistance mechanisms and is often mediated by mutations in regulators of gene expression. Here, we review how diverse gene regulatory mutations confer antibiotic resistance to bacterial pathogens. We view these strategies through the lens of the Gene Expression Demand Theory, originally proposed for inducible operons involved in sugar metabolism, and describe the molecular basis and evolutionary consequences for a few well-studied examples. Broad underlying preferences of when and which kind of regulatory mutations bacteria employ emerge from these examples. A key pattern appears to be a preference for derepression rather than activating mutations, and we highlight potential underlying genetic and evolutionary explanations. Finally, even as our knowledge of molecular mechanisms of antibiotic adaptation continues to expand, we propose that adaptation by regulatory mutations provides a framework for assessing the risk of resistance evolution in the case of novel antibiotics and alternative targets for diagnostic and therapeutic interventions.
records.authors: Vinchhi R, Matange N.

records.title: Microneedle-Assisted CRISPR Biosensing Platform for Presymptomatic Detection of Plant Diseases.
records.abstract: Presymptomatic diagnosis of tomato bacterial speck caused by Pseudomonas syringae requires rapid sample preparation and specific molecular readout. Although existing methods offer high reliability, their requirement for destructive sampling and centralized laboratory infrastructure severely limits their suitability for monitoring of plant diseases. We address this gap with a microneedle-assisted CRISPR platform that integrates on-leaf sample extraction with pathogen-specific detection. A hydrophilic and swelling polyvinyl alcohol microneedle patch mechanically bypasses the cuticle to extract pathogen-associated nucleic acids from the plant apoplast within minutes, and a CRISPR-based fluorescence assay reports the presence of plant pathogens with high detection specificity. The platform can detect unamplified pure target DNA at 0.16 nM, and as few as 103 copies following PCR preamplification. For bacterial suspensions, this platform can achieve a limit of detection at a concentration of 104 CFU/mL without amplification and 103 CFU/mL with PCR within 2 h. In inoculated plants, the platform reliably achieved presymptomatic detection of P. syringaeon day 3 postinoculation, preceding macroscopic necrotic specks by 24 h. These results establish a rapid and minimally invasive sampling-to-molecular biosensing pipeline that significantly accelerates conventional diagnostic turnaround and provides a versatile foundation for presymptomatic plant disease surveillance.
records.authors: Cao C, Jiang D, Zhang X, Pal T, Liu Z, Hadlock T, Neice J, Lu C, Sun W, Vinatzer B, Li S, Chen J.

records.title: Wildlife-associated ecosystems in Algeria harbor internationally distributed ESBL-producing clones and plasmids, including a CTX-M-15 Klebsiella pneumoniae ST17 lineage associated with a conserved IncFIB(K) resistance plasmid.
records.abstract: Expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESC-R-E) have disseminated beyond clinical settings, but their occurrence and genomic epidemiology in wildlife remain poorly characterized, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. ESC-R may result from the production of extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) or AmpC-type cephalosporinases. We investigated the prevalence, resistance mechanisms, and population structure of ESC-R-E in free-ranging wildlife, captive wild animals, and zoo workers in Algeria. Between October 2021 and June 2023, 1,899 fecal samples were collected across six Algerian provinces. ESC-R-E isolates were recovered by selective culture and characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing. Overall, 73 ESC-R-E isolates (3.9%) were identified, including seven OXA-48-like carbapenemase co-producers (0.4%). Carriage was significantly higher in captive animals (13.5%) than in free-ranging wildlife (1.6%) or zoo workers (7.7%). Among the 66 ESBL-producing isolates analyzed, CTX-M enzymes predominated (n = 61), particularly CTX-M-15 (n = 53). Klebsiella pneumoniae was the predominant species (n = 33), with ST17 accounting for 27/33 isolates. Closely related CTX-M-15-producing ST17 isolates were recovered from captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and a zoo worker and carried an IncFIB(K) plasmid harboring blaCTX-M-15 within a multidrug resistance region closely related to globally disseminated plasmids. Globally disseminated high-risk Escherichia coli clones were also detected, namely ST167, ST361, ST410, and a persistent ST38 lineage in Algerian wildlife since 2016. These findings demonstrate the circulation of high-risk Enterobacterales lineages and mobile resistance plasmids in Algerian wildlife-associated ecosystems and highlight the need for integrated One Health surveillance of antimicrobial resistance at the human-animal-environment interface.ImportanceWildlife is increasingly recognized as a potential reservoir and sentinel for antimicrobial resistance, yet genomic data from low- and middle-income countries remain scarce. This study provides one of the largest genomic investigations of expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales in wildlife from North Africa. We demonstrate that internationally disseminated high-risk Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli lineages, together with globally distributed CTX-M-15-carrying plasmids, are circulating among captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and humans in zoological environments. The recovery of closely related K. pneumoniae ST17 isolates from different host species highlights the potential for antimicrobial resistance dissemination across the human-animal-environment interface. These findings extend the known ecological range of clinically important resistant Enterobacterales beyond healthcare settings and identify wildlife-associated ecosystems as part of the broader antimicrobial resistance network. Our study underscores the value of integrating wildlife into One Health surveillance programs to better understand and mitigate the environmental spread of antimicrobial resistance.
records.authors: Mehidi I, Sait-Gharout A, Bougaham AF, Gougam H, Moulai R, Dortet L, Bonnin RA, Girlich D, Ahmim M, Iorga BI, Oueslati S, Naas T.

records.title: Antidepressant desvenlafaxine identified in wastewater promotes transformation and antibiotic resistance risk in Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 via metabolic adaptations.
records.abstract: Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are known reservoirs of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Non-antibiotic compounds, such as antidepressants, may further promote ARG acquisition through horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Desvenlafaxine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) listed on the EU Surface Water Watch List, is among the most frequently detected antidepressants in WWTP effluents, yet its role in HGT has not been examined. Here, we detected desvenlafaxine at the highest concentrations among four antidepressants monitored across three municipal WWTPs in western New York. Using Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 as a model recipient in natural transformation assays (n = 6), we found that desvenlafaxine significantly increased transformation frequency at 10 mg/L (1.74 ± 0.33-fold) and 50 mg/L (1.49 ± 0.19-fold; Padj 20 ~1,300 mg/L). Instead, desvenlafaxine induced dose-dependent increases in membrane fluidity and shifts to less negative zeta potentials, suggesting that electrostatic interactions between its cationic amine group and the negatively charged membrane reduce surface repulsion and facilitate plasmid proximity during uptake. Non-targeted proteomics revealed a biphasic response: at 10 mg/L, competence-associated proteins (PilB, ComM) were upregulated, and STRING analysis identified networks linked to membrane transport, transcriptional regulation, and envelope remodeling, while no connected network was recovered at 50 mg/L. Electron microscopy confirmed higher pilus frequency at both doses. Together, these findings reveal a non-oxidative, envelope-mediated route by which a widely detected antidepressant increases bacterial competence.IMPORTANCEThe spread of antibiotic resistance poses a serious and escalating threat to human health worldwide. While antibiotic use is widely recognized as a key driver, non-antibiotic pharmaceuticals released into the environment through wastewater have received far less attention. Antidepressants are among the most frequently detected drugs in treated wastewater effluents, yet their potential to promote antibiotic resistance transfer in bacteria remains poorly understood. This study demonstrates that desvenlafaxine, one of the most abundant antidepressants found in municipal wastewater, can increase the uptake of antibiotic resistance genes in an environmental bacterium at concentrations above those currently measured in effluent, and identifies the bacterial cell-surface changes that enable this without cytotoxicity.

records.title: Auxiliary glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenases shape central carbon metabolism in Pseudomonas putida.
records.abstract: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenases (GapDHs) are key enzymes in central carbon metabolism, yet their functional diversity extends beyond canonical glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. The soil bacterium Pseudomonas putida KT2440 encodes four GapDH isoenzymes (i.e., GapA, GapB, GapC, and GapD). GapA and GapB have been recently described as gatekeepers of metabolic segregation, with GapA driving glycolysis and GapB associated with gluconeogenesis. However, the physiological roles of GapC and GapD remain poorly defined. In this work, we combined targeted mutagenesis, growth phenotyping, in vitro biochemical analysis, proteomics, and metabolomics to dissect the functions of these lesser-studied GapDH isoforms. GapC and GapD have distinct structural features, diverging from the canonical GapA and GapB enzymes. Physiological characterization of gap-deletion mutants of P. putida across multiple glycolytic and gluconeogenic substrates showed that GapC and GapD exert substrate-specific effects and contribute to network-wide redox balancing. Proteomic and metabolomic profiling further indicated that GapC and GapD are integrated into specialized metabolic modules, supporting auxiliary functions that complement the dominant roles of GapA and GapB. This case of metabolic redundancy at the GapDH node highlights the versatility of central carbon metabolism in bacteria adapted to changing environmental conditions.ImportanceBacteria often carry multiple isoenzymes for the same metabolic step, yet the reasons for such redundancy remain poorly understood. By dissecting the roles of GapDH isoforms in P. putida, we show that these enzymes are not functionally equivalent but rather partition their activity across glycolytic, gluconeogenic, and auxiliary functions. GapC and GapD provide secondary capacity under specific conditions that complement the known roles of GapA and GapB, which dominate glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, respectively. Growth phenotyping, together with proteomic and metabolomic analyses, revealed that isoenzyme specialization is reflected in both substrate-dependent abundance patterns and metabolite profiles. This study underscores the evolutionary diversification of central metabolic enzymes in environmental bacteria and their coordinated regulation across nutritional states. Furthermore, our findings provide a framework for engineering carbon flux in Pseudomonas and related bacteria, with implications for metabolic engineering applications targeting diverse feedstocks.
records.authors: Dekker NK, Partipilo M, Jeeva P, Nieto-Domínguez M, de Jong I, McNaught KJ, Carroll AL, Krink N, Guss AM, Aristilde L, Nikel PI.

records.title: Transcriptomic, untargeted metabolomic, and gut microbiota studies on the anticoccidial activity of the combination formula in broilers.
records.abstract: Coccidiosis, a devastating intracellular parasitic disease, poses a significant threat to the poultry industry. Traditional control methods, which involve the inclusion of anticoccidial drugs in feed, have raised concerns over veterinary drug residues. Consequently, there is a pressing need to identify suitable alternatives or complementary strategies to anticoccidial drugs, with plant-derived natural products emerging as a promising candidate. Our laboratory has previously identified a combination formula that demonstrates good anticoccidial activity. However, the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. This study aims to elucidate the mechanism of action of this formula using a multi-omics approach, including transcriptomics, untargeted metabolomics, and gut microbiota analysis. Cecal transcriptomic analysis revealed significant enrichment in pathways, such as lysosomes, ribosomes, oxidative phosphorylation, and sphingolipid metabolism following treatment with the combination formula. Untargeted metabolomic profiling indicated a pronounced enrichment in the gut IgA generation immune network pathway, with retinoic acid identified as a key differential metabolite. Gut microbiota sequencing analysis suggested that the combination formula modulates the gut microbiota of infected broilers towards a composition resembling that of healthy broilers. Collectively, these results suggest that the combination formula exerts its anticoccidial effects through the regulation of differential gene clusters, metabolites, and microbiota. The results of this study have provided us with a deeper understanding of the good anticoccidial effects of the combination formula.ImportanceEimeria tenella is a significant parasitic protozoan that poses a substantial threat to the development of the poultry industry. The combination formula, a synergistic blend of plant-derived natural products, has been identified in our laboratory for its good anticoccidial effects. In this study, we employed non-targeted metabolomics, transcriptomics, and gut microbiome sequencing to elucidate the mechanism of action against coccidiosis. Our results revealed a multitude of differential gene clusters and metabolites. Furthermore, the gut microbiota structure of the cecal content in the treated group more closely resembled that of the healthy control group.
records.authors: Geng T, Yang H, Liu Y, Zhao J, Zhou Y.

records.title: Bioinspired Mechano-Chemical Titanium Interfaces With Potential for Infection-Resistant Osseointegration.
records.abstract: Bacterial colonization and insufficient osseointegration remain major challenges for titanium-based orthopedic and dental implants. Here, we developed a bioinspired mechano-chemical titanium interface by combining an anodization-derived micro-/nano-pitted topography with a polydopamine-citric acid-quercetin (PCQ) functional layer. Inspired by dragonfly-wing micro-/nanostructures, the resulting OPT@PCQ interface exhibited hierarchical topography, enhanced hydrophilicity, and preserved overall mechanical response. OPT@PCQ showed favorable cytocompatibility and significantly promoted osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells, with increased alkaline phosphatase activity, matrix mineralization, and RUNX2, COL1A1, and OCN expression. It also displayed pronounced antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, accompanied by bacterial morphological deformation and reduced viability. Transcriptomic analysis of S. aureus revealed broad perturbation of central carbon metabolism, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, ribosome-associated processes, and stress-response pathways. In vivo, OPT@PCQ promoted wound closure and markedly enhanced new bone formation and trabecular reconstruction in a noninfected rat femoral defect model. Qualitative hemolysis assessment and major-organ histology provided preliminary evidence of hemocompatibility and systemic biosafety under the tested conditions. Collectively, these findings support OPT@PCQ as a multifunctional titanium interface with potential for infection-resistant osseointegration; however, direct validation in an infected bone-defect model remains necessary.
records.authors: Lu H, Chen R, Chen Y, Zhu M, Liu H, Xu Z, Jian M, Jin K, Wang H, Liu T, Wang J, Zou J, Qiao Y.

records.title: Hybrid membrane vesicle-enabled sonodynamic therapy using ciprofloxacin for treating biofilm-associated infections.
records.abstract: Biofilm-associated infections on indwelling medical devices pose significant clinical challenges due to antibiotic resistance and poor drug penetration. Sonodynamic therapy (SDT) is a promising strategy utilizing ultrasound to activate sonosensitizers for generating reactive oxygen species (ROS). However, the lack of safe and effective sonosensitizers and bacterial-targeting delivery systems limits its application in treating biofilm infection. To address these limitations, we developed antibiotic ciprofloxacin-loaded hybrid membrane vesicles (CIP@HMVs), where ciprofloxacin acts as a safe sonosensitizer and HMVs serve as a detoxified bacterial-targeted delivery system. HMVs were engineered by fusing Pseudomonas aeruginosa-derived outer membrane vesicles (PAEVs) with macrophage membrane vesicles (MMVs), creating a dual-functional nanoplatform with homotypic bacteria-targeting and detoxification capabilities. CIP@HMVs exploited ciprofloxacin's sonosensitizer properties to generate singlet oxygen (1O2) under ultrasound, while HMVs enhanced bacterial uptake in P. aeruginosa. This enabled synergistic bactericidal effects against planktonic bacteria via membrane disruption and intracellular ROS burst, achieving a 5.7-log bacterial reduction in catheter biofilms in vitro. Crucially, HMVs neutralized PAEVs' LPS toxicity in vitro and demonstrated negligible systemic toxicity in vivo. In a murine catheter-infection model, CIP@HMVs under ultrasound achieved 99.8% bacterial eradication and reduced inflammation. This bacterial-targeting sonodynamic platform provides a transformative strategy for treating device-associated biofilm infections with high efficacy and biosafety.
records.authors: Xiao X, Yan M, Yang L, Li Q, He L, Yuan Z, Guo Y, Zhong X, Ding X.

records.title: In silico analysis of SCO, an almost undescribed family of β-lactamases.
records.abstract: Introductionβ-lactamases rank amongst the most common mechanisms of antibiotic resistance, accounting for thousands of different variants. Current genomic tools have resulted in an exponential growth of new variants, most of which, as is the case for SCO, remain undescribed or non-characterised. This study aimed to detect new variants of SCO in GenBank records.Material and methodsThe amino acid sequence of SCO-1 was compared with what is present in GenBank. Only amino acid sequences with >85% identity were considered. No synthetic or partial sequences were included in the analyses.ResultsEleven different SCO variants were detected, 9 of which had previously not been designated as specific variants. Several of the modifications suggested the possible expansion of substrates towards 3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins or the resistance to inhibitors, while others might impair SCO functionality. SCO β-lactamases were detected in 6 bacterial families accounting for 14 genera.ConclusionsThe presence of undescribed SCO variants in GenBank is reported, and the need to establish the exact substrate profile of new variants is highlighted.

records.title: Genetic Variants Associated with Placental Abnormalities in Stillbirths
records.abstract: Background  Placental insufficiency (PI), characterized by impaired placental function, is a leading cause of stillbirth. Although rare coding variants are known to cause a subset of stillbirths, their contribution to PI is poorly understood. Methods  We conducted a secondary analysis of stillbirth cases (N=292) of the Stillbirth Collaborative Research Network study with exome sequencing available on postmortem placental or fetal samples. PI was defined by standardized placental pathological lesions (e.g., maternal vascular malperfusion) and prespecified clinical criteria for placental dysfunction. Candidate gene-based rare-variant burden analysis was performed using the Sequence Kernel Association Test-Optimal framework, focusing on evolutionarily constrained developmental and placental-function genes. Primary analysis compared stillbirths with and without placental vascular malperfusion. Similar comparisons by clinical PI and other placental pathological lesions were conducted in secondary analysis. Results  Stillbirths with PI phenotypes demonstrated different patterns of genetic variation than stillbirths without PI. Specifically, we observed nominal differential enrichment of constrained variants in biologically prioritized placental-function genes, regulating extravillous trophoblast invasion and spiral artery remodeling (  CTNND2 ,  PHACTR1 ,  SLIT1, VEGFA ), placental angiogenesis (  IGF2R ,  TEK ), mitochondrial homeostasis (  OPA1 ), and fetal growth (  DLK1 ,  GNAS ). Secondary analyses on specific placental pathological lesions suggested recurrent enrichment of genes within similar placental developmental pathways.  Conclusions  We observed nominal differential enrichment of constrained developmental and placental-function genes in stillbirths with PI compared to stillbirths without PI. The observed genetic signals across PI phenotypes suggest shared biological pathways underlie placental dysfunction. Our findings advance genotype-phenotype characterization and help prioritize candidate pathways for larger collaborative genomic and functional studies to improve stillbirth risk stratification and prevention.

records.title: Dietary Enhancement for Iron Deficiency and Anaemia Treatment (DEFeAT): study protocol for a randomised controlled trial to assess the effect of a mineral-enriched powder on iron deficiency in women of reproductive age
records.abstract: Background: Iron deficiency (ID) and iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) have global and severe health implications, and disproportionately impact women of reproductive age. Current methods of supplementing diets with iron are challenged by poor adherence and palatability, reducing effectiveness of these treatment strategies. The aim of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of a novel home beverage fortification with a mineral-enriched powder, designed to enhance bioavailability and ease of use, for the treatment of ID in women of reproductive age. Methods: This single-centre, randomised, double-blinded placebo-controlled trial will enrol 150 eligible biologically female participants with ID. Participants will be randomly assigned to the active intervention (iron/zinc-enriched powder) or control group (placebo powder) over 6 months. Primary outcomes will include change in serum ferritin (SF) concentrations and proportion of participants who remain iron deficient at 6-months. Secondary outcomes will include change in SF and haemoglobin (Hb) concentrations across timepoints, and levels of metabolites and key circulating pro-inflammatory biomarkers, changes in dietary intakes, self-reported perceptions of health, barriers to use of the powder, adherence and palatability, safety outcomes, and cost-effectiveness. Exploratory outcomes will assess the gut microbial metagenome and metabolome. Discussion: Fortification, an effective approach for the prevention of ID/IDA, has advantages over some methods of supplementation because it uses low levels of iron, minimising unpleasant side effects, does not risk toxicity, and has high acceptability and compliance rates. This mineral-enriched powder uses electrolytic iron and zinc sulphate monohydrate of a small particle size, which is less irritating to the gut, and facilitates bioavailability. Findings from the study will be shared with those affected by and involved in treating these conditions, as a novel intervention that is both effective and acceptable among women of reproductive age would help to improve treatment compliance, and ultimately, reduce ID/IDA burden. Trial registration: This trial is registered at clinicaltrials.gov (  NCT05990166 ): https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/  NCT05990166 , August 2023.
records.authors: Burns JL, Scott H, Mbuagbaw L, Miller CH, Sheyholislami H, Clouthier BA, Fontaine-Bisson B, Connor KL.

records.title: RecA structure kinetics determine SOS dynamics and predict spontaneous cell death
records.abstract: Even under optimal growth conditions, bacterial cells experience endogenous stresses that threaten cellular function. Individual cells sporadically activate stress responses to restore homeostasis, but some cells ultimately die. The SOS response to DNA damage is particularly heterogeneous, but the origin of its spontaneous activation and its relationship to cell fate remain unclear. Here, we imaged fluorescently labelled RecA in single  Escherichia coli cells under steady-state unperturbed growth using microfluidics. We find that RecA* structures assemble frequently near replication forks and precede SOS response pulses. RecA* structure lifetime quantitatively encodes the magnitude of SOS induction: longer-lived structures promote greater LexA degradation and larger SOS pulses. Thus, cell-to-cell variability in spontaneous SOS activation reflects differences in the repair kinetics of endogenous DNA damage events. By tracking cell lineages over time, we further show that RecA* structures are strong and early predictors of cell fate. Elevated RecA* structure presence emerges up to six generations before spontaneous cell death in over 75% of cases, before other physiological disturbances become detectable. Together, our results establish spontaneous SOS activation as a quantitative readout of endogenous DNA damage processing and identify failure to resolve such damage as a major route to spontaneous bacterial cell death.
records.authors: Pollacco JJ, Haygarth T, Couturier A, Lesterlin C, Sherratt DJ, Baker RE, Maini PK, Uphoff S.
