records.title: Fine Mapping of QTL cqSW.A07 for Thousand-seed Weight in Brassica rapa L.
records.abstract: Abstract    • Background:  Thousand-seed weight serves as a crucial factor influencing rapeseed yield and has historically been a major focus in breeding initiatives for rapeseed. Thus far, quantitative trait locus analyses concerning thousand-seed weight have predominantly been conducted in  Brassica napus  , with similar investigations in  Brassica rapa  being limited. In this study, precise QTL mapping of the thousand-seed weight trait in  Brassica rapa  was conducted by constructing and analyzing residual heterozygous lines. • Results:  This study utilized reduced-representation genome sequencing on 230 F₂ resulting from a cross between the Brassica rapa varieties Dahuang and Haoyou 11. Using these data, a high-density genetic linkage map was established, measuring a total length of 730.585 cM with an average inter-marker distance of 0.015 cM. A significant QTL, identified as  cqSW.A07  , was located on A07 within a 1.44 Mb interval. To refine the mapping of  cqSW.A07  , linked markers were developed, and residual heterozygous lines were generated, narrowing the region to 115.06 kb. Gene expression analysis indicated that  BraA07g035320.3C  is a probable candidate gene associated with  cqSW.A07  . Sequence analysis of the two alleles revealed 31 amino acid differences. • Conclusions:  In this study, the  cqSW.A07  for thousand-seed weight in  Brassica rapa  was mapped to 115.06 kb, and the annotated gene  BraA07g035320.3C  , which may influence the thousand-seed weight was identified. These results provide a molecular basis for high-yield breeding of  Brassica rapa  .
records.authors: Zhao H, Zhao Z, Zhao Z, Xu L, Li Y, Zhang Y, Pan Y, Liu H, Du D, Tang G, Xiao L.

records.title: Genome-Wide Identification of the Potato MAPKKKK Gene Family Reveals StMAPKKKK1 as a Positive Regulator of Salt and Drought Tolerance
records.abstract: Abstract    Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase kinases (MAP4Ks/MAPKKKKs) reside at the apex of MAPK signalling cascades, yet their roles in potato abiotic stress responses remain unexplored. Here, we identified eight  StMAPKKKK  genes via genome-wide identification in potato. StMAPKKKK1 protein was strongly induced by salt and drought stress and localized to the plasma membrane and cytoplasm. Yeast two-hybrid (Y2H), bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), and split-luciferase complementation (SLC) experiments show that StMAPKKKK1 physically interacts with StMAPKK2. To assess its function, we generated  StMAPKKKK1-  overexpressing (OE) and RNA interference (RNAi) lines in potato cultivar  'Atlantic'  . OE lines exhibited improved growth, with higher plant height, biomass, and leaf number, whereas RNAi lines were more sensitive than non-transgenic (NT) controls under both salt and drought stress conditions. Higher activities of ascorbate peroxidase (APX), catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and peroxidase (POD), as well as proline and total chlorophyll contents, along with lower levels of hydrogen peroxide (H  2  O  2  ) and malondialdehyde (MDA) were observed in OE lines. In contrast, RNAi lines showed opposite trends for all above-mentioned parameters. These results indicate alleviated oxidative damage, enhanced osmotic adjustment, and better pigment retention. This study presents the first functional characterization of the  StMAPKKKK  family in potato and establishes  StMAPKKKK1  as a positive regulator of salt and drought tolerance, acting at least partially through interaction with StMAPKK2 and activation of the antioxidant defense system.

records.title: Molecular determinants of Kingella kingae translocation across polarized respiratory epithelium.
records.abstract: Kingella kingae is the leading cause of osteoarticular infections in children under 36 months of age. The pathogenesis of K. kingae disease begins with colonization of the oropharynx followed by translocation across the respiratory epithelium, entry into the bloodstream, and dissemination to distant sites. The bacterial factors that facilitate translocation across the respiratory barrier are poorly understood. In this study, we used polarized Calu-3 cells differentiated at an air-liquid interface (ALI) as a model of the respiratory epithelium combined with molecular genetics, barrier integrity measurements, cytotoxicity assays, and RNA sequencing to interrogate the molecular mechanism by which K. kingae breaches the respiratory epithelium. We found that the pore-forming RtxA toxin drives disruption of the epithelial barrier and is a major contributor to translocation. We observed that type IV pili (T4P) also contribute to translocation and mediate a toxin-independent translocation mechanism. Strains lacking both RtxA and T4P were unable to translocate, confirming that at least one or the other of these factors is required for translocation. Transcriptomic profiling of K. kingae identified 512 differentially expressed bacterial genes during infection and suggested a new role for HprK and a novel esterase in the process of translocation. This study establishes that multiple bacterial factors influence K. kingae translocation across the respiratory epithelial barrier and provides insight into important gene expression changes during K. kingae interaction with host cells.

records.title: B-cell activation markers and cancer risk in people with HIV: An integrative case-control and Mendelian randomization analysis.
records.abstract: Early and continuous antiretroviral therapy (ART) reduces cancer risk in people with HIV (PWH), yet residual risk potentially driven by persistent B-cell activation remains. We used observational and genetic triangulation to evaluate whether baseline B-cell biomarkers are associated with subsequent cancer risk. We conducted: (i) a nested case-control study within the INSIGHT trials (158 cases and 313 matched controls) assessing B-cell biomarkers (sCD23, sCD27, sCD30, CXCL13) in PWH; and (ii) two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) to evaluate likely causal relationships between these proteins and 23 cancer types using general-population genome-wide association studies. Median time from study entry to cancer diagnosis was 2.9 years. In PWH, CXCL13 was associated with overall cancer risk (highest tertile vs. lowest tertile OR 2.36, 95% CI 1.24-4.5), driven by infection-related cancers (N = 82; OR 4.81, 1.76-13.1) and lymphoma (N = 36; OR 9.92, 1.58-62.2). The CXCL13 association remained robust among virally suppressed participants (P = 0.018). sCD30 was also associated with infection-related cancers (OR 2.77, 1.09-7.03). sCD23 showed a linear association with infection-related cancer (OR per SD 1.42, 1.01-2.00), though tertile-based analyses were non-significant. In the general population, MR meta-analyses showed null associations for these biomarkers across 23 cancer types (P > 0.05). Our study links B-cell markers with cancer risk in PWH, identifying CXCL13 as a marker of infection-related cancer risk despite effective ART, highlighting a "residual inflammatory gap" for modern risk stratification. The lack of causal MR signals suggests these proteins are markers of HIV-associated immune activation rather than universal etiological factors for cancer.

records.title: CD6 downregulation from cell surface in human herpesvirus-6A/B-infected T cells.
records.abstract: Human herpesvirus 6A/B (HHV-6A/B) belongs to the Betaherpesvirinae subfamily and mainly replicates in activated T cells. Although HHV-6B establishes lifelong latency after primary infection and infects nearly all adult humans, its immune evasion strategies in vivo remain incompletely understood. CD6 is a key costimulatory receptor that shapes T-cell activation and communication. Here, we identify CD6 as a previously unrecognized target of HHV-6A/B. Infection triggered internalization of CD6 from the plasma membrane into the cytoplasm and led to its proteasome-dependent degradation. CD6 transcription and maturation through the secretory pathway were unaffected, indicating that downregulation occurs through post-transcriptional mechanisms involving altered endolysosomal trafficking. We further demonstrate that the virus-specific U21-U24 gene cluster is required for CD6 downregulation, as deletion of this cluster abolished CD6 degradation in both T-cell lines and primary cord blood mononuclear cells. These findings reveal a viral strategy that disrupts T-cell surface architecture and suggest a role for CD6 modulation in supporting HHV-6A/B persistence.IMPORTANCEHuman herpesvirus 6B (HHV-6B) infects nearly all individuals early in life and persists lifelong, yet the mechanisms by which it modulates host immunity remain poorly defined. CD6 is a critical costimulatory receptor that shapes T-cell activation and communication within the immune system. Here, we identify CD6 as a previously unrecognized target of HHV-6A/B and demonstrate that infection triggers its internalization and proteasome-dependent degradation. We further show that this process is driven by the virus-specific U21-U24 gene cluster, revealing a dedicated viral strategy for altering host protein trafficking. Because degradation of immune surface molecules is a common mechanism of immune evasion among persistent viruses, our findings provide new insight into how HHV-6A/B remodels T-cell function to support long-term persistence. Understanding this pathway may inform future approaches aimed at preventing or mitigating diseases associated with HHV-6 reactivation.
records.authors: Takamiya R, Hayashi M, Hasegawa N, Nishimura M, Mori Y.

records.title: S-nitrosoglutathione reductase deficiency is associated with altered recovery from repeated climate stress across generations in Arabidopsis thaliana.
records.abstract: Climate change exposes plants to recurrent and interacting stresses, yet the extent to which these effects persist across generations, and the mechanisms involved, remain unclear. Here, we compared Arabidopsis thaliana wild type (WT, Col-0) plants with gsnor1-3 (hereafter, gsnor-ko), a mutant deficient in S-nitrosoglutathione reductase (GSNOR), an enzyme involved in nitric oxide homeostasis. Plants were propagated for three successive generations (G1-G3) under control, drought, elevated CO2, O3, heat (warm temperature), and combined treatment scenarios, followed by two recovery generations under control conditions (G4-G5). We quantified rosette growth, photosynthetic traits, seed production, and transcriptome dynamics by RNA-seq. Across environments, gsnor-ko exhibited reduced vegetative growth and reproductive output compared with WT. Transcriptomic responses were strongly scenario- and generation-dependent, with the largest differential expression shifts observed under heat and combined-treatment (combination) conditions. Compared with WT, gsnor-ko showed greater transcriptome similarity across generations and among genes differentially expressed in response to the same treatment. Functional enrichment and candidate-gene analyses identified pathways/components linked to DNA methylation, heterochromatin maintenance, histone ubiquitination, m6A RNA regulation, and methyl-donor metabolism. Together, these findings are consistent with a model in which GSNOR activity contributes to transcriptomic recovery after repeated climate stress, whereas GSNOR deficiency is associated with recurrent or reconfigured stress-associated transcriptional states at G1, G3, and G5, suggesting epigenetically associated regulatory reconfiguration.

records.title: L-Threonine production from acetate by metabolically engineered Corynebacterium glutamicum using a pH-controlled fed-batch process.
records.abstract: Acetate has a considerable potential as a non-food feedstock for microbial bioproduction, yet its use for amino acid production remains underexplored. Here, we developed a process for L-threonine production from acetate as the sole carbon source with Corynebacterium glutamicum by integrating rational, genome-based metabolic engineering with pH-coupled fed-batch cultivation. The engineered strain AT-3 carried five chromosomal mutations that alleviated feedback inhibition of key enzymes and redirected carbon flux toward the aspartate pathway. Substrate supply was controlled using a custom Visual Basic-based feeding script that automatically adjusted the acetic acid feed in response to online pH measurements. Robust process performance was maintained during a tenfold scale-up from 100-mL DASbox to 1-L DASGIP bioreactors. The optimized process achieved an L-threonine titer of 10.04 g/L and a yield of 0.086 g/g acetate. This study provides a basis for further studies on the development and improvement of acetate-based amino acid production process. KEY POINTS: • Plasmid-free C. glutamicum strains produce L-threonine in acetate minimal medium • pH-controlled acetic acid feed in bioreactors improved L-threonine production • Acetate-based production of feed amino acids avoids competition with human food.

records.title: OsPIL1 modulates growth-yield-blast resistance trade-offs involving OsINV3 and jasmonate signaling.
records.abstract: Phytochrome-interacting factor-like proteins coordinate plant growth and defense, but the influence of genetic background on their functions in rice remains unclear. We characterized OsPIL1 in japonica cv. Lijiangxintuanheigu (LTH) and examined its association with OsINV3 in LTH and indica cv. Acuce. Although the cultivars shared identical OsPIL1 coding sequences, OsPIL1 overexpression restricted growth, reduced yield-related traits, and increased blast susceptibility in LTH, contrasting with previously reported effects in Acuce. In uninoculated LTH plants, overexpression increased peroxidase activity and several defense-related transcripts but reduced reactive oxygen species and jasmonate accumulation. Following Magnaporthe oryzae inoculation, OsPIL1 knockout lines showed enhanced resistance, lower fungal biomass, and elevated defense outputs. Exogenous jasmonate alleviated symptoms in wild-type, knockout, and overexpression plants, indicating that this protection did not strictly require functional OsPIL1. Transcriptome profiling linked OsPIL1 perturbation to photosynthesis, phenylpropanoid metabolism, and defense signaling. OsPIL1 overexpression was associated with reduced OsINV3 expression in stems of both cultivars, whereas leaf responses depended on cultivar and developmental stage. Combined loss of OsPIL1 and OsINV3 enhanced resistance in LTH but reduced resistance in Acuce, accompanied by differences in downstream gene expression. These findings establish contrasting phenotypic outcomes of OsPIL1-associated networks in two rice backgrounds and identify candidate relationships for investigating growth and defense coordination.
records.authors: He P, Chen X, Chao Z, Yang S, Deng J, Yang J.

records.title: CelFDrive - multimodal deep learning-assisted microscopy for automated detection of rare events.
records.abstract: The emergence of automated microscopy has enabled the collection of large datasets of rare biological events, accelerating discovery in biology. However, most existing methods cannot be readily integrated into microscopy setups or are limited to a single microscope type. We present CelFDrive, a software package that automatically detects rare events of interest and automates high-resolution three-dimensional imaging of target cells by integrating deep learning-assisted cell classification of auxiliary low-magnification fluorescence images. We show that CelFDrive reduced the mean time required to nominate a mitotic prophase candidate for high-resolution light-sheet imaging by over 30-fold relative to manual expert selection. This approach can be used to define the order of kinetochore assembly upon nuclear envelope breakdown. The trained CelFDrive detector demonstrated transferability by retaining mitotic cell detection capability in an independently generated dataset using a different cell line, DNA marker and imaging setup. As datasets grow and models improve, CelFDrive offers a clear path toward intelligent imaging systems that not only accelerate data collection, but also fundamentally enhance how biological questions are explored.

records.title: Almond Anthracnose Is Caused by a Genetically Diverse Population of Colletotrichum godetiae Fungi Along with a Lower Proportion of C. acutatum.
records.abstract: Almond anthracnose, caused by Colletotrichum spp., has become an increasing threat in modern almond orchards in Portugal. This study aimed to characterize the genetic, phylogenetic, morphological, and virulence diversity of Colletotrichum species associated with symptomatic and asymptomatic almond tree organs collected in the main producing regions of Portugal. A total of 112 isolates were obtained from fruits, leaves, flowers and branches, with most samples originating from the Alentejo region. Almond anthracnose in Portugal is caused by genetically and biologically heterogeneous Colletotrichum species dominated by C. godetiae, which exhibited high multilocus genetic diversity, with most isolates corresponding to unique haplotypes, indicating the coexistence of genetically distinct strains. C. godetiae and C. acutatum were predominantly isolated from symptomatic organs in the field, whereas C. fioriniae, C. karsti, and C. gloeosporioides were detected in asymptomatic organs; however, all species were able to cause disease. This study reports C. karsti and C. gloeosporioides on almond for the first time. This diversity suggests multiple introductions and/or ongoing diversification of Colletotrichum populations associated with almond. Differences in virulence among the representative isolates tested, combined with similar incubation and latency periods, indicate that the severity is related to postpenetration events. Moreover, disease prevalence, averaging 36%, was associated with rainfall during the period from fruit set to early fruit development, highlighting the strong influence of meteorological conditions on anthracnose outbreaks. These findings support targeted monitoring, risk assessment, and integrated disease management under agricultural intensification and climatic variability.

records.title: Molecular Profiling and Precision Oncology for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer in Latin America: Unique Epidemiology, Persistent Barriers, and Paths Toward Equity.
records.abstract: AbstractNon-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) represents a critical public health crisis in Latin America (LA), the leading cause of cancer-associated mortality across the region. Although global incidence rates are shifting, the burden in low- and middle-income countries is projected to increase significantly by 2030. Beyond the impact of tobacco, LA faces unique challenges derived from environmental exposures and diverse genetic ancestry that shape a molecular landscape distinct from other regions. This has resulted in a high prevalence of actionable drivers, particularly EGFR mutations, positioning a large segment of the population as ideal candidates for precision medicine approaches. However, current efforts to address this epidemic fall short of regional needs, as the potential of precision oncology remains largely unrealized due to multilevel systemic and economic barriers. Despite the scientific potential of targeted therapies to drastically improve survival, LA has not broadly or expeditiously adopted these strategies. A profound implementation gap is characterized by a reliance on inefficient single-gene testing, fragmented regulatory frameworks, and severe infrastructural limitations. Consequently, only a minimal proportion of the regional patient population benefits from recent advances, whereas the majority continue to receive empirical chemotherapy with significantly inferior survival outcomes. Addressing these disparities requires a steadfast focus on systemic transformation, ranging from establishing centralized genomic hubs to implementing structured educational programs. Standardizing care through molecular tumor boards (MTBs) and harmonizing regulatory pathways are essential steps in translating research into clinical benefits. In this review, we discuss the unique molecular epidemiology of the region and the challenges of treatment implementation, focusing on the urgent need to integrate new technologies to ensure equitable access to precision oncology. LA has one of the highest potential population-level benefits from precision oncology in NSCLC; however, systemic barriers prevent this molecular opportunity from translating into equitable survival gains (Graphical abstract).Graphical abstract

records.title: Computational tools for biomarker identification in inborn errors of metabolism: A rapid systematic review.
records.abstract: Inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs) are a heterogeneous group of rare genetic diseases characterized by enzymatic, transporter, or cofactor deficiencies that disrupt metabolic homeostasis. Biomarker identification is central to their diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic monitoring, but phenotypic heterogeneity and limited patient cohorts pose persistent challenges. Computational tools, including genome-scale metabolic modeling, systems biology, and quantitative systems pharmacology, are emerging and aiming to address these limitations. This work aimed to identify, characterize, and synthesize the available evidence on computational tools for predicting or identifying metabolic biomarkers in individuals diagnosed with IEMs. A rapid systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed and EMBASE for studies published within the last ten years in English or Spanish. Eligible studies applied computational methodologies, such as in silico modeling, constraint-based modeling, machine learning, or metabolic network analysis, for biomarker discovery, prediction, or validation in IEMs. Three reviewers performed selection independently, resolving discrepancies by consensus. Of 955 records identified, 13 studies met the eligibility criteria. They were classified into four categories: machine learning and artificial intelligence approaches for predictive modeling and risk stratification; genome-scale and constraint-based modeling to simulate enzymatic deficiencies and identify candidate biomarkers; systems biology and network-based modeling for pathway-level signatures and diagnostic visualization; and quantitative systems pharmacology frameworks to model therapeutic response and biomarker trajectories. When combined with conventional methods, computational tools may improve the mechanistic interpretability, scalability, and multi-omics integration during biomarker identification for EIMs. However, most approaches remain exploratory, and prospective clinical validation is limited. Future efforts should prioritize hybrid modeling, standardized reporting, and clinical integration.

records.title: Small molecules targeting SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid reveal a conserved RNA-binding vulnerability across human coronaviruses.
records.abstract: SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 exemplify the persistent threat posed by coronaviruses, with their capacity for zoonotic spill over, rapid transmission, and severe disease resulting in substantial morbidity, mortality, and socio-economic burden. The repeated emergence of highly pathogenic coronaviruses highlights the urgent need for broad-spectrum therapeutic strategies. The nucleocapsid (N) protein, essential for RNA binding, genome packaging, and viral replication, remains a highly conserved yet underexplored antiviral target. Sequence alignment revealed 90% identity between SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV N proteins, and 48.1% identity between SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV N proteins. In our earlier work, we identified two small molecules, ceftazidime and sennoside A, that bind the N-terminal domain of the SARS-CoV-2 N protein and inhibit nucleic acid binding, and identified their binding sites using NMR chemical shift perturbation assays. Here, we observed that several residues involved in inhibitor binding are conserved across betacoronaviruses, suggesting a shared druggable vulnerability. We have purified recombinant N proteins from SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2, and demonstrated by electrophoretic mobility shift assays that both compounds significantly reduced RNA binding. Their inhibitory concentrations (IC50) were determined using fluorescence polarization. The docking analyses indicated that both inhibitors target the RNA-binding pocket of the N-NTD, consistent with a conserved mechanism of action. Collectively, our findings reveal a conserved RNA-binding vulnerability in coronavirus N proteins and highlights the pan-coronavirus therapeutic potential of these inhibitors.
records.authors: Singh S, Gupta GD.

records.title: Provenance-aware handling of identical dengue genome records alters inferred envelope-protein variation in Bangladesh DENV-3
records.abstract: The reliability of interpreting dengue virus (DENV) envelope (E) protein variations depends on whether identical public sequence records are kept as representatives or eliminated based on provenance reviews. We evaluated three record-handling strategies using a frozen Bangladesh-associated dataset of 426 E sequences: exact-sequence deduplication, a prespecified provenance-sensitive exclusion method, and an independently curated Nextstrain accession list. Within the 2021 DENV3 subset (96 accessions), 18 records dated August 2021 were identical across 10,707 nucleotides to the older Sri Lankan genome  AY099336.1 . There were 21 variable E positions within the original 96-accession DENV3 cohort. Whole-cohort deduplication (47 retained) and retaining one representative of the 18-record group (79 retained) preserved all 21 positions. Excluding the group (78 retained) resulted in eight variable positions: 13 of 21 (61.9%) were lost due to differences in state at those positions between the excluded group and retained cohort. Nextstrain reference-specific exclusions selected the same 18 records; applying its full saved list produced 77 accessions and the same eight variable positions. E270 and E383, which had pre-2021 antibody-related evidence, did not meet the sequence-variation criteria for follow-up; however, E223 and E224 remained variable. Antibody-position enrichment was not statistically significant. These results indicate that cohort eligibility decisions may impact dengue E-protein variant prioritization despite representative-retaining deduplication. Genome identity does not indicate specimen identity or an antigenic phenotype.
records.authors: Begum KT, Rafea KAG.

records.title: Acute nicotine exposure produces a spatially organized transcriptional response in mouse olfactory cortex
records.abstract: Nicotine acts on nicotinic receptors throughout the forebrain. Most molecular studies of its effects, however, have focused on reward circuitry and have used bulk tissue, which cannot show which cells respond or how responding cells are arranged relative to one another. We previously found that a single nicotine exposure activates hippocampal astrocytes through the astrocyte-expressed kinase AKT2. Here we asked which cells respond to nicotine in the anterior olfactory cortex, a cholinergic-modulated region that encodes odor associations, and whether their astrocytic surroundings change. Male mice received a single intraperitoneal injection of nicotine or saline, and coronal sections spanning the anterior olfactory nucleus, piriform cortex and adjacent isocortex were sequencing 24 h later using Visium HD. Differential expression on nucleus-based segmentation was concentrated in olfactory excitatory neurons. Pathways centered on calcium-handling, synapse-assembly and extracellular-matrix programs, together with a lasting reduction of the immediate-early gene Egr1. Within the piriform region, the response localized to a continuous population of superficial pyramidal neurons expressing Cartpt and Penk. These neurons upregulated synapse-assembly, receptor-regulation and proteoglycan programs without changes to cell-type proportions. Nicotine also reduced expression of Sparcl1, which encodes astrocyte-secreted synaptogenic protein hevin, within one cell diameter of these neurons. Our study shows that a single nicotine exposure leaves a spatially organized transcriptional program on olfactory circuitry, centered on one neuronal population and the tissue at its border. These results identify candidate cells, genes and tissue locations for testing how nicotine alters sensory cue circuits.
records.authors: Griffioen MK, Lombardi A, Milstead R, Borski C, Zou S, Stitzel J, Ehringer MA, Hoeffer CA.

records.title: In Silico Drug Repurposing: Integrating Network Pharmacology and Structure-Based Virtual Screening to Accelerate Preclinical Drug Development
records.abstract: De novo drug discovery requires over a decade of research and $1.5 billion to $2.5 billion in investment per approved molecule, yet more than 90% of candidates fail during clinical trials due to unforeseen toxicity or poor efficacy. In silico drug repurposing offers a faster, cost-effective alternative by finding new therapeutic uses for regulatory-approved or clinical-stage molecules. However, individual computational methods have clear blind spots. Network biology identifies disease-related genes but lacks atomic-level detail on how a drug physically binds to a receptor. Conversely, standalone molecular docking often produces false-positive hits and relies on an outdated single-target mindset. This review provides a practical blueprint for combining network pharmacology with structure-based virtual screening (SBVS) in preclinical drug repurposing. We first outline how disease genomics databases (DisGeNET, GeneCards) and protein–protein interaction (PPI) networks (STRING) pair with graph-theory tools in Cytoscape (cytoHubba, MCODE) to pinpoint central hub proteins. Next, we detail how to screen curated chemical libraries (DrugBank, ChEMBL) against these prioritized targets using AutoDock Vina and AlphaFold structures. We also explain why approved drugs still require indication-specific pharmacokinetic checks in SwissADME and ADMETlab 3.0, followed by 100–500 ns explicit-solvent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations in GROMACS and MM-PBSA/GBSA free-energy rescoring. Finally, we review recent preclinical applications across infectious, neurological, and oncological diseases and discuss how deep-learning tools like DiffDock and AlphaFold 3 are reshaping virtual screening.
records.authors: Nayem AA, Tarikul Islam Tusher S, Deb S.

records.title: Anti-PBP2a Vaccines and Immunotherapies Against Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus: Current Evidence, Challenges, and Perspectives
records.abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major antimicrobial-resistant pathogen worldwide and a high-priority target for new therapeutic strategies. Methicillin resistance is primarily mediated by the mecA gene, which encodes penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2a), a transpeptidase with reduced affinity for β-lactam antibiotics. Because PBP2a plays a key role in bacterial survival under β-lactam pressure, highly specific to Methicillin-resistant Staphylococci, and immunologically recognizable, it represents an attractive target for immunotherapeutic approaches. This review summarizes current knowledge of PBP2a structure, biological function, and immunological relevance, focusing on vaccine and antibody-based strategies. Studies employing DNA vaccines, recombinant proteins, multi-epitope constructs, and passive immunization have demonstrated protective immune responses and reduced bacterial burden in animal models of MRSA infection. Monoclonal antibodies targeting PBP2a have also shown prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy, including activity independent of Fc-mediated effector functions, suggesting direct interference with PBP2a function. Their potential use in rapid immunodiagnostic assays for methicillin resistance is also discussed. Emerging strategies, including antibody engineering, glycoengineering, antibody-drug conjugates, mucosal vaccination, and combination therapies with antibiotics, may further enhance clinical applicability. Although evidence remains preclinical, PBP2a represents a promising target for active and passive immunization against Methicillin-resistant staphylococci.
records.authors: Senna JP, Boechat JPC.

records.title: Activity of aztreonam-avibactam and comparators against difficult-to-treat resistant Enterobacterales from United States medical centres (2020-24) <sup>†</sup>.
records.abstract: BackgroundThe occurrence of infections caused by Gram-negative bacteria with difficult-to-treat resistance (DTR) is rapidly increasing, generally requiring the use of recently approved, last-resort antimicrobial agents or old compounds that are more toxic and/or less effective. We evaluated the activity of aztreonam-avibactam and comparators against DTR Enterobacterales.MethodsA total of 42 295 Enterobacterales isolates were consecutively collected (one per patient) from 85 US medical centres in 2020-24 and susceptibility tested by Clinical Laboratory Standards Institute broth microdilution. The collection included 450 carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) and 284 DTR isolates, which were screened for β-lactamases by whole genome sequencing.ResultsAztreonam-avibactam was active against 98.2% of DTR (minimum inhibitory concentration for 50%/90% of the collection, 0.25/1 mg/L) and 97.1% of CRE isolates and retained potent activity (≥90.0% susceptibility) against DTR isolates non-susceptible to ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam and/or cefiderocol. Cefiderocol was active against 92.8% of DTR isolates, whereas ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam and the aminoglycosides exhibited limited activity against these organisms. Aztreonam-avibactam and cefiderocol were active against 97.8% and 84.4% of DTR metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) producers, respectively. The most common carbapenemase genes identified among DTR isolates were bla KPC (57.7% of isolates) and bla NDM (29.9%). An MBL gene was observed in 31.7% of DTR and 25.1% of CRE isolates.ConclusionsAztreonam-avibactam retained potent activity against DTR Enterobacterales from US medical centres, and its activity was not adversely affected by clinically relevant carbapenemases or resistance to agents used to treat multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales. The activities of other β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations and cefiderocol were compromised by the increased occurrence of MBL producers.
records.authors: Sader HS, Kimbrough JH, Debabov D, Papp-Wallace KM, Castanheira M.

records.title: A Biocatalytic Cascade-Based Cu-GMP Self-Assembly Nanozyme for Accelerating Infected Diabetic Wound Healing.
records.abstract: Nanozymes with multi-enzyme catalytic properties have emerged as promising multifunctional materials for biosensing and antimicrobial applications. Herein, a copper-guanosine monophosphate (Cu-GMP) nanozyme was synthesized via a simple one-pot method. Its supramolecular network serves as a multifunctional carrier, enabling the encapsulation of functional guest biomolecules and retaining their inherent activity simultaneously. As a proof-of-concept, glucose oxidase (GOx) was incorporated to construct a glucose-responsive cascade catalytic system (GOx@Cu-GMP). In this system, GOx catalyzes glucose oxidation to produce hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and gluconic acid. The latter creates a localized acidic microenvironment, which combined with in situ generated H2O2, effectively activates the peroxidase (POD)-like activity of Cu-GMP and further generates hydroxyl radicals (•OH). Leveraging this cascade reaction, GOx@Cu-GMP was developed as a sensitive colorimetric platform for glucose detection. Furthermore, Cu-GMP exhibits oxidase (OXD)-, laccase (LAC)-, and glutathione peroxidase (GPx)-like activities, facilitating the generation of various reactive oxygen species. Benefiting from multi‑enzyme synergy, it achieves broad‑spectrum antibacterial performance. Moreover, GOx@Cu-GMP can eliminate bacterial infections and accelerate wound healing in a diabetic mouse skin wound model. This work provides a multifunctional nanozyme-based platform for glucose detection and diabetic wound antimicrobial therapy, offering new insights for the development of integrated biosensing and therapeutic materials.
records.authors: Li J, Li L, Wang X, Li Y, An X, Wang S, Lu S, Li W, Feng S, Zhou B.

records.title: Whitefly hijacks host NtWRKY6 to activate NtRGL2 and suppress gibberellin signaling.
records.abstract: BackgroundPiercing-sucking insects severely impair crop productivity by suppressing the growth of host plants. Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) infestation induces a pronounced dwarf phenotype associated with reduced gibberellin (GA) signaling; however, the underlying molecular mechanism remains largely unknown. Here, we investigated the role of the hormone-responsive transcription factor, NtWRKY6, in mediating whitefly-induced inhibition of host growth.ResultsSilencing of NtWRKY6 significantly restored bioactive GA₃ accumulation and alleviated whitefly-induced growth inhibition, whereas NtWRKY6 overexpression further aggravated GA deficiency and dwarfism. Using DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq) as a discovery screen, together with yeast one-hybrid and dual-luciferase assays, we identified NtRGL2, a DELLA-encoding negative regulator of GA signaling, as a direct transcriptional target of NtWRKY6. Intensive whitefly feeding induced NtRGL2 expression in wild-type plants, but this induction was largely abolished in NtWRKY6-silenced plants, demonstrating that NtWRKY6 is required for the whitefly-mediated activation of NtRGL2. Furthermore, silencing NtRGL2 substantially mitigated the inhibitory effects of whitefly infestation on GA₃ accumulation and plant growth, confirming its critical role downstream of NtWRKY6.ConclusionOur findings reveal a previously unrecognized regulatory module in which whitefly infestation exploits the host transcription factor NtWRKY6 to promote NtRGL2 expression, a change consistent with enhanced DELLA-associated repression of GA signaling and suppression of host growth. This study reveals a molecular mechanism by which a piercing-sucking insect modulates host phytohormone homeostasis to alter plant development, providing new insights into plant-insect interactions and potential targets for sustainable pest management. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

records.title: Fragment-based hit-to-lead optimization and preliminary mechanistic investigation of fungicidal thioester derivatives.
records.abstract: BackgroundPlant pathogenic fungi cause substantial crop yield losses worldwide, and chemical fungicides remain indispensable for maintaining crop productivity and food security. However, the widespread use of fungicides with similar chemical structures and modes of action has accelerated the development of cross-resistance, highlighting the urgent need for novel fungicidal scaffolds.ResultsA total of 48 thioester derivatives were designed and synthesized. Among them, compound B22 exhibited the highest antifungal activity against Rhizoctonia solani, with a half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) value of 0.124 μg mL-1, showing approximately tenfold greater potency than fenfuram (EC50 = 1.480 μg mL-1), although it was less active than fluxapyroxad (EC50 = 0.041 μg mL-1). At 100 μg mL-1, compound B22 also showed 79.2% protective control against rice sheath blight under greenhouse conditions. Scanning electron microscopy revealed pronounced morphological abnormalities in R. solani hyphae following B22 treatment. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses indicated substantial perturbations in energy metabolism-related processes, while a preliminary biochemical assay showed that B22 inhibited porcine heart succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) activity. Molecular docking further suggested that B22 could be accommodated in the SDH-binding pocket through hydrogen-bonding and cation-π interactions.ConclusionBioactivity screening and antifungal mechanism studies suggested the potential of thioester derivatives as promising candidates for the development of novel fungicidal agents. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

records.title: Regulation of the 22-nt antiviral silencing pathway in tomato by two RNA viruses.
records.abstract: RNA silencing plays a central role in plant antiviral defence, in which viral RNA is processed into small RNAs (sRNAs) that guide Argonaute-mediated cleavage of viral transcripts. Among these, 22-nucleotide (nt) sRNAs are unique in their ability to trigger secondary sRNA production, thereby amplifying transitive silencing. In tomato, this 22-nt antiviral pathway is strongly activated upon virus infection through the upregulation of DCL2b, yet the underlying mechanism has remained unclear. miR6026, generated by DCL2b and targeting DCL2b itself, forms a feedback loop that fine-tunes this response. Here we show that tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) and tomato bushy stunt virus (TBSV) activate DCL2b transcription via the Dof16 transcription factor. Transcription of MIR6026 is also activated by both TMV and TBSV, while viral infection promotes DCL2b relocalization towards the cytoplasm, preventing pri-miR6026 processing into mature miR6026. This redistribution is associated with reduced phosphorylation of DCL2b at Tyr69, which weakens its interaction with importin-α and limits its nuclear localization. Notably, Arabidopsis DCL2 exhibits a similar virus-induced relocalization pattern, highlighting a conserved mechanism that enhances antiviral silencing during infection while minimizing off-target effects on host genes under normal conditions.

records.title: Expanding the Clinical and Molecular Spectrum of Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis Associated With Biallelic Variants in LSR.
records.abstract: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC) comprises autosomal recessive disorders causing early-onset cholestasis that may progress to cirrhosis and liver failure. Although more than 13 genes are associated with PFIC, some patients remain genetically undiagnosed. LSR, encoding lipolysis-stimulated lipoprotein receptor, has recently emerged as a candidate gene. LSR contributes to tricellular tight-junction integrity and epithelial barrier function. We report four additional patients from three unrelated families with biallelic LSR variants, expanding the reported clinical and molecular spectrum. Features included intractable pruritus, cholestasis with normal or mildly elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), progressive hepatic dysfunction and variable extrahepatic findings, including growth failure, neurodevelopmental delay, seizures and microcephaly. Two patients died from end-stage liver disease. Review of published cases suggests a predominantly progressive cholestatic phenotype with variable syndromic features. These findings support consideration of LSR variants in unresolved PFIC and the value of comprehensive genomic testing.

records.title: Hypoxia orchestrates the natural history of inflammatory bowel disease: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
records.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) arises from a dynamic interplay between epithelial dysfunction, immune activation, microbial dysbiosis and tissue remodelling. Although hypoxia was initially regarded as a consequence of intestinal inflammation, it is now recognized as an active regulator of epithelial, immune and stromal responses that coordinate disease progression. Here, we propose that hypoxia acts as a biological organizer linking oxygen sensing to the transition from intestinal homeostasis to chronic inflammation and structural tissue damage. We use this term in a mechanistic rather than a hierarchical sense: oxygen availability is a shared upstream constraint on epithelial, immune, microbial and stromal programmes, not a single initiating event. This review integrates evidence connecting oxygen sensing with epithelial barrier integrity, immunometabolism, microbial ecology and stromal remodelling, with emphasis on advances in single-cell transcriptomics, spatial biology and microbiome research. Physiological low-oxygen gradients support epithelial metabolism, barrier integrity and immune tolerance, whereas persistent inflammatory hypoxia drives oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming and maladaptive epithelial-immune-microbial interactions. Hypoxia also contributes to spatially distinct epithelial, immune and stromal niches that may sustain chronic inflammation and fibrotic progression. Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids and succinate, together with iron metabolism and ferroptosis, further link oxygen sensing to tissue injury, adaptation and repair. These findings position hypoxia-responsive signalling as a pharmacologically actionable network rather than a downstream consequence of inflammation. Targeting selected components may promote mucosal healing and limit structural disease progression, although successful translation will require cell- and isoform-selective modulation, adequate tissue exposure and careful assessment of long-term safety.

records.title: Self-assembled carboxymethyl cellulose/graphene oxide and chitosan ultra-high oxygen barrier layer on bio-based flexible films for lamb non-contact preservation.
records.abstract: A high-performance natural nanocomposite coating was developed to enhance the barrier properties of bio-based films for meat packaging. The flexible substrate consisted of a bio-based PLLA and graphene oxide (GO)-grafted poly(butylene itaconate) (GO-g-PLBI) copolymer. A high-barrier coating was assembled on this substrate via layer-by-layer (LbL) self-assembly of chitosan (CS) and a carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC)/GO composite. This approach enhanced the dispersion of GO, the mechanical strength, antibacterial activity, UV shielding and oxygen (O2) barrier properties of the film. Additionally, the CMC/GO composite exhibited a stronger hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions with CS. Consequently, the film exhibited higher CS and CMC/GO loadings along with superior water resistance. Notably, alternating the deposition of CS and CMC/GO composite for 9 bilayers led to a dramatic decrease in the O2 transmission rate from 41.9 to 0.05 cm3 m-2·d-1, while maintaining considerable translucency. In the non-contact packaging of chilled lamb, the film's outstanding O2 barrier facilitated the rapid formation of a low-O2, high-CO2 headspace, which was driven by the synergistic effects of meat tissue oxidation and microbial metabolism. Hence, this film achieved better preservation performance for fresh lamb when compared with conventional PA/PE film, as evidenced by improved microbiological quality, physicochemical properties, and texture.
records.authors: Zhang J, Dong T, Liu H, Zhang Y, Wu Y, Guo J, Li Y, Yun X.

records.title: Identification and functional characterization of cGAS, STING and MAVSL in amphioxus Branchiostoma japonicum.
records.abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon (IFN) genes (STING) pathway is an evolutionarily conserved nucleic acid-sensing mechanism in animals, but the identities and signaling relationships of its components in cephalochordates remain incompletely understood. Here, candidate cGAS, STING and mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein-like (MAVSL) homologs were identified in Branchiostoma japonicum. The full-length cDNAs encode proteins of 658, 267 and 546 amino acids, respectively. Sequence analyses identified an N-terminal AT-hook-containing region and a C-terminal Mab21/NTase domain in the candidate cGAS protein, a predicted TMEM173/cyclic dinucleotide-binding domain in the candidate STING protein, and a caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD)-containing candidate MAVSL protein in which a C-terminal transmembrane domain was not detected. Transcripts of all three genes were detected in multiple tissues, with the highest levels in the notochord. After exposure to LPS, poly(I:C), or poly(dA:dT), transcript levels changed transiently. In HEK293T cells, the candidate proteins localized to the cytoplasm, and fluorescent signals for cGAS or STING overlapped with those of MAVSL. Overexpression experiments showed higher IFNα, IRF1, Mx1, Viperin and ISG15 transcript levels after co-expression with candidate MAVSL than after expression of the individual proteins in HEK293T cells. These results provide molecular and heterologous expression evidence for cGAS, STING and MAVSL components in amphioxus.
records.authors: Deng Y, Du Y, Yuan J, Liu R, Chen J, Fan B, Li X, Li B, Nie P, Song X.

records.title: PRKN-independent mitophagy regulators in dopaminergic neurons identified by genome-wide CRISPR screening.
records.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the development of PD. PRKN/Parkin is known to play an essential role in mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy. Indeed, mutations and inactivation of this gene are associated with hereditary and idiopathic forms of PD. Despite extensive studies on PRKN-dependent mitophagy, the molecular regulators of PRKN-independent mitophagy in dopaminergic neurons remain incompletely understood. We generated a PRKN knockout iPSC-derived dopaminergic neuronal line expressing the fluorescent mitophagy biosensor mito-SRAI, which reports the delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes as an increase in the TOLLES/YPet fluorescence ratio. We used this cell line to conduct a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen to reveal genetic regulators involved in PRKN-independent mitophagy. Dozens of genes were identified whose knockout increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in an uncoupler-dependent manner. Of these, several genes emerged as candidates with potential therapeutic implications, one of which was Cathepsin F (CTSF). CCCP treatment increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in neurons with siRNA-mediated CTSF knockdown, and CTSF knockdown partially preserved the proportion of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons after paraquat exposure. These results suggest that CTSF is a candidate regulator of PRKN-independent mitophagy and that this lysosomal enzyme may represent a potentially druggable candidate target for PD.
records.authors: Nishimura T, Kunisada Y, Li HL, Highfill CA, Nagasawa K, Tsujihata Y.

records.title: Rules of the road for loop-extruding motors: loading, unloading, and crowding.
records.abstract: Loop extrusion by structural maintenance of chromosome (SMC) complexes has emerged as a key mechanism of genome organization across domains of life, yet the rules that govern where these motors load, unload, and become enriched remain poorly understood. The canonical model treats cohesin as loading and unloading uniformly but stopping at extrusion barriers. Chromosome architecture is then shaped by where extruding complexes stop. Accumulating evidence broadens this view by uncovering cases of (i) targeted SMC loading across metazoa, plants, and fungi, (ii) sites of specific SMC release, and (iii) domains of crowded loop extrusion. Together, these new Rules of the Road shift the focus from where extruders stop to where they start, end, and dwell-with implications for development, gene regulation, and genome stability.
records.authors: Mirny LA, Zhegalova I, Galitsyna A.

records.title: A single-residue deletion in H9N2 hemagglutinin uncouples viral burden from disease severity.
records.abstract: H9N2 avian influenza viruses are characterized by significant genetic diversity. Deletions within the hemagglutinin (HA) receptor-binding domain represent a notable, albeit rare, evolutionary trajectory. Here, we systematically characterized the multifaceted impact of a single-amino-acid deletion at residue 227 of HA (designated HAΔ227), a naturally occurring deletion within the 220-loop that overlaps a key antigenic epitope, using isogenic reverse genetics H9N2 viruses. Paradoxically, the HAΔ227 imposed a fitness cost and was associated with enhanced HA receptor-binding avidity, reduced apparent virion-associated NA activity, altered HA/NA functional balance, attenuated viral replication in vitro, and reduced respiratory shedding in vivo. Notably, despite this compromised replicative fitness, infection with the mutant virus was associated with an altered host immune response in chickens, characterized by elevated levels of interferon-γ (IFN-γ), interleukin-10 (IL-10), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1). These altered immune responses were associated with more severe pulmonary lesions, indicating a dissociation between disease severity and viral RNA load. Furthermore, the deletion increased the pH threshold for HA-mediated membrane fusion and substantially altered antigenic relationships. Collectively, our findings identify HA residue 227 as a functionally important site at which a single-residue deletion is associated with a phenotypic trade-off between replicative capacity and disease severity: reduced replicative fitness accompanied by altered inflammatory responses and greater tissue injury. This study highlights the potential phenotypic significance of a rare deletion in influenza virus HA and demonstrates that viral burden alone may not adequately predict disease severity.
records.authors: Sun Y, Zhu Y, Zhang P, Sheng S, Gai L, Li S, Zhang F, Cao P, He A, Wang W, Li X, Cong Y.

records.title: Domain Swapping Reveals Direction-Dependent Compatibility of Fungal Polyketide Synthase-Nonribosomal Peptide Synthetase Off-Loading Domains.
records.abstract: Two fungal natural products, hirsutellone and didymellamide, are proposed to be biosynthesized from closely related β-ketoamide intermediates despite producing structurally distinct cyclic products. This unusual biosynthetic relationship raises the question of whether the corresponding polyketide synthase-nonribosomal peptide synthetase (PKS-NRPS) off-loading domains are functionally interchangeable. Here, we identified and characterized HirA, a PKS-NRPS involved in hirsutellone biosynthesis, and used it together with AsolS, a PKS-NRPS involved in didymellamide biosynthesis, as a model system to investigate the compatibility of fungal PKS-NRPS off-loading domains. Heterologous expression in Aspergillus oryzae established that HirA produces a β-ketoamide intermediate possessing a nonaketide polyketide chain closely related to that generated by AsolS. Reciprocal domain swapping revealed asymmetric compatibility: artificial fusion of the HirA-derived reductase domain to the AsolS assembly line supported productive processing of the AsolS-derived intermediate, whereas reciprocal fusion of the Dieckmann cyclase domain yielded the C18-derived product at a low level but did not produce the expected tetramic acid derivative. These results demonstrate that off-loading activity can be retained following domain swapping between distinct fungal PKS-NRPS systems, but the extent of productive processing is strongly direction-dependent. Taken together, our findings identify direction-dependent compatibility and fusion-site dependence as important constraints for engineering fungal PKS-NRPS off-loading domains.
records.authors: Sato S, Ugai T, Yamane M, Liu X, Oikawa H, Minami A.

records.title: Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses prioritize candidate genes associated with lysosomes and ferroptosis in rheumatoid arthritis synovium.
records.abstract: ObjectivesTo prioritize candidate genes associated with lysosome-related and ferroptosis-related annotations in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) synovium and characterize their expression across synovial cell populations.MethodsPublicly available bulk and single-cell transcriptomic data from patients with RA and osteoarthritis (OA) were integrated with curated lysosome-related genes (LRGs) and ferroptosis-related genes (FRGs). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) shared by both gene sets were identified. Gene-set expression scoring and high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA) were used to characterize cellular expression patterns and prioritize candidate genes. Candidate-gene expression was assessed in external datasets and by exploratory quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR).ResultsMyeloid cells and fibroblast-like synoviocyte (FLS) populations showed relatively high expression scores for the shared gene set. Intersection analysis of the shared DEGs and selected co-expression module genes identified four candidates: VAMP2, HRAS, GRN, and BGN. External datasets supported lower VAMP2 expression in RA than in OA. Exploratory qRT-PCR analysis of synovial samples from four patients with RA and four patients with OA showed a consistent expression difference.ConclusionIntegrated transcriptomic analyses prioritized VAMP2 as a candidate gene associated with lysosome-related and ferroptosis-related annotations in RA synovium. External datasets and exploratory qRT-PCR supported its lower expression in RA. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish a causal role for VAMP2 in lysosomal regulation or ferroptosis. Key Points • Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses prioritized four candidate genes associated with lysosome-related and ferroptosis-related annotations. • Myeloid cells and FLS populations showed relatively high expression scores for the shared gene set. • External datasets and exploratory qRT-PCR supported lower VAMP2 expression in RA, prioritizing it for further functional investigation.
records.authors: Yan G, Yan H, Yu P, Xiang Y, Yang G, Zhang Y, Long L, Huang X.

records.title: Gene-metabolite-cardiac associations in the Chronic Kidney Disease in Children (CKiD) study.
records.abstract: BackgroundCharacterizing gene-metabolite-cardiac associations in childhood chronic kidney disease (CKD) has the potential to identify new research directions or therapeutic targets for mitigating the excessive cardiovascular risk in childhood CKD.MethodsThe Chronic Kidney Disease in Children (CKiD) is a prospective cohort that recruited children with eGFR 30-90 ml/min/1.73 m2 across 54 North American centers. Predictor and outcome variables included genotypes, metabolite levels, left ventricular mass index (LVMI) z-score, and left ventricular filling pressure (E/e'). Multivariable linear regression analyses assessed metabolite associations with either LVMI z-score or E/e', adjusting for age, sex, CKD duration, glomerular etiology, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system blockade, hypertension, anemia, dyslipidemia, eGFR, and proteinuria. Significance was based on the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate Results556 unique participants with 574 metabolites and ~8.4 million SNPs were included. Sphingomyelin (d18:2/d18:1) and hypotaurine were associated with LVMI z-score. Isobutyrylglycine and 3beta-hydroxy-5-cholestenoate were associated with E/e'. Multiple genetic variants associated with these metabolites at p ConclusionsWe identified metabolites associated with cardiac markers in children with CKD. We identified genetic associations with variability in these metabolites. Collectively, these gene-metabolite associations suggest roles for inflammation, increased oxidative stress, mitochondrial and energy dysmetabolism, and gut microbial dysbiosis in mediating cardiac pathology in childhood CKD. A higher resolution version of the Graphical abstract is available as Supplementary information.

records.title: BK polyomavirus viraemia after kidney transplantation: incidence, graft survival and its association with urinary tract malignancies.
records.abstract: BackgroundBK polyomavirus (BKPyV) nephropathy is an important cause of graft dysfunction and loss after kidney transplant. Treatment options are limited and predominately involve immunosuppression reduction with a limited role for anti-viral medications. There have been some reports of BKPyV-DNAemia and its association with bladder cancer.MethodsWe examined the incidence and impact of BKPyV in 1372 first-time kidney transplant recipients from 2011 to 2022, using prospectively collected data from the National Renal Transplant Registry and the National Virus Reference Laboratory. We assessed risk factors, graft survival, and development of post-transplant bladder cancer. Recipients underwent regular viral load monitoring with BKPyV-DNAemia defined as >1000 copies per millilitre (CPM).ResultsBKPyV-DNAemia was detected in 22.2% of recipients. Graft survival was comparable between groups; five-year survival was 91% in the BKPyV-DNAemia-positive group versus 88% in the BKPyV-DNAemia-negative group. Post-transplant bladder cancer occurred in .87% (n = 12) of recipients. However, bladder cancer occurred in 2.6% (n = 8) of BKPyV-DNAemia-positive compared to 0.37% (n = 4) of BKPyV-DNAemia-negative recipients. Multivariate analysis revealed a significantly increased risk of bladder cancer in the BKPyV-DNAemia group (adjusted hazard ratio 4.95, P = .008), furthermore we noticed a marked increase in hazard ratio as levels increased from 1000 CPM to 10 000 CPM. In BKPyV-DNAemia patients, median time to cancer diagnosis was 72 months post-transplant, with median survival of 25 months after diagnosis.ConclusionsThis association between BKPyV-DNAemia and post-transplant bladder cancer suggests the need for close surveillance for signs of bladder cancer in these patients.

records.title: SARS-CoV-2 Nsp2 reprograms host immunity to drive pathogenic inflammation.
records.abstract: Despite the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate endemically, highlighting the need to better understand the viral determinants of pathogenesis. Putative functions of the non-structural protein 2 (Nsp2) have been studied in vitro, but how Nsp2 affects pathogenesis and overall viral fitness in vivo has yet to be demonstrated. Here, we generated a recombinant SARS-CoV-2 lacking Nsp2 (ΔNsp2) to investigate its role in viral replication and disease. While ΔNsp2 replicated comparably to wild-type virus in vitro and in vivo, its deletion resulted in markedly attenuated disease in K18-hACE2 mice. Wild-type virus infection induced a strong pro-inflammatory response associated with increased recruitment of monocytes and macrophages, whereas ΔNsp2 virus infection promoted a more balanced antiviral response characterized by enhanced lymphocyte and NK cell recruitment. This was accompanied by reduced pulmonary and systemic inflammation and distinct transcriptional programs, including downregulation of pathways related to RNA processing and translation. Mechanistically, CLIP-seq and proximity labeling suggest that Nsp2 interacts with host RNA and components of the translational machinery. Together, our findings identify Nsp2 as a key virulence factor that drives immunopathology by skewing host immune responses, highlighting its role as a regulator of host-pathogen interactions.IMPORTANCEThe COVID-19 pandemic has officially ended, yet the virus that causes it continues to circulate and evolve, making it important to understand what makes it cause severe disease. This study focuses on a viral protein called Nsp2 and asks what role it plays in driving illness. Using an animal model, we observed that when Nsp2 was removed from the virus, infected animals became far less sick, even though the virus itself replicated just as well. Instead of triggering the harmful, excessive inflammation typically seen with the full virus, the modified virus prompted a more balanced immune response. Further investigation revealed that Nsp2 interacts directly with the host's genetic machinery, suggesting a mechanism by which the virus hijacks immune signaling to worsen disease. These findings pinpoint Nsp2 as a driver of COVID-19 severity and a promising target for future therapies aimed at reducing inflammation rather than simply fighting the virus itself.
records.authors: Lacasse É, Dubuc I, Leclerc J, Gravel A, Gudimard L, Joly-Beauparlant C, Faure M, Fortin P, Blanchet M-R, Droit A, Flamand L.

records.title: ZmSGT1-mediated competitive protection of ZmBBI1 enhances maize resistance to Rhizoctonia solani.
records.abstract: Banded leaf and sheath blight (BLSB), incited by the necrotrophic basidiomycete Rhizoctonia solani, is a devastating soil-borne disease that severely constrains global maize (Zea mays) production. Bowman-Birk inhibitors (BBIs) constitute a critical class of protease inhibitors in plant innate immunity; yet, their biological functions and upstream regulatory circuits in maize defense against necrotrophic pathogens remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we show that ZmBBI1, a BBI family member transcriptionally upregulated upon R. solani infection, positively modulates BLSB resistance. Its defense activity is strictly dependent on trypsin-inhibitory function, mediated by the evolutionarily conserved Thr52 and Arg53 residues in its canonical reactive loop. We identify Rs03254, a secreted virulence effector from R. solani, that directly engages ZmBBI1 and biochemically inactivates its protease-inhibitory activity to promote fungal colonization. We further demonstrate that the conserved immune co-chaperone ZmSGT1 physically interacts with ZmBBI1 and is genetically required for its full defense function. Mechanistically, ZmSGT1 competes with Rs03254 for binding to ZmBBI1, displacing the pathogen effector and restoring ZmBBI1's trypsin-inhibitory activity. Our work defines a tripartite molecular arms race module in the maize-R. solani pathosystem and uncovers a noncanonical role for SGT1 as a molecular bodyguard that protects host defense factors from effector-mediated suppression, providing actionable targets for engineering durable BLSB resistance in maize.
records.authors: Sun Y, Wang L, He X, Zhu B, Ma Z, Wan K, Li N.

records.title: An IoT-enabled hybrid paper/polymer-based microfluidic device for rapid detection of Campylobacter jejuni in foods.
records.abstract: Campylobacter jejuni is the leading bacterial cause of foodborne gastroenteritis worldwide and represents a major public health concern. We report an IoT-enabled hybrid paper/polymer-based microfluidic device for rapid detection of C. jejuni in food matrices. This platform integrates recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA), CRISPR/Cas12a-based sequence recognition, and lateral flow readout within a foldable paper-based architecture incorporating PDMS reservoirs. An IoT workflow was established to enable automated image capture, result classification, and centralized data transmission. Analytical performance was evaluated using both pure cultures and food samples. This assay specifically detected C. jejuni with no observed cross-reactivity among the tested strains and achieved a limit of detection of 5800 CFU mL-1 using the developed microfluidic device. In chicken breast samples, C. jejuni was reliably detected at initial inoculation levels of 100 to 103 CFU g-1 following 6-12 h of enrichment, while higher contamination levels (>103 CFU g-1) were detectable without enrichment. The complete workflow from DNA extraction to visual readout was completed in ∼1 h. By integrating microfluidic sensing, automated data interpretation, and IoT-enabled connectivity, this platform provides a practical and scalable approach for decentralized screening and rapid monitoring of C. jejuni in agri-food system.
records.authors: He Y, Liu J, Li S, Zhao X, Lu X.

records.title: Adeno-associated virus gene therapy for hemophilia B: a comparative appraisal of the licensed products.
records.abstract: Among the inherited bleeding disorders, hemophilia B has become the leading target for adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapy. The compact factor IX (FIX) coding sequence, the abundance and durability of hepatocyte-derived FIX expression and the hyperactive FIX-Padua variant together made single-infusion phenotypic correction achievable earlier and more convincingly for FIX deficiency than for factor VIII (FVIII) deficiency. Three FIX-Padua AAV products have reached regulatory approval: etranacogene dezaparvovec, licensed in the United States, Canada and Europe; fidanacogene elaparvovec, initially licensed in the same regions but discontinued worldwide by its manufacturer; and dalnacogene ponparvovec (BBM-H901), licensed in China. This review outlines the biological differences between FVIII and FIX, the immunological and analytical challenges common to all AAV FIX products, and the pivotal trial data for each licensed therapy. Because FIX-Padua activity is reagent dependent, activity is standardized throughout to a single one-stage scale (HemosIL SynthASil), permitting a like-for-like comparison: mean activity 27-55 IU/dL, annualized bleeding rates 0.6-1.5 and reductions in FIX consumption exceeding 90% for all three products, sustained to five years for etranacogene dezaparvovec and six for the fidanacogene elaparvovec phase 1/2a cohort. Only dalnacogene ponparvovec has published data in adolescents. The review compares the three products' capsids, genome configurations, doses, impact of pre-existing anti-AAV immunity and immunomodulation, and weighs their reassuring but surveillance-dependent long-term safety, including the theoretical risk of insertional oncogenesis. Finally, it considers why the clearest efficacy successes have coincided with limited real-world uptake, and what the divergent commercial and regulatory trajectories imply for equitable global access.
records.authors: Miesbach W, Pierce GF.

records.title: From long-term progeny trials to genomic selection: empirical prediction and simulation-guided redesign of Scots pine breeding in Germany.
records.abstract: In Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.), long generation intervals limit genetic gain, but mature progeny trials may provide reference populations for genomic selection. We combined repeated phenotypes from two German trials established in 1990 with single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotypes, parentage auditing, duplicate filtering, and empirically calibrated forward simulations. Of 1,986 phenotype-matched genotyped trees, 1,651 remained after quality control. Across 14 trait-by-age combinations, genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) gave modest but consistent improvements in predictive ability for diameter and volume from age 20 onwards. For volume at age 20 (V20), repeated leave-progeny-out predictive ability increased from 0.233 with pedigree-based additive best linear unbiased prediction (ABLUP) to 0.268 with GBLUP, and GBLUP exceeded ABLUP in all 20 matched partitions. Paired jackknife intervals did not establish systematic differences in narrow-sense heritability. ABLUP and GBLUP rankings were highly correlated, but only 75.9% of the top 10% V20 candidates overlapped. Simulations calibrated to empirical V20 variance components and family relationships compared phenotypic selection, ABLUP, progeny testing, direct genomic selection, and genomic selection followed by phenotypic thinning. After five cycles, progeny testing produced the greatest cumulative additive genetic gain (163.3%), whereas direct genomic selection produced the greatest annual gain (1.208% yr-1) because of shorter cycles. Faster genomic pathways accumulated more kinship, and a kinship-aware penalty reduced relatedness with pathway-specific effects on gain. These results support staged genomic implementation with continual reference-population updating, field validation, and explicit coancestry management.
records.authors: Degen B, Leite Montalvão AP, Schneck V.

records.title: Dysregulated CSF T-cell responses and their evolution after intravenous immunoglobulin in Guillain-Barré syndrome.
records.abstract: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated neuropathy that frequently results in long-term disability. The cellular mechanisms underlying GBS and the immunomodulatory effects of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) remain incompletely understood. In this prospective observational cohort study, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing with paired T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing on peripheral blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) collected before and after IVIg treatment from treatment-naïve patients with GBS. Pre-treatment blood and CSF were obtained from nine and eight patients, respectively; post-treatment samples were available from six patients for blood and three patients for CSF. Previously published healthy control (HC) blood and CSF single-cell datasets were analyzed for comparison. We characterized immune cell composition, transcriptional states, TCR clonality, and clonal dynamics across peripheral and CSF compartments as well as following treatment. Individuals with GBS exhibited enrichment of T helper 1 (Th1)-polarized CD4+ T cells, activated and resident-memory CD8+ T cells, and macrophages in CSF relative to paired peripheral blood. This CSF-to-blood enrichment was greater than in healthy controls (HCs) for Th1 cells, activated effector-memory CD8+ T cells, and inflammatory macrophages, although the overall degree of T-cell clonal expansion was similar between groups. In both GBS and HCs, expanded CSF CD4+ clonotypes were predominantly Th1-polarized and largely absent from blood, whereas expanded CD8+ clonotypes showed greater overlap between compartments. Among clonotypes detected in both blood and CSF, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells exhibited more activated transcriptional states in the CSF, a shift that was particularly pronounced in GBS. Following IVIg treatment, peripheral blood showed minimal changes, whereas CSF T-cell populations exhibited more substantial alterations, including reductions in Th1-associated and activated effector-memory states, increases in T helper 2 (Th2) and regulatory T cell populations, and changes in the clonal repertoire. Expanded T cell clonotypes with sequence-based predicted specificity for pathogens associated with GBS were identified in six patients, and convergent clonotype groups were detected both within and across patients. Demyelinating GBS is characterized by compartmentalized enrichment and activation of pro-inflammatory T-cell populations within the CSF rather than an overall increase in T-cell clonal expansion. Exploratory longitudinal findings further suggest that CSF T-cell populations are altered following IVIg treatment. Integrated single-cell transcriptomic and TCR analyses provide insight into the early immune response in GBS and identify candidate cellular pathways for biomarker development and therapeutic investigation.
records.authors: Morrison AH, Yao T, Isfort MC, Morena J, Liu T, Roell J, Akkaya B, Kolb SJ, Bell EH, Saligrama N, Segal BM.

records.title: R-loopBase v2.0: species- and cell type-resolved quantitative R-loop maps and R-loop regulatory resources.
records.abstract: R-loops are non-canonical nucleic acid structures implicated in diverse cellular processes and diseases. We previously developed R-loopBase to address the pressing challenges of inaccurate R-loop maps and the limited understanding of the R-loop regulatory network. However, R-loopBase provided only human R-loop maps with categorical confidence and did not account for cell type specificity. These limitations, coupled with the emerging R-loop profiling technologies and advances in R-loop regulatory mechanisms, have motivated the development of R-loopBase v2.0 (https://rloopbase.nju.edu.cn). After uniformly re-analysing 358 R-loop mapping datasets generated by 16 technologies, we introduce a quantitative R-loop scoring framework that assesses genome-wide R-loop confidence in human, demonstrating strong concordance with known R-loop biology. We further extend the framework to specific cell types and mouse, fruit fly, and yeast. In parallel, we substantially expand the collection of R-loop regulators across species, enabling the inference of changes in R-loop homeostasis. Building on these expanded datasets, we implement several new interactive features and analytical tools, including an expanded multi-species genome browser, deep learning-based R-loop prediction, R-loop homeostasis analysis, and a streamlined data download portal. We anticipate that R-loopBase v2.0 will serve as an enhanced, up-to-date one-stop resource for the R-loop research community.
records.authors: Gu R, Hu J, Gao Y, Yang H, Lin R, Zhong X, Zhang KX, Li W, Hu Q, Wei L, Xing Z, Chen JY.

records.title: Pneumocystis phosphoglucomutase links glucose-phosphate metabolism to β-1,3-glucan synthesis and cell-wall integrity
records.abstract: The fungal cell wall is a dynamic, carbohydrate-rich structure whose composition is closely coordinated with cellular metabolism. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, linking carbon metabolism with UDP-glucose-dependent cell-wall biosynthesis. We previously identified functional Pgm2 homologs from Pneumocystis jirovecii and Pneumocystis murina. Here, using a Saccharomyces cerevisiae pgm2Δ complementation model, we examined the relationship between Pgm2 activity, β-1,3-glucan, and cell-wall integrity. Pgm2 deficiency reduced β-1,3-glucan content and altered zymolyase sensitivity without major changes in cell-wall thickness. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed that the pgm2Δ mutant exhibited coordinated metabolic and cell-wall transcriptional responses, including increased SLT2/MPK1, RLM1, FKS2/GSC2, GFA1, CHS1, CRH1, SED1, and CWP1 expression and decreased FKS1, GAS1, GAS3, and CHS2 expression. Expression of either Pjpgm2 or Pmpgm2 broadly shifted these responses toward wild-type levels. Selected transcriptional changes were further evaluated by qRT-PCR, which supported the major stress and cell-wall responses identified by RNA sequencing. FKS2/GSC2 showed the same directional pattern, although differences were not statistically significant by qRT-PCR. Despite this compensatory response, Pgm2-deficient cells were markedly more susceptible to sublethal caspofungin, whereas either Pneumocystis Pgm2 homolog restored tolerance toward wild-type levels. These findings link Pgm2-dependent glucose-phosphate metabolism with β-1,3-glucan levels and cell-wall function. Given the importance of β-1,3-glucan to the Pneumocystis cyst wall and its limited cell-wall biosynthetic pathways, these findings further support Pgm2 as an important component of Pneumocystis cell-wall biology and a potential antifungal target.
