records.title: Temperature alters Culex tarsalis West Nile virus vector competence, tissue bottlenecks, and transcriptional responses
records.abstract: West Nile virus is an arbovirus transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Temperature is frequently the strongest abiotic factor impacting transmission in many virus-vector pairings, including WNV and Culex. However, it is unknown how temperature impacts WNV population bottlenecks and transcriptional responses to infection in Culex tarsalis. We found that elevated temperatures led to increased likelihood of transmission of rare virus variants due to increased vector competence and less stringent tissue barriers. Analysis of Cx. tarsalis transcriptional responses confirmed that WNV infection had minimal impacts on transcriptional activity. Temperature, however, induced significant changes to mosquito gene expression, whereas canonical immune gene expression minimally changed in response to infection. Thus, temperature impacts bottlenecks in the Culex-WNV system independent of known antiviral pathways, possibly by altering virus replication dynamics. While temperature had a dramatic impact on bottleneck stringency, this is likely independent of antiviral pathways and instead some other change to mosquito biology. Together, these results shed light on the relationships between temperature, virus evolutionary dynamics and antiviral immunity.
records.authors: Gallichotte EN, King DC, Marsico B, Fitzmeyer EA, Ogg HA, Kimball KX, Ebel N, Campbell CL, Ebel GD.

records.title: RNA Polymerase Backtracking Promotes Type III-A CRISPR DNA Targeting
records.abstract: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems provide transcription-dependent immunity against mobile genetic elements, yet the mechanism underlying their DNA targeting remains unclear. Although the type III effector Cas10-Csm functions as a single-stranded DNase  in vitro , type III systems eliminate double-stranded DNA targets  in vivo , suggesting that transcription generates critical DNA substrates. Here, we show that conserved RNA polymerase anti-backtracking factors, such as GreA, selectively inhibit DNA-targeting of type III immunity. GreA overexpression abolishes protection against both phages and conjugative plasmids, whereas mutations that disrupt GreA anti-backtracking activity eliminate this effect. In contrast, immunity mediated by the type II CRISPR-Cas system or the auxiliary type III RNase Csm6 remain unaffected, demonstrating that GreA specifically suppresses Cas10-dependent DNA interference. These findings identify RNA polymerase backtracking as a key determinant of Cas10-Csm activity and support a model in which arrested transcription complexes generate substrates for DNA degradation, opening up new anti-CRISPR strategies against type III.
records.authors: Hernandez Viera AJ, Gross NR, Tran PQ, Shahin O, Kosmopoulos JC, Anantharaman K, Mo CY.

records.title: Highly prevalent cargo genes of F plasmids harbored in pathogenic Escherichia coli
records.abstract: Analysis of prevalent orthogroups (OGs) in a collection of F plasmids from extraintestinal Escherichia coli ST131 isolates has led to the identification of two groups of previously uncharacterized cargo genes that may be widely distributed among F plasmids of pathogenic E. coli. Group 1 comprises four OGs whose encoded proteins are predicted to be involved in transport-related functions. The corresponding genes cluster with other genes associated with metabolism and are highly prevalent in extraintestinal ST131 isolates. Group 2 comprises several OGs whose encoded proteins currently have unknown functions. These OGs are present in a large proportion of F plasmids from both intestinal and extraintestinal E. coli isolates. The corresponding genes cluster within an F-plasmid region that also contains genes involved in DNA metabolism, suggesting that the proteins encoded by these newly identified OGs may likewise contribute to F-plasmid DNA biology. Characterizing the functions of these newly identified proteins may improve our understanding of the contribution of F plasmid to E. coli virulence and reveal novel targets for antimicrobial intervention, either by limiting F-plasmid dissemination among multidrug-resistant (MDR) E. coli strains or by directly targeting plasmid-carrying bacteria.
records.authors: Guirao-Rico S, Flament-Simon SC, Madrid C, Balsalobre C, Huttener M, Blanco JE, Blanco J, Rozas J, Juarez A.

records.title: Live attenuated YFV-17D vaccine induces robust B and T cell immunity in vaccine-draining lymph nodes
records.abstract: The yellow fever virus-17D (YFV-17D) vaccine is widely regarded as one of the most effective vaccines in existence, with protection linked to robust elicitation of neutralising antibodies1. The features of the germinal centre (GC) reaction driving this durable and potent antibody responses remain unclear. Here we examined immune dynamics in blood and lymph nodes (LNs) after primary YFV-17D immunisation in humans. Using fine needle biopsy (FNB), we identified robust T and B lymphocyte responses within draining LNs, underpinning maturation of antibodies targeting the viral envelope (E). Early antibody responses were largely IgM, with gradual accumulation of E-specific memory B cells and anti-viral IgG in the subsequent months. Monoclonal antibodies derived from GC B cells had specificity for E, with diversification in the LN capable of driving increases in binding and neutralising potency. While circulating vaccine-specific CD4+ T cells peaked two weeks post-vaccination, clonally related GC and IL-10+ T follicular helper populations progressively accumulated in the LN. Comparison of FNB transcriptional datasets following YFV-17D, SARS-CoV-2 mRNA/LNP, and seasonal influenza vaccination identified a conserved GC program involving similar B and T lymphocyte subpopulations. Collectively, we find that while YFV-17D induces robust GC activity, this trait is shared with other vaccine platforms and the notably durable protection against infection may reflect an incapacity of the virus to escape host immunity.

records.title: A Concentration-Matrix Approach to Assess Planktonic Growth and Biofilm Biomass in Pseudomonas aeruginosa Exposed to Rifampicin and Moringa oleifera Leaf Ethanolic Extract
records.abstract: Biofilm formation by Pseudomonas aeruginosa complicates antimicrobial treatment, particularly in persistent infections, and motivates the assessment of plant-derived antibiotic adjuncts. The influence of Moringa oleifera leaf ethanolic extract on rifampicin responses across planktonic growth and biofilm formation requires concentration-resolved evaluation. Three independent experiments assessed planktonic growth and crystal violet-stained biofilm biomass across ethanolic extract–rifampicin concentration matrices. Conventional PCR screened selected biofilm-associated genes. The ethanolic extract alone yielded 99.33–119.33% planktonic growth relative to controls at 1–64 µg/mL. Rifampicin alone reduced growth to 58.67 ± 1.15% and 6.67 ± 0.58% at 16 and 32 µg/mL, respectively. Adding 16 µg/mL ethanol fraction to 16 µg/mL rifampicin yielded 44.67 ± 30.99% growth, compared with 58.67 ± 1.15% for rifampicin alone. At 32 µg/mL rifampicin, the same fraction addition yielded 16.00 ± 13.00% growth, compared with 6.67 ± 0.58% for rifampicin alone. Biofilm biomass at 16 µg/mL rifampicin was 55.67 ± 67.00%, reaching 70.00 ± 86.88% with ethanol fraction addition. All 49 paired comparisons per assay yielded false-discovery-rate-adjusted q-values above 0.05. PCR detected pelA, pslA, pslD, pqsA, lasR, and ndvB. The concentration matrices revealed distinct planktonic growth and biofilm biomass responses. These findings position complementary planktonic and biofilm measurements as essential criteria for assessing plant–antibiotic combinations, providing concentration-specific evidence to guide formulation screening and antimicrobial candidate prioritization.
records.authors: Hapsari BK, Natzir R, Sultan AR, Syamsuri F, Astuti I, Bahar B, Aswad M, Hatta M.

records.title: TRIM63-associated signal in sunitinib-resistant xenografts and an eight- gene prognostic score in renal cell carcinoma
records.abstract: Abstract  Background  Sunitinib resistance limits the durable activity of anti-angiogenic therapy in renal cell carcinoma (RCC). This study screened TRIM-family expression in the GSE64052 786-O xenograft model and evaluated a TRIM63-anchored eight-gene risk score (TRIM-8RS) comprising OTX1, LIMCH1, ANK3, TRIM63, CAVIN2, CLTRN, WFDC10B and BBOX1 for prognostic association. Methods  The score was evaluated in The Cancer Genome Atlas kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (TCGA-KIRC) development cohort (508 patients; 171 deaths) and an independent Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium operational primary-RCC cohort (183 patients; 31 deaths). Model development was repeated with all outcome-dependent candidate screening confined to outer training folds, and discrimination was assessed with Uno's concordance index and inverse-probability-of-censoring-weighted time-dependent receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results  TRIM63 expression was directionally higher in resistant xenografts, but the association did not survive genome-wide false-discovery-rate adjustment (log2 fold change, 1.84; nominal P = 0.038; adjusted P = 0.291). The apparent Uno concordance index was 0.738 in the development cohort and 0.716 in the external cohort. The 1- and 3-year areas under the curve were 0.804 and 0.745 in TCGA-KIRC and 0.793 and 0.770 in the external cohort, and overall survival differed between risk groups defined by the frozen TCGA median score in both cohorts (hazard ratios, 4.56 and 4.51, respectively). The leakage-controlled reconstruction yielded a mean outer-fold concordance index of 0.699, and multivariable models further adjusted for age, sex and, in TCGA-KIRC, stage and grade. In public single-cell data, TRIM63 was detected in 49 of 17,986 cells, each with one raw unique molecular identifier, and spatial data showed low and variable fractions of TRIM63-positive spots across 11 slides. Conclusion  These findings support a preliminary prognostic association and further biological validation. They do not establish a causal resistance mechanism or predict clinical benefit.

records.title: Genome Mining-Driven Discovery of the Sactipeptide Smithiosin in Probiotic, Thermophilic Strain Bacillus smithii.
records.abstract: Sactipeptides are a class of ribosomally synthesised and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs), which have a cyclic topology formed by unique thioether crosslinks called sactionines. Sactionines are introduced by radical S-adenosylmethionine (rSAM) enzymes between cysteine residues and the α-carbon of other amino acids. Genome sequencing has revealed many putative sactipeptide biosynthetic gene clusters; however, few sactipeptides have been isolated and characterised. Here, we use genome mining to identify a novel sactipeptide from Bacillus smithii. The novel sactipeptide, named smithiosin, was extracted from the industrially important thermophile B. smithii and characterised as a novel homologue of the previously characterised sactipeptide subtilosin A from B. subtilis. Furthermore, the smithiosin precursor peptide gene was heterologously expressed in the subtilosin A producer Bacillus subtilis 168 without knockout of the native precursor peptide, successfully leading to the production of both subtilosin A and smithiosin. This demonstrates for the first time that a non-native precursor peptide is able to outcompete the subtilosin A precursor for all of the native biosynthetic enzymes in B. subtilis, including the radical SAM enzyme AlbA. It also opens a potential new opportunity for screening non-native precursor peptides with the subtilosin A biosynthetic enzymes via heterologous expression in B. subtilis.
records.authors: Vasciaveo S, Zhou Y, Ding Y, Hind CK, Gräff ÁT, Camp AH, Sutton JM, Barry SM, Dickman R.

records.title: Modeling of Therapist-Client Dynamics in Psychotherapy Using Large Language Model-Based Assessments: Retrospective Observational Study of 1573 Psychotherapy Sessions.
records.abstract: BackgroundPsychotherapy is a primary treatment for many mental health conditions, yet the dynamic interplay among therapist behaviors, client responses, and the therapeutic relationship remains difficult to disentangle at scale. Traditional process research relies on labor-intensive human coding, limiting the ability to model moment-to-moment therapeutic dynamics across large datasets.ObjectiveThis study aimed to develop and validate a computational framework for modeling therapist-client interaction processes and to examine how therapist behaviors and relational qualities relate to client self-disclosure and emotional expression in psychotherapy sessions.MethodsWe developed automated assessment pipelines using large language models (LLMs) to measure therapist behaviors (empathy or exploration), relational quality (rapport), and client outcomes (self-disclosure, self-directed negative emotion, or outward-directed negative emotion). Model-generated scores were validated against human annotations. We then applied these measures to approximately 2000 hours of psychotherapy transcripts from the Alexander Street corpus. This yielded an estimation sample of 119,233 client utterances from 1573 sessions and 37 clients. Because utterances are nested within sessions and sessions within clients, we estimated a saturated multivariate structural equation model with SEs clustered at the session level. Results were confirmed in a multilevel regression model with random intercepts for session and client.ResultsFollowing comparative validation of 6 candidate language models, automated measures showed good to excellent agreement with human annotations (intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC]=0.60-0.81) for rapport (ICC=0.81), self-disclosure (ICC=0.78), empathy components (ICC=0.60-0.75), and emotion measurements (ICC=0.66-0.80). Structural equation modeling analyses revealed that therapist empathy and exploration were each associated with increased client disclosure (empathy: β=.086, 95% CI 0.078-0.095; exploration: β=.086, 95% CI 0.078-0.094; both PConclusionsThis study demonstrates that LLM-based measurement combined with structural modeling can capture core therapeutic processes at scale. Empathy and exploration showed small but consistent turn-level associations with client disclosure and emotional expression, whereas prior-session rapport did not show a robust association. These findings provide a computational foundation for precision modeling of psychotherapy processes and may offer actionable insights for scalable therapist training and AI-supported clinical education systems.
records.authors: Chen AH, Jin S, Wang C, Swartz HA, Wu T, Kraut RE, Zhu H.

records.title: Resistance to SDHI Fungicides in Monilinia fructicola Field Isolates Is Associated with Amino Acid Substitutions Across SDH Subunits.
records.abstract: Brown rot, caused by Monilinia fructicola, is the most destructive pre- and postharvest fruit rot of peach worldwide. In 2024, a disease outbreak occurred in a South Carolina orchard despite a rigorous chemical management program consisting of preharvest applications of succinate dehydrogenase inhibitor (SDHI), quinone outside inhibitor, and demethylation inhibitor (DMI) fungicides. Isolates from affected orchards carried the Mona element upstream of the MfCYP51 gene, and propiconazole discriminatory dose assays confirmed reduced sensitivity in vitro, with all 2024 isolates exhibiting relative growth greater than 20%. They displayed either low, moderate, or high levels of resistance to boscalid, isofetamid, fluopyram, and fluxapyroxad based on EC50 values ranging from 0.30 to 14.74, 0.07 to 1.93, 0.26 to 3.48, and 0.19 to 2.82 µg/ml, respectively. In contrast, EC50 values obtained for historic isolates were ≤0.05 µg/ml for all SDHI fungicides. Whole-genome sequencing, followed by targeted amplification and sequencing of SDH subunits across the isolate collection, identified five SDH genotypes: wild type (no amino acid substitutions), G1 (N226H in SDHB), G2 (P80H in SDHC), G3 (N226H in SDHB and V26I in SDHD), and G4 (N226H in SDHB, P80H in SDHC, and T24A in SDHD). Isolates harboring amino acid changes in multiple SDH subunits had the highest EC50 values and were resistant to all SDHIs tested. Detached fruit assays confirmed that label rates of SDHI fungicides failed to control isolates carrying multiple amino acid changes. To the best of our knowledge, this study provides the first report worldwide of SDHI resistance in Monilinia species field isolates linked to amino acid changes in the SDH subunits and combined SDHI and DMI resistance in peach orchards, highlighting the need for resistance monitoring and management.
records.authors: Gelain J, Wesche J, Trotter EK, Beger M, Ortiz M, Schnabel G.

records.title: Comparison of Next-Generation Sequencing and Quantitative PCR Methodologies for Quantification of Fungicide Resistance in Mixed Samples of Colletotrichum siamense.
records.abstract: Measuring the frequency of fungicide resistance alleles in pathogen populations is critical for understanding resistance spread and severity. TaqMan quantitative PCR (qPCR) is a standard method for allele quantification, whereas next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies offer an alternative for high-resolution detection. Because studies exploring NGS for this purpose are limited, the objective of this study was to compare the accuracy and feasibility of Illumina NGS amplicon sequencing with that of a previously validated TaqMan qPCR assay to quantify resistance alleles to thiophanate-methyl fungicide in a set of mixed Colletotrichum siamense DNA samples. For validation, a set with known frequencies of resistance to thiophanate-methyl was used as a control. Both the NGS- and qPCR-based methods were highly precise, with an R2 of 0.99 and 0.97, respectively, for the C. siamense DNA samples with known resistance frequencies. However, with the samples of unknown resistance frequencies that were collected from detached blueberry fruit assays, the NGS method demonstrated more variability than the TaqMan method (P < 0.001). This variability was likely associated with low target DNA concentration and the presence of host and nontarget fungal DNA, which reduced PCR efficiency. This study highlighted strengths and weaknesses of both technologies and important assay design considerations. It was concluded that NGS-based methodologies may be preferential for large sample sizes and for detecting multiple or novel mutations within a region, whereas the qPCR assay can be more efficient for rapid quantification of known alleles.

records.title: Antimicrobial Nanoparticles Against Resistant Bacteria and Biofilms: From Material Design to Clinical Translation
records.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and biofilm-associated infections continue to compromise the effectiveness of conventional antibiotics, highlighting the need for complementary therapeutic approaches. Nanoparticle-based systems offer two distinct but potentially convergent strategies: direct antibacterial activity and improved delivery of antimicrobial agents. This narrative review critically examines inorganic, organic, and hybrid nanoplatforms, including metal and metal-oxide nanoparticles, carbon-derived materials, mesoporous silica, polymeric carriers, lipid-based systems, and stimuli-responsive formulations. Their mechanisms of action, physicochemical determinants of efficacy, and potential applications against multidrug-resistant bacteria and biofilm-associated infections are discussed. Particular attention is given to the distinction between bacterial resistance, tolerance, and persistence, as well as the challenges associated with nanoparticle penetration, antimicrobial synergy, and reproducible antibacterial activity. Although preclinical findings demonstrate considerable therapeutic potential, translation into clinical practice remains limited. Inhaled liposomal amikacin illustrates the clinical relevance of indication-specific nanodelivery, while emphasizing that therapeutic benefits cannot be generalized across nanoparticle formulations. Major challenges include cytotoxicity, bacterial adaptation, biodistribution, stability in biological environments, manufacturing scalability, regulatory requirements, and environmental safety. Future research should prioritize standardized characterization, clinically relevant infection models, robust comparisons with conventional treatments, and integrated assessments of safety and resistance evolution. Within a One Health framework, nanoparticle-based technologies may contribute to more effective antimicrobial therapies, provided that their development is guided by demonstrable clinical benefits, responsible antimicrobial use, and consideration of their broader environmental impact.

records.title: A Transcriptome-Inferred Binucleation State of CD10⁺ (MME⁺) Macrophages Consistent with Incomplete Cytokinesis: Morphology–Metabolism Coupling and a “Don’t-Eat-Me” Immune-Evasion Profile
records.abstract: Background:  Binucleated and multinucleated macrophages (cells carrying two or more nuclei in one cell body) occur in granulomas and tumors, yet their origins beyond cell–cell fusion, and the macrophage role of CD10 (MME), remain unresolved. We asked who CD10⁺ macrophages are, whether their binucleation reflects incomplete cytokinesis (failure of the final separation step of cell division), and how this state relates to phagocytic immune evasion. Methods: Analyzing 20,000 lung adenocarcinoma myeloid cells (GSE131907), we applied a three-axis discrimination rule (molecular-output level, lineage concordance, G2/M activity), a six-module prediction model, and a 35-molecule eat-me/don’t-eat-me panel. Results: CD10⁺ cells comprised 16.2% of myeloid cells (87.6% C1QC⁺ tumor-associated macrophage (TAM)-derived, predominantly normal-lung-derived alveolar macrophages) and split by origin into scavenger and inflammatory–pro-angiogenic types (Type-1 and Type-2). Transcriptome-inferred binucleated candidates constituted 27.0% of CD10⁺ cells with G2/M programs directionally elevated (consistent with incomplete cytokinesis over fusion; attenuated after library-size control); the state and its key contrasts replicated in tumor-restricted cells and an independent NSCLC atlas. The lysosome module showed the largest association (unadjusted Δ = +0.222; persists after library-size control, residual Δ = +0.068); the classifier reached an AUC of 0.77 (same-cohort, not externally validated). These cells also showed a transcript-level shift of the don’t-eat-me/eat-me balance centered on CD47 (Δ = +0.127; calreticulin unchanged)—itself both an anti-phagocytic checkpoint and a multinucleation participant. Conclusions: We hypothesize that lysosomal stress drives cytokinesis failure and barrier co-assembly, nominating the CD10⁺ binucleated state as a testable node of phagocytic immune evasion for combination checkpoint targeting.

records.title: Genetic code expansion for site-specific encoding of a switchable, intrinsic fluorophore-quencher pair to monitor protein dynamics.
records.abstract: Precisely modifying proteins at multiple sites in their native, folded structures offers unique opportunities to answer molecular and cellular-level biological questions. Here, we present a genetic code expansion strategy for site-specific integration of a fluorophore-quencher pair comprising two non-canonical amino acids-acridonylalanine (Acd) and methyltetrazinyl phenylalanine (Tet)-into a protein expressed in E. coli. The Acd and Tet pair requires no post-translational labeling, and quenching can be switched off by bioorthogonal or photochemical reactions of Tet for convenient internal control experiments. Mechanistic studies based on Stern-Volmer quenching, fluorescence lifetime measurements, and "proline ruler" peptides established the distance dependence of quenching. As proof-of-concept, we applied this strategy to study: (1) calmodulin, a calcium-sensing protein, (2) RecA, a DNA damage sensor in bacteria, and (3) LexA, a transcriptional repressor whose activation by RecA governs acquired antibiotic resistance in bacteria. Using these proteins, we demonstrate that dual Acd/Tet labeling provides molecular-level insights into protein dynamics, shows potential for adaptation to high-throughput drug screening, and advances tools for studying protein structure-function relationships.
records.authors: Giri P, Venkatesh Y, Mathis MH, Hurley CM, Jones CM, Ndogo Eteme O, Hostetler ZM, Cooley RB, Kohli RM, Mehl RA, Petersson EJ.

records.title: Engineering cyanobacterial carbonic anhydrase surface mutations for fast CO<sub>2</sub> hydration and capture.
records.abstract: Equilibration between CO2 and the other forms of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is slow under ambient conditions, bottlenecked by the hydration of dissolved CO2 to form bicarbonate and a proton. This step is often rate-limiting for aqueous CO2 capture processes under ambient temperature and pressure, and is precisely the chemistry catalyzed by the family of carbonic anhydrase enzymes. As a result, incorporation of carbonic anhydrases (CAs) into various CO2 capture schemes may be used to accelerate CO2 hydration, increasing the rates of downstream processes coupled to this DIC equilibrium. While this potential use for CA has been long-studied, extending these basic chemical principles to real applications have been hampered by practical questions of how to economically source carbonic anhydrase enzymes at mass scale. This work explores the use of modified cyanobacterial expression hosts as a potential resolution to that problem. Successful engineering of carbonic anhydrase surface display in fast-growing, marine cyanobacteria would yield a self-sustaining CO2 hydration catalyst that requires only sunlight, CO2 itself, and nutrients freely available in seawater, as inputs for passively generating carbonic anhydrases on the cell envelope during cell growth.

records.title: Continuous Capture of Recombinant Adeno-Associated Virus Particles Using Twin-Column CaptureSMB.
records.abstract: Recombinant adeno-associated viruses (rAAVs) have gained increasing importance in gene therapy due to their safe and precise gene delivery. However, certain indications require substantially higher vector doses, pushing manufacturing capacity and cost of goods (COG) to its limits. In this study, we present a proof-of-concept evaluation of a continuous twin-column capture process (CaptureSMB) enabling direct purification of rAAV5 from minimally processed, nonlysed perfusion harvest without prior enzymatic nuclease digestion, concentration or buffer exchange. This approach differs fundamentally from conventional batch workflows which typically mandate clarification and concentration before affinity capture and offers a novel process integration in viral vector manufacturing. A single-column batch capture process was developed first and subsequently compared to continuous CaptureSMB configurations. Optimized CaptureSMB operation achieved consistent yields over four cycles, with recoveries exceeding batch operation (+14.3%) with concomitant higher productivity (+11.4%) and reduced buffer consumption (-79.2%). Critical quality attribute (CQA) analysis showed lower host cell protein levels and lower residual DNA in early CaptureSMB cycles, while full capsid ratios, thermal stability and transduction efficiency of rAAV5 particles remained unaltered across cycles and process modes. However, progressive backpressure and residual impurity accumulation in later cycles highlight operational challenges associated with direct capture of low-titer feed streams. These findings highlight that continuous twin-column CaptureSMB directly from secretion-derived perfusion harvest can improve operational efficiency, lower buffer requirements, and also maintain and, in some respects, enhance product quality. This novel strategy provides a promising route to address manufacturing capacity and cost challenges in rAAV gene therapy production.
records.authors: Müller JM, Tobler D, Bühler J, Hauri D, Plieninger R, Göbel S, Saygili E, Higuchi Y, Takahashi R, Vogg S, Müller-Späth T, Villiger TK.

records.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity.
records.abstract: Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1-8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9-13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)-a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution-and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

records.title: Tetraspanin CD81 restricts Ebola virus infection and is antagonized by glycoprotein GP and matrix protein VP40.
records.abstract: Viruses manipulate host cell membranes to evade antiviral immunity, prevent superinfection, and optimize their replication and spread. The Ebola virus glycoprotein GP mediates viral entry but also contributes to the subversion of host antiviral immune responses. Here, we characterize the impact of Ebola virus GP on cell surface proteins and show that it reduces cell surface availability of tetraspanins CD81, CD63, and CD9. This function is conserved among several filoviral glycoproteins but not observed for glycoproteins of other viral families. Whereas CD63 and CD9 are largely dispensable for Ebola virus replication, CD81 suppresses virus-like particle entry and viral replication. This activity might be attributed to CD81-mediated suppression of NF-κB signaling, which is induced by the Ebola virus matrix protein VP40 and transcription- and replication-competent virus-like particle (trVLP) replication. Our results further indicate that both GP, which interacts directly with CD81, and VP40, which also associates with CD81, function to reduce total and surface expression levels of CD81. CD81 is shown to reduce levels of Ebola virus RNA species, and its antibody-mediated clustering can suppress Ebola virus infection. Our study provides insights into the roles of NF-κB signaling in Ebola virus replication and immunopathogenesis, and identifies tetraspanin CD81 as a potentially druggable Ebola virus-inhibitory host factor.

records.title: A homozygous C2ORF78 variant is associated with mTOR hyperactivation and neurodevelopmental defects in focal cortical dysplasia.
records.abstract: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a malformation of cortical brain development, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate type II FCD in a proband with behavioral disturbances, including aggression, hyperactivity, and sleep dysfunction, but with normal early development and cognition. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the proband revealed focal cortical thickening, abnormal sulcation, and gray-white matter blurring in the left temporal lobe, consistent with FCD type II. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous missense variant in C2ORF78 (c.1264 A > G; p.Ser422Gly), absent in population databases. The S422 residue is evolutionarily conserved, resides within a disordered, solvent-accessible region, and its substitution with glycine caused marked structural destabilization, cytosolic mislocalization, and protein aggregation. Functional studies in proband fibroblasts revealed no significant reduction of C2ORF78 protein, deregulated mTOR signaling, impaired autophagy, ER stress, and G0/G1 cell cycle arrest. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed significant loss of protein stability and compactness in the S422G mutant. C2ORF78 interacts with RNA-binding and transcriptional regulators, and gene ontology analyses indicated roles in transcription and RNA splicing. We propose that C2ORF78 functions as a transcriptional coregulator of genes negatively regulating mTOR signaling. Mislocalization of the S422G mutant leads to a loss of nuclear function, resulting in hyperactivation of mTOR and disrupted cellular homeostasis. High expression of C2ORF78 in cerebral cortex and hippocampus supports its relevance to brain physiology. Our findings identify C2ORF78 as a novel candidate gene associated with FCD type II and highlight transcriptional dysregulation of mTOR signaling as a potential pathogenic mechanism.
records.authors: Ahmad SR, Zeyaullah M, Zahrani Y, Altijani AA, Hummad H, Mohamed AOA, Dhiman NK.

records.title: Engineering commensal Lachnospiraceae for programmable therapeutic delivery in the mouse gut.
records.abstract: Engineered native gut bacteria could offer persistent, programmable therapeutic delivery in the gut, but many dominant taxa remain genetically intractable. Members of one such family of obligate anaerobic Clostridia, Lachnospiraceae, are prevalent in the human gut microbiome and produce metabolites linked to intestinal and metabolic health. Here we report a modular toolkit for engineering Lachnospiraceae, including constitutive and inducible expression, chromosomal integration and secretion systems. Applying this toolkit to gut native Coprococcus comes, we programmed the secretion of cytokine interleukin-22 (IL-22) in the mouse intestinal tract, where it induces epithelial defence transcriptional programmes. In a mouse model of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, IL-22-secreting C. comes improved glucose homeostasis, reduced systemic endotoxemia and attenuated hepatic steatosis. This work demonstrates that native Lachnospiraceae can be genetically programmed to modulate host metabolic and immune physiology. The toolkit provides a foundation for the development of Lachnospiraceae-derived engineered therapeutics and for dissecting causal relationships between commensal gene programmes and host physiology.
records.authors: Arnold J, McClure S, Glazier J, Shakya S, Jansen Z, Ahan RE, Villegas D, Chen TL, Fuerte-Stone J, McGann R, Mimee M.

records.title: The microbial making and breaking of dimethylsulfoniopropionate and related compounds.
records.abstract: Dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) is one of Earth's most abundant organosulfur compounds, made by marine algae, bacteria, corals and plants to cope with diverse environmental stressors and predation. Once released into the environment, DMSP serves as a widespread signalling molecule and a source of carbon, sulfur and/or energy for marine organisms. Diverse organisms can also produce a suite of DMSP-related compounds (DRCs) with important biological roles and environmental impacts, including the climate-cooling gases dimethylsulfide and methanethiol (MeSH) that are generated through microbial DMSP catabolism or H2S/MeSH S-methylation. This Review reports the current understanding of DMSP and DRC biosynthesis and catabolism, emphasizing recent discoveries that challenged common beliefs on their sources and fates. It explores the biodiversity, regulation and importance of the genes and pathways that drive the production, import and degradation of these sulfur compounds. Finally, it highlights current challenges and priority areas to guide future DMSP and DRC research.
records.authors: Carrión O, Zhu XY, Azizah M, Liu J, González JM, Pohnert G, Raina JB, Todd JD.

records.title: Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals Vitamin D Metabolism, Hyper-IgE Genes, and Epithelial Barrier Dysfunction in Hazelnut Allergy.
records.abstract: BackgroundHazelnut allergy is a major cause of food-induced anaphylaxis yet remains poorly defined at the molecular level. We aimed to identify molecular differences between individuals with primary hazelnut allergy and nonallergic controls by investigating a comprehensive spectrum of omics profiles in immune cells.MethodsWe analysed DNA methylation, transcriptomic, and proteomic profiles in hazelnut-stimulated and unstimulated immune cells.ResultsAcross analyses, we identified 87 differentially methylated signatures, 125 unique differentially expressed genes, and 11 unique differentially secreted proteins associated with hazelnut allergy. DNA methylation signatures were largely preserved irrespective of antigen stimulation, indicating stable epigenetic remodelling. Key findings implicated ZNF341, associated with a rare monogenic hyper-IgE syndrome, and ARL2, both linked to STAT3-mediated IgE dysregulation. We identified a hypermethylated region overlapping TH2LCRR in the cytokine gene cluster, suggesting an epigenetic mechanism contributing to IL-5 and IL-13 upregulation. Antigen stimulation was required to reveal hazelnut-specific transcriptional and proteomic signals. Integration of these data demonstrated that IL-5 expression could distinguish both groups. Moreover, integrated analysis of all multi-omics data revealed prominent innate immune activation programs involving antimicrobial, antiviral, and cytokine-mediated inflammatory responses. Finally, we identified signals in epithelial barrier genes of the gut and skin (TRIM31, TRIM40, CDSN), activation of the vitamin D pathway (CYP27B1, IL32), and nominated additional signals (PHACTR1, MFHAS1, SPRED2, NSMCE1-DT) for follow-up.ConclusionThis study provides the first antigen-specific multi-omics characterization of hazelnut allergy, confirming coordinated alterations in type 2-immunity and uncovering novel links to monogenic hyper-IgE syndrome, innate inflammatory pathways, activation of vitamin-D pathways, and gut/skin barrier genes, yielding a catalogue of candidate biomarkers for mechanistic studies and prospective validation.

records.title: HIV-1 Tat drives genotype-dependent neuroimmune programs that promote Parkinson Disease-like neurodegeneration in the hSNCA<sup>A53T</sup>Gba1 mouse model.
records.abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type I (HIV-1) infection can induce both motor and cognitive impairments even in patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy (cART). These neurological alterations are related to direct and indirect mechanisms represented by viral and immune mediated processes, respectively. HIV-1 directly elicits neurological damages through some viral proteins including transactivator of transcription (Tat), a protein involved in the HIV-1 replication and able to affect neural cell through autocrine and paracrine pathways. In this study, we investigated the functional and transcriptional effects of intrastriatal Tat injection in pre-symptomatic mice carrying the hSNCAA53TGba1+/+ and hSNCAA53TGba1+/L444P mutations, common genetic risk factors for Parkinson's disease (PD). Behavioural assessment revealed that Tat administration anticipated motor symptoms onset in both genotypes, with some behavioural measures suggesting greater impairment in mice carrying both mutations, whereas spatial memory was not affected. In line with these findings, Tat injection induced significant loss of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive cells and fibre density in hSNCAA53TGba1+/L444P mice. HIV-1 Tat injection did not significantly modify TH-positive fibre density in hSNCAA53TGba1+/+ mice, whereas a marked reduction was observed in hSNCAA53TGba1+/L444P mice. Transcriptomic analysis revealed genotype-dependent responses, with a predominant innate immune-related signatures in hSNCAA53TGba1+/+ mice and transcriptional alterations involving immune, lysosomal, proteostatic, and autophagy-related pathways hSNCAA53TGba1+/L444P mice. Altogether, these findings indicate that HIV-1 Tat administration is associated with genotype-dependent PD-related motor deficits and that the Gba1 deficiency is linked to a more pronounced dopaminergic and transcriptional response to Tat exposure.
records.authors: Bertasini C, Lotti V, Lagni A, Grisotto J, Picari R, Diani E, Cecchetto R, Raniero D, Turrina S, Mazzariol A, Gibellini D, Paolone G.

records.title: DNA methylation remodeling across adulthood in the rhesus macaque hippocampus.
records.abstract: DNA methylation (DNAm) is a key epigenetic mechanism implicated in brain aging, yet methylation trajectories across the lifespan in the primate brain remain poorly understood. To characterize age-associated DNAm patterns in the hippocampus, we generated reduced representation bisulfite sequencing (RRBS) data from 86 rhesus macaque hippocampus samples spanning ~3-35 years of age (females = 56; males = 30). CpG-level analyses revealed minimal age-associated changes in mean methylation, with sites trending toward intermediate states, but widespread increases in methylation variability, consistent with epigenetic drift and reduced regulatory fidelity. Region-level modeling identified 5163 age-associated methylation regions exhibiting both monotonic and nonlinear trajectories across age. Nonlinear clusters revealed midlife inflections centered around 12.3 and 13.2 years, suggesting that hippocampal epigenetic aging may involve molecular transition periods that shape later-life brain aging trajectories. Integration of these age-associated DNAm regions with matched RNAseq data identified candidate cis-regulatory loci where age-associated methylation may be linked to transcriptional changes, including IGF1R. In addition, direct testing of associations between mean gene methylation and expression revealed a significant repressive directional bias (higher methylation associated with lower expression) highlighting genes involved in neuroinflammation, amyloid processing, and myelin maintenance. Intergenic regions overlapped annotated human brain enhancers, indicating that age-associated methylation remodeling extends to distal cis-regulatory elements. Together, these findings indicate that hippocampal DNAm aging in a long-lived primate is dominated by increasing epigenetic variability at the CpG level alongside regional remodeling of both genic and intergenic regulatory loci, with potential implications for transcriptional remodeling during brain aging.

records.title: TWIST family in cervical cancer biology: From molecular mechanisms to clinical implications.
records.abstract: Despite ongoing clinical efforts, cervical cancer remains one of the most common gynecologic tumors, largely due to its metastatic potential and resistance to chemotherapy. The transcriptional regulator TWIST has been implicated in these features, in part through the induction of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). The expression of TWIST is delicately regulated by several exogenous factors, including hypoxia-driven HIF-1α signaling and TGF-β pathways, as well as endogenous oncogenic cascades such as Wnt/β-catenin, NF-κB, PI3K/Akt, Hedgehog, Notch, and IL-6/JAK2/STAT3. Moreover, the E6 and E7 proteins from high-risk human papillomavirus strains promote TWIST upregulation, facilitating cellular plasticity and evasion of senescence. Post-transcriptional and epigenetic regulation is orchestrated by complex networks of non-coding RNAs and key transcription factors such as Mist1, FOXC1, and LMX-1A. Importantly, hypermethylation of the TWIST1 promoter has been proposed as a candidate biomarker for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. TWIST has been reported to promote tumor-associated phenotypes through E-cadherin downregulation, induction of matrix metalloproteinases, and maintenance of stem cell-like properties. TWIST has been associated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy resistance, potentially through mechanisms involving DNA-damage responses and MDR1/P-glycoprotein-mediated drug efflux. The tumor microenvironment affects its expression and activity, including hypoxia, cancer-associated fibroblasts, inflammatory cytokines, tumor-associated macrophages, and extracellular vesicles. In a clinical context, high levels of TWIST are linked to poor outcomes in cervical cancer. Growing evidence links it to immune evasion through regulation of PD-L1, immunosuppressive cytokine signaling, macrophage polarization, T-cell exclusion, and immune resistance associated with cancer stem cells, underscoring its importance for translation in the current era of immune checkpoint blockade.
records.authors: Sayed U, Kubaev A, Polatova D, Ali MK, Mishra S, Singhal D, Bainsal N, Vahdati SN.

records.title: Shared genetic architecture and pleiotropic loci linking prurigo nodularis to allergic diseases.
records.abstract: Prurigo nodularis (PN) frequently co-occurs with allergic diseases, but the underlying shared genetic architecture and specific loci contributing to this overlap remain incompletely understood. We integrated genome-wide association study summary statistics for PN and multiple allergic diseases. Genetic sharing was assessed at genome-wide and regional levels, directional associations were examined using bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR), and shared signals were refined through cross-trait pleiotropy, colocalization, and complementary gene-prioritization analyses. Immune-cell analyses were used to provide additional cellular context. PN showed positive genetic correlations with multiple allergic diseases, with regionally heterogeneous local sharing. MR suggested associations of several allergic liabilities with increased PN susceptibility. Cross-trait pleiotropy identified shared loci with enrichment in cytokine signaling, T-cell regulation, and lipid metabolism, while regional colocalization further refined a subset of shared signals. Across complementary genetic evidence, IL2RA, FADS1, PRR5L, and LRRC43 emerged as the most consistently supported candidate genes. Exploratory immune-cell analyses provided suggestive CD25-related T-cell context for IL2RA signal. PN and allergic diseases share a broad but regionally heterogeneous genetic architecture. Convergent evidence prioritizes a restricted set of shared loci and candidate genes, including IL2RA, providing a genetic framework for further functional investigation of PN-allergy overlap.
records.authors: Yin M, Zhu G, Zhou Z, Zhang X, Song Z.

records.title: First epidemiological and molecular characterization of bovine leukemia virus in Holstein dairy cattle from two cities in Shandong Province, China.
records.abstract: Bovine leukemia virus (BLV) is the etiological origin of enzootic bovine leukosis, a chronic lymphoproliferative disorder causing significant economic losses to the global cattle industry. Shandong Province in eastern China is a major dairy cattle-breeding region. However, the molecular prevalence and genetic characteristics of BLV in this area remain unclear. In this study, 289 blood samples were collected from Holstein dairy cattle across three large-scale commercial farms in Shandong Province, China, and BLV infection was determined using nested PCR targeting the long terminal repeat (LTR) of the virus. Of 289 samples, 59 (20.4%) were positive for BLV provirus. Phylogenetic analysis was performed based on 423 bp partial sequences of the env-gp51 gene from 24 BLV isolates, which were positive for BLV provirus by PCR targeting both the LTR and the env-gp51 gene. Maximum likelihood phylogenetic trees revealed that the 24 BLV sequences from Shandong Province were clustered into three distinct genotypes-namely, Genotypes-4, -6, and -7-among the 12 known BLV genotypes worldwide. Bayesian phylogenetic trees indicated that BLV sequences belonging to Genotypes-4 and -6 were further classified into four and two distinct phylogenetic clusters, respectively. This study reports the coexistence of Genotype-4 (G4-1, G4-2, G4-3, and G4-4), Genotype-6 (G6-1 and G6-2), and Genotype-7 in the cattle population from two cities in Shandong Province. These findings provide important baseline information on the molecular epidemiology and genetic diversity of BLV in Shandong Province.
records.authors: Guo G, Matsuura R, Dong L, Wang J, Bao A, Wang C, Wang J, Aida Y.

records.title: Immunoinformatics-based design of a multi-epitope vaccine against Fusobacterium nucleatum-associated colorectal cancer.
records.abstract: A multi-epitope vaccine candidate, A-20EFγ, was rationally designed against Fusobacterium nucleatum using proteomic and genomic information. The construct comprises a B-cell epitope (epitope 20) derived from the ABC transporter permease, along with cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CTL) and helper T-lymphocyte (HTL) epitopes (epitopes E, F, and γ) selected from the nickel ABC transporter permease. All epitopes demonstrated favorable immunological properties, including high antigenicity, surface accessibility, and the absence of allergenicity and toxicity. These epitopes were assembled using suitable linkers, and outer membrane protein A was incorporated as an adjuvant to enhance immunogenicity. Additionally, the PADRE sequence was included to improve immune stimulation and population coverage, resulting in a remarkable increase in predicted MHC class II and combined population coverage to 99.98%. The three-dimensional structure of the finalized vaccine was modeled using multiple computational approaches and validated through structural quality assessments and molecular dynamics simulations, with the RoseTTAFold model showing superior stability. Molecular docking, network normal mode, and binding free energy analyses revealed stable interactions between the vaccine and Toll-like receptors 2 and 4. Immune simulations further suggested that A-20EFγ could elicit a robust and long-lasting humoral immune response, characterized by high IgG and IgM levels and enhanced memory B-cell activity. Lastly, codon optimization and in silico cloning were conducted to facilitate in vitro synthesis and predict efficient expression in E. coli using the pET-28a (+) vector. Overall, these preliminary findings suggest A-20EFγ as a potential prophylactic vaccine candidate for the prevention of F. nucleatum-associated colorectal cancer.

records.title: Novel Regulators of Sugar-dependent Food Consumption in  Drosophila melanogaster
records.abstract: Diet and genetic background interact to influence food consumption, yet the genetic basis of diet-dependent feeding behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we used genome-wide association analysis (GWAS) to investigate the genetic regulation of sugar-dependent food consumption in  Drosophila melanogaster . Food intake was quantified in 176 lines of the  Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) using the Con-Ex (  Con sumption-  Ex cretion) assay on low- and high-sugar foods. Flies showed compensatory feeding, consuming more low-sugar food than high-sugar food, and this behavior was largely maintained across genotypes. Additionally, the magnitude and overall consumption varied several-fold among lines, with broad-sense heritability of 0.53 to 0.66 across sexes and diets. Association analysis across six sex- and diet-specific phenotypes identified 161 variants mapping to 118 candidate genes, which shared almost no loci between dietary conditions, indicating that consumption on the two foods is largely under separate genetic control. RNAi knockdown of candidate genes identified  CG42673 and  Tmtc2 , whose knockdown increased consumption across sexes and diets and was reproduced in independent experiments. Together, these findings show that natural genetic variation contributes substantially to diet-dependent feeding and identify candidate regulators of sugar-based food consumption in  Drosophila .

records.title: Histopathological and virus-associated features of Boid Inclusion Body Disease in  Boa constrictor
records.abstract: Boid inclusion body disease (BIBD) is a reptarenavirus-induced fatal disease of boid snakes that, while diagnosed with ease due to the pathognomonic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (IB), is not yet fully characterized pathomorphologically and with regards to its pathogenesis. The present study retrospectively investigated a random cohort of 50 captive male and female boa constrictors of variable age (neonate to 25 years) for histopathological changes and  in situ viral protein (nucleoprotein, NP, and glycoprotein 2, GP2) expression patterns. IB formation and NP expression were scored semiquantitatively. The vast majority of snakes (42/50; 84%) exhibited histopathological changes; these mainly (39/42; 93%) represented inflammatory processes that most frequently affected the gastrointestinal tract. Overall, IB and NP scores were significantly higher in the more recent cases (2020-2025) compared to the older cases (2000-2003). NP scores did not differ between age groups or sex, but were lower in animals with clinical signs and higher in those with histopathological changes. No statistically significant association was found between NP scores and inflammatory processes, neither in general nor in individual organs. GP2 expression, as an indicator of virion assembly, was less consistent than NP expression and generally restricted to individual cells with and without IBs. There was no histological evidence of overt damage in infected cells. Jointly, the results indicate different phases of restrictive and systemic viral replication that are not directly associated with pathological processes and/or clinical signs.
records.authors: Bogner M, Dervas E, De Neck S, Hepojoki J, Baggio F, Hetzel U, Kipar A.

records.title: Reference-Guided De Novo Retrieval of 3D Chromatin Organizational Features with Representation Learning
records.abstract: Chromosome conformation maps reveal spatial genome organization through recurring contact patterns, some associated with established architectural features and others with less understood biological processes. Identifying instances of a pattern across these maps is necessary to investigate its biological associations and recurrence across experimental settings. However, conventional feature callers typically target predefined patterns, offering limited support when researchers can provide examples of a feature of interest but lack a dedicated detection method. We introduce Chromatin Fetch (C-Fetch), a reference-guided retrieval framework that uses examples of a desired feature and a contrasting class to rank and assign contact-map patches at provided candidate coordinates. C-Fetch learns a generalized representation through weakly KL-regularized 3D autoencoding of structurally related, non-temporal Hi-C and Micro-C patches without architectural feature labels. We demonstrate retrieval of biologically defined contacts, visually specified patterns, and established architectural features. Polycomb-guided retrieval identifies contacts enriched for PRC2-associated signals, exceeding enrichment from loop-guided assignments at 5 kb, while queries resembling condensed domains retrieve patches with progressively stronger rectangular enrichment at higher ranks. Loop-guided retrieval increases aggregate focal enrichment relative to complete Mustache proposal sets across four held-out maps, and selected contacts show greater focality loss after cohesin depletion than matched remaining candidates. Retrieval also extends to Region Capture Micro-C and HiChIP, with ranking agreement retained across biological replicates and reduced sequencing depths. Together, these results establish reference examples as a flexible means of specifying contact-map features of interest, enabling biological investigation, exploration of visual patterns, and refinement of existing calls across datasets and technologies.

records.title: Cross-species epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity: Insights from Jonathan the Giant Tortoise and human centenarians
records.abstract: Can epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity transcend species boundaries? By comparing findings from a previously published epigenomic study of Jonathan, a 194-year-old giant tortoise, based on buccal scrape and saliva samples, with the analyses of publicly available DNA methylation data from exceptionally long-lived humans based on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), this comparative study reveals intriguing molecular parallels across evolutionarily distant species. Human individuals aged 110+ years exhibited significantly higher global methylation entropy than those aged 60-82 years. Furthermore, 12 candidate genes displayed a distinctive promoter methylation entropy profile, with lower values at the youngest and oldest ages than in intermediate-age groups. Strikingly, these genes were enriched in telomere-related biological processes, highlighting a compelling link between epigenomic patterns and pathways implicated in aging. The correspondence between the findings in humans and previously reported observations in Jonathan suggests testable hypotheses about epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity that may be conserved across species and extend beyond tissue-specific effects.
records.authors: Pischedda S, Gómez-Carballa A, Martinón-Torres F, Salas A.

records.title: CryoID2: deep learning-enhanced identification of protein and RNA from cryoEM maps
records.abstract: SUMMARY  Identifying the molecular components of cryoEM/cryoET maps of endogenous or poorly characterized complexes remains a major bottleneck. CryoID2 addresses this by integrating deep learning–based feature prediction with sequence prioritization and structural evaluation. Three 3D U-Nets extract structure classes, key-atom positions, and reduced residue/nucleotide types from the input map. These predictions support backbone tracing and the generation of short sequence queries that rank candidates from a user-supplied pool—using BLASTp for proteins and a maximin strategy for RNA. Corresponding PDB or AlphaFold models are then retrieved, rigidly fitted using predicted features and experimental density, and ranked by map agreement. Module-level tests show high-recall feature prediction and resolution-dependent atom clustering, while a 52-case benchmark recovers near-reference fitting quality. In practice, cryoID2 correctly identified PfA-M17 from a 166-protein mass-spectrometry pool and the unannotated Ca-raiA RNA from a genome-derived non-coding sequence set, demonstrating a unified sequence-plus-structure route to molecular identification in cryoEM maps.
records.authors: Xu Q, Yu X, Wu L, Feng S, Zhou ZH.

records.title: Functional analysis of small-molecule and protein binding domains using monomeric streptavidin-based two-component biosensors
records.abstract: Protein biosensors are important analytical and diagnostic tools that convert molecular recognition into measurable activity. Most common two-component biosensors require two non-competing recognition domains, yet binding affinity and specificity alone do not reliably predict their compatibility with the rest of the biosensor. We report a modular platform that exploits monomeric streptavidin (mSA2) as a surrogate recognition domain, enabling rapid functional evaluation of candidate binders in the context of biosensor scaffold without requiring a second ligand-specific binding protein. We established a chromatography-free protocol for recovering functional mSA2-based biosensor components from  Escherichia coli . Using biotinylated small molecules methotrexate and vitamin D  3 , as well as heart failure protein biomarkers galectin-3 and S100A7 we demonstrate ligand-dependent reporter biosensor activation. The developed platform provides a scalable approach for rapid binder evaluation and biosensor prototyping, streamlining biosensor development using binding domains generated by directed evolution or computational protein design.
records.authors: Mutschler R, Guo Z, Fiorito MM, Alexandrov K, Cui Z.

records.title: Decoupled geogenic and faecal hazards in shallow coastal groundwater: evidence and a screening framework from the lower Indus Delta, Pakistan
records.abstract: Abstract  Shallow hand pumps supply drinking water to millions of people in low-lying deltas worldwide, where groundwater is exposed to geogenic salinisation and faecal contamination. Because these hazards are usually assessed together, it remains unclear whether they share a pathway and, therefore, which interventions are needed. In the lower Indus Delta (Pakistan), we analysed 93 hand pumps for 16 physicochemical variables, total coliforms and Escherichia coli, and combined hydrochemical diagnostics, a seawater mixing index (SMI), multivariate statistics, entropy-weighted and weighted-arithmetic water quality indices (EWQI, WA-WQI) and deterministic and Monte Carlo health-risk models. TDS exceeded 1000 mg/L in 58.1% of wells. A single salinity factor (65.9% of variance) integrated evaporation, cation exchange (slope −0.95, R² = 0.97) and limited marine mixing (SMI > 1 in 23.7%). E. coli occurred in 23.7% of wells, was independent of salinity (OR = 0.83, p = 0.81), was predicted only by turbidity (OR = 4.18 per log₁₀ NTU; AUC = 0.82) and, unlike salinity, was not spatially clustered, indicating wellhead ingress. WA-WQI assigned 66% of its weight to F⁻ and turbidity and agreed poorly with EWQI (weighted κ = 0.20). Child hazard index exceeded 1 with 46.1% probability, driven by F⁻, and drinking water supplied up to 122% of the WHO daily sodium limit. A well-by-well typology showed that only 26.9% of wells were safe, 8.6% needed only wellhead repair and 64.6% required treatment or a new source. The framework uses only routine monitoring data and is transferable to other salinising coastal deltas.

records.title: Detecting chlorophylls and carotenoids utilizing a novel chromatographic method designed for HPLC-PDA-MS analyses and application to environmental and cultured algae and cyanobacteria
records.abstract: Abstract    Chlorophylls and carotenoid analyses are important in aquaculture and freshwater and marine research as they are used to quantify algal biomass, food and supplement analyses, and to determine ecological diversity. The methods used for these analyses have often been limited to photometric detection, with some methods incorporating chromatographic separation. Mass spectrometric detection offers improved sensitivity, selectivity, and structural information compared to spectroscopy, but requires a full redesign of the separation system as previous chromatographic separations used solvent additives incompatible with mass spectrometry. The separation developed here used a YMC C30 “Carotenoid Column” with a novel mobile phase and elution scheme to separate a suite of algal pigments. Detection can be performed using a photodiode array alone, or in conjunction with mass spectrometry (MS). We report that the carotenoid echinenone (CAS 432-68-8) is actually an isomeric pair, which may have important implications for cyanobacterial photosynthesis and the orange carotenoid protein complex. New chlorophyll analogs, that could be hydroxylated or dehydroxylated derivatives, were detected in  Caulerpa  and  Planktothricoides  sp. BLCC-F182. This cyanobacterium produced novel chlorophylls, and it uniquely contained no echinenone or 3-OH echinenone. There was marked diversity in the types of pigments produced in the multiple strains analyzed, and the analyses demonstrated that there is likely to be more to discover in the pigments produced by algae and cyanobacteria. The inclusion of MS added significant value for the analysis of carotenoids and chlorophylls, and novel methodologies such as this may lead the field into important discoveries and advancements.

records.abstract: Abstract  Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is an aggressive malignancy driven partly by epigenetic and epitranscriptomic dysregulation. ZNF677 is a candidate tumor suppressor, but its regulation by DNA methylation and N6-methyladenosine (m6A), and its prognostic significance, remain unclear.We integrated clinical, RNA-sequencing and DNA-methylation data from a TCGA-derived OSCC cohort (n = 25). Associations were assessed using Spearman correlation, false-discovery rate control, and bootstrap confidence intervals. Prognostic value was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier and multivariable Cox regression. ZNF677 expression inversely correlated with YTHDF2 (ρ=−0.35) and promoter methylation (ρ=−0.36). Although median-dichotomized survival was not significant, continuous ZNF677 independently predicted better survival (HR = 0.10, 95% CI 0.02–0.67; p = 0.017; C-index = 0.85). Restoring ZNF677 suppressed pro-tumorigenic phenotypes (Hedges’ g = − 0.90; p = 0.003) and cancer-stemness markers (g = − 1.59; p = 0.016). records.title: New insights into the Cenangiaceae: Marsonomyces, gen. nov., the first case of true polyspory in Helotiales, and taxonomic revisions in Neomelanconium.
records.abstract: The new genus Marsonomyces is proposed to accommodate two new species, M. pinicola and M. salicacearum, collected between 1990 and 2020 at four locations in Europe (Germany, the Netherlands, Poland) and Macaronesia (Tenerife). The most striking characteristics of the genus are large, long-cylindrical, ~128-spored asci with inamyloid, thin-walled, hemispherical apices and minute, allantoid ascospores aggregating prior to discharge in a large, elongated spore cluster. The observed polyspory is a result of seven nuclear divisions prior to spore wall formation. Phylogenetic rDNA and multigene analyses suggest placement in the family Cenangiaceae, in sister position to a clade comprising Encoelia/Velutarina, Cenangiopsis, and Trochila. This relationship is supported by morphological traits, such as brown, coriaceous, drought-tolerant apothecia growing on xeric branches, erumpent from bark (but also superficially on wood), the presence of refractive vacuolar bodies in the living paraphyses, the absence of an ionomidotic reaction, and allantoid ascospores. The two new species are morphologically very similar but can be distinguished by wider spores, the presence of hairs and occurrence on gymnosperms in M. pinicola, and the presence of rhomboid crystals and occurrence on angiosperms in M. salicacearum. Marsonomyces represents the first known case of true polyspory within the Helotiales. A possible parasitism on perithecia and pycnidia of unidentified Diaporthales is discussed. Another fungicolous member of Cenangiaceae, Hymenobolus kmetii, was investigated. Morphological reexamination of the holotype confirmed its conspecificity with Mycosphaerangium quercinum. The phylogenetically closely related genera Mycosphaerangium and Neomelanconium share numerous morphological characteristics. Consequently, Mycosphaerangium is synonymized with the older Neomelanconium, and the new combinations N. kmetii, N. magnisporum, and N. tetrasporum are proposed.

records.title: Stony coral symbioses show variable responses to future ocean conditions.
records.abstract: Coral reefs support over a quarter of marine species and nearly a billion people worldwide but are also among the ecosystems most threatened by anthropogenic impacts. There is long-standing debate about whether coral symbioses will be disrupted or respond adaptively under future ocean conditions. Using a factorial 2.5-year future-ocean mesocosm experiment across eight coral species representing the major coral lineages, we tracked symbiont community shifts within replicate fragments from the same individual coral. Some corals exhibited stochastic divergence, whereas others showed deterministic shifts in symbiont community composition. Heat stress generally reduced symbiont diversity and promoted predictable restructuring, consistent with deterministic adaptation to moderate thermal stress but stochastic accumulation of diversity under extreme conditions. We propose that adaptive and stochastic responses represent endpoints along a continuum of host-orchestrated symbiont sorting. This study bridges coral reef ecology with broader host-microbiome theory, offering an integrated perspective on how symbiotic systems may respond to environmental change.

records.title: Identification and validation of biomarkers associated with mitochondrial dynamics dysfunction in Parkinson's disease based on GEO datasets.
records.abstract: BackgroundParkinson's disease (PD), the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, is characterized by an unclear etiology and a lack of specific early diagnostic biomarkers. This study investigated novel biomarkers associated with mitochondrial dynamics (MD) dysfunction in PD.MethodsTranscriptomic data from the Gene Expression Omnibus database (training set: GSE6613, n = 72; validation set: GSE99039, n = 438) and 23 MD-related genes (MDRGs) were integrated. Three machine learning algorithms (random forest, support vector machine, and generalized linear model) were employed to construct diagnostic models. Feature importance analysis identified key candidate biomarkers, which were preliminarily validated in clinical samples via reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Functional enrichment, immune infiltration, and compound prediction analyses were subsequently performed.ResultsCysteinyl leukotriene receptor 2 (CYSLTR2) and alpha‑tocopherol transfer protein‑like gene (TTPAL) were identified as MDRG score-correlated biomarkers. records.title: Dynamic virulence decomposition disentangles host and pathogen contributions over the course of infection.
records.abstract: Decomposing virulence into host and pathogen effects is key to understanding how virulence is generated during infection, and how host and pathogen contributions evolve over time. Conventional virulence decomposition is, however, not designed to quantify how these contributions vary throughout an infection. Building on conventional virulence decomposition, we developed a dynamic framework that integrates disease space analysis to quantify these changing contributions. We applied this framework to existing data from house finches (Haemorhous mexicanus) experimentally infected with the emerging bacterial pathogen, Mycoplasma gallisepticum, examining two biologically meaningful infection phases: an early phase dominated by innate immune responses and a later phase in which the adaptive immune response is fully activated. Our analyses revealed that virulence components evolved differently across infection phases, with pathogen exploitation, per-parasite-pathogenicity (PPP), and host resistance each exhibiting distinct trajectories. These findings corroborated several known evolutionary patterns, while also revealing the evolution of increased PPP in this system. In contrast, the apparent evolution of host tolerance inferred from aggregated peak measurements was not supported by phase-specific analyses, demonstrating that aggregated and phase-specific measures can provide different mechanistic insights into virulence. By linking conventional virulence decomposition with disease space analysis, our dynamic virulence decomposition framework provides a general approach for quantifying how host and pathogen processes shape virulence over the course of infection.

records.title: The effect of varying levels of irrigation on Tuber melanosporum mycelia and the ectomycorrhizal fungal community in a black truffle orchard in British Columbia, Canada.
records.abstract: The French black truffle is the prized fruiting body of the ectomycorrhizal fungus Tuber melanosporum Vittad. Optimizing the growth of T. melanosporum while mitigating ectomycorrhizal fungal competitors are important goals for producers, particularly in novel growing regions. We investigated the influence irrigation on (1) the abundance of T. melanosporum extramatrical mycelium and (2) the communities of ectomycorrhizal fungi in soil and roots in an 8 year old T. melanosporum-Quercus robur L. orchard located in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada that had yet to produce truffles. Irrigation treatments were characterized by high (- 30 kPa mean soil water potential), moderate (- 80 kPa), or low (non-irrigated) soil moisture. Soil samples were collected monthly from July to September 2021, at 50 cm and 100 cm from the base of trees. Droplet digital PCR was used to estimate the abundance and distribution of T. melanosporum extramatrical mycelia in the soil. The ectomycorrhizal fungal community in soil and on mycorrhizal root tips were examined using PacBio Sequel II. Moderate irrigation had 17% more DNA than low irrigation, and high irrigation had 39% less DNA, but neither treatment was significantly different from the low irrigation treatment. Still soil DNA content decreased exponentially and significantly with soil water content (p < 0.001). Irrigation treatments did not affect the fungal community composition or richness, though several species of Scleroderma were found in high frequency. To our knowledge, this is the first study of a North American T. melanosporum truffle orchard in which a management variable (irrigation) was manipulated.

records.title: Modern breeding of root, tuber, and bulb crops to enhance food and nutritional security.
records.abstract: Key messageUnlocking the molecular mechanisms and pathways of underground storage organ development and nutrient and non-nutrient traits may provide more avenues to tailor elite germplasm enriched with these characteristics in root, tuber, and bulb crops. Biofortified cassava, potato, and sweet potato provide food and nutritional security to millions of people in Africa, Asia, and Latin American regions. Root and tuber crops provide food and nutritional security to millions of people in Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean, while garlic and onions, in addition to strong therapeutic potential, are widely used in food preparation to add flavour and taste. Root, tuber, and bulb (RTB) crops are a good source of carbohydrates, minerals, and bioactive compounds. However, these crops also possess a variety of allergens and toxic compounds, limiting their consumption. Here, we synthesized i) the contribution of RTB crops on food and nutrition security in the Global South, ii) the various types of allergens and toxic compounds detected in these crops, iii) catalogue germplasm resources across national and international genebanks, iv) document the range of genetic variation in edible organs morphology, nutrient and non-nutrient traits, v) discuss advances in high-throughput phenomics to monitor variability, vi) assess population structure and diversity in germplasm pool, vii) list genomic regions (QTL) and genes (both functionally characterized and candidate genes and QTL) associated with storage organs (roots or tubers) morphology, nutrient and non-nutrient traits, viii) uptake, transport, and storage of minerals in edible vegetable organs and their effects on consumers, and ix) advances in genetic improvement of nutritionally enhanced (nutrient and non-nutrient traits) and productive germplasm through crossbreeding and biotechnological interventions. Assessing and exploiting functional diversity, combined with the use of functionally characterized genes and associated markers for storage root growth/thickening, and nutrient and non-nutrient traits, can be deployed in breeding programs to improve these characteristics in RTB crops. Numerous candidate genes and genomic regions (or quantitative trait loci) reported herein must be functionally validated before being deployed in crop breeding programs. A greater emphasis should be placed on genetically and phenotypically characterizing RTB germplasm, and on combining empirical breeding with molecular tools to enhance precision, efficiency, and rapid genetic gain. Millions of rural households in parts of Africa, Asia, and Latin America are currently benefiting from the commercialization of provitamin A-enriched cassava, potato, and sweet potato. The development of orange-fleshed sweet potato cultivars with higher levels of provitamin A was awarded the ''World Food Prize'' in 2016. There are more opportunities to enhance nutrition status and food security through improvement of root, tuber, and bulb crops.
