records.title: Molecular basis for bile sensitivity of Escherichia coli with defective LPS O-antigen assembly.
records.abstract: The periplasmic space between the inner (IM) and outer membranes (OM) of diderm gram-negative bacteria is densely filled with proteins and peptidoglycan cell wall. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is transported through this crowded compartment and then installed at the cell surface. While laboratory-adapted Escherichia coli K-12 strains produce a truncated "rough" LPS, clinical E. coli strains decorate rough LPS with an O-antigen (O-Ag) polysaccharide. At the periplasmic leaflet of the IM, WaaL ligates O-Ag chains onto LPS once it has transited the IM, yielding long "smooth" LPS molecules that are subsequently transported to the OM. Recent reports claim that periplasmic O-Ag chains in ΔwaaL cells disrupt cell envelope integrity to cause bile sensitivity. The presence of long periplasmic O-Ag chains is suggested to stress envelope architecture. Notably, this bile sensitivity is suppressed by disrupting OM-peptidoglycan interactions. Here, we show that even O-Ag repeat units trapped in the cytosol cause bile sensitivity that can be similarly suppressed by disruption of OM-peptidoglycan interactions, despite O-Ag never entering the periplasm. We show that stalled O-Ag chains cause bile sensitivity because they sequester a lipid carrier, limiting its availability for other biosynthetic processes, especially peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis. Indeed, providing more lipid carrier effectively suppressed severe bile sensitivity in ΔwaaL even while increasing the accumulation of long O-Ag chains in the periplasm. Our study clearly shows that periplasmic O-Ag chains do not inherently damage the cell envelope. Rather, stalled O-Ag biogenesis causes a detrimental lipid carrier sequestration that presents as bile sensitivity.IMPORTANCELipopolysaccharide O-antigen (O-Ag) covers the cell surface of wild-type Escherichia coli strains. These long molecules are made inside the crowded periplasmic space and must be accommodated in this compartment. Recent studies reported that long O-Ag chains are toxic molecules in the periplasm, stressing the cell envelope architecture to cause bile sensitivity. We demonstrate that long O-Ag chains in the periplasm are not inherently toxic and that short cytosolic O-Ag repeat units similarly cause bile sensitivity. The accumulation of these O-Ag repeat units or chains acts to sequester an essential lipid carrier, which causes bile sensitivity by impinging on cell wall synthesis. Our study shows that enteric bacteria are vulnerable when lipid carrier availability is reduced, making them more susceptible to the antibacterial effects of bile.
records.authors: May KL, Muthuraman SM, Grabowicz M.

records.title: Structure of MPXV DNA ligase complex reveals a virus-specific pocket for selective inhibition.
records.abstract: Mpox, caused by monkeypox virus (MPXV), remains a public health concern, yet the structural basis of poxvirus DNA ligase function has been poorly defined despite strong genetic and biochemical evidence supporting its essential role in viral DNA replication and repair. Here, we report the crystal structure of MPXV DNA ligase (MpxvLig) in complex with nicked DNA at 2.04 Å resolution. MpxvLig adopts the canonical three-domain architecture of ATP-dependent DNA ligases, comprising an N-terminal DNA-binding domain (DBD), a nucleotidyltransferase domain, and a C-terminal oligonucleotide-binding fold domain (OBD), which together form a clamp-like configuration that embraces nicked DNA for catalysis. The structure captures MpxvLig in an active catalytic state corresponding to the adenylylation step, in which Lys233 forms a covalent ligase-AMP intermediate. Comparative structural and biochemical analyses with the catalytic core of human DNA ligase III reveal substantial differences in domain arrangement and DNA engagement, consistent with the stronger DNA-binding capacity and higher ligation activity of MpxvLig in vitro. Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) further shows that apo-MpxvLig adopts an extended flashlight-like conformation in solution. Notably, we identify a virus-specific small-molecule-binding pocket within the DNA-binding domain. Mitoxantrone binds directly to this pocket and inhibits MpxvLig activity at micromolar concentrations, while exerting minimal effects on the human ligase. Mutations in pocket-defining residues markedly attenuate this inhibition, supporting an on-target mechanism. Together, these findings establish the structural basis of poxvirus DNA ligation and provide a framework for the rational development of selective antiviral inhibitors targeting MpxvLig.
records.authors: Chen A, Fang N, Ye M, Qiu Y, Zhang Y, Huang J, Ding J, Ji C, Li J.

records.title: Two Ume6 target gene classes in the biofilm regulatory network of Candida albicans.
records.abstract: Biofilm formation by the fungal pathogen Candida albicans is a major source of infection. The biofilm regulator Ume6 forms complexes with partner transcription factors Efg1, Ndt80, and Upc2 to drive expression of biofilm-related genes. Here, we present chromatin immunoprecipitation with sequencing data for Ume6-chromatin association in both wild-type and efg1Δ/Δ ndt80Δ/Δ upc2Δ/Δ backgrounds. Ume6 associates with two promoter region classes. For one class, Ume6 association is significantly decreased in the efg1Δ/Δ ndt80Δ/Δ upc2Δ/Δ background. This class includes 577 genes, many with well-established roles in biofilm formation or the related process of filamentation. For the second class, Ume6 association is unperturbed in the triple mutant background. This class includes 534 genes, some with roles in iron homeostasis (e.g., SFU1) and ergosterol synthesis (e.g., ERG11), which may contribute to the impact of Ume6 on ndt80Δ/Δ mutant azole drug sensitivity. It also includes FLO9, a putative adhesin gene that is required for the emergent biofilm state produced by efg1Δ/Δ ndt80Δ/Δ double mutants. The data show that Ume6 binding to about half of its targets requires known partners, and Ume6 binding to about half of its targets does not. Ume6 may bind to the latter set of promoter regions independently of any partner, or perhaps with additional partners that have yet to be discovered.IMPORTANCEBiofilm formation has a central role in infection by the fungal pathogen Candida albicans. Here, we focus on a key regulator, Ume6, that can drive biofilm formation. It is known to form protein complexes with three partner transcription factors, and here, we investigate Ume6-promoter binding in the presence and absence of those partners. Ume6 binds to two promoter classes: one depends on known partners, and many associated genes have roles in biofilm formation. The second class is independent of known partners, and some associated genes are functionally connected to iron metabolism and ergosterol synthesis. The second class may mediate effects of Ume6 on azole drug sensitivity. Our results suggest that Ume6 may bind to some promoter regions independently of any partner, or perhaps with additional partners that have yet to be discovered.

records.title: Investigating the Distinctive Clinical and Genetic Landscape of PPA2 Deficiency.
records.abstract: BackgroundPPA2 encodes for inorganic pyrophosphatase 2, a mitochondrial enzyme that hydrolyzes inorganic pyrophosphates into orthophosphate. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause PPA2 deficiency, an emerging recessive cardiac condition that causes heart failure and sudden cardiac death in infants and young people.MethodsUsing published case reports and large-scale genomics resources, we defined the clinical and molecular spectrum of this disease, classified variants using a customized American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics pipeline, assessed genotype-phenotype correlations, calculated predicted prevalence using the gnomAD GenIE tool, and investigated monoallelic associations in the UK Biobank.ResultsA total of 63 cases from 37 families were identified from 12 publications. The natural history of this disease is characterized by clinical heterogeneity and high mortality (79% by 20 years of age), typically presenting as a highly arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with 2 distinct risk periods: in infancy, where viral infections can lead to heart failure, and in adolescence, where minimal alcohol exposure can trigger sudden cardiac death. The disease is genetically heterogeneous, with 29 distinct variants described (18 of which were classified as [likely] pathogenic), usually in compound heterozygosity. As complete gene knockout appears to be incompatible with life, PPA2 deficiency is caused by biallelic variants within a particular loss-of-function window, with deficiency mitigated by hypomorphic effects, variants in nonconstitutive exons, and particular compound heterozygous combinations. The spectrum of phenotypic effect extends to monoallelic carriers of pathogenic variants, which demonstrate an apparent mitohormesis-like compensatory protection from heart failure. The disease has an estimated prevalence of at least 1/135 000 in European ancestry populations.ConclusionsPPA2 deficiency is a genetically complex and clinically severe disease. Given the potential for effective life-saving interventions, PPA2 may warrant inclusion in emerging newborn genomic screening programs.
records.authors: Low BSH, Corver ME, Lipov A, Wardle JPR, Mazzarotto F, Bezzina CR, Behr ER, Jurgens SJ, Carroll CJ, Walsh R.

records.title: Optimizing Genetic Analyses for Movement Disorders: A Unified Panel Approach and Targeted Reanalysis of 4,046 Clinical Exomes.
records.abstract: BackgroundMolecular testing for genetic movement disorders (MDs) increasingly relies on exome- or genome-based virtual gene panels. In the absence of consensus guidelines, MD panel design remains heterogeneous across laboratories, with international variation in panel configuration and gene content.ObjectiveThe aim of this work was to develop a reproducible framework for a unified MD panel design, generate a comprehensive, curated gene-phenotype dataset, and evaluate clinical utility via targeted exome reanalysis.MethodsCandidate genes were extracted from multiple resources and assessed using predefined criteria for panel inclusion and gene-disease validity. Genes were tiered as Green, Amber, or Red based on evidence strength. Phenotypic spectrum and age at onset were assessed for Green genes based on published literature. Newly added Green and Amber genes were investigated in 4,046 exomes from previously undiagnosed MD cases.ResultsAmong 2,090 extracted genes, 640 were selected. The final panel included 537 Green, 36 Amber, and 67 Red genes, expanding the prior panel by 283 genes and removing 42. Across Green genes, only 17% were linked to a single MD feature, whereas the remainder associated up to eight. Age-at-onset data indicated both pediatric and adult presentations in 43% of genes. Targeted exome reanalysis using a 220-gene list identified 37 clinically relevant variants across 28 genes, resolving 16 cases and increasing diagnostic yield by 0.4%.ConclusionsThis study offers a systematic framework for designing a unified MD panel by integrating evidence from multiple sources and accounting for phenotypic and age heterogeneity. Targeted reanalysis yielded actionable diagnoses, confirming its benefit in routine clinical practice. © 2026 The Author(s). records.title: IDENTIFICATION OF CANDIDATE GENES UNDERLYING A NOVEL QTL FOR ROOT LENGTH AND DIAMETER IN BARLEY IN RESPONSE TO SALINITY
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Salinity is a major agricultural problem that decreases growth and yield of crops and is expected to worsen with climate change. Improving salt tolerance through breeding could be facilitated by identification of genetic loci and candidate genes affecting root traits that enhance water and nutrient uptake while limiting accumulation of toxic ions. In this study, a Clipper x Sahara 3771 doubled haploid (DH) barley mapping population was screened for root growth responses to saline conditions in a controlled environment. Quantitative trait loci (QTLs) were mapped for root traits including seminal root length, root diameter and root potassium. Major QTLs affecting seminal root length and average root diameter were detected in the distal region of the short arm of chromosome 2H, indicating that this region is a key determinant of root architecture under both control and saline conditions. The linkage map was improved by using newly designed assays for SNPs on chromosome 2H and a 2.5-Mb interval was identified for investigation of candidate genes. Bulked segregant RNA sequencing (BSR-Seq) of contrasting salt-tolerant and salt-sensitive DH lines identified differentially expressed genes associated with root growth maintenance and ion homeostasis in root tips. These findings identify specific region on chromosome 2H as a major genomic region affecting barley root architecture, especially under saline conditions, and identify differentially expressed candidate genes in that region.

records.title: Spatial transcriptomics of pediatric tuberculosis lymph nodes reveals a conserved hypoxia–SPP1 niche
records.abstract: Pediatric tuberculosis (TB) often presents as primary disease involving the mediastinal lymph nodes; however, its granuloma microenvironment remains poorly characterized because these population patient tissues are rarely available for study. Here, we use spatial transcriptomics to profile 60 granulomas from four children aged 4 to 36 months. We identified nine recurrent transcriptional microenvironments shared across granulomas, despite their marked histological heterogeneity. One macrophage-rich microenvironment showed strong hypoxia-associated activity and  secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) enrichment. This microenvironment was present in both non-necrotic and necrotic lesions and overlapped with a Mtb-persistence macrophage signature previously identified in murine TB lymph nodes. Pathway analysis revealed the enrichment of both antimicrobial and regulatory programs within this microenvironment, suggesting partial immune control rather than uniform inflammatory or suppressive activity in this region. SPP1 expression was associated with regions enriched for both M1- and M2-like macrophages, suggesting a macrophage program that extends beyond conventional polarization classifications and may be influenced by the local granuloma microenvironment. We further observed a similar spatial association between hypoxia-associated activity and SPP1 expression in an independent adult TB dataset (pooled Spearman ρ=0.65) and validated this association at protein level by multiplex immunofluorescence in our pediatric TB granuloma sample. Overall, this study identified a hypoxia-associated  SPP1 -enriched microenvironment that may contribute to incomplete bacterial clearance and could provide a framework for evaluating host-directed strategies to enhance sterilizing immunity without exacerbating tissue damage.

records.title: Compost-associated microbiota modulates root transcriptional responses and enhances tomato drought resilience
records.abstract: Summary  Compost is a promising sustainable alternative to mineral fertilization because it supplies nutrients and organic matter while hosting diverse microbial communities. However, even if its application to plants has been proven to alleviate different biotic and abiotic stresses, it remains unclear whether its benefits arise from its physico-chemical properties, its associated microbiota, or both. In this study, we compared the impact of compost, sterile compost and an NPK treatment providing equivalent macronutrient inputs on tomato plants cv. Micro-Tom. After assessing physiological parameters of the leaves and molecular responses of the roots under optimal conditions, we performed a drought stress experiment under the three fertilization treatments, complementing the analysis with the investigation of substrate water-retention properties. Although all fertilized treatments improved plant performance relative to nutrient-poor soil, RNA sequencing revealed distinct root transcriptional profiles among compost, sterile compost and NPK, with the compost treatment upregulating several pathways related to plant growth and health, such as hormone signaling, nutrient metabolism, and stress responses. When subjected to severe water stress, compost-treated plants retained the highest photosynthetic efficiency and compost showed the highest available water content compared to the other treatments. These findings suggest that compost may enhance tomato drought resilience through combined effects of substrate water availability and compost-associated microbiota.
records.authors: Cipriani R, Strickler SR, Petruzzellis F, Ghirardello G, Greggio L, Zanardi W, Bonato T, Baldan B, Nigris S.

records.title: Molecular insights into the regulation of coenzyme selection in NADP-specific glutamate dehydrogenase from  Saccharomyces cerevisiae
records.abstract: Coenzyme specificity is one of the crucial aspects of the functional regulations in enzymes. Understanding the molecular basis of coenzyme specificity in glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is highly essential as this is the only enzyme that fulfils various physiological demands in terms of energy production and/or nitrogen assimilation via its strict functional regulation by connecting carbon and nitrogen metabolic cycles in every living organism. We have studied  S. cerevisiae GDH3 (ScGDH3), as a model system for NADP-specific fungal GDHs. K272R and S250E mutants of ScGDH3 exhibited remarkable alteration in coenzyme specificity, with 15-55-fold and 3-14-fold more preference towards non-specific coenzymes [NAD(H)], respectively. S250E exhibited higher NADH affinity (∼ 1.3-fold) than that of towards NADPH. K272R showed ∼ 10-fold increased coenzyme affinity (  1/K  M ) and binding affinity (  1/k  d ) towards NADH, compared to the wild type enzyme (ScGDH3-WT). We solved the crystal structure of ScGDH3-K272R complexed with NADP  + at 2.50 Å resolution with a unique oligomeric arrangement having two distinct subunit conformations (“open” and “super-closed”) and it is the first structure of a GDH from  S. cerevisiae . Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide insights into NADH binding and its increased affinity to ScGDH3-K272R. Further structure-based sequence analyses unravelled that a lysine and an arginine are naturally preferred residues for providing NADP(H) and NAD(H) specificity, respectively for various amino acid dehydrogenases. Taken together biochemical and structural data, our study successfully illustrates the evolutionary conserved mechanism of coenzyme related regulation in fungal and other GDHs; as well as amino acid dehydrogenases.
records.authors: Banerjee A, Roy A, Saha S, Godsora BKJ, Bhaumik P.

records.title: NRT2.2 is essential for nitrate uptake and carbon-nitrogen balance in  Nannochloropsis oceanica
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Nitrate is the dominant nitrogen source for marine microalgae, yet how it is taken up remains poorly understood in many ecologically and biotechnologically relevant species. Here we show that NITRATE TRANSPORTER 2.2 (NRT2.2) is the principal nitrate transporter of the oleaginous marine microalga  Nannochloropsis oceanica .  N. oceanica encodes only two NRT2 proteins and, unlike land plants and green algae, lacks a recognizable homolog of NITRATE ASSIMILATION-RELATED 2 (NAR2), the partner protein that green-lineage NRT2s require for activity and plasma membrane targeting. CRISPR knock-outs and confocal imaging showed that NRT2.2 is located at the plasma membrane and is required for nitrate uptake, whereas its paralog NRT2.1 cannot compensate for its loss. When nitrate was resupplied after nitrogen starvation,  nrt2.2 mutants did not take up nitrate and did not resume growth, while they recovered normally with ammonium. Their photosystem II efficiency fell below that of fully nitrogen-starved wild-type cells, and chlorophyll content was reduced, while total protein remained stable. Fixed carbon was redirected into storage, with lipids and carbohydrates accumulating above the levels of all strains after 3 days of nitrogen starvation. Loss of NRT2.2 therefore mimics a prolonged nitrogen starvation, even though nitrate is available. Because nitrate was present but could not be used, recovery from starvation depends on the capacity to take up nitrate, not only on its availability. In the ocean, where nitrate is depleted for long periods and resupplied episodically, NRT2.2 is thus likely to set how quickly  Nannochloropsis can use new nitrate inputs and resume growth.
records.authors: Santin A, Verdesca L, Bellan A, Minio M, Gerotto C, Morosinotto T, Perin G, Alboresi A.

records.title: Establishing  de novo  microbial biosynthesis of anisole
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Anisole is a valuable aromatic ether and promising green solvent whose industrial manufacture relies exclusively on petroleum-derived phenol and hazardous alkali-mediated methylation. Here, we establish the first  de novo microbial biosynthesis of anisole from glucose in  Pseudomonas putida KT2440 by integrating retrosynthetic pathway design with growth-coupled directed evolution. Using a selection platform in an engineered double auxotroph, in which growth depends on S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation, we evolved a promiscuous plant chavicol O-methyltransferase to yield phenol O-methyltransferase 1 (POMT1; bearing a key D264N substitution), which improved anisole production by 2.3-fold over the wild-type enzyme. To overcome product volatility, we integrated an  in situ two-phase extraction system using dodecane that achieved near-quantitative product recovery. Then, we compared two phenol routes from the shikimate pathway, selected the 4-hydroxybenzoate route, and raised precursor supply by deleting competing reactions and introducing feedback-resistant and reduced-flux variants in two shikimate pathway enzymes. The final strain produced up to 0.57 mM anisole (62 mg/L) from glucose.
records.authors: Bruinsma L, Rosas Gomez D, La Rocca C, Escrig Molina JE, Martins dos Santos VAP, Batianis C.

records.title: Urban enrichment of  molestus  ancestry and opposing temperature clines in a metropolitan  Culex pipiens  hybrid zone
records.abstract: Hybridization between ecologically distinct lineages can fuel rapid adaptation when introgressed alleles are locally favored. The North American  Culex pipiens assemblage, a principal West Nile virus vector east of the Mississippi, comprises three lineages—temperate  Cx. pipiens f.  pipiens , urban-specialist  Cx. pipiens f.  molestus , and subtropical  Cx. quinquefasciatus —that meet in a mid-Atlantic hybrid zone where temperature and urbanization gradients intersect. Using whole-genome Pool-seq of 24 field populations and three lineage-reference pools across the Baltimore–Washington corridor, we find a weakly differentiated,  Cx. pipiens f.  pipiens -like background, richer in  molestus - and  quinquefasciatus -like ancestry toward the warmer end of the corridor. Urbanization impacts allele frequencies across the genome:  molestus -like ancestry rises with impervious surface, independently of temperature and position, while  Cx. quinquefasciatus -like ancestry does not. An 11.6 Mb chromosome 3 inversion is  molestus -like in every population, most of all in urban ones, and tracks genome-wide  molestus -like ancestry. Temperature acts locus by locus. On chromosome 1, a cluster of six CYP6 paralogs, a family implicated in insecticide resistance and thermal-stress response, shows rising  Cx. quinquefasciatus -like ancestry and read depth with temperature. A chromosome 2 interval centered on a  Yan ortholog, a repressor of cell differentiation, shows non-  quinquefasciatus ancestry increasing with temperature, consistent with selection against  Cx. quinquefasciatus - like introgression. Urban populations therefore carry more ancestry from the human-commensal lineage, while temperature moves ancestry both ways at individual loci. Both  molestus and  Cx. quinquefasciatus donors carry human-contact traits, so these patterns bear on how warming and urbanization will reshape arboviral risk.
records.authors: Gregory BP, Arsenault-Benoit A, Bell KL, Fritz ML.

records.title: How to name dark fungal taxa outside the Code: The International Standard to Catalogue Dark Fungal Taxa (ISCDFT)
records.abstract: There is an exponential increase in the number of fungal OTUs being documented by environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding. Many of these, the so-called dark fungal taxa (DFT), are known only from eDNA data, with no associated physical specimen or derived culture. Of the millions of fungal species predicted to exist, only ~205,000 are currently described, making it likely that many of these unknown or undescribed fungi are represented only by eDNA data. For more than a decade mycologists have struggled with whether the  International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (the  Code ) should allow for formal description of fungal taxa from eDNA data alone, i.e. with a DNA sequence serving as a type. It is, however, unlikely that an amendment to the  Code with this provision will pass in the near future. It is therefore imperative to establish an informal yet structured naming system to allow unified communication about DFT. The system proposed herein applies most of the principles of the  Code to generate designations that, while nomenclatorially invalid, can nonetheless be integrated into fungal classifications and diversity assessments. We used the 2025 Westerdijk Spring Symposium "DNA Sequences as Type" to bring mycologists together to work out community consensus-driven conventions and standards for what we call the International Standard to Catalogue Dark Fungal Taxa (ISCDFT). The established guidelines principally refer to naming conventions, quality and standards for the underlying data, and standards regarding the underlying analysis leading to the detection of new DFT. The ISCDFT does not compete with the  Code but enables the community to catalogue DFT and integrate these into fungal classifications while adhering to broadly established principles. For ease of immediate implementation, we provide examples to illustrate these newly established guidelines, a checklist for publishing new DFTs under the ISCDFT, and convert some previously published fungal names based on eDNA sequences to ISCDFT-compliant names.

records.title: A multidimensional “omics” approach reveals biased signaling through flg22- and UDP-glucose-induced, AtRGS1-driven signaling circuits
records.abstract: Abstract  Different cellular inputs into a central signaling core elicit different outputs in a process called biased signaling. Often this occurs by imprinting the signaling core with a phosphorylation bar code, functionally analogous to a microprocessor. The bacterial peptide flg22 and UDP-glucose both utilize a heterologous G protein core that contains a 7-transmembrane RGS protein, AtRGS1, to mediate changes differentially in plant defense and growth. Both flg22 and UDP-glucose launch rapid endocytosis of AtRGS1 at the plasma membrane but the destination and route are signal specific. flg22 directs plasma membrane AtRGS1 to the nucleus followed by different gene expression profiles. UDP-glucose does not direct AtRGS1 to the nucleus and does not elicit transcriptional reprogramming. Instead, UDP-glucose causes a massive, time-dependent restructuring of the G protein complex that likely traffics to the endosomal compartment. Associated with these two outcomes are phosphorylation bar codes that correlate with different patterns of AtRGS1-associated partners over time.
records.authors: Walley J, Li Z, Simoni E, Yang J, Montes C, Jones A.

records.title: Critical regions for human brain development include SON and ITSN1 defined by a panel with chromosome 21 interstitial deletions.
records.abstract: Abstract    Aneuploidies of chromosome 21 (CHR21), including Down syndrome and partial monosomy 21, are major causes of mental retardation and provide unique opportunities to identify candidate genes regulating human brain development. We identified 10 individuals with partial CHR21 deletions and defined molecular breakpoints with high resolution genomic arrays, FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) and quantitative Southern blots. Patient records and neuroimaging generated by the authors or by referring physicians were reviewed. We defined regions from proximal to distal on CHR21, a region consistent with a normal range of cognition, a region associated with microcephaly, and a third region associated with polymicrogyria and partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. Three individuals with severe cortical dysgenesis including polymicrogyria (PMG) with callosal hypoplasia or agenesis shared a ~649 kb minimal region at 21q22.11-22.2 whose distal border lies within  ITSN1  and contains SON. Seven individuals with large proximal deletions outside this interval, had mild cognitive deficits and did not share this phenotype. Comparison of the human phenotypes with those seen with loss-of function mutations in  SON  or  ITSN1  indicate that the 649kb deleted region disturbs vertebrate brain development with components likely attributable to ITSN1 and SON.
records.authors: Korenberg JR, Sarnat HB, Pulst S, Hattori M, Chen X.

records.title: Strigolactone analog GR24 modulates hyphal growth, mitochondrial activity, and superoxide accumulation in the ectomycorrhizal fungus Rhizopogon roseolus
records.abstract: Abstract    Plant hormone strigolactone (SL) is an important rhizosphere signal that mediate communication between plants and diverse soil organisms. However, the role of SL in ectomycorrhizal (ECM) fungi remains largely unexplored, despite ECM fungi representing a major group of plant symbiotic fungi. To address this knowledge gap, we examined the effects of widely used SL analog GR24 with different stereoisomers and concentrations on several ECM fungal species. Deeper investigation on cellular and transcriptional response to GR24 was conducted on  Rhizopogon roseolus  . The evaluated parameters include fungal growth and branching, mitochondrial activity, superoxide accumulation, Ca  2+  signaling, and gene expression. Our findings reveal that ECM fungal responses to GR24 depend on fungal species, as well as GR24 stereoisomers and concentration. Further analysis on  R. roseolus  suggested that GR24 enhanced mitochondrial activity and increased mitochondria-associated superoxide accumulation. Based on pharmacological approach, the response of  R. roseolus  to GR24 required extracellular Ca  2+  influx. Consistent with these morphological and cellular responses, GR24 induce transcriptional response in genes related to cell-wall biosynthesis, mitochondrial respiratory chain, superoxide detoxification, and Ca  2+  signaling. Together, these findings provide novel insight into SL responsiveness in ECM fungi by integrating morphological, cellular, and transcriptional analyses.
records.authors: Pratiwi MN, Nathawan K, Chollada S, Hiroyuki A, Aimi T, Shimomura N.

records.title: Turning Large Electron Microscopy Datasets into Quantitative Measurements with Model-Assisted Analysis
records.abstract: Abstract  Large electron microscopy datasets require extensive annotation and review before they can be converted into reliable measurements. ACORN is an open-source, locally executable application that offers image preparation, reviewed annotation, task-specific model training, batch inference, calibrated measurement, and statistical analysis in a single format. Users can create and correct annotations manually or with promptable segmentation and use the reviewed annotations to train models directly within ACORN. Its Cryo-EM Lab Utility (CLU) assistant also allows users to request any analysis or training operations in plain language. To show its use cases, we evaluated ACORN using low-dose cryogenic TEM images of polymeric nanoparticles and SEM images of bacterial spores. YOLO models trained in ACORN produced validation F1 scores of \(0.906\pm0.013\) and \(0.624\pm0.016\), respectively. Controlled simulations built in ACORN provided 25,983 exact object annotations for further model development and a controlled evaluation of software performance. On held-out simulation images, equivalent-circular-diameter mean absolute error was 3.60~nm (10.1\%) for TEM particles and 31.48~nm (3.7\%) for SEM spores among matched detections. The software logs every interaction, training step, and annotation in a sample history for provenance tracking. ACORN provides an environment where annotations, image calibration, model checkpoints, object measurements, and statistical records are easily accessible and traceable. This software provides a traceable path from electron microscopy images to quantitative results in multiple user-friendly formats.

records.title: Selection and validation of intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) alone beneficiaries among elderly patients with stage T1-2N1M0 nasopharyngeal carcinoma and ACE-27 scores < 2: a multi-center study
records.abstract: Abstract  Background  Elderly patients are underrepresented in clinical trials supporting concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) as the standard treatment for patients with stage T1-2N1M0 nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). This study aimed to develop and validate a prognostic nomogram in elderly patients (≥ 60 years) with stage T1-2N1M0 NPC to distinguish low-risk subgroup for whom intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) alone is sufficient. Methods  This multi-center study retrospectively analyzed 615 elderly patients with stage T1-2N1M0 NPC and Adult Comorbidity Evaluation-27 (ACE-27) scores
records.authors: Zhang Y, Yu H, Mo H, Cai H, Zhang L, Yang Q, Lin X, Tian Y, Chen X, Wen Y.

records.title: Ecological niche and plantation composition differentially shape bacterial community composition and assembly across the root-soil continuum in Populus simonii plantations
records.abstract: Abstract    Mixed plantations are widely established to restore degraded sandy landscapes, yet bacterial community patterns across roots and surrounding soils remain poorly understood. This study examined bacterial diversity, composition, inferred assembly patterns, environmental associations, and predicted functional potential in contrasting  Populus simonii  plantations. We analysed 60 composite samples from root (R), rhizosphere (RS), and non-rhizosphere soil (NRS) in four stands in the Kubuqi Desert, northern China. These comprised a  P. simonii  monoculture and mixtures with  Salix psammophila  ,  Caragana korshinskii  , and  Pinus sylvestris  var.  Mongolica  , with five plots sampled per stand. Root communities exhibited lower richness and diversity and distinct taxonomic composition compared with the two soil compartments. PERMANOVA confirmed significant effects of both ecological niche (  F   = 24.995,  p   = 0.001) than stand type (  F   = 2.649,  p   = 0.005) on community composition, with niche showing the stronger association. Null-model classifications varied among sample groups. Homogeneous selection was the most frequently assigned category in most groups, whereas dispersal limitation accounted for a larger proportion of comparisons in the sampled  P. simonii  and  C. korshinskii  mixture. Co-occurrence patterns also varied across ecological niches and plantation types, with the rhizosphere showing the highest connectivity and mixed plantations generally exhibiting greater connectivity than the monoculture. Soil water content was strongly associated with bacterial community variation (  r²  =0.815,  p   = 0.0005). Predicted KEGG and COG profiles varied among niche and plantation combinations, but no consistent functional response to mixed planting was observed. Together, these results reveal that bacterial taxonomic composition and community assembly responded to different ecological dimensions, ecological niche was more strongly associated with compositional differentiation, whereas assembly processes varied more clearly among the four sampled stands. This decoupling highlights the multidimensional organization of bacterial communities across the root-soil continuum in sandy plantations.
records.authors: Ren Y, Yang G, Su M, Guo X, Qiao S, Shang J.

records.title: Docosahexaenoic Acid and the Gut-Ovarian Axis: A Potential Protective Role Against Environmental Endocrine-Disrupting Chemical-Induced Female Reproductive Toxicity.
records.abstract: The global burden of female infertility is substantial and rising, with environmental endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EEDs) now recognized as important modifiable contributors. Bisphenol A (BPA), phthalates, and their analogues have been shown to impair folliculogenesis, steroidogenesis, oocyte quality, and endometrial receptivity. These toxicants also reshape the gut microbiota, damage intestinal barrier integrity, and promote metabolic endotoxemia, thereby amplifying systemic inflammation and endocrine perturbations. Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), a long-chain n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid, exerts anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and pro-resolving activities, and is increasingly recognized as a modulator of the gut microbial ecosystem. This review proposes that DHA may antagonize EED-induced female reproductive toxicity through a gut-ovarian axis, by (i) restoring microbial diversity and beneficial taxa, (ii) strengthening tight-junction integrity and reducing lipopolysaccharide translocation, (iii) blunting Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB)-mediated inflammation, and (iv) directly protecting granulosa cells and oocytes against oxidative stress. The strongest available evidence comes from DHA-enriched phosphatidylserine, which attenuates BPA-induced intestinal injury via restoration of Akkermansia, Butyricicoccus, and Lachnospiraceae and inhibition of TLR4/NF-κB signaling. Translational data from polycystic ovary syndrome models and in vitro oocyte maturation studies further support an ovary-protective role of n-3 fatty acids. However, ovarian protection mediated by the gut microbiota remains unproven: the strongest available data derive from rodent models with intestinal rather than ovarian endpoints, and human evidence is largely limited to metabolic and inflammatory outcomes that cannot be equated with preserved follicles or improved fertility. Responses may also vary with genetic background. Future studies should integrate multi-omics of the gut microbiota, metabolome, bile acids, and ovarian transcriptome, and evaluate DHA formulation, dose, and timing in at-risk populations.

records.title: Prioritizing Osteoporosis-Associated Candidates Through Multi-Omics Mendelian Randomization, Transcriptomic Modeling, and in vitro Validation.
records.abstract: BackgroundGut microbiota, immune traits, and circulating metabolites may contribute to skeletal biology. We integrated genetic association analyses, transcriptomic profiling, and cell experiments to prioritize osteoporosis-associated molecular candidates.MethodsTwo-sample Mendelian randomization (MR), gene prioritization, and three GEO datasets comprising 110 samples were integrated. MR estimates were recalculated while retaining outcome-associated instruments, followed by false-discovery-rate correction. Exploratory classifiers and a five-gene nomogram were evaluated internally. Protein expression and osteoclast formation were examined in control and RANKL-treated RAW264.7 cells in three independent experiments per group. Supplementary validation repeated normalization, screening and tuning within training folds.ResultsAmong 2,329 IVW tests, the metabolite exposure indexed by GCST90200621 was associated with osteoporosis after multiplicity adjustment (odds ratio 1.296, 95% confidence interval 1.155-1.454; within-domain adjusted P = 0.0135). No colocalization record had PP.H4 above 0.5. The transcriptomic workflow prioritized CCR1, TRMT2A, FADS2, FBXL14, and TTLL12. The original nine-gene RF analysis had an internal test-partition AUC of 0.805. Expression of all five proteins increased during RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis. Additional nested validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.528; cross-study performance remained limited. Fixed-five-gene ridge sensitivity analysis yielded a mean internal AUC of 0.756, conditional on prior gene selection.ConclusionIntegrating genetic and transcriptomic analyses with cell experiments prioritized five osteoporosis-associated candidates whose protein expression increased during osteoclast differentiation. These complementary findings provide a focused basis for biological follow-up; predictive and gene-specific functional applications require further validation.
records.authors: Sun L, Ni S, Yang K, Zhu X, Tang J, Shi H, Sun X, Ding H.

records.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and DNA Methylation Analysis Identifies KRT6B and CHI3L2 as Candidate Shared Biomarkers of Psoriasis and Cutaneous Melanoma.
records.abstract: BackgroundDifferent studies have drawn inconsistent conclusions on whether psoriasis increases the risk of cutaneous melanoma (CM). Although shared gene expression or methylation pathways between the two diseases have been independently reported, suggesting a potential molecular basis for their comorbidity, whether expression and methylation synergistically contribute to their pathogenesis remains unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to identify common methylation-regulated genes (co-MRGs) as potential biomarkers for the association between psoriasis and CM.MethodsTranscriptomic and DNA methylation data of psoriasis and CM, comprising 53 cases and 55 normal controls in total, from GEO and ArrayExpress were used as the main dataset. Differential expression and differential methylation analyses were performed on the main dataset using limma and DMRcate; co-MRGs were further identified. TCGA-GTEx data (472 CM cases and 326 normal controls) served as the external validation dataset to validate the expression regulation of the identified co-MRGs in CM. Network analyses were based on the main dataset; immune infiltration and survival analyses were based on the validation dataset; and IHC analyses were based on the HPA database.ResultsThree co-MRGs (KRT6B, CHI3L2, and TSPAN8) were identified. KRT6B was hypomethylated/upregulated in psoriasis but hypermethylated/downregulated in CM, with enrichment in epidermal development and keratinization. CHI3L2 was hypomethylated and upregulated in both, exhibiting superior diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.867). TSPAN8 was hypermethylated/downregulated in both. KRT6B trended toward poor CM prognosis, whereas CHI3L2 high expression correlated with better survival. HPA-based IHC validation confirmed differential expression of KRT6B and CHI3L2.ConclusionThis study identified two novel promising candidate co-MRG biomarkers, KRT6B and CHI3L2, providing preliminary evidence for a shared molecular link between psoriasis and CM. However, limitations remain, as psoriasis and CM data were derived from separate datasets, and further experimental validation is required.
records.authors: Gao L, RenChen X, Li H, Li B.

records.title: Identification and validation of circadian rhythm-related diagnostic biomarkers for endometriosis through integrating machine learning and single-cell analysis.
records.abstract: BackgroundEndometriosis (EMs) is a chronic inflammatory disease, and the lack of candidate molecular biomarkers remain a major clinical challenge. Circadian rhythm disruption plays a non-negligible role in EMs. However, the diagnostic potential of circadian rhythm-related biomarkers remains insufficiently validated.MethodsWe performed weighted gene co-expression network analysis to screen for endometriosis-related hub modules. Four machine learning algorithms were used for feature selection in the training cohort, and the resulting diagnostic model was evaluated in three independent GEO validation cohorts. To evaluate the immune microenvironment, we applied MCPcounter, CIBERSORT, and single-sample gene set enrichment analysis. Single‑cell RNA‑seq data were processed with Seurat for cell clustering and annotation, cell‑cell communication networks were constructed using CellChat, and pseudotime trajectory analysis was performed with Monocle.ResultsSMC2, SUV39H2, and TIMELESS were identified as candidate molecular biomarkers, demonstrating favorable diagnostic performance across three independent validation sets. Computational immune infiltration analysis suggested higher enrichment scores for B cells and CD8+ T cells, along with lower scores for Tregs and NK cells in EMs samples. Single-cell analysis revealed an increased proportion of mesenchymal cells in EMs samples and altered cell-cell communication involving BMP, CHEMERIN, and GRN signaling pathways. Pseudotime analysis further suggested transcriptional relationships among distinct stromal cell populations.ConclusionThis study identified SMC2, SUV39H2, and TIMELESS as candidate tissue-based molecular biomarkers for EMs and revealed alterations in stromal cell populations and immune-related features associated with the disease.

records.title: Evaluating ANO6 as a Parkinson's disease candidate gene: A human genetic investigation of common and rare variant associations.
records.abstract: ANO6 (TMEM16F), a Ca2+-activated lipid scramblase and ion channel, has been implicated in α-synuclein secretion and propagation, a hallmark of Parkinson's disease (PD). To evaluate whether genetic variation in ANO6 contributes to PD risk, we analyzed common and rare variants across large-scale datasets. Relying on genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from 63,555 PD cases, 17,700 proxy cases, and 1.7 million controls, we identified seven noncoding common variants within ANO6 that reached genome-wide significance, but these signals were driven by linkage disequilibrium (LD) with the nearby LRRK2 p.G2019S variant. We further tested rare variant burden in 4879 PD cases and 65,279 controls. Rare variant burden analysis showed significant enrichment only when all rare variants were aggregated (meta-analysis PFDR = 0.02), with no signal detected in functional categories. Overall, human genetic data does not support an important role for ANO6 in PD.

records.title: Caspase-1 and -11 defend against environmental but not host-adapted pathogens in genetically complex mice
records.abstract: Caspase-1 and -11 are inflammatory caspases that trigger pyroptosis, yet in most infection models they confer only a modest survival benefit. We have proposed that caspase-1 and -11 evolved primarily to defend against ubiquitous environmental microbes that have not been under selective pressure to evade them, whereas host-adapted pathogens have evolved evasion strategies. Testing this idea is complicated because the inbred mouse strains used in most infection studies carry mutations in innate immune genes: i.e., C57BL/6 (B6) mice carry a loss-of-function  Nramp1 allele, and 129 mice lack functional caspase-11. Here we generated B6 × 129 F1 hybrid mice, which are gene-sufficient at both  Nramp1 and  Casp11 , and used them to measure the fold change in lethal dose (ΔLD  100 ) caused by caspase-1 and -11 deficiency for four pathogens on the B6, 129, and F1 backgrounds. Caspase-1 and -11 conferred little or no survival benefit against the host-adapted pathogens  Listeria monocytogenes and  Salmonella Typhimurium on any of the three backgrounds, apart from a modest benefit at the lowest  S . Typhimurium inoculum in F1 mice. In contrast, caspase-1 and -11 were required to survive infection with the environmental pathogens  Burkholderia thailandensis and  Chromobacterium violaceum , where caspase-1 and -11 deficiency lowered the lethal dose by up to six orders of magnitude. The failure of caspase-1 and -11 against host-adapted pathogens therefore persists on a genetically robust hybrid background, supporting the view that a major evolutionary role of caspase-1 and -11 is defense against environmental microbes that have not been selected to evade them.  Importance  Cells can sense bacteria growing inside them and destroy themselves, killing the invader along with the cell. Two enzymes, caspase-1 and caspase-11, carry this out, yet mice lacking both die from host-adapted bacteria such as  Salmonella and  Listeria almost as readily as normal mice. We proposed that these enzymes instead evolved to stop the ubiquitous bacteria of soil and water, microbes that have never faced selective pressure to hide from them. Testing this has been difficult because the standard inbred strains each carry defective immune genes. We crossed two strains to produce hybrid mice with a complete set, then measured the dose of bacteria needed to kill them. Caspase-1 and caspase-11 gave almost no protection against  Salmonella or  Listeria , but raised the lethal dose of the environmental bacteria  Burkholderia thailandensis and  Chromobacterium violaceum by up to a millionfold. This defense therefore appears aimed at environmental microbes.
records.authors: Li L, McGlaughon BD, Larson HN, Koller BH, Miao EA.

records.title: Long-Read Reference Transcriptomes for Five Species of Rosaceae Tribe Spiraeeae: A Resource for Investigating Sequence Divergence, Species-Associated Expression Variation, and Leaf-Developmental Candidate Genes.
records.abstract: Species in the Rosaceae tribe Spiraeeae occupy diverse habitats and vary strikingly in growth form and leaf morphology. Still, no reference transcriptomes have been published for the tribe, and its transcriptome-level variation is uncharacterized. We generated long-read (PacBio Iso-Seq) reference transcriptomes of five species spanning three genera: Petrophytum caespitosum (Nutt.) Rydb., Spiraea lucida Douglas ex Greene, Spiraea splendens Baumann ex K. Koch, Aruncus dioicus (Walter) Fernald var. dioicus, and Aruncus aethusifolius (H.Lév.) Nakai. We then quantified expression across 20 individuals using 3'-tag RNA sequencing (TagSeq) to characterize expression patterns, ortholog sequence divergence, and gene repertoire. Multivariate analyses (principal component analysis [PCA] and hierarchical clustering) resolved replicates into three groups corresponding to the sampled genera. Because the material combined field-collected and potted plants, we treat expression comparisons as descriptive and do not attribute them to genetic control of interspecific differences. Pairwise analyses revealed extensive transcriptional divergence between genera, including thousands of differentially expressed transcripts in comparisons such as A. aethusifolius vs. P. caespitosum. Functional enrichment highlighted variation in transport and catabolism, plastid organization, and biotic-stress responses, implicating both metabolic and organelle-associated processes. Transcription factor families, particularly bHLH and bZIP, varied most among differentially expressed transcripts. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA) recovered modules correlated with species identity; because between-species variation dominates this dataset, we treat these as descriptive summaries of coexpression structure and do not regard them as independent evidence of species-specific regulatory programs. Because reads were quantified against a reference assembled from species-specific contigs, mapping rates were higher within species (70.5%-85.1%) than across species (25.1%-77.0%), and between-species expression comparisons are interpreted with this asymmetry in mind. Sequence-level analysis of orthologous transcript pairs indicated that protein-coding genes are predominantly under purifying selection. A small fraction (2.7%-5.0% of retained pairs) showed Ka/Ks > 1, but these were concentrated at low synonymous divergence, where ratio estimates are unstable; we therefore treat them as screening-level candidates for rapid divergence, enriched for stress-response, membrane-trafficking, and ion-transport annotations, and we make no claim of positive selection. These results provide a comparative transcriptomic framework for Spiraeeae and identify candidate transcripts and protein-coding differences for future studies of ecological and morphological variation in Rosaceae.
records.authors: Mafakheri AM, Potter D.

records.title: Biofilm-induced drag in natural seawater.
records.abstract: The mechanisms underlying the drag produced by soft biofilms are complex due to the interaction between the flow and the biological communities. To fully understand this phenomenon, hydrodynamic studies need to be paired with biological analysis involving the characteristics of what is present on the drag-producing surfaces. Here, the drag production and biological characterization of flat inert PVC plates exposed to natural seawater for up to 14 weeks are analyzed. At successive growth stages, biofilm samples were collected and drag forces were measured using a turbulent channel flow. Although biofilm age dominated drag penalty, this varied widely for plates grown under nominally equal conditions, ranging from 20% to 60% for 14-week biofilms tested at 3 m s-1. While bacterial community composition within biofilms varied significantly with both age and shear disturbance frequency, biofilm age was the primary driver of community structure. Communities were dominated by Planctomycetia, Bacteroidia, and Alphaproteobacteria, with shifts in relative abundance over time. Genus-level patterns indicated successional changes and revealed that taxa within the class Alphaproteobacteria may be resilient to multiple shear disturbances. Overall, biofouling composition may be identified as a contributing factor to the wide variance in drag measurements, although other aspects, such as fouling arrangement and volume, can also produce drag variations.
records.authors: Vilumbrales Garcia R, Mugge RL, Elsouht M, Molina V, First M, Lee J, Ganesh H.

records.title: Identification and binding-site mapping of RNA-binding proteins interacting with microRNA precursors in Arabidopsis.
records.abstract: BackgroundMicroRNAs (miRNAs) play key roles in modulating gene expression. Upon transcription, primary miRNA transcripts (pri-miRNAs or MIRNAs) fold into stem-loop structures. Endonucleolytic cleavage releases a miRNA/miRNA* duplex from the stem, which is subsequently matured. In higher plants, the pri-miRNA hairpins vary widely in length and structure. Pri-miRNA processing is extensively regulated by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and the range of underlying mechanisms continues to expand.ResultsHere, we performed an unbiased screen to identify Arabidopisis thaliana candidate RBPs that interact with pri-miRNAs, using pri-miRNA159a and pri-miRNA398b as paradigms. Nucleoplasmic proteins were significantly enriched in pulldowns with bead-immobilized in vitro transcripts of the stem-loop regions of these pri-miRNAs compared with pulldowns using empty beads. The enriched proteins included several serine/arginine-rich (SR) splicing factors, notably RS31 and SR34a, extending previous findings that RS40 and RS41 bind pri-miRNAs and participate in miRNA biogenesis. Mutant analysis indicated that selected candidate interactors affect pri-miRNA and/or mature miRNA accumulation. To validate candidate interactions with pri-miRNAs in vivo, we performed individual-nucleotide resolution crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (iCLIP). Whereas our conventional plant iCLIP procedure detected only a few crosslink sites on pri-miRNAs, likely because of the low abundance of these transcripts, our improved plant iCLIP2 protocol enabled the identification of binding sites on numerous pri-miRNAs. RS31 and SR34a bound overlapping sets of pri-miRNAs and contacted both stem-loop regions and flanking regions upstream and downstream of the stem-loop. Binding-site mapping resolved overlapping and distinct contact regions and highlighted the importance of complete pri-miRNA annotations for interpreting interactions beyond annotated transcript boundaries.ConclusionIn vitro pulldowns of nucleoplasmic proteins identified candidate RBPs associated with pri-miRNA stem-loops, and the improved plant iCLIP2 protocol revealed in vivo binding of RS31 and SR34a to a subset of pri-miRNAs. Together, these findings expand the repertoire of candidate RBPs implicated in plant miRNA biogenesis and support a role for SR proteins as candidate regulators of miRNA abundance.
records.authors: Winkel AR, Bitterer VW, Lewinski M, Reichel M, Lüders J, Scheibe M, Kalyna M, Laloum T, Duque P, Staiger D, Butter F, Köster T.

records.title: Neoadjuvant botensilimab with or without balstilimab in pMMR and dMMR colon cancer: the phase 2 UNICORN trial.
records.abstract: Preoperative immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are active in patients with deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) colon cancer (CC), whereas proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) CC has been consistently considered resistant to first-generation ICIs. In the phase 2 UNICORN trial, we evaluated short-course preoperative botensilimab (BOT; multifunctional Fc-enhanced anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody) alone or in combination with the anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody balstilimab (BOT + BAL) in 56 patients with resectable, locally advanced CC. Twenty-eight patients with pMMR CC were sequentially enrolled in BOT (n = 14) and BOT + BAL (n = 14) cohorts. Twenty-eight patients with dMMR CC followed the same sequential allocation strategy. The primary endpoint of centrally assessed pathological major response (pMR) rate (≤10% of residual viable tumor) was met in all cohorts, except pMMR BOT. Specifically, the pMR rate was 0% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0-23.2%) in pMMR BOT, 36% (95% CI: 12.8-64.9%) in pMMR BOT + BAL, 36% (95% CI: 12.8-64.9%) in dMMR BOT and 100% (95% CI: 76.8-100%) in dMMR BOT + BAL. Secondary endpoints included safety, quality of life, describing treatment-induced transcriptional dynamics, peripheral blood mononuclear cell dynamics, radiomics and radiogenomics features, fecal microbiota composition and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) dynamics. Eight (29%) and 15 (54%) patients treated with BOT and BOT + BAL, respectively, experienced immune-related adverse events, most commonly flu-like syndrome and diarrhea. Single-cell spatial transcriptomic analysis of matched baseline and post-treatment samples highlighted high baseline PD-L1 stromal expression and low post-treatment regulatory T cell signatures in pMMR responders, whereas dMMR responders displayed high baseline FCGR2A and FCGR3A expression on intratumoral macrophages. Clearance of ctDNA before surgery correlated with pathological response and lack of recurrence at data cutoff. Preoperative BOT + BAL elicits pathological responses in patients with pMMR or dMMR CC, supporting the combination as a promising strategy to expand ICI benefits to the early-stage setting. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05845450 .

records.title: Pheno+: An Electronic Health Record-Integrated, Clinician-in-the-Loop Application for Efficient Phenotyping in Clinical Genomics
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Objective  To evaluate the efficiency and diagnostic utility of Pheno+, an electronic health record (EHR)-integrated application that streamlines the generation of structured phenotypes for genomic testing and analysis. Materials and Methods  We developed Pheno+ as a Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies on Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (SMART on FHIR) application embedded within the University of Utah Health EHR. Pheno+ applies ClinPhen to clinician-selected clinical notes to identify candidate Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, which clinicians review and curate within the EHR. We conducted an eight-case crossover evaluation comparing workflow time between Pheno+ and a standard workflow that involved physician chart review and molecular geneticist-led HPO term selection. In a separate cohort of 17 patients with confirmed monogenic diagnoses, we assessed the diagnostic utility of Pheno+-derived HPO terms by evaluating Exomiser gene prioritization performance using these terms. Results  Pheno+ reduced mean total workflow time by 66%, from 31.1 to 10.5 minutes (p Discussion and Conclusion  Pheno+ reduced the time and personnel required to generate clinician-curated HPO term lists while producing phenotypes that improved causative gene prioritization. These findings support EHR-integrated, clinician-in-the-loop phenotyping as an efficient approach to generating diagnostically informative phenotype data for clinical genomic workflows.

records.title: Decoding adenomyosis: integrative insights from genetics, multiomics, and advanced computational analyses.
records.abstract: Adenomyosis is an oestrogen-driven, inflammatory uterine disorder characterised by endometrial glands and stroma in the myometrium resulting in abnormal bleeding, pain, and poor reproductive outcomes. Multiple contributors to its pathogenesis and pathophysiology have been identified over the years using a variety of experimental approaches and technologies, with gaps in integrating these approaches into a comprehensive paradigm of adenomyosis pathobiology. This review provides integrative insights from recent studies focused on genetics, multiomics, and advanced computational approaches. These demonstrate that select genes are causally linked to adenomyosis and that genomic and epigenetic mechanisms promote the enhanced oestrogen and diminished progesterone signalling and associated inflammation that are pathognomonic of the disorder, supported by orthogonal validation including novel 3D in vitro cell models. In addition, advanced computational tools, including AI-driven platforms that integrate multiomics data, reveal promising therapeutic candidates for mitigating disease progression and symptoms and improving fertility and pregnancy success.
records.authors: Liu B, Irwin JC, Giudice LC.

records.title: Cachexia defined by the Asian Working group for cachexia 2023 criteria and gut microbiota diversity in post-stroke patients capable of oral intake.
records.abstract: Background & aimsCachexia defined by the Asian Working Group for Cachexia (AWGC) 2023 criteria is associated with adverse outcomes in older adults, but its relationship with gut microbiota diversity remains unclear. This study aimed to examine the association between cachexia and gut microbiota diversity in stroke patients.MethodsThis cross-sectional study examined post-acute stroke patients capable of oral intake. Cachexia was assessed at admission using the AWGC 2023 criteria. Gut microbiota diversity was evaluated using the Shannon index, amplicon sequence variant (ASV) richness, and Faith's phylogenetic diversity (PD) based on 16 S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples. Multiple linear regression analyses were performed after adjustment for potential confounders.ResultsA total of 130 patients were included; the mean (SD) age was 78.4 (7.1) years, and 58% were men. Cachexia was diagnosed in 15% (19/130) of patients. After adjustment, cachexia was independently and negatively associated with the Shannon index (β = -0.282, p = 0.002), ASV richness (β = -0.279, p = 0.001), and Faith's PD (β = -0.264, p = 0.006). Among the AWGC 2023 components, underlying disease, low body mass index, decreased handgrip strength, and elevated C-reactive protein were independently associated with lower gut microbiota diversity.ConclusionsIn this cross-sectional study, cachexia was independently associated with lower gut microbiota diversity in post-acute stroke patients. These findings are associative rather than causal and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.
records.authors: Nagano F, Yoshimura Y, Wakabayashi H, Matsumoto A, Shimazu S, Bise T, Kido Y, Kuzuhara A, Yoneda K, Maeda K.

records.title: Treatment of viral retinitis after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with maribavir: A report of three cases and a review of the literature.
records.abstract: Viral retinitis subsequent to allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo - HSCT) is a severe post - transplant ocular complication. This study presents data on three patients who developed viral retinitis after allo - HSCT. All three patients received letermovir and acyclovir prophylaxis for cytomegalovirus (CMV) or other viral infections post - transplantation. They exhibited Epstein - Barr (EB) virus and/or CMV viremia and were associated with post - transplant lymphoproliferative disorders, which improved after rituximab therapy. Viral retinitis was diagnosed during immunosuppressive therapy (7-8 months post - transplantation), with negative peripheral blood viral DNA quantification at the time of diagnosis. Intravitreal injection of ganciclovir or foscarnet sodium demonstrated suboptimal efficacy, whereas visual improvement was achieved through combined oral antiviral therapy using maribavir. These findings imply that enhanced vigilance for viral retinitis and intensified fundus monitoring are necessary for patients with prior CMV or EB virus viremia during letermovir prophylaxis for CMV. Intravitreal injection combined with oral maribavir represents a novel therapeutic approach for patients with suboptimal responses to ganciclovir or foscarnet sodium.
records.authors: Shi Y, Wang X.

records.title: Biogenic gold nanoparticles in breast cancer nanomedicine: sustainable synthesis, multifunctional engineering, and the road to clinical translation.
records.abstract: The use of plant, algal, microbial or biomolecule based reducing and capping agents to synthesize gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) has paved the way for the use of these materials as versatile candidates for breast-cancer nanomedicine. In addition to being a more sustainable synthetic pathway, the biological elements attached to the surface of AuNP can have an impact on the formation process, the stability of AuNP in solution, the interaction with cells and the therapeutic activity of the particles. This review critically assesses the recent advances of biogenic AuNPs for application in breast cancer, ranging from direct phytogenic anticancer formulations, engineered drug delivery system, HER2 associated biosensing platform, photoresponsive therapies, and multimodal theranostic constructs. Preclinical reported mechanisms are increased cellular uptake, increased oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, increased DNA damage, cell-cycle arrest, and apoptosis. Additionally, Biogenic AuNPs offer flexible surfaces for the conjugation of chemotherapeutics, phytochemicals, nucleic acids, antibodies, photosensitizers and tumour-targeting ligands, thus providing opportunities for subtype-specific strategies for HER2-positive disease and triple-negative breast cancer. Currently however, in vitro studies dominate the evidence base, and many of these studies make use of limited models of cell lines. Although the bioinorganic nature of Biogenic AuNPs is scientifically interesting, their clinical applicability will rely on the development of reproducible synthesis procedures, characterization in biological environments, validation for the respective sub-type, quantitative biodistribution and clinically representative preclinical models.
records.authors: Singh UR, Mishra G, Leharwani M, Abourehab MAS, Gupta G, Wen Goh K, Kesharwani P.

records.title: Microplastic exposure and obesity-related metabolic dysfunction: A proposed gut microbiota-metabolite framework.
records.abstract: Microplastics (MPs), as emerging global contaminants, have infiltrated aquatic systems, soil, and food chains, raising concerns about their health risks, particularly their potential link to metabolic disorders like obesity. This review evaluates evidence that MP exposure may influence host energy metabolism and adipogenesis and examines the potential involvement of the gut microbiota and its metabolites. Dietary MP exposure can alter microbial communities and associated metabolic pathways. Such dysbiosis may impair intestinal barrier integrity, trigger chronic inflammation, and promote adipose dysfunction, thereby potentially contributing to obesity-related metabolic disturbances. We synthesize findings from animal studies, in vitro models, and multi-omics approaches, highlighting the roles of MP physicochemical properties, exposure dose, and duration in obesity-related metabolic effects. Current limitations include insufficient long-term assessments at environmentally relevant concentrations, uncertainties in cross-species extrapolation, and unclear interactions with co-pollutants. Future studies could combine organ-on-a-chip (OoC) models with microbial and host single-cell or spatial approaches to test microbiota-host crosstalk. Overall, this review synthesizes emerging evidence on the potential links between MP exposure and adipogenesis dysregulation and identifies priorities for future mechanistic research and risk assessment.

records.title: Characterization of peritrophin-like protein PvPT-L1 from Penaeus Vannamei: Potential association with dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase DLD from Lactiplantibacillus plantarum Ep-M17 and implications for probiotic adhesion and immune modulation.
records.abstract: Probiotics are widely used to promote growth and health in Penaeus vannamei; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying their interaction with the host remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified a peritrophin-like factor, PvPT-L1, as a putative critical mediator of the probiotic effects of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum Ep-M17. Full-length cloning revealed that PvPT-L1 contains three typical chitin-binding domains and shares high homology with Penaeus japonicus PT-L1. PvPT-L1 was predominantly expressed in the midgut, with considerable transcript abundance in the hepatopancreas and foregut. In vitro binding assays confirmed that recombinant rPvPT-L1 may bind to chitin and associated with both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Notably, PvPT-L1 significantly enhanced the intestinal adherence of L. plantarum Ep-M17 in a HEK-293 T cell model. RNA interference (RNAi) against PvPT-L1 resulted in 466 differentially expressed genes, disrupting redox homeostasis, proteostasis, and transmembrane transport, suggesting its essential role in maintaining gut barrier integrity. Using His pull-down and LC-MS/MS, we identified dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (DLD) that may be associated with bacterial cells as a potential interacting partner of PvPT-L1; this interaction was further validated by molecular docking, dynamics simulations, and co-immunoprecipitation. Functionally, oral administration of recombinant rDLD appeared to mitigated intestinal epithelial apoptosis. Interestingly, although rDLD suppressed hemocyte phagocytic activity, it effectively reprogrammed immune effector transcription and alleviated pathogen-induced apoptosis, hinting at a shift from robust internalization toward balanced immunomodulation. Collectively, these findings provide insights into a potential DLD-PvPT-L1 axis that may link physical adhesion and immune calibration, offering new mechanistic clues into probiotic-host immune interactions in crustaceans.
records.authors: Du Y, Li B, Yang X, Chen J.

records.title: Polystyrene nanoplastics exacerbate hepatic insulin resistance and glycolipid metabolism disorders in high‑fat diet‑induced obese mice.
records.abstract: Nanoplastics are emerging environmental contaminants with potential metabolic health risks, yet their chronic effects on high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity‑related metabolic disorders remain poorly understood. This study investigated whether long‑term oral exposure to polystyrene nanoplastics (PS‑NPs) aggravates hepatic insulin resistance and glycolipid metabolism disorders in HFD‑induced obese mice, and elucidated the underlying molecular mechanisms. Male C57BL/6 J mice were fed a HFD for 32 weeks with concurrent oral gavage of PS‑NPs (10 mg/kg, every 3 days). PS‑NPs co‑exposure significantly exacerbated body weight gain, fasting hyperglycemia, glucose intolerance, and insulin resistance compared with HFD alone. Hepatic histopathology revealed aggravated steatosis, inflammatory infiltration, and glycogen depletion in PS‑NPs‑treated obese mice. Mechanistically, PS‑NPs further suppressed hepatic protein levels of phosphorylated AKT (Ser473), insulin receptor (INSR), and glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2), while upregulating mRNA expression of gluconeogenic regulators (FOXO1, PCK1) and lipogenic genes (SREBF1, ACACA). In vitro, using HepG2 cells with high‑concentration insulin‑induced insulin resistance, PS‑NPs reduced insulin‑stimulated AKT phosphorylation, decreased INSR and GLUT2 protein expression, upregulated G6PC1 and ACACA, and downregulated SLC2A2, suggesting a cell‑autonomous sensitization to metabolic stress. Gut microbiota analysis revealed that PS‑NPs co-exposure further reduced microbial diversity and increased the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio in HFD-fed mice. Collectively, these findings indicate that HFD-induced obesity creates a metabolically vulnerable state that amplifies nanoplastic-induced hepatic insulin resistance and glycolipid dysregulation via interference with insulin signaling and transcriptional reprogramming. This positions chronic nanoplastic exposure as an underappreciated environmental driver in the obesity-diabetes nexus, highlighting the need for future risk assessment that considers host metabolic vulnerability and diet-pollutant interactions.
records.authors: Tang Y, Li T, Kuang X, Wu J, Qin D, Luo M, Han Z, Zheng Y.

records.title: 3D confinement reshapes RNA folding and enhances circularization in the Zika virus.
records.abstract: Many RNA molecules function within confined environments, but the effect of confinement on RNA folding remains poorly understood. Proximity ligation experiments reveal altered long-range contacts in confined vs. unconfined states, yet they do not explain how spatial constraints give rise to these differences. Here, we develop a physical modeling approach that incorporates proximity ligation data into coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to reconstruct RNA 3D structures under confinement. We test our model on the [Formula: see text]11 kb genome of the Zika virus, comparing the folding in virions (confined) and in cells (unconfined). We observe that the probability of contact between two regions of the genome vs. linear distance follows different scaling laws in the confined and unconfined cases, in agreement with proximity ligation experiments. We find that genome circularization-an interaction that regulates replication in Zika-occurs more frequently under confinement in both experiments and simulations. Our model reveals that the formation of long double-stranded stems through stacking confers local nematic liquid crystalline order to the RNA, and predicts pseudoknot topologies consistent with those seen in crystallographic structures of shorter RNAs. These results provide insight into the mechanism through which confinement alters the ensemble of 3D structures accessible to a long RNA molecule.
records.authors: Novev JK, Lau JY, Marenduzzo D, Kudla G.

records.title: Comparative transcriptomic responses of tomato to Xanthomonas strains isolated from different hosts.
records.abstract: Bacterial spot disease, caused by several Xanthomonas species, poses a significant threat to tomato and pepper production worldwide. Among these pathogens, Xanthomonas vesicatoria and Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. euvesicatoria have emerged as particularly important pathogens due to their widespread distribution and economic impact. While both pathogens cause similar symptoms, their genetic and pathogenic differences influence infection dynamics. In this study, we conducted a comparative transcriptomic analysis of tomato plants infected with one strain of X. vesicatoria (isolated from tomato) and one of X. euvesicatoria pv. euvesicatoria (isolated from pepper) to elucidate differential gene expression patterns associated with tomato defense responses. RNA sequencing at 48 hours post-infection revealed a higher number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in response to X. vesicatoria, with significant enrichment in pathways related to cell wall modification, secondary metabolism, and phytohormone signaling. On the other hand, infection with X. euvesicatoria pv. euvesicatoria induced a more limited transcriptomic response, with upregulation of a lesser number of genes involved in stress response. Key defense-related genes, including pathogenesis-related proteins (PR1, PR2, PR5), chitinases, and peroxidases, were activated in both infections but showed higher expression levels in response to X. vesicatoria. These findings suggest that X. vesicatoria elicits a stronger immune response in tomato plants than X. euvesicatoria pv. euvesicatoria under the conditions tested. This differential response likely reflects distinct interaction strategies employed by these strains during host colonization. Overall, our study provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying tomato-Xanthomonas interactions and identifies potential molecular targets for developing bacterial spot-resistant cultivars.
records.authors: Sánchez-Giménez L, Llorens E, Farvardin A, Cubero J, Scalschi L, Vicedo B, Camañes G.

records.title: Protocol for isolating intracellular Salmonella RNA from primary murine macrophages.
records.abstract: Isolation of intracellular bacterial RNA from infected cells remains challenging, limiting studies of bacterial transcription during host cell infection. Here, we present a protocol for isolating intracellular Salmonella enterica RNA from primary murine macrophages for transcriptomic analysis. We describe steps for macrophage infection, selective host cell lysis, bacterial recovery, and RNA purification for sequencing. This protocol uses standard laboratory equipment, is completed in 3 days, and can be adapted to other bacteria that replicate within macrophages. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Massicotte et al.1.
records.authors: Massicotte MA, Coombes BK.
