records.title: Monitoring-Network Composition and Analytical-Method History Shape Temporal Inference of Fecal-Coliform Exceedance in an Urban River-Lake Network, Taihu Basin, China.
records.abstract: Changing station composition and analytical methods can complicate microbial water-quality trends. We analyzed 2573 fecal-coliform (FC) observations from 64 reconciled sections in the Wuxi river-lake network, Taihu Basin, between December 2021 and August 2026. Records were available for 53 of 57 calendar months; four monthly files were irretrievably lost following a system error. Overall, 853 observations (33.15%) exceeded the common Class III FC benchmark of 10,000 counts L-1. A fixed panel of 21 sections contributed 1113 observations. Pooled and fixed-panel Sen slopes were 0.503 and 0.344 percentage points per month; their paired difference was 0.158 (section-bootstrap 95% interval 0.011-0.327). Binomial mixed models with calendar-month effects and section random intercepts gave annual odds ratios of 1.59 and 1.51, respectively. Adding an indicator for the reported October 2023 change from the rapid paper-strip method to the enzyme-substrate method reduced these estimates to 1.26 (section-clustered 95% interval 1.08-1.47) and 1.36 (1.02-1.81). Within the enzyme-substrate period alone, annual odds ratios were 1.17 (0.96-1.43) and 1.35 (0.93-1.98). Thus, the full-period association remained positive under seasonal and method-period adjustment, but the shorter, single-method record did not resolve a temporal association. Between-section heterogeneity and sensitivity to the monitoring population support reporting station coverage and analytical-method history alongside pooled trends. The method-period contrast cannot separate analytical effects from environmental changes occurring at the same time.

records.title: Ramping up the heat: Induction of systemic and pulmonary immune responses and metabolic adaptations in mice.
records.abstract: Heatwaves are an increasing public health concern, yet most animal studies use sudden extreme heat exposure that poorly reflects real-world conditions. This study examined the effects of gradual exposure to extreme heat on mice. Adult male and female C57Bl/6 mice were randomly assigned to heat-exposed, control, or pair-fed experimental groups. Heat-exposed mice underwent a single 8-h temperature ramp from 20°C to 38°C; control and pair-fed mice remained at ambient temperature. Multi-omics analyses after heat exposure included cytokine profiling in serum and lung, cecal microbiome characterization, lung transcriptomics, and serum metabolomics. Heat exposure altered several serum and lung cytokines (IL-17α, MIP-1α, MIP-1β, IL-1α, IL-12(p40), and RANTES). Random forest analysis identified microbial taxa that distinguished experimental groups, with a reduction in Lactobacillus observed in males; however, these effects were not statistically significant. Lung transcriptomics revealed changes in immune-related gene expression, particularly in pathways associated with B-cell activation. Serum metabolomics indicated modest disruptions in amino acid and energy metabolism, with enrichment of the glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism pathway. Integrated analyses identified associations among cytokines, gene expression, and bile acid-related metabolites. These findings demonstrate that gradual exposure to extreme heat triggers systemic and pulmonary responses in mice.

records.title: Divergent dependence on host gene sigma-1 receptor shapes hepatitis C and orthoflavivirus infection.
records.abstract: The Flaviviridae family encompasses major human pathogens, such as hepatitis C virus (HCV) and dengue virus (DENV). Despite shared genome organization and replication strategies, these viruses differ in host interactions, tissue tropism and replication dynamics, leading to distinct disease outcomes. Sigma-1 receptor (SIGMAR1) encodes an endoplasmic reticulum-associated protein that regulates lipid transport, autophagy and proteostasis. We previously showed that SIGMAR1 silencing reduces early HCV infection efficiency without affecting unrelated viruses. Here, we demonstrate that SIGMAR1 is rate-limiting for the formation of normal double-membrane vesicles (DMVs), the putative HCV replication compartments. In contrast, DENV and West Nile virus (WNV) RNA replication remained efficient following SIGMAR1 depletion, indicating a selective requirement for SIGMAR1 in HCV DMV formation. Notably, SIGMAR1 knockdown markedly impaired secretion of infectious DENV and WNV particles without reducing intracellular progeny, suggesting a role for SIGMAR1 in orthoflavivirus virion release. SIGMAR1 silencing also disrupted Golgi architecture and altered cellular detergent-resistant membrane composition, consistent with defects in vesicular trafficking. These findings identify SIGMAR1 as a host factor with distinct functions in the replication cycles of hepaciviruses and orthoflaviviruses and highlight its broader role in maintaining membrane organization required for efficient infection by Flaviviridae.
records.authors: García-Crespo C, Venturini V, Calvo G, Díaz-Piñero E, Castro V, Gastaminza P.

records.title: Follistatin-like 1 Promotes Neutrophil-mediated Host Defense against  Klebsiella pneumoniae
records.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of pneumonia and highly burdensome etiology of antibiotic-resistant infections constituting an urgent public health threat. Follistatin-like 1 (FSTL-1) is implicated in many processes including lung development and homeostasis, tissue remodeling, and inflammation though its role in antibacterial immunity remains poorly defined. We have observed that FSTL-1 is elevated in the lungs of both humans and mice during bacterial pneumonia. Using an inducible  Fstl1 knockout mouse model, we demonstrate that FSTL-1 is required for pulmonary bacterial clearance and neutrophil recruitment during  K. pneumoniae infection. Recombinant FSTL-1 rescues  Fstl1 -deficient susceptibility and enhances clearance of  K. pneumoniae in wild-type mice. Mechanistically, FSTL-1-mediated protection was lost upon neutrophil depletion and in  Cd14 -deficient or  Nr4a1 deficient mice – components of a lung-specific neutrophil transcriptional program. These findings identify FSTL-1 as a lung-derived factor that licenses neutrophil-mediated antibacterial defense via a novel FSTL-1/CD14/NR4A1-dependent signaling pathway critical for protection against bacterial pneumonia.
records.authors: Sugitani N, Henkel M, Applegate A, Partyka J, Wu T, Froelich NW, Dewicki A, Campfield BT.

records.title: From Biopsy to Pathology: A Retrospective Cohort Study of Predictors of Gleason Score Upgrading in Grade Group 1 Prostate Cancer.
records.abstract: Background/aimThis study aimed to identify pre-treatment predictors of Gleason score (GS) upgrading in patients with biopsy-confirmed Grade Group 1 (GS 3+3) prostate cancer (PCa) - those typically considered candidates for active surveillance according to National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines - so as to refine risk stratification and avoid under-treatment.Patients and methodsA retrospective analysis was conducted on patients with biopsy-proven GS 3+3 PCa who underwent radical prostatectomy (RP) at a tertiary referral center between 2010 and 2023. Preoperative clinical, pathological, and biochemical data were collected, including prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, prostate volume (PV). Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of GS upgrading. Collinearity among PSA, PV, and PSA density was assessed using variance inflation factors and correlation matrix analysis.ResultsAmong the 121 patients included in the study, 64.46% experienced GS upgrading at the final pathology. Patients with GS upgrading were older (median age 67.5 years), had higher PSA density (median 0.3 ng/ml/cm³ vs. 0.18 ng/ml/cm³, p=0.0033), and exhibited a smaller median PV (36.4 ml vs. 41 ml, p=0.0145) compared to those without upgrading. These findings highlight the limitations of biopsy-based grading in accurately assessing tumor aggressiveness.ConclusionGS upgrading is common in patients initially diagnosed with GS 3+3 PCa and is associated with pre-treatment clinical factors, including PSA density and smaller PV. Identifying these predictors preoperatively may improve risk stratification and guide personalized treatment strategies. Future research should focus on integrating genomic and molecular markers to increase the predictive accuracy and optimize patient management.
records.authors: Su HC, Su YC, Lee HY, Juan YS, Wu WJ, Lu K.

records.title: Crystallographic fragment screening in cancer and antiviral drug discovery: from electron density to translational outcomes.
records.abstract: IntroductionCrystallographic fragment screening (CFS) provides an experimental starting point for small-molecule discovery by defining a fragment's binding site, pose and routes for chemical elaboration. By establishing a structural hypothesis before major medicinal-chemistry investment, CFS reduces early uncertainty and the risk of pursuing a binding mode inferred from activity or modeling but not supported by experimental structural evidence.Areas coveredThis review examines how CFS advances fragments into lead series, preclinical candidates and clinical molecules. Oncology examples include kinase inhibitors, the PHIP2 bromodomain, the transcription factor brachyury and the metabolic enzyme PYCR1. Antiviral examples include viral proteases, polymerases, the influenza PA endonuclease and the SARS-CoV-2 immune-evasion protein Mac1. It also considers the practical requirements and limitations of CFS, criteria for hit validation and prioritization, and how high-throughput crystallography, reusable structural datasets and computational or machine-learning methods can support chemical elaboration and translational decision-making. Relevant literature was identified through targeted PubMed searches conducted from March to September 2026, supplemented by reference-list screening of relevant primary studies and reviews.Expert opinionCFS is most powerful when it provides an experimentally grounded binding hypothesis early in discovery. It converts weak binding into actionable geometry, reveals ligandable pockets and supplies credible design starting points. Computational and machine-learning methods can extend this information by exploring chemical space, ranking fragment elaborations and supporting multiparameter prioritization, but they do not replace experimental determination of binding modes or functional validation. Future progress will depend on reusable structure-affinity datasets and tighter structure-design-synthesis-test cycles that connect crystallographic evidence to biological decisions.
records.authors: Balıkçı E, Grimes JM.

records.title: EXPRESS: Feline granulocytic anaplasmosis in Europe: anamnesis, clinicopathological abnormalities, bacterial DNA load, treatment, and outcome.
records.abstract: Feline granulocytic anaplasmosis (FGA) is caused by Anaplasma (A.) phagocytophilum. Fever and thrombocytopenia are the most common clinicopathological abnormalities.ObjectivesThe aim was to investigate regionality, seasonality, clinicopathological parameters, treatment, and outcomes in cats with FGA.MethodsThe database of a commercial laboratory was retrospectively screened for A. phagocytophilum-polymerase chain (PCR)-results on EDTA-blood submitted by European veterinarians from 01/2022 to 12/2025. Hematological data and bacterial DNA loads quantified by digital droplet-PCR were analyzed. Questionnaires were sent to the veterinarians asking for underlying diseases, anamnesis, clinicopathological abnormalities, treatment, and outcome in cats with FGA.Results43/702 cats (6.1%) tested positive by A. phagocytophilum-PCR in Europe. Questionnaires were available for 29/43 cats (67.4%), all of which had outdoor access. Lethargy (23/29; 79.3%), anorexia (22/29, 75.9%), and fever (>39.5°C, 18/29, 62.0%) were the most reported findings. Thrombocytopenia was detected in 14/18 cats (77.8%) without concurrent diseases, anemia and leukopenia in 2/20 cats each (10.0%), eosinopenia in 10/17 (58.8%), and lymphopenia in 8/17 cats (47.1%). The bacterial DNA load was available for 27/43 cats (25 x 102-87 x 106, median 124 x 105/ml EDTA-blood), revealing no significant correlation with hematological parameters. 20/21 cats (95.2%) were treated with doxycycline and one (4.8%) with enrofloxacin. Uncomplicated course of disease was reported in 19/21 cats (90.5%). In one cat treated with doxycycline for 10 days, another positive PCR was recorded one month later. Clinical signs recurred immediately in another cat treated with doxycycline for five days only.Conclusions and relevanceFGA should be considered in cats with outdoor access, lethargy, inappetence, and most often mild thrombocytopenia and/or anemia, regardless of fever. Infected cats usually responded well to doxycycline with individual relapses if treated for 10 days or shorter. Treatment for 14 days to clear the infection, and PCR monitoring after finishing treatment are recommended.
records.journal: Journal of feline medicine and surgery
records.authors: Meyer L, Moritz A, Baneth G, Strube C, Jindal K, Müller E, Schäfer I.

records.title: Occult Hepatitis B Virus Infection Among HBsAg-Negative Maintenance Haemodialysis Patients in Malaysia: Association with Anti-HBs Serostatus
records.abstract: Abstract  Background  Occult Hepatitis B infection (OBI)—defined as the presence of replication-competent HBV DNA in HBsAg-negative individuals—poses a severe transmission and reactivation risk in haemodialysis units. This study aims to investigate the prevalence and clinical characteristics of detectable HBV DNA among HBsAg-negative maintenance haemodialysis patients, particularly those with anti-HBc positivity. Methods  A retrospective observational study was conducted involving 2,146 patients who attended the dialysis unit at Universiti Malaya Medical Centre (UMMC) from 1 January 2019 to 30 June 2024. Patients established on maintenance haemodialysis were included, while those with HBsAg positivity or missing data were excluded. Patient demographics, clinical variables, and biochemical information were extracted from the Electronic Medical Record (EMR). Data collection was conducted using REDCap version 14.3.13, and statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 29.0 and Python version 3.10.16. A Firth penalised multivariable binary logistic regression model was constructed utilising OBI status as the dependent variable to identify independent clinical predictors, addressing potential small-sample bias inherent in standard logistic regression. Results  Among 2,146 screened patients, 1,635 patients were included. Anti-HBc IgG positivity was identified in 23.5% (N = 384) of the cohort. HBV DNA testing was not performed in 146 patients under the testing practices prevailing during the study period. Within the tested core-positive subgroup (N = 238), overall OBI prevalence was 9.2% (N = 22). In patients with positive HBV DNA, 54.6% were concurrently Anti-HBs IgG positive (≥ 10 IU/L), and 18.2% possessed an Anti-HBs IgG level ≥ 100 IU/L. The multivariable Firth penalised logistic regression model revealed that while an Anti-HBs titre ≥ 10 IU/L was a significant negative predictor of OBI (OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.07–0.50, p = 0.001), it failed to exclude active viraemia entirely. Conclusion  Our study identified an overall OBI prevalence of 9.2% in a tested Malaysian ESKD cohort. Firth penalised logistic regression model utilising OBI status as the dependent variable confirmed that relying solely on Anti-HBs IgG to infer viral clearance is inadequate in this immunocompromised population, especially given that over half (54.6%) of OBI patients maintained Anti-HBs IgG positivity.
records.authors: Tan XYJ, Em JM, Ng ML, Lim SE, Abdullah A, Kun LS.

records.title: Integrated single-cell transcriptomics reveal E2F1-driven multidrug resistance in medulloblastoma and identify Palbociclib as a therapeutic candidate
records.abstract: Abstract    Purpose  Medulloblastoma (MB) is a malignant pediatric brain tumor where tumor recurrence driven by acquired multidrug resistance remains a paramount clinical challenge. Resolving the intratumoral heterogeneity underlying this resistance is urgently required to identify novel therapeutic targets. Methods  Single-cell RNA sequencing data and large-scale bulk transcriptomes were integrated and comprehensively analyzed. Multidrug-resistant subpopulations were identified by mapping ridge regression-based drug sensitivity predictions to single-cell profiles. Developmental trajectories and core regulatory networks were reconstructed, and essential transcription factors were functionally evaluated by computational vector field perturbations. The prognostic value of specific cellular states was assessed, and potential therapeutic antagonists were screened using computational databases and spatial molecular docking. Results  Two distinct multidrug-resistant reservoirs were identified, an  E2F1  -driven DNA repair state exhibiting cross-resistance to genotoxic agents, and a  ZIC5  -regulated neuronal differentiation state associated with Hedgehog signaling. Trajectory inference and in silico perturbations demonstrated that the continuous accumulation of  E2F1  is critical for maintaining the chemoresistant DNA repair phenotype. Clinical deconvolution revealed that elevated  E2F1  expression acts as a robust indicator of poor overall survival. Subsequently, computational pharmacogenomic screening and molecular docking identified palbociclib as a highly potent inhibitor capable of precisely binding and targeting the CDK4/6-E2F1 axis. Conclusion  An  E2F1  -driven DNA repair program and a  ZIC5  -associated differentiation state directly govern distinct multidrug resistance mechanisms in MB. Targeting the CDK4/6-E2F1 axis with palbociclib represents a promising precision therapeutic strategy to overcome chemoresistance in high-risk patients.
records.authors: Yao Y, Zhang J, Liang P, Ji H.

records.title: Long-term Glucocorticoid Exposure in Angiostrongylus cantonensis Meningoencephalitis Without Eosinophilic Response—Insights Into Treatment Withdrawal From a Medical- Humanities Perspective: A case report
records.abstract: Abstract    Background  Angiostrongylus cantonensis is the primary pathogen responsible for human eosinophilic meningitis. Atypical infection presentations lacking peripheral or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) eosinophilia occasionally occur under immune-modulated conditions. Long-term glucocorticoid use is a plausible contributor to blunted eosinophilic inflammatory responses. This case highlights that chronic steroid-induced immune alteration may lead to diagnostically challenging, eosinophil-negative neuroangiostrongyliasis, requiring heightened clinical vigilance.  Case presentation  A 48-year-old male with a 30-year history of psoriasis and chronic irregular oral dexamethasone use presented with generalized pain, fever, and altered mental status. Admission laboratory tests revealed neither peripheral nor cerebrospinal fluid eosinophilia. CSF metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) identified 1853 specific reads of  Angiostrongylus cantonensis  , confirming the diagnosis of neuroangiostrongyliasis. Given the patient’s critical neurological deterioration and family concerns regarding irreversible severe neurological sequelae, the family declined antiparasitic treatment; the standard albendazole-glucocorticoid regimen was not administered.  Conclusions  To our knowledge, this is a real-world case of molecularly confirmed  A. cantonensis  meningoencephalitis characterized by double-negative eosinophil results, strongly associated with decades-long irregular glucocorticoid exposure. Normal eosinophil counts cannot rule out parasitic neuroinfection in patients receiving chronic glucocorticoid therapy. CSF-mNGS successfully resolved this diagnostic deadlock, validating its role as a critical alternative diagnostic tool when conventional testing yields negative results. Family-initiated treatment withdrawal illustrates prevalent real-world challenges in prognostic expectation management, risk communication, and shared decision-making for severe neglected tropical central nervous system infections.
records.authors: Wang Z, Xue Z, Pu Q, Zhi D, Wang W, Yu A, Dong Z, Wang G, Liu A.

records.title: Transcriptomic Features Associated With Kinase Inhibitor Sensitivity in KMT2A-Rearranged AML.
records.abstract: Background/aimKMT2A-rearranged (KMT2A-r) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has a transcriptional program, but its relationship to drug sensitivity remains incompletely characterized. This study investigated whether a KMT2A-r-like transcriptomic state is associated with ex vivo kinase inhibitor sensitivity.Materials and methodsTARGET-AML RNA-sequencing data with fusion and cytogenetic annotations were used to define a predefined, biology-informed, continuous KMT2A-r identity score based on KMT2A-rearrangement-associated genes. The score was applied to Beat AML primary samples with matched normalized expression, ex vivo drug-response area under the curve (AUC) values, malignant cell-type scores, and FLT3-internal tandem duplication status. Associations were assessed using Spearman correlation and covariate-adjusted linear regression.ResultsKMT2A-r AML exhibited increased expression of HOXA genes, MEIS1, PBX3, MEF2C, and FLT3 in TARGET-AML. The identity score differentiated KMT2A-r AML from other fusion groups in TARGET-AML; when applied to Beat AML, higher KMT2A-r identity scores were associated with lower AUC values for kinase inhibitors. After adjustment for malignant cell-type scores and FLT3-internal tandem duplication status, cabozantinib, sorafenib, and pelitinib retained significant negative associations with AUC. Further adjustment for FLT3 expression attenuated these associations, whereas an FLT3-excluded score preserved their direction.ConclusionA KMT2A-r-like transcriptomic state is associated with candidate kinase inhibitor sensitivity patterns in primary AML datasets and appears linked to, but not fully explained by, FLT3-related biology.
records.authors: Choi W, Lee S.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Graph Methods for Microbiome Research: A Systematic Review.
records.abstract: The complexity of high-throughput sequencing data in microbiome research necessitates advanced analytical methods to decipher microbial community structures and interactions. Graph-based methods, which model taxa as nodes and their relationships as edges, have emerged as a powerful framework for this purpose. However, the rapid evolution of these techniques, from classical network analysis to modern graph representation learning, has created a fragmented and complex methodological landscape. This systematic review provides a comprehensive synthesis and structured overview of the field. We systematically review the literature and propose a three-part classification to categorize the primary contribution of each study: (1) novel methods for microbial network representation, (2) applications of classical graph analysis, and (3) the emerging use of graph representation learning for predictive modeling. We summarize the most frequent applications within each class, including keystone species identification, community clustering, and graph-based disease classification. Furthermore, we identify critical cross-cutting challenges, such as the lack of standardized tools and the need for improved model interpretability. By structuring the current landscape of graph-based methods, this review serves as a crucial guide for researchers to select appropriate models and highlights key gaps to direct future research.
records.authors: Shum-Tim C, Islam P, Boyajian JL, Abosalha A, Kassab A, Santos M, Khan KA, Stern K, Emad A, Prakash S.

records.title: Bacterial effectors targeting the host ubiquitin system.
records.abstract: Intracellular bacteria are largely shielded from humoral immunity but remain vulnerable to cell-autonomous defense mechanisms, many of which depend on the ubiquitin system. To evade autophagy and lysosomal targeting, numerous bacteria have evolved secreted effectors that disrupt or manipulate the host ubiquitin machinery to their advantage. Bacterial deubiquitinases can protect bacterial surfaces or their enclosing vacuoles from ubiquitin coating and interfere with host inflammatory and cell death pathways. Conversely, bacterial ubiquitin ligases may induce the degradation of host proteins, engaging in an evolutionary arms race with host ligases. In addition, ubiquitin-modifying and ubiquitin-crosslinking effectors can disable major host defense signaling pathways. In the present overview, we summarize currently known ubiquitin-directed effectors, their targets, and their roles in bacteria-host interaction.
records.authors: Eschger P, Hermanns T, Hofmann K.

records.title: Rare and Novel Hepatitis C Virus Genotype Subtypes and Response to Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir in A5360 (MINMON) Clinical Trial.
records.abstract: The introduction of potent, well-tolerated direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) has transformed hepatitis C virus (HCV) therapy and spurred global elimination efforts. However, the extensive genetic diversity of HCV may affect antiviral efficacy, particularly in low and middle-income regions where limited data currently exist. Using samples from the ACTG A5360 (MINMON) trial, which evaluated a minimal-monitoring strategy with 12 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) across five countries, we characterized rare and novel HCV subtypes and assessed baseline resistance-associated substitutions (RASs) and treatment response. Genotype/subtype assignments were obtained by NS5B short-fragment sequencing and confirmed through next-generation and whole-genome sequencing. Among 399 participants, 389 (97.5%) were successfully genotyped; whole-genome sequencing in unresolved genotypes identified several provisional novel genotype 4 subtypes and a putative new genotype 7 subtype (7c). Despite the presence of baseline NS5A RASs, all participants with initially unsubtyped infections achieved sustained virologic response (SVR12). Reduced SVR was observed primarily among genotype 3b infections (78%), consistent with prior data linking A30K + L31M RASs to decreased NS5A inhibitor susceptibility. Overall, SOF/VEL achieved high SVR across genotypes, including rare and novel subtypes. These findings underscore both the increased recognition of global HCV genetic diversity and the robust performance of pangenotypic DAA regimens, supporting universal adoption of simplified treatment strategies, as proposed by the MINMON trial, towards HCV elimination. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03512210.
records.authors: Han WM, Solomon S, Wagner-Cardoso S, Li J, Parvangada A, Sulkowski M, Naggie S, Martin R, Mo H, Maiorova E, Wyles D, ACTG A5360 study team.

records.title: Modulation of the FAK-Src Signalling Axis by Oncoviruses: Molecular Mechanisms, Functional Consequences, and Therapeutic Opportunities.
records.abstract: Oncoviruses play a role in cellular transformation and cancer progression by manipulating host signalling pathways, such as the FAK-Src axis. Preclinical evidence suggests that viral proteins can modulate this axis through direct interactions, integrin signalling, tumour suppressor inactivation, transcriptional and kinase reprogramming, calcium/ROS signalling, regulation of phosphatases, and epigenetic modifications. Important examples include HPV E2 and E6/E7, EBV LMP1 and LMP2A, HBV HBx, HCV Core and E2, and KSHV proteins. FAK-Src disruption can activate pathways such as PI3K/AKT, Rho GTPase, AP-1, and NF-κB, thereby enhancing migration, invasion, survival, angiogenesis, and modulation of the immune response. In some infections, this axis may also be involved at different stages of the viral life cycle. This review examines the molecular mechanisms of FAK-Src regulation by oncoviruses and its functional and therapeutic implications. It also reviews FAK/Src targeting strategies, distinguishing experimental inhibitors, multitargeted agents, and compounds under clinical evaluation, emphasising the limited clinical evidence specific to each virus. Finally, pFAK and pSrc are reviewed as potential markers of pathway activation and pharmacodynamic interaction with the target; however, current evidence is insufficient for their use as valid diagnostic or predictive biomarkers. A better understanding of the virus-host-FAK/Src interaction could help develop mechanism-based therapeutic approaches and biomarker-based patient selection.
records.authors: Albalawi YA, Deebani AO, Almadani HM, Almessiry BK, Mohammedsaleh ZM, Kaabi AMH, Abdulfattah AM, Assiri RA.

records.title: Immune-Excluded Mucosal Melanoma: Spatial Mechanisms of Checkpoint Resistance and Biomarker-Guided Therapeutic Opportunities.
records.abstract: Mucosal melanoma is a rare, aggressive melanoma subtype arising from melanocytes within mucosal surfaces of the head and neck, anorectal, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts. Unlike ultraviolet-driven cutaneous melanoma, mucosal melanoma has lower tumor mutational burden, fewer BRAF V600 alterations, greater structural genomic complexity, and recurrent drivers including mutations in KIT, NRAS, NF1, SF3B1, and copy-number alterations. It is often diagnosed at advanced stages, recurs locally, disseminates early, and responds less favorably to immune checkpoint inhibition than cutaneous melanoma. Low neoantigen burden contributes to this resistance, but emerging evidence indicates that antitumor immunity is also shaped by spatially organized tumor-immune interactions, site-specific mucosal biology, suppressive myeloid and stromal programs, angiogenic signaling, and underexplored innate checkpoint pathways. Here, we review mucosal melanoma as a biologically distinct model of immune-excluded melanoma, summarizing its clinical behavior, genomic architecture, immunotherapy outcomes, and mechanisms of checkpoint resistance, with emphasis on restricted intratumoral CD8-positive T-cell infiltration, macrophage- and stroma-rich barriers, angiogenic remodeling, and candidate innate checkpoints including B7-H3, CD24-Siglec-10, CD47-SIRPα, and B7-H6/NKp30. We further discuss how spatial and circulating biomarkers may support response-adapted translational studies and define actionable immune states across mucosal melanoma sites.
records.authors: Truong-Balderas KM, Chang RC, Lasalle C, Rogers MC, Wang Y, Amber KT, Mansini AP.

records.title: Microeukaryotic Diversity and Habitat Structuring in a Desiccating Alkaline Maar Lake (Central Mexico).
records.abstract: Microeukaryotes are important components of microbial food webs in saline and alkaline lakes, yet their diversity and distribution across distinct microhabitats remain poorly understood. We characterized microeukaryotic communities associated with microbialites, microbial mats, hypersaline waters, and sediments in the desiccating maar lake Rincón de Parangueo (central Mexico) using 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. After quality filtering and rarefaction, 417 amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) belonging to 17 eukaryotic phyla were identified. Community composition differed among microhabitats, with mats harboring the highest number of exclusive genera and water containing the fewest. No genus was shared across all four microhabitats. The greatest taxonomic overlap occurred between mats and water, suggesting ecological connectivity between benthic and planktonic environments. Ordination analyses and environmental data indicated strong habitat filtering associated primarily with salinity and conductivity. Co-occurrence network analysis revealed a highly modular community structure (Q = 0.789), with distinct habitat-associated modules and limited connectivity among them. Chlorophyta dominated assemblages, particularly in microbialites and water, whereas Bacillariophyta, Amoebozoa, Discoba, Aphelidiomycota, and Rotifera were present. Recurrent taxa such as Dunaliella and Picocystis occupied central network positions. These results demonstrate strong microhabitat-scale structuring and highlight the importance of fine-scale environmental heterogeneity in shaping diversity within alkaline maar lakes.
records.authors: Moguel B, Cerca M, Sanchez-Sanchez J, Muñoz-Velasco I, Vega-González M, Olmedo-Álvarez G.

records.title: Diversity of Ascetosporeans Associated With Feather Hydroids in New Caledonia.
records.abstract: Ascetosporea is a group of parasitic protists within Endomyxa that primarily infect marine invertebrates and can cause serious damage to fishery resources such as oysters and prawns. Although approximately 50 species have been formally described, environmental DNA (eDNA) studies suggest that their diversity remains largely underestimated, with many lineages yet to be discovered. Their ecological roles and host ranges are also poorly understood, partly because no complete life cycle has been elucidated, likely due to the difficulty of maintaining live cells in laboratory conditions. In this study, we investigated feather hydroids as potential hosts of ascetosporeans in New Caledonia, where this group has not been previously examined. Using metabarcoding with ascetosporean-specific primers, we detected 46 operational taxonomic units (OTUs) from three hydroid individuals. Of these, 31 OTUs were affiliated with environmental clades ENDO-3a and ENDO-2, whereas two and four OTUs were assigned to Paradinida and Haplosporida, respectively. Notably, seven OTUs were consistently detected across all samples, suggesting that they may have been broadly associated with the feather hydroids in this environment. These findings indicate that ascetosporean diversity and host associations in marine ecosystems are substantially underestimated.
records.authors: Yabuki A, Yamazaki A, Yamakita T, Miwa T, Fukuba T, Olu K, Toyofuku T.

records.title: 6PPD-Quinone Promotes Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease through Immune-Inflammatory Disruption.
records.abstract: 6PPD-quinone (6PPDQ), a transformation product of the tire antioxidant 6PPD, is widely detected in environmental and human matrices, yet its relevance to metabolic liver disease remains unclear. We examined its potential contribution to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) by integrating disease-burden analysis, computational toxicology, human transcriptomics, and cross-model validation. The intersection of predicted 6PPDQ targets with MASLD transcriptomic signatures identified 103 candidate genes enriched predominantly in immune and inflammatory pathways. Three machine-learning algorithms prioritized six hub genes, ASPM, ERN1, GADD45B, GINS2, LDLR, and MYPOP, which discriminated MASLD from controls with a combined AUC of 0.997. Immune deconvolution and single-cell analyses were associated with this signature with hepatic immune remodeling and intercellular communication. Molecular docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations predicted stable interactions between 6PPDQ and several targets, particularly ERN1. Environmentally informed low-dose oral exposure produced hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and injury in mice, while LC-MS/MS confirmed internal exposure. Concordant transcriptional responses were reproduced in the hiPSC-derived liver organoids. Integration of these findings supported a provisional adverse outcome pathway linking 6PPDQ exposure to MASLD-related liver injuries. Collectively, these results implicate 6PPDQ as a plausible environmental hazard for metabolic liver injury and support expanding the risk assessment of tire-derived contaminants beyond that of aquatic ecotoxicity.
records.authors: Zuo X, Ma L, Hou X, Zhang C, Tan S, Zhang Y, Pu Y, Zhang J.

records.title: A semi-automated genetic screen using genome-wide association analysis identifies modulators of stress-induced sleep in Caenorhabditis elegans.
records.abstract: Animals sleep more when they are sick. In Caenorhabditis elegans, stress-induced sleep (SIS) follows cellular injury such as exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light. The genetic regulators of SIS remain incompletely defined. Using robotic automation, high-throughput imaging, and genome-wide association analysis, we performed a semi-automated screen of 940 whole-genome-sequenced Million Mutation Project (MMP) strains. We quantified behavioral activity and quiescence before and after ultraviolet (UV) radiation. We applied the Sequence Kernel Association Test (SKAT) to this behavioral data to prioritize a set of associated genes and observed significant enrichment of known SIS genetic regulators. Based on these results, we conducted a candidate validation screen for additional genes regulating SIS. We identified three genes (strd-1, cla-1, and egl-8), mutations in which reproducibly influence SIS. Further exploration of these genes holds potential for enhancing our understanding of the molecular basis of SIS. These findings establish a pipeline for automated behavioral phenotyping coupled with gene-based association to accelerate studies of C. elegans neurogenetics.
records.authors: Li ZJ, Honarpisheh H, Kutagulla S, LeCure KM, Liang J, Raizen DM, Fang-Yen C.

records.title: The 2027 BCPT Perspectives on Studies Involving Natural Products, Traditional Chinese Medicine and Systems Pharmacology.
records.abstract: Natural products, including isolated compounds, complex extracts, traditional medicinal preparations and marine, microbial, fungal and animal-derived materials, remain important sources of therapeutic agents and pharmacological discovery. However, variation in biological source materials, preparation methods, chemical composition and experimental design may compromise reproducibility and interpretation. This guideline presents the requirements of Basic & Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology for studies involving natural products and their semisynthetic or biotransformed derivatives. It provides recommendations for documenting scientific and ethnopharmacological rationale, taxonomy, authentication, provenance, sustainable and lawful sourcing, extraction, chemical characterisation, dosing, bioactivity, safety and data accessibility. Particular emphasis is placed on studying the preparation actually administered, using pharmacologically relevant concentrations and doses, controlling vehicle effects and assay interference and aligning mechanistic and therapeutic claims with the supporting evidence. Complex mixtures do not necessarily need to be reduced to a single active constituent; however, their composition must be adequately characterised, and claims concerning individual constituents, additivity, synergy or antagonism require experimental substantiation. Computational, network and systems-pharmacology analyses should be transparent and reproducible, with experimental validation of central predictions. These recommendations apply equivalent standards to natural products and other interventions while recognising the additional information required to define complex biological materials and improve overall translational relevance.
records.authors: Tveden-Nyborg P, Yang B, Albayrak G, Simonsen U, Lykkesfeldt J.

records.title: Alr2204-Alr2205 form a functional modular thioredoxin system that enhances oxidative stress tolerance in cyanobacteria.
records.abstract: The cysteine-mediated catalytic reactions are essential for redox homeostasis in photosynthetic organisms. In the genome of cyanobacterium Anabaena PCC 7120 (Anabaena), the genes encoding thioredoxin reductase (TR; alr2204) and the atypical thioredoxin (Trx; alr2205) are contiguously located, but whether these proteins function as a redox pair remains unknown. Interestingly, Alr2204 and Alr2205, respectively, show high homology to the TR and Trx domains of the chloroplast NADPH-thioredoxin reductase C (NTRC). To delve into its possible role, Alr2204 was overexpressed in Anabaena. The resulting strain displayed elevated TR activity and demonstrated enhanced resistance to oxidative stresses. Biochemical characterization showed Alr2204 to be a FAD-associated, predominantly alpha helical protein with NADPH-dependent TR activity. Notably, Alr2204 supported the function of Trx Alr2205, indicating that Alr2204-Alr2205 formed a cognate redox pair wherein Alr2204 donated electrons to Alr2205. When co-expressed in Anabaena, Alr2204 copurified with Alr2205, and together these proteins enhanced the cellular levels of the reduced form of 2-Cys-Prx, a physiologically vital antioxidant protein. Importantly, Alr2204-Alr2205 also sustained peroxidase activity of 2-Cys-Prx. This is the first study to show that Alr2204-Alr2205, though independently synthesized, are functionally analogous to the NTRC protein, and Trx systems can be modulated to enhance stress resistance in organisms.
records.authors: Waghamare N, Hurali DT, Patwardhan RS, Banerjee M, Ballal A.

records.title: Sphingosine-1-Phosphate Attenuates LPS-Induced Inflammatory Cardiac Injury in Association With RASGRP1-S100A9-NLRP3 Signaling.
records.abstract: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induces endotoxemia-associated inflammatory cardiac injury rather than classical viral or autoimmune myocarditis. Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) regulates cardiovascular and immune responses, predominantly through S1P receptors, but whether it also modulates macrophage-associated inflammatory signaling during LPS-induced cardiac injury remains incompletely understood. This study investigated the role of the RASGRP1-S100A9-NLRP3 signaling axis in the cardioprotective effects of S1P. Transcriptomic and single-cell RNA-sequencing analyses were used to identify inflammation-associated candidate genes and their cellular distribution. Male Sprague-Dawley rats received a single intraperitoneal injection of LPS (8 mg/kg) followed by S1P treatment for 6 weeks. Histopathology, echocardiography, serum cardiac-injury markers, oxidative-stress indices, inflammatory cytokines, Western blotting, and cellular metabolic-flux assays were evaluated. RAW264.7 macrophages were used for mechanistic cellular studies. RASGRP1 or NLRP3 overexpression and S100A9-R101Q mutation were used to assess functional contributions. Molecular docking and molecular-dynamics simulations were complemented by SPR, MST, CETSA, DARTS, and Co-IP assays to evaluate S1P-RASGRP1 target engagement and pathway-associated protein interactions. Bioinformatic analyses identified RASGRP1 as a macrophage-enriched, inflammation-associated hub gene. In LPS-treated rats, S1P reduced myocardial inflammatory injury and collagen deposition, improved ejection fraction and fractional shortening, and decreased cardiac-injury, oxidative-stress, and inflammatory markers. In RAW264.7 macrophages, S1P attenuated inflammatory and oxidative-stress responses, restored oxidative phosphorylation and glycolytic capacity, and reduced the abundance of RASGRP1, S100A9, NLRP3, and ASC. SPR and MST supported a concentration-dependent biophysical interaction between S1P and RASGRP1; CETSA and DARTS provided complementary target-stability evidence. The molecular-dynamics trajectory showed substantial rearrangement of S1P from the starting pose before reaching a plateau and therefore supports conformational sampling rather than preservation of the original docked pose. Co-IP supported protein associations within the proposed inflammatory network. RASGRP1 or NLRP3 overexpression attenuated several S1P-associated protective effects. The S100A9-R101Q mutation also weakened several S1P-associated protective responses. SPR indicated a lower apparent dissociation constant for R101Q than for WT S100A9 after model-specific fitting, which is consistent with stronger or more persistent NLRP3 binding rather than loss of the S100A9-NLRP3 interaction. S1P mitigates LPS-induced inflammatory cardiac injury in association with altered macrophage RASGRP1-S100A9-NLRP3 signaling. Biophysical and target-stability assays support direct engagement of RASGRP1 by S1P. However, these findings do not establish RASGRP1 as the sole mediator of S1P activity, exclude contributions from canonical S1P receptor signaling, or demonstrate a strictly linear RASGRP1-S100A9-NLRP3 signaling cascade. Because the LPS model primarily represents endotoxemia-associated inflammatory cardiac injury, extrapolation of these findings to classical viral or autoimmune myocarditis should be made with caution.
records.authors: Yue C, Li Q, Li C, Yang T, Huang X, Yue F, Long Q, Li R, Lei R, Ma Q, Hu C, Yang Q, Yan Y, Liu Y, Yan Q, Yang M.

records.title: Novel ex vivo models reveal segment-specific infection of the human efferent ducts and epididymis: implications for Zika virus persistence and shedding in semen.
records.abstract: Study questionCan human epididymis and efferent ducts (ED) support Zika virus (ZIKV) replication ex vivo and act as a source of prolonged viral shedding in semen of infected men?Summary answerOur novel ex vivo models demonstrate that ZIKV exhibits segment-specific tropism, with sustained replication in the ED epithelium and restricted infection of epididymal stromal macrophages, identifying these organs as distinct reservoirs for viral persistence in semen.What is known alreadyThe 2015-2017 ZIKV outbreak revealed that the virus persists in semen and can be sexually transmitted by men long after the acute phase of infection. While the human testis is an established reservoir, animal studies and longitudinal semen analyses suggest that additional organs within the male genital tract contribute to the prolonged excretion of infectious ZIKV. However, the specific roles of the human EDs and epididymis have remained unexplored due to the lack of physiologically relevant human models.Study design, size, durationOrganotypic cultures of human EDs and epididymis corpus (EC) were developed and characterized using post-mortem tissues obtained from 11 uninfected organ donors (age range 29-79 years, median age: 58 years). Using this innovative ex vivo platform, we investigated ZIKV replication kinetics, cellular tropism, and the resulting impact on tissue viability and innate immune responses over a 9-day culture period.Participants/materials, setting, methodsED and EC tissues were dissected and cultured on PET inserts at the air/medium interface. Tissue integrity was validated via histology, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) viability assays, and transcriptomic/protein marker expression, assessed by RT-qPCR and immunohistochemistry. Explants were exposed to ZIKV, with replication monitored via viral RNA (vRNA) quantification, as assessed by RT-qPCR, and plaque assays for infectious virion release. Cellular targets were identified using RNAscope combined with immunohistochemistry. To determine the impact of the infection, we analyzed the innate immune response by RT-qPCR and ELISA and cell viability by LDH assays and cleaved caspase 3 expression, as well as the transcriptional and protein expression of a selected panel of cell markers, assessed by RT-qPCR and immunohistochemistry.Main results and the role of chanceThe ex vivo models preserved global tissue architecture, viability, and the expression of epithelial, macrophage and smooth muscle markers throughout the study. ZIKV infected the ED epithelium, with replicative vRNA persisting from 3 days post-infection (dpi) until the end of culture (P = 0.01). Conversely, in the EC, infection was limited to stromal macrophages and smooth muscle cells, peaking at 3 dpi before diminishing (P = 0.002). Both segments exhibited robustly repeatable results across donors. Notably, both ED and EC exhibited limited antiviral responses and weak pro-inflammatory responses to ZIKV infection. ZIKV replication did not induce significant changes in morphology, viability or functional marker expression, suggesting a non-cytopathic infection mechanism.Limitations, reasons for cautionWhile these organotypic cultures preserved multi-lineage cell types for 9 days, epithelial morphology and organization were gradually impacted, and the expression of a subset of functional and hormone-responsive markers (e.g. AQP1, ESR1, AR) decreased. Furthermore, the ex vivo setup cannot replicate in vivo viral entry via systemic circulation or luminal flow from the testis, nor can it account for the influence of infiltrating systemic leukocytes and global inflammation.Wider implications of the findingsThese novel human ED and EC culture systems bridge a critical gap in reproductive research. Our findings reveal a dual cellular pathway for ZIKV shedding, epithelial in the ED and macrophage-mediated in the EC, offering a mechanistic explanation for the prolonged presence of ZIKV in human semen. Furthermore, this ex vivo platform provides a new tool for studying male reproductive tract-pathogen interactions, as well as the efficacy of antiviral drugs.FundingThis study received funding from the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under grant agreement no. 733176, ZikaPLAN (grant agreement no. 734584) and ZIKAlliance (grant agreement no. 734548), and was funded in part by Inserm and the University of Rennes.DisclosuresWe declare no conflict of interest.Trial registration numberN/A.

records.title: Human airspace macrophage signatures are conserved during sterile lung injury and repair.
records.abstract: RationaleAirspace macrophages (AM) are implicated in both persistent inflammation and tissue repair following acute lung injury. Distinct subsets of AM are associated with lung pathology in humans, but whether unique AM signatures are specific to disease states or represent a conserved response to lung inflammation is unknown.ObjectivesWe sought to test the hypothesis that conserved subsets of inflammatory and reparative AM could be identified by transcriptional programming in a human model of self-resolving acute lung injury.MethodsA total of 15 participants underwent BAL before and at a pre-assigned time point after endobronchial exposure to bacterial endotoxin. Bronchoalveolar lavage cells were subjected to single cell RNA sequencing, and longitudinal assessment of AM programming during resolution of inflammation and lung repair was performed.Measurements and main resultsWe identify transcriptionally distinct subsets of tissue resident and recruited AM present at all time points, in all participants. Two recruited AM populations increase following inflammation: one that aligns with classical monocytes and one with interstitial macrophages (IAM). Airspace macrophage subsets display unique patterns of gene expression throughout the time course. Comparison of subset-specific markers to those identified in disease states reveals that IAM express many so-called pathogenic markers during normal lung repair.ConclusionsBy applying a uniform inflammatory stimulus to healthy adults and examining BAL cells obtained at precise time points thereafter, we construct a time-resolved kinetic of AM transcriptional programming during typical lung repair. Our data demonstrate that IAM share transcriptional similarity to AM identified in disease states and suggest they may reflect a conserved cellular response to tissue injury.

records.title: Genetic mapping of fruit texture in American cranberry reveals multitrait QTL and a complex genetic architecture.
records.abstract: Fruit texture is a key quality trait in cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon Ait.), with a direct impact on processing efficiency and overall profitability for the industry. To elucidate the genetic basis of cranberry texture, we conducted the first QTL mapping study in this crop, implementing a fruit compression method with 10 mechanical texture traits in 2 biparental populations, CNJ02 (n = 168) and CNJ04 (n = 67), over 2 years. These 10 traits, associated with flesh hardness/stiffness and elasticity, showed similar phenotypic patterns of transgressive segregation and generally strong positive correlations. However, traits accounting for fruit size and shape effects (stress/strain-related traits and maximum contact pressure), together with slope-related parameters, exhibited consistently high heritability across populations, supporting their potential utility for breeding and genetic analyses. Genetic mapping revealed multiple consistently detected multitrait QTL distributed across chromosomes 1,2,3,4,5,8,9,10,11 and 12, suggesting a complex genetic architecture. These genomic regions explained, on average, 4.67% to 18.6% of the phenotypic variance in CNJ02 and 10.97% to 27.75% in CNJ04. Candidate genes identified within these regions point to cell wall dynamics, including pectin modification, cellulose biosynthesis, and hemicellulose metabolism, as potentially relevant processes underlying cranberry fruit texture. Our findings provide loci in association with texture traits in cranberry and insights for the genetic improvement of this essential trait, informing the design of genotyping platforms and the implementation of genomic-assisted breeding approaches. Furthermore, we anticipate that these results will guide future studies aimed at optimizing postharvest fruit handling and management practices.

records.title: Integrative Analysis of Nucleotide Metabolism-Related Genes Reveals a Diagnostic Signature and In Silico Functional Disruption in Hypertrophic Scarring.
records.abstract: Hypertrophic scar (HTS) is a fibrotic skin disease characterized by excessive extracellular matrix accumulation and chronic inflammation. This study aimed to investigate cellular heterogeneity, immune alterations, and nucleotide metabolism-related biomarkers in HTS and to explore their potential mechanisms. Single-cell RNA sequencing data were analyzed using Seurat for cell clustering and annotation. Nucleotide metabolism activity was evaluated to identify key cell populations and candidate genes. Bulk transcriptomic datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were used for differential expression analysis, and machine learning algorithms were applied to develop a diagnostic model. Sixteen cell clusters were identified, with macrophages showing prominent activation of nucleotide metabolism pathways and immune-related signaling. The optimal Enet + svmLinear model achieved strong predictive performance (area under the curve = 0.934), and Shapley Additive exPlanations analysis identified NCF1 and GPR34 as key predictive genes. These genes were also associated with immune cell infiltration. In vitro validation using THP-1-derived M2 macrophages showed that NCF1 and GPR34 promoted transforming growth factor-β1 secretion and enhanced fibroblast activation, while their knockdown reduced α-smooth muscle actin and collagen I expression. Collectively, this study reveals the important role of macrophage-associated nucleotide metabolism in HTS and identifies NCF1 and GPR34 as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

records.title: Unveiling the antioxidant and antimicrobial potential of Astragalus tephrosoides methanol extract: Phytochemical screening, GC-MS profiling, computational and experimental approaches.
records.abstract: BackgroundPlant-derived bioactive compounds have significant pharmaceutical applications.ObjectivesThis study focused on the methanol extract of Astragalus tephrosoides (A. tephrosoides) to evaluate its phytochemical composition, biological activities and in-silico properties.MethodPhytochemical screening, GC-MS profiling, antioxidant (DPPH), antimicrobial and phytotoxic assays were performed. Molecular docking against bacterial proteins (DNA gyrase, lanosterol-14-α-demethylase, PBP2A and chitin synthase) and density functional theory (DFT) analyses were conducted for the bioactive compounds identified by GC-MS.ResultsPhytochemical analysis confirmed the presence of alkaloids, steroids, terpenoids, saponins, phenolics, volatile oils and coumarins in the extract. GC-MS analysis revealed the presence of 17 bioactive compounds. The extract exhibited notable antioxidant activity (IC50 = 0.66 mg/mL), comparable to that of ascorbic acid (IC50 = 0.58 mg/mL). Antibacterial effects were observed with net absorbance values of 0.860 (E. coli, P. aeruginosa), 0.770 (B. subtilis), 0.656 (S. aureus) and 0.550 (S. typhi) and MICs of 1.0-0.12 µg/mL. The extract exhibited antifungal activity comparable to that of miconazole and moderate phytotoxicity (66.6%) at 1000 μg/mL. Docking revealed moderate binding affinities, while DFT analysis revealed significant HOMO/LUMO gaps, indicating their thermodynamic stability.ConclusionA. tephrosoides contains bioactive compounds with promising antioxidant, antimicrobial and moderate phytotoxic activities, as supported by computational studies.
records.authors: Batool F, Wajid M, Alzahrani HA, Chohan TA, Mansour AA, Imran M, Khan A, Masroor D.

records.title: The Gain-of-Function GLP1R R131Q Variant Preserves β-Cell Function and Enhances Response to GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.
records.abstract: ObjectiveGenetic variation in the glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor (GLP1R) has been implicated in type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk and treatment response. We investigated whether GLP1R R131Q, which was previously reported as a T2D-protective variant in genome-wide association studies, alters receptor signaling, β-cell function, and response to glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs).Research design and methodsTrajectory of β-cell function was evaluated in a 20-year community-based prospective cohort in Korea (n = 6,373), where participants underwent biennial 2-h 75-g oral glucose tolerance tests, and disposition index was used as surrogate marker. Pharmacogenetic response to GLP-1RAs was assessed in a hospital-based T2D cohort in Korea (n = 177). Hyperglycemic clamp studies (n = 17), human islet experiments (n = 21), and in vitro assays were conducted to characterize GLP1R R131Q effects on receptor signaling and islet function.ResultsGLP1R R131Q was associated with slower decline in disposition index in individuals without T2D, with reductions from baseline of 30% in homozygous carriers, 35% in heterozygotes, and 37% in wild-type individuals. In people with T2D, each allele conferred an additional 0.53% or 5.8 mmol/mol reduction in HbA1c after 6 months of GLP-1RA treatment (P = 5.8 × 10-4). Hyperglycemic clamp and human islet experiments demonstrated allele-dependent enhancement of GLP-1RA-stimulated insulin secretion (P = 0.050 and P = 0.037, respectively). In vitro, GLP1R R131Q increased GLP-1RA-stimulated cAMP production with directional observations consistent with pathway bias.ConclusionsGLP1R R131Q is a gain-of-function variant associated with preservation of β-cell function and enhanced glycemic response to GLP-1RA treatment, supporting further investigation as a candidate pharmacogenetic marker for precision diabetes care.

records.title: Distinct Transcriptomic Profiles in ART-Treated People With HIV Are Associated With NF-κB-Regulated Gene Expression and Inflammatory Cytokine Signatures.
records.abstract: ObjectiveDespite effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), people with HIV (PWH) continue to experience elevated morbidity, potentially driven by persistent immune dysregulation. This study aimed to define transcriptomic heterogeneity in peripheral CD4 + T cells and identify immune signatures associated with clinical stratification in ART-treated PWH.DesignWe analyzed transcriptomic and immunologic (plasma cytokine) data from a well-characterized cohort of ART-suppressed PWH to identify biologically meaningful subgroups.MethodsBulk RNA sequencing was performed on peripheral CD4 + T cells from 154 ART-treated PWH. Plasma levels of immune mediators were also quantified. We applied Pairwise Controlled Manifold Approximation (PaCMAP), a novel dimensionality reduction technique, to identify transcriptomic clusters and assessed their associations with clinical and immunological parameters, including CD4:CD8 ratio and cell-associated HIV DNA/RNA.ResultsPaCMAP identified 3 distinct transcriptomic clusters among PWH. These clusters were enriched for differential expression of genes regulated by NF-κB, suggesting a role for chronic immune activation and inflammation. While clustering was not associated with HIV reservoir size, there was a modest association with CD4:CD8 ratio, a key marker of immune recovery. In addition, plasma levels of IL-1β, TNF-α, and G-CSF differed across clusters, supporting a link between plasma cytokines and CD4 + T-cell transcriptomic diversity.ConclusionsOur findings define transcriptomic subgroups in ART-treated PWH that are characterized by NF-κB-driven gene expression and distinct inflammatory cytokine profiles. These immune signatures may serve as biomarkers for immunological stratification and provide insights into persistent immune dysfunction despite viral suppression.

records.title: A C. elegans model for functional analysis of conserved ADPKD variants in cilia, extracellular vesicles, and sensory signaling.
records.abstract: Interpreting the pathogenic significance of missense variants in human disease gene candidates remains a major challenge in precision medicine. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), a common cause of kidney failure, results from mutations in PKD1 or PKD2, encoding polycystin-1 and polycystin-2. Here, we establish C. elegans as a platform for the functional classification of PC2 variants by characterizing PKD-2C180S, the C. elegans ortholog of the likely pathogenic human variant PC2C331S. Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing with dual-color fluorescent reporters and super-resolution imaging, we show that PKD-2C180S reduces cell-body protein levels, abolishes ciliary and extracellular vesicle (EV) localization, and eliminates sensory function, phenocopying a pkd-2 null allele. In heterozygous animals, PKD-2C180S is recessive and exerts no dominant-negative effect on wild-type PKD-2 trafficking, protein levels, or function, establishing that PKD-2 is haplosufficient in this model. PKD-2C180S also abolishes ciliary and EV localization of the PC1 homolog LOV-1 and reduces LOV-1 cell-body levels, phenocopying pkd-2 null animals, consistent with PC2 acting as a molecular chaperone for PC1 stability and trafficking. Genetic epistasis analysis shows that PKD-2C180S protein levels and ciliary trafficking defects are intrinsic to the mutant protein and independent of lov-1 and the ciliary kinesin-3 klp-6. Quantitative analysis reveals that LOV-1•PKD-2 is more abundant at the ciliary membrane and more efficiently packaged into EVs than PKD-2 alone in lov-1 mutants. We conclude that PC2C331S may perturb protein stability and/or polycystin complex formation prior to ciliary/EV trafficking. This work establishes a C. elegans pipeline for mechanistic classification of conserved ADPKD-associated missense variants.
records.authors: Wang J, Nava Cruz C, Walsh JD, desRanleau E, Nikonorova IA, Barr MM.

records.title: Optimization of RNA Sequencing Workflow in Brush Swabs of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
records.abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is associated with poor survival due to challenges with timely diagnosis and surveillance. Noninvasive biopsy methods, such as brush swab biopsy, have emerged as a promising approach with several clinical advantages over surgical biopsies, which may help overcome challenges in diagnosis, prognostication, and surveillance. We aimed to evaluate a noninvasive brush swab method for nucleic acid collection suitable for RNA sequencing in patients with OSCC. Brush swabs were collected from tumor sites before surgery, followed by corresponding fresh-frozen tissue samples from the same sites during surgical resection. Thirty-nine patients were enrolled [median age, 65 years (IQR, 55-73)]. As expected, tissue samples yielded higher RNA concentration and integrity than swabs [456.3 ng/μL (IQR, 291.3-651.3) vs. 73.2 ng/μL (IQR, 34.9-106.3); DV200, 91.6% (IQR, 85.9-93) vs. 82% (IQR, 77.3-87.8); both P Prevention relevanceBrush swab sampling is a simple, minimally invasive method to assess molecular changes in oral cancer, yielding results comparable with tissue samples. Its low burden and repeatability support early detection, monitoring, and risk assessment. Its practicality in dental and community settings enables broader access to screening and preventive care.
records.authors: Luong BA, Dong MP, Nguyen-Le DM, Arambula M, Asam K, Thomas CM, Callahan NF, Walker PC, Nguyen KK, Chen Wongworawat Y, Ye Y, Xu K, Aouizerat BE, Viet CT.

records.title: Tumor Microbial Burden Drives Immune Responses through Regulation of Interferon Signaling.
records.abstract: Tumor microbes are increasingly recognized for modulating tumor behavior and therapy responses. Intratumoral microbial burden (ITMB) analysis across cancers revealed regulation of immune pathways and activated mast cells, mostly in colorectal and gastric cancers. High-ITMB colorectal cancer leads to interferon (IFN) regulation and is associated with improved outcomes in advanced disease. Single-cell sequencing revealed induction of IFN-related genes (IRG) within microbe-containing human colorectal cancer. Gastrointestinal-luminal mismatch repair-deficient (MMRd) tumors had higher ITMB than proficient tumors. In a rectal MMRd cohort with 100% remission after immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), tumor microbes and microbe-containing mast cells increased. In ICB-sensitive syngeneic murine MMRd tumor models, local tumor microbial depletion impaired ICB efficacy while downregulating IFN signaling. Forced upregulation of IRGs in ADAR1-deficient cancer cells restored immunotherapy responses during microbial ablation. These data highlight dynamic interplay among ITMB, host defense, and immunogenicity, which seems key to determine therapy responses.SignificanceThe ITMB is linked to transcriptional and immune functional changes that seem to determine tumor sensitivity to immunotherapy. These findings highlight the key role of tumor-resident microbes in shaping the tumor ecosystem, which could be targeted to modulate therapy responses.

records.title: A Highly Sensitive ERA-CRISPR/Cas13a Assay for Detection of Vibrio vulnificus.
records.abstract: BackgroundVibrio vulnificus is a halophilic marine bacterium widely distributed in coastal environments and seafood products and is responsible for severe human infections and foodborne disease outbreaks. Rapid and sensitive detection of V. vulnificus is therefore critical for clinical diagnosis and seafood safety monitoring.ObjectiveThe objective of this study was to develop and evaluate a rapid, sensitive, and specific nucleic acid detection method for V. vulnificus suitable for application in complex biological and food matrices.MethodsAn enzymatic recombinase amplification (ERA)-clustered regularly interspaced short panlindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 13a (Cas13a)-based nucleic acid detection assay was established by coupling ERA with Cas13a-mediated collateral cleavage of fluorescent RNA reporters. The analytical performance of the assay was systematically evaluated using V. vulnificus standard plasmids, artificially contaminated human serum samples, and spiked oyster homogenates.ResultsThe assay exhibited high specificity for V. vulnificus, with no cross-reactivity observed for other common Vibrio species. The LOD was 1 × 10-1 copies/μL for standard plasmid templates. In complex matrices, including human serum and oyster samples, the assay achieved an LOD of 1 × 101 CFU/mL. The entire detection process was completed under isothermal conditions within 45 min.ConclusionA sensitive and specific ERA-CRISPR/Cas13a-based assay for the detection of V. vulnificus was successfully developed and validated. The method demonstrates strong analytical performance in both biological and seafood matrices.HighlightsA rapid isothermal ERA-CRISPR/Cas13a assay for V. vulnificus detection was developed. High specificity was achieved without cross-reactivity to other Vibrio species. The assay enables sensitive detection in serum and oyster samples. The method shows potential for routine seafood safety surveillance and marine pathogen monitoring.
records.authors: Pan Y, Nie X, Lü P.

records.title: An interdisciplinary comparative framework for antimicrobial efficacy and environmental risk assessment of antibiotics integrating human and environmental health: A case study from patient to river.
records.abstract: Pharmaceutical residues in aquatic environments are a global concern. The "benign by design" concept seeks to reduce pharmaceutical pollution, among others, through the development of environmentally less persistent derivatives of active pharmaceutical ingredients on the market. Here, we go beyond persistence alone by applying an interdisciplinary framework for comparative environmental risk assessment (ERA) to evaluate a novel fluoroquinolone derivative, ciprofloxacin-hemi (CIP-hemi), versus its conventional counterpart, ciprofloxacin (CIP). The framework integrates antibiotic efficacy, human pharmacokinetics, environmental degradability, and ecotoxicity to nontarget organisms to evaluate the balance of human health needs and environmental protection, combining experimental data with in silico modeling. We show that CIP-hemi, despite its higher overall degradability than CIP, does not exhibit lower risk to aquatic ecosystems at comparable therapeutic efficiency, except in a few specific scenarios where clinically unrealistically high doses are administered to patients. While CIP-hemi has lower predicted environmental concentrations than CIP when the same dose is administered, due to its faster hydrolysis in urine, higher doses of CIP-hemi are required to match the therapeutic efficacy of CIP due to the higher minimum inhibitory concentrations for pathogenic bacteria that are commonly treated with CIP. Consequently, even though CIP-hemi has higher predicted no-effect concentrations for aquatic ecosystems (201 ng L-1) and antimicrobial resistance selection in aquatic environments (56,000 ng L-1) than CIP (22 and 79 ng L-1, respectively), the higher doses needed generally cause higher environmental risks. Ciprofloxacin-hemi could achieve lower risk than CIP for antimicrobial resistance selection in some scenarios but only when administered intravenously and at unrealistically high doses. On the basis of this comparative ERA, we conclude that focusing on higher degradability alone is insufficient in searching for "greener" derivatives of existing antibiotics. Rather, an interdisciplinary framework is needed that integrates degradability, therapeutic efficacy, human pharmacokinetics, and ERA to improve the development of environmentally safer pharmaceuticals.

records.title: Lipid droplets and viruses: a dynamic battlefield of cellular resources.
records.abstract: Lipid droplets (LDs) are highly conserved, evolutionarily dynamic organelles. In addition to their canonical roles in energy homeostasis, membrane biosynthesis, and lipid signaling, accumulating evidence highlights their critical involvement in viral pathogenesis. As obligate intracellular parasites, viruses are entirely dependent on their host's cellular machinery. To replicate, they must hijack LDs to obtain essential lipids and energy, which are critical for assembling viral replication complexes and producing new virions. However, host cells do not passively accept viral invasion. Recent evidence demonstrates that pathogen infection triggers the innate immune response of host cells. This response, in turn, rewires lipid metabolism to drive the formation of new LDs. These newly formed LDs are characterized by surfaces enriched with immune proteins. These specialized lipid droplets serve as defensive structures that combat pathogen invasion through both direct and indirect mechanisms. This article provides a systematic review of the dual roles of LDs in viral infection: on the one hand, LDs are hijacked by viruses to facilitate their replication; on the other hand, they serve as central hubs in innate immunity, participating in host cell antiviral defense mechanisms. These findings lend substantial support to the hypothesis that "LDs constitute critical components of innate immunity", while offering novel perspectives for understanding virus-host interactions. Future investigations should focus on elucidating the specific molecular mechanisms by which LDs mediate immune regulation, and explore innovative antiviral therapeutic strategies through targeted modulation of LD metabolism.
records.authors: Ling X, Zheng Z, Qiao S, Zhang S, Wu J, Xiao S.

records.title: Differential pathogenicity of A3B2 infectious bursal disease virus strains associated with distinct inflammatory transcriptional signatures.
records.abstract: The emergence of novel lineages of infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV) raises questions about the relationship between viral genotype, pathogenicity, and host responses. This study compared the pathogenicity and bursal transcriptional responses induced by two genotype A3B2 strains exhibiting contrasting clinical phenotypes: the newly identified Polish strain 222/20 and the previously characterized very virulent field strain 75/11. Experimental infection of specific-pathogen-free chickens demonstrated that strain 222/20 caused no clinical signs or mortality, despite marked bursal atrophy and histopathological lesions, whereas strain 75/11 caused 56% mortality. Viral RNA loads in the examined tissues did not differ significantly between strains after correction for multiple comparisons. RNA sequencing of the bursa of Fabricius at 3 days post-infection (dpi), selected to characterize the early acute phase of infection, identified 703 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the 222/20-infected group and 3,573 DEGs in the 75/11-infected group relative to uninfected controls. Both strains induced interferon-associated and antiviral transcriptional responses. However, the 75/11-infected group exhibited a broader enrichment of pathways associated with cytokine signaling, inflammation, and cell death, accompanied by increased expression of inflammatory mediators and interferon-associated genes. These findings demonstrate that genetically related A3B2 strains can exhibit markedly different clinical pathogenicity despite the absence of statistically significant differences in the measured tissue viral RNA loads. The more severe phenotype of strain 75/11 was associated with a broader inflammatory and antiviral transcriptional response in the bursa. However, these associations do not establish causality, and additional functional studies are required to determine the mechanisms underlying the contrasting pathogenic phenotypes.
records.authors: Pikuła A, Lisowska A, Opolska J, Kycko A.

records.title: Targeted Metagenomic Sequencing for the Rapid Diagnosis of Chlamydia Caviae Pneumonia in an Elderly Patient without Known Immunosuppression or Animal Exposure: A Case Report and Literature Review.
records.abstract: BackgroundChlamydia caviae, a pathogen primarily causing conjunctivitis and respiratory diseases in guinea pigs, rarely infects humans. Previous human cases were mostly associated with direct contact with sick guinea pigs or occurred in immunocompromised individuals.Case presentationWe report a case of a 79-year-old female from Sichuan, China, without known immunosuppressive disease or therapy who presented with fever, fatigue, and left upper lobe consolidation, and was diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). She had no documented history of contact with guinea pigs or other pets. Empirical antibiotic therapy proved ineffective. Subsequently, probe capture-based targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS, specifically the MetaCAP™ panel) of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) rapidly identified C. caviae (sequence count: 1107, relative abundance: 54.50%) as the highly probable causative pathogen. Following targeted therapy with a doxycycline-moxifloxacin combination regimen, the patient's temperature rapidly normalized, achieving significant clinical and radiological improvement before discharge.ConclusionThis case demonstrates that pulmonary infection caused by C. caviae can occur in individuals without known immunosuppressive conditions and without direct animal contact, raising questions about potential alternative transmission routes and zoonotic reservoirs. The early application of targeted next-generation sequencing is of critical clinical value for the precise diagnosis and prompt management of rare and elusive respiratory pathogens.
records.authors: Li J, Li L, Wang J, Liu C, Rong X, Yang J, Si G.

records.title: Integrative transcriptomic, molecular dynamic simulation and in vitro analysis identify Evodiamine as a multi-target therapeutic agent against cisplatin-resistant non-small cell lung cancer.
records.abstract: An integrative transcriptomic, computational, and experimental approach was employed to identify molecular determinants of cisplatin resistance in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and to investigate the therapeutic potential of Evodiamine (Evo). Analysis of multiple Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets identified 100 overlapping differentially expressed genes, followed by protein-protein interaction network analysis that prioritized SPP1, GPX3, HBEGF, and KLF2 as key hub genes. Expression analysis demonstrated significantly increased SPP1 and reduced GPX3 and KLF2 expression in NSCLC tissues, while survival analysis revealed an association between elevated SPP1 expression and poor overall survival. Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment analyses indicated that the identified hub genes were predominantly associated with extracellular matrix organization, ErbB signaling, glutathione metabolism, and apelin signaling. Molecular docking analysis demonstrated favourable binding of Evo to the identified hub proteins, with SPP1, GPX3, HBEGF, and KLF2 showing docking scores of -9.1, -8.9, -8.9, and - 8.5 kcal/mol, respectively. Subsequently, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated stable SPP1-Evo interactions throughout the simulation period. In vitro validation further demonstrated that Evo significantly reduced cell viability (A549: IC50 = 4 ± 0.23 µM, A549CR: IC50 = 2 ± 0.31 µM), clonogenic growth, migration, and invasion in both cisplatin-sensitive and cisplatin-resistant NSCLC (A549, A549CR) cells. Interestingly, Evo showed better sensitivity towards A549CR cells than parental A549. Evo treatment also increased intracellular reactive oxygen species generation, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, DNA damage, and apoptotic cell death. Furthermore, Evo modulated the expression of the identified hub genes in NSCLC cells, supporting their potential involvement in its anticancer activity. Collectively, the integrated bioinformatics, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, and experimental findings identify SPP1, GPX3, HBEGF, and KLF2 as potential molecular regulators associated with cisplatin resistance and demonstrate the multi-target anticancer activity of Evo against cisplatin-sensitive and cisplatin-resistant NSCLC, supporting its potential as a therapeutic candidate for overcoming cisplatin resistance.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05107-0.
