records.title: Colonic Epithelial Differentiation-associated Remodeling and Gut Barrier Damage are Associated with Depressive-like Behaviors Under Chronic Stress.
records.abstract: IntroductionMajor depressive disorder and gastrointestinal dysfunction are frequently comorbid in clinical populations, but the colonic epithelial programs that accompany stress-associated behavioral changes remain incompletely defined. The cellular heterogeneity of the intestinal epithelium further limits high-resolution dissection of stress-induced colonic dysfunction. We therefore profiled crypt-enriched colonic epithelium from a Chronic Social Defeat Stress (CSDS) model in male mice at single-cell resolution.MethodsWe assessed behavior, colonic histology, permeability, and crypt-enriched single-cell transcriptomes during CSDS. Separate intervention experiments used systemic DAPT, a γ-secretase inhibitor, or intramucosal AAV-mediated Occludin expression; an antibiotic-depletion experiment was also performed.ResultsEarly CSDS was accompanied by social avoidance and detectable colonic inflammation, crypt injury, and barrier dysfunction, before the broader multidomain behavioral phenotype observed at day 10. Stress was associated with expansion of cycling colonic stem and transit-amplifying cells, impaired secretory-lineage maturation, disrupted tight-junction-associated programs, mucus-barrier impairment, bacterial encroachment, and enrichment of a Reg3b-high epithelial state. In the specific interventions used here, systemic pharmacological Notch inhibition or local AAV-mediated Occludin expression was accompanied by improvement in selected barrier-related readouts and stress-associated behavioral phenotypes.DiscussionThese findings identify temporally coordinated colonic epithelial remodeling and barrier damage in male mice exposed to CSDS and support an association between epithelial homeostasis and depressive-like behaviors. This crypt-enriched dataset should therefore be interpreted as a cell-state-resolved resource that generates hypotheses for future epithelial-specific, lineage-tracing, and mechanistic studies.ConclusionColonic epithelial remodeling and barrier damage are associated with CSDS-associated depressive-like behaviors in male mice.
records.authors: Gao J, Xiao S, Gao Z, Yang A, Cheng J, Wen J, Zhou H, Wang G, Aa J, Zhang Y.

records.title: Microbial dynamics across commercial spaceflights of varying duration.
records.abstract: Spaceflight introduces environmental stressors that can alter human microbiomes and immune responses. We analyzed 259 and 17 biospecimens for microbiome and single-cell studies from n = 6 astronauts across two commercial International Space Station (ISS) missions: Axiom 2 (10-day mission) and Axiom 3 (21-day mission). Samples included saliva, stool, urine, and body swabs from 10 anatomical sites, profiled via 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene amplicon sequencing. Gut and oral microbiomes remained stable, while skin-associated communities exhibited transient diversity shifts post-flight. Taxonomic analysis revealed individual and site-specific patterns, as well as from the spaceflight/ISS environment. Cytokine profiling from single-cell data indicated immune activation, with IL-32 and IL-16 transcripts elevated in Axiom 2 and Axiom 3. Microbiome and interleukin correlation analyses found 14 significant associations in Axiom 2 data. These findings provide an integrated view of microbiome individuality. Our study represents a descriptive comparison of two missions, informing strategies for crew health on future long-duration missions.

records.title: Rapid visual and direct detection of Acinetobacter baumannii and carbapenem resistance by oligoDNA-gold nanoparticles biosensor in clinical samples.
records.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a major nosocomial pathogen responsible for extensively drug-resistant (XDR) infections in healthcare settings and is ranked as a critical priority one pathogen on World Health Organisation list. However, clinical diagnosis generally is given as (Acinetobacter calcoaceticus-baumannii) ACB complex, including A. baumannii, A. calcoaceticus, A. nosocomialis, and A. pittii, and among these, A. baumannii is the most clinically significant species. Further the conventional diagnostic methods take 4-48 h and many of them require sophisticated infrastructure, highlighting the urgent need for rapid and economical detection methods both for A. baumannii and its carbapenem resistance determinants. Among the carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii, blaOXA-23 and blaNDM are the predominant β-lactamase genes, with New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) conferring broad-spectrum carbapenem resistance and severely limiting the therapeutic options. In the present study, oligoDNA-gold nanoparticle (AuNP)-based biosensors were developed for the direct, rapid and visual detection of A. baumannii, blaOXA-23 and blaNDM in clinical respiratory samples without the need for DNA purification or amplification. The biosensor for the detection of A. baumannii targeted a conserved region of the Outer Membrane Nuclease encoding nucAb gene, enabling its accurate identification. blaOXA-23 biosensor detected blaOXA-23 gene, which is the highly prevalent carbapenem resistance gene in A. baumannii while the other biosensor, based on the conserved region of blaNDM gene, detected blaNDM-1 not only in A. baumannii but also its variants in Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. These biosensors produced visual results within 30 min, with a detection limit of 0.5 ng/µL DNA or 10³ CFU/mL to support early clinical decision-making for optimised therapy and antimicrobial resistance surveillance.

records.title: Myristic acid promotes cell-to-cell spread of Marek's disease virus by inhibiting STING-mediated IFN-β production and reprograming metabolic profiles.
records.abstract: Myristic acid (MA), which is typically synthesized by various cellular processes as a physiological metabolite, has recently emerged as an endogenous immune regulator through N-myristoylation. This post-translational modification (PTM) has been shown to suppress STING-mediated production of type I interferon (IFN-I), leading to inhibition of antiviral innate immunity in mammals. Although a variety of mammalian viruses manipulate N-myristoylation for efficient replication and immune evasion, little is known about whether avian viruses also exploit MA-induced PTM for their benefits. For this purpose, our present study used primary chicken embryo fibroblasts (CEFs) as a model to analyze the effects of MA on the IFN-I production induced by the STING signaling pathway, and evaluated whether MA facilitates replication of Marek's disease virus (MDV) in vitro. In the context of cGAMP stimulation, the mRNA levels of both TBK1 and IRF7 were decreased by MA treatment, leading to suppression of IFN-β synthesis. Interestingly, the presence of MA significantly dampened the expression of IRF7 and IFN-β transcripts at 72 h post-infection with MDV. This inhibitory effect can be reversed by the N-myristoyltransferase inhibitor DDD85646. Noticeably, MA treatment significantly elevated the expression of MDV glycoprotein gC and led to larger viral plaques, indicating enhanced cell-to-cell spread; however, MDV replication was not improved in the presence of MA. Moreover, metabolomic analysis revealed that MDV infection caused significant alterations in multiple metabolic pathways, including glycerophospholipid metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, and cofactor biosynthesis. In MDV-infected CEFs, MA exacerbated abnormalities of lipid metabolism and specifically activated inflammation-related pathways such as arachidonic acid metabolism and α-linolenic acid metabolism. Taken together, the present study provides a novel understanding on how MDV manipulates N-myristoylation to establish a favorable metabolic program for efficient cell-to-cell spread.

records.title: Multi-omics insights into the effects of selenium yeast-enriched water on the hepatic responses of hybrid (Megalobrama amblycephala ♀ × Ancherythroculter nigrocauda ♂).
records.abstract: The health-promoting effects of selenium (Se) in fish have been well established; however, current research mainly focuses on dietary Se supplementation. Waterborne Se exposure serves as a complementary approach, yet the regulatory effects and underlying molecular mechanisms of farming fish in Se yeast-enriched water on hepatic function remain unclear. This study used the hybrid fish "Xianfeng No. 2" (Megalobrama amblycephala ♀ × Ancherythroculter nigrocauda ♂) as the experimental animal model. After three weeks of culture in Se yeast-enriched water at a target total Se concentration of 0.07 mg L-1, integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses were conducted to explore the hepatic responses to organic Se. Firstly, metabolomic analysis identified 399 metabolites, among which 16 high-confidence characteristic markers potentially closely associated with flesh quality were screened out, including nutritionally valuable metabolites such as docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), clupanodonic acid (DPA), and leucinic acid. Differential metabolites were significantly enriched in pathways pertaining to amino acid metabolism, substance transport and biosynthesis. Secondly, transcriptomic analysis revealed that multiple redox-and immune-related genes were significantly up-regulated in the Se-treated group, including selenoproteins (SELENON, GPX2, and TXNRD3), the complement system (CFB, CFH, and C3), and antioxidant-regulatory genes (GFER and FOXO3), pointing to potential molecular signatures of altered hepatic immune function and antioxidant defense. Thirdly, integrated multi-omics analysis preliminarily identified coordinated changes in retinol and vitamin B6 metabolic pathways. Elevated expression of CYP26A1 and PDXP was associated with the accumulation of vitamin A and pyridoxamine, which may provide a molecular basis for alterations in hepatic antioxidant defense. This study preliminarily reveals potential regulatory mechanisms underlying Se biofortification and quality improvement in fish reared in Se yeast-enriched water at the molecular and metabolic levels, providing a theoretical basis and candidate targets for Se-enriched fish culture and molecular breeding.
records.journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part D, Genomics & proteomics
records.authors: Fang Y, Lan M, Qin Q, Wang G, Yu Y, Li Q, Bai Q, Song Z, Ye L, Ji W, Sun Y, Zhang L.

records.title: Thymic single-cell RNA sequencing reveals the immunosuppressive microenvironment in chicken model simulating vertical transmission of recombinant ALV.
records.abstract: Avian leukosis virus (ALV) induces immunosuppression and tumorigenesis. In this study, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was used to analyze the transcriptional dynamics of thymic immune cells in specific-pathogen-free (SPF) chickens, which were intra-embryonic infected with the naturally recombinant ALV-FJ15TH0, at 1-day-old (d), 28d, and 56d post-hatch. Using subgroup-specific marker genes and cell state analysis, we identified six T-cell clusters, two B-cell clusters, and a macrophage cell cluster. Differential gene analysis revealed that ALV infection resulted in a significant enrichment of downregulated genes across all immune cell subsets at 28d. Functional enrichment analysis indicated that ALV infection activated the FoxO immunosuppressive pathway, PI3K pathway, MAPK pathway (CD4+CD8+ T cells and M2 macrophages at 1d), multicellular synergistic regulation of the cancer pathway (CD4+CD8+ T cells, M2 macrophages, and Cytotoxic T cells at 28d), and ErbB signaling pathway, Notch signaling pathway (CD4+CD8+ T cells and M2 macrophages at 56d). Cell-cell communication analysis revealed that ALV infection induced the strongest predicted communication via the PPIA-BSG axis at 28 d. Analysis further inferred that CD147 (BSG) was associated with multiple signaling pathways, including MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT, which may contribute to the immunosuppressive microenvironment. BCL11B, SP3, and EP300 were identified as potential regulatory components with subset-specific associations with JUN, BRAF, and MYB, potentially involving the MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and FoxO signaling pathways. This study reveals the dynamic evolution of the thymic immune microenvironment following ALV-FJ15TH0 infection, providing a resource for understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying ALV-induced immunosuppression and offering a foundation for future investigation of its potential relationship with tumorigenesis.
records.authors: Zhang D, Pan Y, Zhong Z, Gu Q, Qiu W, Chen N, Meng K, Gong Z, Zeng Y, Zhao J, Liu P, Wu Y, Wu X.

records.title: Genomic characterization and selection signals in Italian black Atriana chickens using high-density SNP array.
records.abstract: The black Atriana (ATRI) is a local Italian chicken breed of historical and cultural importance. This study evaluated its genetic diversity and population structure and identified putative signatures of selection using runs of homozygosity (ROH) and the integrated haplotype score (iHS). Nineteen ATRI birds and 494 birds from 24 Mediterranean local breeds were genotyped with the Affymetrix Axiom 600 K Chicken Genotyping Array. After quality control, 505 birds and 495,454 autosomal SNPs were retained. In ATRI, observed heterozygosity, expected heterozygosity, and minor allele frequency averaged 0.345, 0.358, and 0.270, respectively. The inbreeding coefficients based on observed versus expected homozygosity and on ROH were 0.037 and 0.222, respectively. Principal component, NeighborNet, and ADMIXTURE analyses supported a distinguishable ATRI genomic profile while indicating affinities with several Mediterranean breeds. ROH and iHS analyses identified six candidate regions each, including two overlapping regions on chromosomes 2 and 14. These regions contained genes previously associated with growth, production, and environmental-response traits, including PTP4A3, TSNARE1, NDUFB6, WFIKKN1, and IFT140. Given the limited ATRI sample size, these candidate signals should be interpreted as exploratory and validated in larger independent populations. The findings provide baseline genomic information to support genetic monitoring and conservation planning for ATRI.
records.authors: Saleh MS, Perini F, Camarda A, Bettini S, Mugnai C, Landi V, Lasagna E.

records.title: Psl exopolysaccharide regulates biofilm formation and environmental adaptation in Pseudomonas fluorescens PF07.
records.abstract: Pseudomonas fluorescens PF07, a prevalent psychrotrophic spoilage bacterium, relies heavily on robust biofilm formation to persist in food environments and exert spoilage effects. Nevertheless, the distinct contributions of exopolysaccharides to its biofilm maturation and stress adaptation remain unclear. Herein, we systematically characterized the genetic determinants and biological functions of three exopolysaccharides (Psl, alginate and PNAG) in modulating PF07 biofilm development and resistance to food-processing-associated stressors. Single, double, and triple deletion mutants targeting the pslB, alg8, and pgaC genes were constructed to evaluate the contributions of these biosynthetic systems, and transcriptomic analysis was performed to explore the underlying responses. Deletion of pslB markedly impaired biofilm formation, pellicle development, and extracellular matrix production, whereas deficiency of alg8 or pgaC caused only minor phenotypic changes compared with the wild-type strain, indicating that Psl is the primary structural determinant of the PF07 biofilm matrix. Furthermore, double- and triple-mutants lacking pslB exhibited more severe reductions in biofilm biomass and thickness, suggesting that alginate and PNAG make supplementary but secondary contributions to the Psl-dominated biofilm matrix. In addition, ΔpslB exhibited substantially reduced biofilm formation under low temperature and ionic stress and decreased tolerance to sodium hypochlorite and benzalkonium chloride, in contrast with limited alterations for the Δalg8 and ΔpgaC mutants. Consistently, catalase and superoxide dismutase activities were significantly weakened in the ΔpslB mutant but largely unaltered in the Δalg8 mutant, indicating that Psl deficiency was associated with reduced antioxidant enzyme activities and suggesting a potential role of Psl in the antioxidant response of PF07. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed significant changes in genes associated with stress adaptation and metabolism, including the upregulation of aqpZ, the downregulation of osmY, and alterations in multiple metabolism-related genes. Thus, these findings demonstrate that Psl is a pivotal structural polysaccharide in the biofilm matrix of P. fluorescens PF07 and plays critical roles in biofilm structure and tolerance to cold, ionic, and oxidative stresses, providing new insights into potential strategies for controlling P. fluorescens biofilms in food-processing environments.
records.authors: Lu Z, Zhou Z, Feng L, Zhu J.

records.title: Immune profile dysregulation of high grade- compared to low grade-pseudomyxomas.
records.abstract: BackgroundPseudomyxoma peritonei is a rare and poorly understood cancer. The histological characteristics that classify pseudomyxoma as either low-grade or high-grade are major prognostic factors. The present study aimed to identify differentially expressed genes in low-grade and high-grade pseudomyxomas using transcriptomic analysis, in order to improve our understanding of their pathophysiology.MethodsTwo cohorts of pseudomyxoma peritonei FFPE samples composed by 13 low grade and 11 high grade tumours respectively were selected. The expression of several biomarkers (CK7, CK20, MUC2, MUC5AC, Ki67) were analysed by immunohistochemistry. Gene expression profiles were studied using Nanostring™ technology and included the tumour signalling 360™ panel (760 tumour signalling related genes and 20 internal reference controls) and the inflammation v2 panel (249 inflammation-related human genes and 6 internal reference controls).ResultsThe study revealed distinct transcriptomic profiles of the immune response in low grade and high grade, indicating dysregulation of immune cell migration and/or chemotaxis, as well as modulation of cellular metabolic activities and cell signalling. In addition, in high grade pseudomyxoma peritonei, there are genes and signalling pathways linked to the response to lipopolysaccharides and bacterial molecules were also downregulated. Our results strengthen both the role of immune response and the role of bacterial involvement in pseudomyxoma peritonei pathophysiology.
records.authors: Bourgin C, Golias M, Ollivier E, Levergeois R, Cochonneau D, Thibaudeau E, Dumont F, Vignaud T, Heymann MF, Heymann D.

records.title: Ancestral Quadruplication of Protein Kinase R in Tarsiers Hints Towards Novel Primate-Virus Innovations
records.abstract: Tarsiers, an elusive family of primates found in Indonesia and the Philippines, sit at an essential point in primate evolution, with their divergence between that of Strepsirrhini (lemurs) and Simiiformes (monkeys and apes). Through homology searches, we have discovered that tarsiers carry the first known case in primates of a gene expansion of protein kinase R (PKR), a kinase involved in the response to viral infection. PKR was quadruplicated in the ancestor of tarsiers and has been maintained since then in all sequenced tarsier species. The extra copies lack the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) binding domains necessary for detecting viral infection yet largely maintain the residues necessary for the kinase function that carries out PKR’s antiviral function. We show that three of the four PKR copies indeed maintain kinase activity, one of which appears to be resistant to the viral PKR antagonist K3 from vaccinia virus. Our analyses of site and branch-site positive selection reveal that the tarsier PKRs are under positive selection. We propose that these extra copies could serve as a diversification strategy to bypass viral inhibitors that bind PKR’s kinase domain, or they could alternatively serve as decoys that shield the canonical PKR from viral inhibition. This is the first instance of mammal PKR duplicates lacking dsRNA-binding domains and may highlight an innovation in an ancient, long-standing molecular arms race between viruses and a close relative of humans.
records.authors: Heneghan PG, Grieve TR, Sadhu MJ.

records.title: A Review of Rhizosphere Processes, Plant Performance and Production Trade‑Offs in Soil Versus Solid‑Substrate Cultivation of Greenhouse Strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa)
records.abstract: Strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) is an economically important berry crop in protected horticulture, mainly produced through soil‑based and solid‑substrate soilless systems. Soil cultivation possesses strong physicochemical buffering and abundant indigenous microbial resources, but suffers from continuous cropping obstacles including soil degradation and soil‑borne pathogen accumulation. Solid‑substrate cultivation can isolate soil‑borne pathogens and enables precise rhizosphere manipulation; however, it is constrained by low buffering capacity, unstable microbial assembly, peat‑related ecological costs, and waste‑substrate disposal risks. This review builds a unified analytical framework centered on the cascade "medium physicochemical properties – microbial community – extracellular enzymes – root physiology – yield‑quality performance" and clarifies the conceptual boundaries among soil cultivation, solid‑substrate cultivation, and hydroponics. We analyze the sources of heterogeneity across published results, including cultivar genotype, medium properties, water‑fertilizer management, growth stage, and analytical methodology. Most existing evidence is correlational, whereas rigorous causal manipulation experiments remain scarce, which explains why no universal consensus has been reached on the relative superiority of the two production modes. Key research gaps include fragmented rhizospheric mechanism research, lack of cross‑study standardized experimental conditions, insufficient normalization of enzyme and microbiome datasets, and a shortage of long‑term multi‑objective field assessments. We highlight that microbial–functional decoupling frequently occurs in both soil and solid‑substrate systems, indicating that microbial community composition alone cannot represent real rhizosphere biogeochemical processes. Based on evidence synthesis, differentiated optimization strategies are proposed: soil systems should prioritize soil‑health restoration, whereas solid‑substrate systems need peat‑substitute development, microbial–habitat compatible inoculation, and substrate circular regeneration. Shared future directions cover in‑situ rhizosphere sensing, causal validation experiments, and multi‑objective evaluation balancing yield, fruit quality, resource cost, and environmental footprints. This review provides theoretical references for sustainable protected strawberry production.
records.authors: Zha Y, Hu S, Liu A, Li C, Lai W, Li X, Wang J, Yu H, Xiao W.

records.title: Hydrogels in Pharmacy and Medicine: An Illustrated Review of Preparation Methods, Process Control and Drug Delivery Applications
records.abstract: Hydrogels, three-dimensional hydrophilic polymer networks that can imbibe large volumes of water or biological fluids without dissolving, have become one of the most versatile platforms in pharmaceutical and biomaterial science. Their high water content, soft tissue-like mechanics, biocompatibility and tunable network architecture allow them to be engineered as topical, ophthalmic, mucosal, oral and injectable dosage forms and as scaffolds for regenerative medicine. This illustrated review provides a critical, practice-oriented account of the field, with particular emphasis on how hydrogel dosage forms are prepared. Physical cross-linking methods (ionic gelation, polyelectrolyte complexation, thermoresponsive gelation, freeze–thaw cycling and supramolecular assembly) and chemical cross-linking methods (free-radical and photo-initiated polymerization, small-molecule cross-linkers, click and dynamic covalent chemistries, and enzyme-mediated and radiation cross-linking) are examined in terms of their mechanisms, typical materials and conditions, critical process parameters, advantages and limitations. The preparation of conventional pharmaceutical gels based on carbomers, cellulose ethers, poloxamers and polysaccharides is described step by step, together with drug-loading strategies, processing into beads, micro- and nanogels, films, sponges, microneedles and printed constructs, and a troubleshooting guide for the most frequent formulation failures. Advanced architectures that overcome the intrinsic weakness of conventional networks, including hybrid, interpenetrating, nanocomposite, double-network and Tetra-PEG hydrogels, are then discussed, followed by the characterization and quality-control methods needed to establish critical quality attributes such as gel fraction, swelling and mesh size, rheology, morphology, release kinetics, stability, microbiological quality and biocompatibility. The review subsequently analyzes drug release mechanisms, route-specific delivery strategies, stimuli-responsive and hierarchical systems, the selection of drug candidates with reference to physicochemical properties and the Biopharmaceutics Classification System, and applications in tissue engineering and wound care. Finally, clinically approved products and the main translational barriers, namely mechanical fragility, burst release, residual reagents, sterilization, batch-to-batch variability and regulatory classification, are critically evaluated to identify realistic routes towards next-generation, clinically useful hydrogel dosage forms.
records.authors: Ramesh KA, Mawazi SM.

records.title: Modulating DNA Methylation in Mature Hair Cells to Mitigate Cisplatin-Induced Hearing Loss: A Review
records.abstract: Cisplatin-induced hearing loss (CIHL) is a debilitating side effect in cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy. So far, epigenetic studies in the inner ear have largely focused on developmental biology to regenerate hair cells. In post-mitotic hair cells, on the other hand, DNA methylation regulates transcriptomic response to external stimuli. Adult mammalian hair cells are locked in the G0 phase, and passive demethylation via DNA replication does not occur under normal physiological conditions. However, external stimuli such as cisplatin can aberrantly upregulate DNMT methyltransferases (DNMTs), resulting in promoter methylation and silencing protective genes. From this angle, DNMTs modulation is an attractive therapeutic strategy to protect hearing during chemotherapy. Recent studies suggest that non-nucleoside inhibitors such as RG108 and natural polyphenolic compounds downregulate DNMTs, and at the same time, protect auditory cells. These compounds function via the inhibition of the DNMT catalytic site but can also act through downregulating DNMT1 and DNMT3A/B at mRNA and protein levels. Polyphenols are also antioxidants, decreasing reactive oxygen species, thereby increasing cell survival. Furthermore, it is suggested that upregulating TET-mediated active demethylation can be another angle to modify DNA methylation in cancer and CIHL models. However, functional DNA methylation should be distinguished from non-functional, passenger DNA methylation to elucidate the compounds’ otoprotective effects. In addition, the candidate compounds should not interfere with cisplatin’s antitumor effect. In this review, we investigate the relationship between DNA methylation and CIHL in the post-mitotic inner ear and evaluate the therapeutic potential of candidate DNMT inhibitors.
records.authors: Koo C, Fuentes R, Tan X.

records.title: Investigation of the molecular mechanisms of action of sophorolipids in MCF-7 cells: therapeutic potential against breast cancer.
records.abstract: A mixture of lactonic and acidic sophorolipids exerted concentration-dependent cytotoxicity against human breast ductal adenocarcinoma (MCF-7) cells, with an IC₅₀ of 82.54 µg/mL as determined by resazurin assay. Phase-contrast microscopy revealed morphological alterations including cell swelling, loss of adhesion, and impaired membrane integrity. Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated cell cycle arrest in the S phase, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, and a predominance of necrosis-like cell death at higher concentrations. Transcriptional profiling by RT-qPCR identified overexpression of CDKN1A, GADD45A, ERN1, and BBC3, alongside repression of ACTB and GAPDH, indicating activation of DNA damage and stress-response pathways, endoplasmic reticulum stress, structural collapse, and metabolic dysfunction. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that sophorolipids induce mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum stress, culminating in homeostatic failure and cell death in MCF-7 cells, positioning these biosurfactants as promising candidates for the development of natural antiproliferative therapies.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05096-0.

records.title: Investigation of Polyethylene (PE) Exposure in Labeo rohita (Hamilton, 1822): Accumulation, Stress Responses and In Vitro Biodegradation of PE by a Gut-Associated Bacterium.
records.abstract: The aquatic biome is exposed to a significant threat of persistent contamination by polyethylene (PE) in the ecosystem. A critical research gap exists in PE-induced tissue-specific bioaccumulation, associated immune and stress responses in fish, followed by potential bioremediation solutions. The present study investigated the bioaccumulation of PE particles and subsequent oxidative stress in Labeo rohita induced by two different doses (0.1 and 0.5 mg/L) over 2 weeks. Additionally, the biodegradation potential of gut-associated microbial isolates was also evaluated. We found that PE accumulation was highest in the intestine (33.0 ± 2.5 particles/g), followed by gills (20.5 ± 1.9 particles/g) and liver (8.0 ± 1.4 particles/g), indicating a significant, dose- and time-dependent increase. Substantially, it triggered a tissue-wise oxidative stress response of antioxidant (SOD, CAT, GPx) and stress marker (Hsp70) genes, showing significant upregulation in gill, liver, and intestine. Furthermore, this work identified a gut-associated bacterium, Proteus vulgaris KG-SD-15807, demonstrating significant PE biodegradation capability. Quantitative analysis revealed achievement of 3.00% ± 0.16% weight loss over 30 days of incubation. Qualitative characterization through FT-IR, FE-SEM, and GC-MS analyses indicated polymer oxidation, surface erosion, and formation of distinct metabolic degradation intermediates. The present findings reveal the significant bioaccumulation and stress response due to PE in a commercially important fish, Labeo rohita. Moreover, the identified bacterium acted as a PE biodegradation agent. This research has significant implications for future explorations focused on the long-term impacts of PE in aquatic animals and the optimization of biodegradation efficiency of Proteus vulgaris for applied bioremediation.
records.authors: Dey S, Rout AK, Ghosh K, Kumar V, Saha A, Das BK, Behera BK.

records.title: Comprehensive regulatory network construction highlights lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA-TF interactions and key molecular drivers in rheumatoid arthritis.
records.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent inflammation and progressive joint damage. Although numerous molecular contributors have been reported, the integrated regulatory architecture linking coding and non-coding transcripts remains incompletely defined. This study aimed to construct a multilayer lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA-transcription factor (TF) network to prioritize candidate regulators associated with RA. Publicly available RNA-sequencing datasets from RA and control samples were retrieved from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive. Differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2. High-confidence miRNA-mRNA interactions were obtained from miRDip, miRNA-lncRNA associations from miRNet, and TF annotations from AnimalTFDB. Functional enrichment analyses were conducted to identify overrepresented biological themes. Network topology and module structure were evaluated in Cytoscape using CytoHubba and MCODE. Integration of interaction datasets identified 179 mRNAs targeted by 93 miRNAs, of which 90 miRNAs were connected to 404 annotated lncRNAs. Twenty-five TFs were incorporated into the regulatory framework. Degree-based analysis highlighted QKI, hsa-miR-497-5p, and KCNQ1OT1 as the most connected nodes within their respective categories. Module detection revealed five densely interconnected sub-networks, indicating coordinated regulatory organization. Several prioritized elements have previously been implicated in immune or inflammatory regulation, supporting the biological relevance of the network. This integrative analysis delineates a comprehensive regulatory landscape of RA and provides a ranked set of candidate molecules for future experimental validation. Among these, CCDC6 was identified as a downregulated gene positioned within a highly connected module and linked to multiple hub miRNAs and lncRNAs, suggesting potential functional importance in RA pathobiology.

records.title: Microbiome interactions in renal cell carcinoma: evidence, challenges and opportunities.
records.abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is a heterogeneous malignancy with limited predictive biomarkers to guide treatment. Emerging evidence suggests that the microbiome might influence systemic immunity, therapeutic response and clinical outcomes. In metastatic RCC, the gut microbiome has been linked to the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors, whereas the existence of a tumour microbiome remains a topic of debate. Circulating microbial DNA in blood has been proposed as a minimally invasive window into systemic immune status, offering a potential tool for monitoring treatment response, but its role in RCC is largely unexplored. Evidence from mechanistic studies, primarily from other solid cancer types, suggests that microbiome-immune crosstalk, microbial metabolites and functionally redundant pathways across taxa could modulate tumour biology. However, progress in RCC microbiome research remains limited by small cohorts, methodological variability and challenges in working with samples with a low microbial biomass, which are highly prone to contamination. Emerging spatial and multi-omics technologies now enable high-resolution mapping of these complex interactions, offering the potential to transform our understanding of the cancer microbiome. A structured roadmap is required to overcome technical and analytical challenges in RCC microbiome studies, enabling the identification of clinically relevant microbial signatures and their role in shaping tumour immunity.
records.authors: Lindgaard C, Hvidt AK, Keller AK, Thingholm L, Kristensen SS, Lyskjær I.

records.title: Pobacilamides A and B, two linear depsipeptides from a marine-derived Bacillus sp. ROA-056.
records.abstract: Through the intensive investigation of the chemical components for the culture broth of marine-derived Bacillus sp. ROA-056, two new linear peptides, namely, pobacilamides A (1) and B (2), have been discovered. Their planar structures were elucidated through mass spectrometry, and 1D and 2D NMR analyses. Both peptides were composed of valine (Val), 2-hydroxyisovaleric acid (HIVA), and 2-hydroxyisocaproic acid (HICA), while pobacilamide A (1) contained leucine (Leu). The absolute configurations of Val and Leu were defined by acid hydrolysis and advanced Marfey's method, while those of HIVA and HICA were established by GC-MS analysis of O-trifluoroacetylated (S)-(+)-3-methyl-2-butyl ester. Compounds 1 and 2 displayed selective antibacterial activity against Gram-positive bacteria, including Bacillus subtilis and Kocuria rhizophila, with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) values from 0.25 μg/mL to 4 μg/mL. Pobacilamide B (2) showed the strongest activity against K. rhizophila with an MIC of 0.25 μg/mL. No antibacterial activity was observed against Gram-negative strains. These results suggested that compounds 1 and 2 have considerable potential as targeted antibacterial agents for Gram-positive pathogens.

records.title: Mapping human genetic associations to drug targets in valvular heart disease: an integrative evidence synthesis.
records.abstract: BackgroundValvular heart disease (VHD) lacks disease-modifying pharmacological therapies. Drug repurposing guided by human genetics may help identify therapeutic opportunities. We aimed to integrate human genetic associations, drug-target information, and clinical evidence to identify repurposing opportunities and prioritise potentially druggable targets across the VHD spectrum.MethodsWe retrieved VHD-associated genetic variants from the NHGRI-EBI Genome-Wide Association Studies Catalogue and Ensembl, interrogated annotated genes in the Open Targets Platform, and evaluated linked drugs through structured searches of MEDLINE and ClinicalTrials.gov. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251071741).FindingsWe identified 1464 genetic associations corresponding to 844 unique variants and 582 candidate genes. Of these genes, 431 had tractability information and 51 had linked compounds, comprising 388 distinct pharmacological agents, 273 in phase 3 or 4 of clinical development. Drug-linked targets were concentrated in aortic stenosis. Clinical evidence supported therapeutic potential for 14 drugs, with preclinical or mechanistic cardiovascular support for eight additional drugs and adverse cardiovascular signals for four. An exploratory evidence-weighted framework prioritised targets according to genetic-functional evidence, tissue and mechanistic context, and translational tractability.InterpretationThis genetics-informed evidence synthesis identifies drug-repurposing opportunities and a substantial gap between genetically supported targets and available therapies. The findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework for mechanistic validation and future valve-focused studies.FundingLimburg Clinical Research Centre of UHasselt, Jessa and ZOL; British Heart Foundation; National Institute for Health and Care Research; UK Research and Innovation; European Research Council; Horizon Europe.

records.title: First evidence of measles virus detected from exhaled breath in humans.
records.abstract: ObjectivesMeasles is among the most transmissible human infections, yet direct capture of measles virus from an infected person's exhaled breath has not been described. We assessed whether measles virus RNA can be detected from exhaled breath using facemask sampling (FMS).MethodsWe studied a 23-year-old unvaccinated woman with laboratory-confirmed measles (throat-swab RT-qPCR positive on day 5 post symptom onset). From day 10 post symptom onset, longitudinal sampling was performed for six consecutive days with duplicate specimens collected at each timepoint from the throat, face, cutaneous lesions and exhaled breath using a surgical mask fitted with polyvinyl alcohol sampling strips (FMS). Dissolved mask strips and swab eluates underwent RNA extraction followed by RT-qPCR targeting measles nucleoprotein and haemagglutinin genes, with human RNase P as a sample adequacy control. Quantification was derived from nucleoprotein-gene standards and normalised per strip or per 100 μL of swab eluate.ResultsMeasles virus RNA was consistently detected in exhaled breath captured by FMS and remained >10ˆ4 genome copies per sampling strip despite sampling beginning 10 days after symptom onset. During FMS collection, the participant reported no respiratory symptoms and did not vocalise. RNA kinetics differed by sampling site: throat and facial swabs increased even after complete rash resolution, whereas cutaneous-lesion swabs yielded comparatively low RNA levels. FMS kinetics diverged from throat swabs over time, suggesting distinct patterns of virus emission across compartments.ConclusionsThis study provides the first empirical evidence that measles virus RNA can be captured directly from the exhaled breath of an individual with measles. Although RNA detection does not confirm infectious virus, persistent high-level exhaled RNA supports FMS as a practical, non-invasive tool to study measles respiratory emission and may inform understanding of transmission and the duration of potential contagiousness. Empirical sampling of different respiratory compartments may help refine infection-prevention guidance during resurgent outbreaks.

records.title: Particle size-dependent developmental and neurotoxic effects of epoxiconazole nanoformulations and its active ingredient in zebrafish larvae.
records.abstract: Epoxiconazole (EPO), a widely used triazole fungicide that can enter aquatic ecosystems through agricultural runoff, poses potential risks to non-target aquatic organisms. Although nano-enabled pesticide formulations can control release and reduce application rates, their toxicological evaluation remains insufficient, particularly with respect to size-dependent biological effects. Here, zebrafish larvae were exposed to free EPO and EPO-loaded mesoporous silica nanoparticles (EPO@MSNs) with particle sizes of 30, 150 and 450 nm to investigate size-associated differences in developmental toxicity and their underlying mechanisms. Overall, EPO exposure induced developmental and neurovascular abnormalities, neurobehavioral impairment, and neurotransmitter imbalance, accompanied by oxidative stress, innate immune activation, inflammation, and apoptosis. Nanoencapsulation reshaped the toxicological profile of EPO, with the overall toxicity, as integrated by PCA, following the order EPO@MSNs-30 < EPO@MSNs-150 < EPO@MSNs-450 < free EPO. Transcriptomic analyses further demonstrated that nanoformulation shifted the dominant molecular responses from metabolism- and detoxification-related processes in free EPO toward nanoparticle-associated intracellular processing in EPO@MSNs-30 and broader extracellular matrix, vascular, and inflammatory responses in EPO@MSNs-450. These findings demonstrate that particle size is associated with both the overall toxicological profile and the molecular response patterns of MSN-based pesticide formulations, providing mechanistic insights for the biosafety assessment and rational design of nano-enabled pesticide formulations.

records.title: A nuclease-associated short pAgo system from Pleomorphomonas koreensis with dual DNA and RNA collateral activity.
records.abstract: Argonaute (Ago) proteins play pivotal roles in nucleic acid targeting across eukaryotes and prokaryotes. While eukaryotic Ago (eAgo) proteins utilize RNA guides to cleave complementary RNA, prokaryotic Ago (pAgo) proteins often employ DNA guides for DNA targeting. This study focuses on the short pAgo system from Pleomorphomonas koreensis (Pko-SPARDA), which consists of a DUF4365-APAZ protein (PkoRE) and an Ago protein (PkoAgo). Upon RNA-guided target DNA recognition, Pko-SPARDA exhibits nonspecific cleavage activity toward ssDNA, dsDNA, and RNA, demonstrating potential for nucleic acid detection. Biochemical characterization revealed that Pko-SPARDA prefers Mn2+ or Mg2+ as cofactors, operates optimally at 40-45 °C, and is sensitive to mismatches in the central and 3'-supplementary regions of the guide RNA. Notably, the system accommodates a range of guide lengths (14-40 nt) and shows higher activity with 5'-phosphorylated guides. Additionally, guide RNA 5'-phosphorylation universally enhances Pko-SPARDA trans-cleavage activity, and this principle extends to microRNA-guided activation, advancing the understanding of short pAgos and highlighting Pko-SPARDA's utility in molecular diagnostics by bridging a gap left by CRISPR systems due to its lack of sequence constraints like PAM motifs.

records.title: Active components alignment of Gegen Qinlian Decoction for inflammatory bowel disease: exploring the possible role of the SphK1/S1P/NF-κB pathway.
records.abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceGegenqinlian Decoction (GQD) has been used as a folk remedy for gastrointestinal diseases in China over thousands of years, and demonstrates significant efficacy against inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We previously showed that the active components alignment of GQD inhibits nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) p65 signal transduction and plays a key role in preventing and treating IBD. With growing insights into the gut microbiota and its metabolites, the molecular mechanisms underlying therapeutic effects of GQD against IBD require further elucidation. This is particularly relevant given the previously reported relationship between the host NF-κB pathway and the gut microbiota.Aim of the studyTo explore the therapeutic mechanisms of GQD and its aligned active components against IBD, with a focus on microbiota-involved regulation of the host sphingosine kinase 1 (SphK1)/sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P)/NF-κB signaling pathway, using both 2,4,6-Trinitrobenzenesulfonic acid (TNBS)-induced rat colitis and dextran sulfate sodium salt (DSS)-induced mouse colitis models and cultured cells.Material and methodsIn this research, the therapeutic effect of GQD on TNBS-induced colitis rats was evaluated through the measurement of body weight, colorectal length, disease activity index (DAI), colon length and hematoxylin-eosin staining. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomic analyses were performed to evaluate the restoration of gut microbial and metabolic homeostasis by GQD. Network pharmacology and molecular docking were then utilized to explore the potential relationships between specific targets and the active components alignment (ACA) of GQD on IBD treatment. To further validate the in vivo effects of the ACA, a dextran sulfate sodium salt (DSS)-induced mouse colitis model was established, and body weight, DAI, colorectum length, histopathology, S1P levels, and SphK1/S1PR1 expression were assessed. Experimental validation in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages and NCM460 colonic epithelial cells was subsequently conducted to determine whether this active components alignment suppressed the SphK1/S1P/NF-κB pathway via molecular and cellular assays, including cell metabolomics, ELISA, Western blot, and immunofluorescence staining.ResultsGQD significantly relieved symptoms, colonic inflammation, and intestinal damage in TNBS-induced colitis rats. It partially reversed gut microbiota dysbiosis, modulated sphingolipid metabolic pathways, and downregulated the expression of sphingolipid-related Sphk1 and S1PR1 proteins, as well as S1P levels, in colon tissues (p ConclusionGQD restored gut microecological homeostasis and rectified sphingolipid metabolic disturbances. Its active components alignment afforded anti-inflammatory and colitis-protective effects, partially via modulation of the SphK1/S1P/NF-κB signaling pathway. The consistent therapeutic and mechanistic effects observed in both TNBS-induced rat colitis and DSS-induced mouse colitis support that the eight-component alignment largely recapitulates the key effects of the complete GQD formulation. These findings provide novel mechanistic insights and a scientific rationale for the clinical application of GQD in the management of IBD.
records.authors: Liu S, Zhang D, Zong Z, Hu Y, Bai J, Li J, Sun W, Yang X, Chen Y, Yang B, Wang H, Wang J, Wu D, Li W, Liu J, Xu B.

records.title: Therapeutic advances in chronic hepatitis B and Delta: where are we now and where are we headed?
records.abstract: Chronic hepatitis B (HBV) and delta (HDV) infections remain major global health challenges. Nucleos(t)ide analogues (NUCs) and bulevirtide, a recently approved entry inhibitor, effectively suppress HBV and HDV replication, respectively, thereby reducing the risk of liver-related complications. However, they rarely induce functional cure, defined as sustained HBsAg loss, and generally require long-term administration. This limitation is primarily driven by the persistence of covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) and integrated HBV DNA, which are not targeted by existing treatments. A broad range of novel therapeutic strategies is currently under investigation. Virus-directing agents, including small interfering RNAs, antisense oligonucleotides, nucleic acid polymers, and capsid assembly modulators, have shown promising antiviral activity. However, their efficacy as monotherapy remains modest, with HBsAg loss observed at moderate rates and mainly among patients with a favorable baseline profile. Combination strategies integrating direct antivirals with immune modulation (therapeutic vaccines, toll-like receptor agonists or monoclonal antibodies) may represent a promising pathway to increase the rates of functional cure. In HDV infection, emerging phase 3 combination strategies are also showing promising results, supporting a shift toward more effective, multi-targeted treatment approaches. Building on these advances, the convergence of novel antivirals and immune-modulating strategies, together with precision biomarkers, makes functional cure a realistic long-term objective in HBV and HDV infection.
records.authors: Pocurull A, Battistella S, Forns X, Lens S.

records.title: Recombinant spinach ribosome-inactivating protein induces cytotoxicity and alters gene expression associated with PTEN/AKT/mTOR signaling, apoptosis, and stemness in HT29 cells.
records.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major therapeutic challenge, highlighting the need for novel anticancer strategies. These challenges have increased interest in bioactive natural molecules with anticancer potential. In this study, we investigated the antitumor activity of a recombinant spinach (Spinacia oleracea) type I ribosome-inactivating protein (SoRIP) in HT29 colorectal cancer cells and evaluated its effects on cellular survival, apoptosis, and stemness-associated pathways. The SoRIP coding sequence was cloned, heterologously expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3), and purified by Ni-affinity chromatography, yielding a recombinant protein of approximately 22 kDa. Recombinant SoRIP reduced HT29 cell viability in a concentration-dependent manner after 48 h of treatment, with an IC50 of 48 μg/mL and cell viability of 51.3 ± 2.5% at this concentration. Annexin V-FITC/PI flow cytometry demonstrated a concentration-dependent increase in total apoptotic cells, reaching approximately 15%, 58%, and 79% following exposure to 12, 48, and 180 μg/mL SoRIP, respectively. At the transcriptional level, SoRIP increased CASP3 expression by up to 3.8-fold and PTEN expression by up to 4.3-fold, while reducing AKT and mTOR expression to 0.60- and 0.70-fold, respectively, at 48 μg/mL. BCL2 and CD44 expression were also reduced to approximately 0.65- and 0.70-fold, respectively. These findings indicate that recombinant SoRIP is associated with reduced cell viability, enhanced apoptosis, and coordinated transcriptional modulation of PTEN/AKT/mTOR-related, apoptosis-associated, and stemness-associated genes in HT29 cells. Collectively, these results support SoRIP as a candidate for further investigation in the HT29 colorectal cancer model.
records.authors: Ranjbar M, Maghsodiyan S, Khakdan F, Bayram M.

records.title: The clinical relevance of multiple sclerosis genetics: from susceptibility to disease severity and progression.
records.abstract: Large-scale genome-wide association studies have identified hundreds of multiple sclerosis risk loci, most of which implicate immune pathways and establish multiple sclerosis as a highly polygenic, immune-mediated disease. These findings help explain why immune-modifying therapies suppress relapses and new lesion formation. However, susceptibility genetics does not adequately explain disability accumulation, variation in disease course, or treatment response. Evidence from rare-variant studies, genetic studies of disease severity and disability progression, epigenetic analyses, gene-environment studies, and Epstein-Barr virus research is beginning to extend this genetic framework from susceptibility to disease expression. Still, the direct clinical relevance of this research remains constrained by modest individual-level predictive value, underpowered studies of genetic determinants of disease severity and disability progression, complex regulatory mechanisms linking variants to function, and restricted generalisability across populations. At present, multiple sclerosis genetics is most useful for interpreting mechanisms, prioritising therapeutic targets, supporting causal inference, informing biomarker discovery, and enriching research cohorts. Future clinical value will likely depend on integrating genetic architecture with longitudinal clinical, imaging, biomarker, and multi-omic data to identify the contexts in which prevention or treatment is most likely to succeed.
records.authors: Jensen LT, Gold R, McVean G, Attfield KE, Fugger L.

records.title: Biomarker tests for invasive Candida infection in critically ill patients in the UK (A-Stop): a multicentre diagnostic test accuracy study.
records.abstract: BackgroundThe current practice of empirical antifungal treatment for suspected invasive Candida infection in the intensive care unit (ICU) leads to overtreatment. Biomarkers might better target treatment; however, their diagnostic accuracy in this patient group is uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate whether a biomarker or a combination of biomarkers has sufficiently high negative predictive value (NPV) to enable early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in patients in ICUs.MethodsIn this prospective, multicentre, diagnostic test accuracy study, we recruited patients who had been started on empirical antifungal treatment for suspected candidiasis and had blood cultures drawn within 24 h of starting treatment from 43 UK ICUs. We tested a research blood sample, collected within 24 h of the standard-of-care care blood culture (ie, within 48 h of starting empirical antifungal treatment), with three DNA detection tests (Fungiplex, T2Candida, and CandID) and one (1,3)-β-D-glucan test (Fungitell). We assessed the accuracy of these tests against an international consensus definition of proven invasive Candida infection and a constructed reference standard for proven or probable infection. The primary outcome was NPV for exclusion of proven Candida infection; we also reported sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios.FindingsAmong 4005 patients screened, 1251 were enrolled. A total of 1225 participants, recruited between April, 2018 and Feb, 2023, were evaluable, among whom 54 (4·4%) had proven invasive Candida infection. The median duration of antifungal treatment was 9 days (IQR 5-15), and survival at 28 days was 76·8%. The index tests had similar NPVs: 96·6% (95·3-97·6) for Fungiplex, 97·1% (94·7-98·6) for T2Candida, 96·7% (95·4-97·8) for CandID, and 97·2% (95·5-98·4) for Fungitell; however, sensitivity varied widely among the tests, from 27·5% to 68·6%. The optimal test combination was Fungitell and CandID, which had an NPV of 97·5% (95·7-98·7) and a sensitivity of 75·0%. Combining these biomarkers with standard-of-care blood culture testing further increased the NPV to 98·6% (97·0-99·4), with a sensitivity of 85·1%.InterpretationNo single biomarker had sufficiently high sensitivity to justify stopping empirical antifungal treatment. Combining Fungitell and CandID with standard-of-care blood culture testing could provide a sufficiently high NPV to allow early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in this patient group, thereby reducing overtreatment, although this gain in sensitivity is accompanied by a reduction in specificity. Randomised trials are needed to confirm the clinical and cost-effectiveness of this diagnostic strategy before it is adopted in practice.FundingUK National Institute for Health and Care Research Health Technology Assessment Programme and the Research Charitable Trust Fund of the Belfast Health & Social Care Trust.
records.authors: McMullan R, Loughlin L, Toase S, Campbell C, Clarke M, Curran T, Dark P, Guiney M, Harrison DA, Lindsay J, Mills C, Morris KP, Perkins GD, Simpson AJ, Stevenson M, Walsh T, White PL, McAuley DF, A-Stop Study Investigators.

records.title: NF-κB phosphorylation controls enhancer selection to shape the inflammatory gene program.
records.abstract: Inflammatory transcriptional responses mediated by NF-κB are diverse despite similar upstream activation signals. Because phosphorylation of the NF-κB subunit RelA/p65 promotes interaction with co-activators CREB-binding protein/E1A binding protein p300 (CBP/p300) and selectively affects gene expression, we asked whether this modification distinguishes regulatory architectures underlying distinct immune functions. In macrophages carrying a Rela Ser276Ala mutation, p65 phosphorylation at serine 276 (S276) was dispensable for NF-κB binding to primed enhancers but essential for recruitment to nucleosome-occluded regions lacking pre-bound transcription factors (TFs) and activating histone marks. Such latent enhancers required phosphorylated NF-κB to recruit CBP/p300, promote histone acetylation, and open chromatin. Genes linked to these enhancers, including inflammatory mediators, were selectively impaired in S276A macrophages. Although antiviral responses remained intact, Rela Ser276Ala mice resisted endotoxin shock but were susceptible to bacterial infection. Thus, NF-κB responses are functionally partitioned by enhancer architecture: phosphorylation-sensitive sites define a latent enhancer compartment with NF-κB-dominated regulatory architecture, whereas primed sites are embedded in broader networks of lineage-determining and inducible TFs, yielding distinct biological outputs.

records.title: In silico conservation and HLA-binding profiles of HMPV F and G protein epitopes: implications for universal vaccine development.
records.abstract: BackgroundHuman metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a significant cause of respiratory infection, yet no licensed vaccine exists. Variability across viral subgroups, particularly in the attachment (G) protein, can complicate universal design. We assessed the immunogenetic regions in the fusion (F) and G proteins to identify stable vaccine targets.MethodsWe analyzed N = 324 Pittsburgh and N = 655 global HMPV genomes (2017-2022) for genome diversity per viral subgroup. Previously identified epitope sequences were obtained from the Immune Epitope DataBase (IEDB) for F and G proteins and sequence similarity was determined. Using NetMHCpan-4.1, we identified and computed inferred human leukocyte antigen (HLA) binding affinities for 15 epitope variants (1 or 2 substitutions) against universally common human alleles.ResultsThe F protein was highly conserved across all subgroups (>96% amino acid sequence identity). In the G protein, we identified a conserved epitope cluster (G3-G7) where epitope G7 was present in 91% of A2 genomes. Functional modeling of the G-protein epitope variants revealed that the majority of HLA alleles maintained or gained binding affinity, a subset exhibited diminished binding (escape), suggesting these regions are subject to ongoing antigenic drift. B-genotypes showed fewer retained binders and were notably underrepresented in the current epitope databases.ConclusionThe conserved F protein remains an optimal target for neutralization, while the G3-G7 cluster provides a robust secondary target for T-cell mediated immunity. A bivalent vaccine strategy could pair the stable F protein with these high-frequency G-protein epitopes to elicit an immune response. This approach addresses the A2 subgroup, and incorporating B-genotypes through ongoing surveillance and epitope mapping will be essential to achieve comprehensive, multi-antigen coverage across circulating HMPV strains.

records.title: Towards forecasting antimicrobial resistance evolution: concordance of  in vitro  and  in vivo  studies
records.abstract: Summary  Antimicrobial resistance is a major global health concern, and current measures to address the problem are new drugs, prudent use and rapid diagnostics. Recently, the idea of forecasting resistance evolution experimentally to prevent resistance  a priori has gained attention. But how well do experimental data on antimicrobial resistance evolution reflect resistance in strains from patients?  We conducted a systematic review and analysis to compare  in vitro and  in vivo data. We collected and analysed literature on experimental resistance evolution published between 1977 and 2024 available on PubMed for ESKAPE pathogens plus  E .  coli (ESKAPEE). We catalogued the magnitude of resistance evolution via minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) changes across antimicrobial classes. We then focussed on  P. aeruginosa and  E. coli under ciprofloxacin (CIP) selection, as these were most frequent bacterial species used in experimental evolution. CIP-selected gene mutations and amino acid substitutions, as well as the associated MICs in experimentally evolved  P. aeruginosa and  E. coli isolates, were compared with corresponding  in vivo data.  In vitro and  in vivo isolates of  E. coli showed high concordance in the selected gene mutations and the specific amino-acid changes. Similar results were found for  P. aeruginosa Evolved MIC values differed significantly depending on the respective gene mutation and the total number of mutations, but not due to the origin of the strains –  in vitro or  in vivo . Our findings clearly show that experimental resistance evolution  in vitro could predict the emergence of antimicrobial resistance evolution  in vivo .  This study supports the idea that experimental data can be used to forecast the risks of resistance emergence and therefore contribute to antimicrobial stewardship. It will be important to investigate how generalizable these findings are for other bacteria-antimicrobial combinations.
records.authors: Herzog M, Murphy RA, Rolff J.

records.title: COGNITIVE HETEROGENEITY AND AGING: AN AGE-INDEPENDENT CILIARY GENE PROGRAM TRACKS COGNITIVE RESILIENCE IN MICE
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Cognitive decline with age is often viewed as inevitable, yet older animals show striking heterogeneity in functional trajectories, with many preserving cognitive integrity despite physiological decline. The biological basis of this resilience remains poorly understood, partly due to insensitive behavioral testing paradigms. Using an automated home-cage platform and hippocampal RNA sequencing, we integrated behavioral phenotyping with transcriptomic profiling to disentangle molecular programs linked to cognitive performance from chronological age. Behavioral data from 906 C57BL/6 mice across 129 standardized studies, trajectory-based modeling, variance-partitioned correlation, and stability-driven gene prioritization identified a transcriptional signature (271 genes) linked to cognitive state independent of age. Preserved cognition was associated with higher expression of genes governing ciliary structure and motility, neurite organization, and synaptic architecture, while impairment was associated with neuroimmune and metabolic-stress programs. A 38-gene cilia structural module score remained associated with resilience after controlling for age (partial rho = −0.81), with consistent effects across leave-one-out resampling. Because the constituent genes were selected on this same outcome, the module-level magnitude is not an unbiased effect-size estimate; recalibration against a null that reapplies the full selection procedure gave an empirical p of 0.026. This divergence emerged among genetically identical mice, indicating non-genetic, discrete hippocampal molecular signatures underlying individual differences. Cell-type attribution against the Allen Brain Cell Atlas localized the module predominantly to ependymal cells, with 27 of 38 genes ependymal-restricted (median detection 90.2% in ependymal cells versus 1.1% in CA1 glutamatergic neurons) and three genes (Dnah9, Dnai4, Kif9) also detected in CA1. The association was not attributable to ependymal tissue content: the module score was unrelated to Foxj1 expression (rho = −0.016) and the partial correlation was unchanged after adjustment for ependymal and choroid plexus marker panels, indicating that the module reflects how strongly the ciliary program is expressed rather than how many ependymal cells each sample contained. These findings support a conceptual shift: cognitive trajectories appear shaped by intrinsic molecular set points rather than by chronological age, with expression of a motile ciliary program at the cerebrospinal fluid interface, rather than the abundance of the cells carrying it, emerging as a candidate correlate of resilience. This approach offers a generalizable strategy for dissecting functional heterogeneity from aging and identifying pathways for hypothesis-driven tests of resilience across the lifespan.

records.title: Daphnia magna bioconverts eicosapentaenoic acid continuously and independently of dietary supply.
records.abstract: Freshwater food webs are increasingly exposed to eutrophication and warming, which can shift phytoplankton community composition and reduce the availability of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids to higher trophic levels. We investigated whether the model freshwater crustacean Daphnia magna can compensate for a dietary lack of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) through endogenous EPA synthesis from its precursors, and whether this response depends on food quality, temperature, and genetic background. Two D. magna strains, isolated from contrasting temperate regions, were exposed to four diets ranging from edible cyanobacteria-dominated to cryptophyte-enriched communities at 15, 20, and 25 °C. Using deuterium labelling, compound-specific hydrogen isotope analysis, fatty acid quantification and fitness measurements, we assessed EPA bioconversion and its consequences for consumer performance. Cyanobacteria-rich food reduced biomass accrual, delayed reproduction, decreased body size, and lowered offspring production. Despite these pronounced fitness effects, endogenous EPA production remained stable across all dietary treatments. Instead, bioconversion was primarily governed by water temperature, reaching a maximum at approximately 20 °C, and was slightly higher in the cold-adapted strain, consistent with underlying biochemical constraints on metabolic processes. Slight differences between the two strains suggest an important contribution of genetic background in determining EPA biosynthesis. These results indicate that endogenous EPA synthesis in D. magna was not actively regulated but was constantly active and potentially buffered against low dietary EPA levels, but did not fully compensate for poor food quality.
records.journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part B, Biochemistry & molecular biology
records.authors: Pilecky M, Kesti P, Amorim C, Fuchs I, Ruiz T, Taipale SJ, Kouba A, Wassenaar LI, Jardine T, Guo F, Kainz MJ.

records.title: Sequence-programmed peptide nanozyme hydrogel with microenvironment-responsive dual catalytic activity for infected wound healing.
records.abstract: Natural enzymes orchestrate complex biological processes through highly coordinated and multifunctional catalysis, yet their practical translation is limited by poor stability and environmental sensitivity. Here, we report a peptide-engineered nanozyme hydrogel that enables programmable, microenvironment-responsive catalytic switching in response to the wound microenvironment for active regulation of wound healing. Inspired by the catalytic motifs of natural hydrolases and oxidases, an amphiphilic peptide (C16-GAVFFAHHGGEE) was rationally designed to coordinate Cu2+ and self-assemble into a β-sheet-rich nanofibrous hydrogel. The resulting system exhibits pH-dependent catalytic switching, functioning as an oxidase (OXD)-like nanozyme under acidic conditions to generate bactericidal reactive oxygen species for localized antibacterial activity (Km = 32.45 mM, vmax = 0.61 µM s-1), while transitioning to hydrolases (HYD)-like activity under alkaline conditions to hydrolyze prodrugs and modulate inflammatory responses (Km = 888.15 mM, vmax = 3.55 mM s-1). Distinct from conventional nanozyme-based wound dressings that provide isolated or static functionalities, this system dynamically links catalytic activity with the evolving wound microenvironment, thereby enabling coordinated intervention in bacterial infection, redox imbalance, and inflammation. In vitro studies demonstrate high cytocompatibility and broad-spectrum antibacterial activity. In a diabetic infected wound model, the hydrogel achieved almost complete wound closure within 12 days, accompanied by enhanced re-epithelialization, reduced inflammation, collagen deposition, and angiogenesis. This work establishes a strategy for integrating environment-responsive, dual enzyme-mimetic catalytic switching within a single peptide-based material, offering a programmable platform for actively modulating complex wound healing processes. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Chronic infected wounds require biomaterials capable of dynamically adapting to complex and evolving pathological microenvironments; however, most existing nanozyme systems exhibit static or single-function catalytic behavior. Here, we report a sequence-programmed peptide nanozyme hydrogel that integrates switchable multienzyme-mimetic catalysis within a single self-assembled peptide sequence. By coordinating Cu2+ within a β-sheet nanofibrous network, the hydrogel achieves microenvironment-responsive catalytic switching between antibacterial oxidase-like activity under acidic conditions and anti-inflammatory hydrolase-like activity under alkaline conditions. This work establishes a direct structure-function relationship between peptide molecular design, supramolecular assembly, and adaptive therapeutic performance. The study provides a structurally simple yet multifunctional biomaterial platform for active microenvironment modulation and offers new insights into the design of peptide-based catalytic biomaterials for wound healing and other biomedical applications.

records.title: Time-fractional modeling framework for Microcystis blooms and microcystin dynamics.
records.abstract: Microcystin risk in cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms cannot be inferred reliably from total biomass alone because toxin concentrations depend on toxigenic biomass, toxin synthesis, intracellular retention, extracellular release, removal, and transport. This study developed a toxin-explicit, spatiotemporal time-fractional advection-dispersion-reaction (TF-ADR) framework for coupled cyanobacterial biomass and microcystin dynamics, using Lake Pontchartrain Estuary as a case-study implementation. The model resolves four transported state variables: toxigenic Microcystis biomass, non-toxigenic Microcystis biomass, intracellular microcystin, and extracellular microcystin. Environmental forcing fields, hydrodynamic velocities, and field observations from July-December 2021 were used to evaluate biomass structure, toxin partitioning, biomass-toxin decoupling, and process-level source-sink controls. Results showed that biomass-growth and toxin-synthesis favorability were related but not identical, reflecting different environmental controls on biomass accumulation and toxin production. The biomass module reproduced broad bloom structure, while the toxin simulation showed that microcystin was dominated by the intracellular pool, with median modeled intracellular and extracellular fractions of 0.978 and 0.022, respectively. Estuary-wide diagnostics showed that upper-tail total microcystin peaked before upper-tail total biomass, despite strong temporal association between the two signals. Pooled station-node analysis also showed a monotonic but non-linear biomass-toxin relationship, with total microcystin more strongly associated with toxigenic biomass than with total biomass. Process diagnostics indicated that toxin behavior reflected intracellular synthesis, release to the extracellular pool, dissolved-phase removal, and hydrodynamic redistribution. These findings demonstrate that separating toxigenic biomass, non-toxigenic biomass, intracellular toxin, and extracellular toxin provides a process-based modeling framework for interpreting microcystin risk in spatially heterogeneous estuarine systems, allowing government agencies to take proactive measures for protecting seafood and human health.
records.authors: Hofioni SO, Deng Z, Bargu S.

records.title: Frequency-dependent fitness effects are ubiquitous in rapidly adapting microbial populations.
records.abstract: In simple microbial populations, the fitness effects of selected mutations are typically assumed to be constant, regardless of mutant frequency. This assumption underpins predictions about evolutionary dynamics, epistasis, and the maintenance of genetic diversity. Here, we systematically test this assumption using beneficial mutations from early generations of the Escherichia coli long-term evolution experiment (LTEE). Using flow cytometry-based competition assays, we find that frequency-dependent fitness effects are the norm rather than the exception, occurring in ∼80% of strain pairs tested. Most competitions exhibit negative frequency dependence, where fitness advantages decline as mutant frequency increases. We demonstrate that the strength of frequency dependence is predictable from invasion fitness measurements, which explain approximately half of the biological variation in frequency-dependent slopes. We also observe violations of fitness transitivity in several strain combinations, indicating that competitive outcomes cannot always be predicted from fitness measured against a single reference strain. High-resolution measurements reveal that frequency dependence changes substantially within the growth cycle, with the net per-cycle effect reflecting the balance of opposing dynamics at different growth phases. Our results demonstrate that, even in a model system designed to minimize ecological complexity, subtle interactions between closely related genotypes create frequency-dependent selection that can fundamentally alter evolutionary trajectories.
records.authors: Ascensao JA, Abedi KD, Prasad AN, Hallatschek O.

records.title: HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection of macrophages escapes restriction by the BST-2 host cell factor independently of the Vpu counteracting viral protein.
records.abstract: As HIV-1 target cells, macrophages can be infected by cell-to-cell virus transfer from infected T cells through cell-cell fusion leading to the formation of virus-productive multinucleated giant cells (MGCs). We recently demonstrated that this route of infection escaped host cell restriction acting on the early steps of the viral life cycle. Here, we investigated whether restriction factors acting on late steps of HIV-1 replication were also bypassed in virus cell-to-cell infection of macrophages. We focused on the impact of the interferon(IFN)-induced factor BST-2/tetherin acting on virus release, a process counteracted by the Vpu viral protein. We show that deletion of Vpu did not significantly affect HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection of IFN-stimulated macrophages, and virus assembly in virus containing compartments was not affected in MGCs. Accordingly, depletion of BST-2 in IFN-stimulated macrophages had no impact on virus cell-to-cell transfer, formation of MGCs and virus production. However, cell-to-cell infection of macrophages was still sensitive to the nelfinavir protease inhibitor, whereas we previously showed that this route of infection was resistant to antiviral drugs acting on early steps of virus replication. Our results show that HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection of macrophages escapes restriction factors acting on both early and late steps of the virus life cycle, but displays resistance to antiviral drugs specifically acting on the early steps of virus replication.
records.authors: Yan S, Durringer A, Woottum M, Benichou S.

records.title: Host genotype, resistance status and seasonal temperature shape the Norway spruce phyllosphere mycobiome.
records.abstract: The influence of the phyllosphere microbiome on plant health and disease development is well established. However, the roles of host resistance phenotype, seasonal variations, and accumulated temperature in shaping the phyllosphere mycobiome of Norway spruce (Picea abies) remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated (i) the phyllosphere mycobiome assembly of a subset of Heterobasidion partially resistant and susceptible Norway spruce genotypes, (ii) how fungal community composition in these genotypes changes across seasons and with temperature, and (iii) the extent to which the phyllosphere mycobiome shared taxa with the seed-associated fungal communities of the same genotypes. Needle samples were collected from Heterobasidion partially resistant and susceptible Norway spruce seedlings growing in an open field in May, July and September 2022. Fungal communities were characterized using internal transcribed spacer (ITS) amplicon sequencing. Alpha diversity metrics (richness, diversity and evenness) of the phyllosphere fungal community were significantly different between susceptible and partially resistant Norway spruce genotypes. Although the distributions showed substantial overlap between resistance classes, all three alpha-diversity metrics differed significantly between the groups (p < 0.05). Community composition was associated with both host resistance phenotype and temperature-related variables, with average and accumulated temperature explaining a greater proportion of variation than host resistance phenotype. Less than 1% of phyllosphere fungal taxa overlapped with the seed-associated fungal communities. Network analyses further revealed seasonal differences in fungal association patterns between partially resistant and susceptible seedlings.
