records.title: Selective Cognitive and Affective Benefits of 3D-Printed Bacteriophage T4 Models in High School Molecular Biology Instruction: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
records.abstract: Teaching abstract molecular concepts poses persistent challenges in high school biology education. This study evaluated a custom-developed three-dimensional (3D) bacteriophage T4 model for teaching the Hershey-Chase experiment in a Grade 11 classroom. Using a quasi-experimental design, 92 students were assigned to either model-based instruction (n = 46) incorporating hands-on assembly of a disassemblable 3D-printed phage model, or conventional instruction (n = 46). Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires assessed conceptual understanding and affective outcomes. ANCOVA revealed no significant overall cognitive difference between groups, F(1, 89) = 1.42, p = 0.237. However, item-level analysis showed the model group significantly outperformed on structural component identification (52.2% vs 26.1%, p = 0.018, ϕ = 0.27). Affective outcomes significantly favored the model condition, including lesson enjoyment (p = 0.038), model construction interest (p = 0.028), perceived knowledge mastery (p = 0.033), perceived instructional utility (p = 0.028), and modeling skill need (p = 0.049). These findings suggest that curriculum-aligned 3D model-based instruction selectively enhances representational competence for spatially complex concepts and improves situational affective engagement.
records.authors: Xu L, Li Y, Wang L, Yang C.

records.title: Combined toxicity of cyanotoxins and anthropogenic contaminants on Chlorella vulgaris: insights from single and binary mixture exposures.
records.abstract: Aquatic organisms in eutrophic brackish and freshwater systems are chronically exposed to natural and anthropogenic contaminants, including cyanotoxins, metals and pesticides, mainly driven by cyanobacterial blooms and human activities. However, the environmental risks posed by their combinations to the aquatic environment remain poorly understood. This study investigated the growth response of Chlorella vulgaris exposed to four single-chemical compounds (microcystin-LR, cylindrospermopsin, terbuthylazine, and cadmium) and five binary mixtures for 7 days. In single-chemical exposures, terbuthylazine was the most toxic to C. vulgaris, followed by cadmium, cylindrospermopsin and microcystin-LR. The obtained growth data were compared with concentration addition predictions based on individual toxicities using the MIXTOX tool, testing deviations for synergistic/antagonistic interactions, dose ratio and dose level dependencies. Mixture effects varied with composition and exposure time. Antagonism was the prevailing type of interaction between the chemical compounds after 4 days of exposure, while dose level dependency was the only deviation observed after 7 days. Regarding dose level dependency, synergism was observed at low doses of each chemical in three of the five tested binary mixtures. Time was an important factor in the change in the toxicity pattern. This synergistic effect poses a significant risk to aquatic organisms exposed simultaneously to cyanotoxins and anthropogenic contaminants in the environment.
records.authors: Pinheiro C, Azevedo J, Campos A, Silva PV, Vasconcelos V, Loureiro S.

records.title: Identical consensus genomes of bovine coronavirus in respiratory and enteric specimens from a single cow and sequence variation after cell culture passage.
records.abstract: Bovine coronavirus (BCoV) causes respiratory and enteric diseases in cattle, but the relationship between viral genetic variation and anatomical distribution remains unclear. We compared BCoV genomes detected in a tracheal swab and diarrheic intestinal content from the same adult cow. The two clinical specimens had identical 31,015-nt consensus genomes. After five passages in HRT-18 cells, the recovered tracheal isolate differed at three consensus-level amino acid positions (HE N104D, S Q179K, and S E965D) and showed marked within-sample heterogeneity. These findings highlight the importance of direct sequencing of clinical specimens because cell-culture passage can alter viral population composition.
records.authors: Nakagawa K, Yoshida A, Kuwata K, Kitamura Y.

records.title: CaSNF1 interacts with and phosphorylates CaHD-ZIP to enhance cold tolerance in pepper.
records.abstract: Cold stress severely restricts pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) growth and productivity by disrupting cellular homeostasis and inducing oxidative damage. Although HD-ZIP transcription factors play important roles in plant abiotic stress responses, the molecular mechanisms regulating their function during cold stress remain largely unknown. Here, we characterized the pepper HD-ZIP transcription factor CaHD-ZIP and demonstrated that it is a nuclear-localized, cold-responsive protein that positively contributes to cold stress tolerance. To further investigate the regulatory mechanism underlying CaHD-ZIP function, a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) screen identified the sucrose non-fermenting 1-related protein kinase CaSNF1 as a previously unrecognized interacting partner of CaHD-ZIP. Their interaction was confirmed by yeast two-hybrid, luciferase complementation imaging, and bimolecular fluorescence complementation assays, with BiFC indicating that the interaction occurs predominantly in the nucleus. In vitro phosphorylation analysis further demonstrated that CaSNF1 directly phosphorylates CaHD-ZIP, providing biochemical evidence for a functional regulatory relationship between these proteins. Complementary loss- and gain-of-function analyses, including virus-induced gene silencing and transient overexpression in pepper together with stable overexpression in Arabidopsis, demonstrated that CaSNF1 positively regulates cold tolerance. Silencing of CaSNF1 increased oxidative damage, impaired antioxidant enzyme activities, and suppressed the expression of antioxidant and cold-responsive genes, whereas overexpression produced the opposite effects and significantly enhanced cold tolerance. Together, these findings identify CaSNF1 as a CaHD-ZIP-interacting kinase and reveal a potential CaSNF1-CaHD-ZIP regulatory module involved in pepper cold stress adaptation. This study advances our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying pepper cold tolerance and provides potential genetic targets for improving cold resilience in pepper and other Solanaceae crops.
records.journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
records.authors: Ullah I, Pei Y, Wang M, Hussain A, Guo J, Zhang H, Chen R.

records.title: Revisiting porcine circovirus infections in Uruguay: first evidence of PCV3 circulation and PCV2d as the sole genotype detected.
records.abstract: Porcine circoviruses (PCVs) are widespread among pig populations, and porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2) is a major pathogen affecting swine health and productivity worldwide. Although PCV2 genetic diversity was previously characterized in Uruguay, updated information has been lacking for more than a decade, and porcine circovirus type 3 (PCV3) has not been reported. This study aimed to characterize recent PCV2 clinical cases and retrospectively investigate PCV3 circulation in archived samples previously analysed for PCV2. Complete PCV2 genomes obtained from clinical cases detected between 2017 and 2020 belonged to PCV2d. PCV3 was detected in archived samples from 2010 to 2014, including domestic pigs and wild boars, providing the first evidence of PCV3 circulation in Uruguay. All characterized PCV3 strains clustered within PCV3a, and PCV2/PCV3 coinfection was observed in several PCV3-positive samples. These findings indicate that PCV2d predominated among the investigated clinical cases from non-vaccinated farms and confirm PCV3 circulation in Uruguay, making it the fifth South American country to report the virus. Continued molecular surveillance is warranted to monitor PCV2 and PCV3 diversity and better understand the epidemiology of PCVs in Uruguay and across South America.
records.authors: Ramos N, Galiano A, Betancour G, de Oliveira LGS, Buroni F, Boabaid F, Arbiza J.

records.title: The Sensitivity of  13  C-Metabolic Flux Analysis to Biomass Composition Underscores the Need for Accurate Biomass Formulation in  Escherichia coli
records.abstract: Quantifying intracellular fluxes through  13 C-metabolic flux analysis (  13 C-MFA) provides a detailed view of cellular metabolism. While model formulation, including biomass synthesis reactions, is known to influence flux estimations, the degree to which biomass composition affects  13 C-MFA outcomes in  Escherichia coli remains debated. Here, we reconstructed a genome-scale  13 C-MFA model of  E. coli incorporating explicit nucleotide biosynthesis and a modular biomass formulation that separates protein, RNA, and other components. Using isotopic labeling experiments and systematic perturbations of biomass composition, we demonstrate that  13 C-MFA can robustly differentiate subtle shifts in the protein/RNA ratio, with deviations as small as 2–3% producing statistically significant but biologically interpretable changes in model fit. Reaction-level analyses revealed consistent flux adjustments across amino acid and nucleotide biosynthesis, while pathways in one-carbon metabolism, particularly serine, glycine, and threonine interconversions, exhibited the strongest responses. Collectively, these results highlight the robustness and discriminative power of  13 C-MFA and also demonstrate the importance of accurate biomass composition measurement in  E. coli 13 C-MFA, given the method’s intrinsic sensitivity to macromolecular stoichiometry.
records.authors: Cai Y, Antoniewicz MR.

records.title: CST–Polα/primase, backed up by Rif1, protects telomeric ss-dsDNA junctions from damage recognition and resection
records.abstract: The yeast Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 (CST) complex is critical for telomere length regulation and telomere protection. Recent studies further implicate Polα/primase (PP) as an essential partner of CST in executing these functions, but the mechanistic bases remain poorly understood. Using the pathogenic yeast  Nakaseomyces glabratus , a model amenable to mechanistic dissection of CST-PP, we analyzed the protection mechanisms of CST-PP by combining mutations that disrupt individual subunits or complex assembly with mutations in DNA damage response (DDR) and DNA repair factors. The complete loss of Cdc13 – which eliminates the CST-PP assembly – results in telomere damage recognition involving Rad9, Rad24 and Mec3, as well as aberrant resection mediated by Exo1 and Sgs1. In contrast, disrupting the interaction between CST and PP leads to proliferation defects triggered primarily by Exo1, implying a more selective protection function for PP. The involvement of the DDR clamp loader and clamp together with Exo1 points to ss-dsDNA junctions with recessed 5’ ends as a crucial lesion in the absence of Cdc13. Further analysis implicates RNase H1 and H2 in promoting DNA damage, possibly by exposing such junctions. Based on similarities between Cdc13 and POT1, a telomere protein previously implicated in junctional protection, we modeled Cdc13 binding to a ss-dsDNA junction and showed that point mutations at the proposed interaction site impaired telomere protection and altered the distribution of the telomere C-strand 5’ ends  in vivo . We further demonstrate that Rif1, another telomere protein with junctional binding activity, supports the protection function of CST-PP. Together, our findings illuminate the molecular basis of telomere DNA damage and of CST-PP mediated telomere protection.
records.authors: Yu EY, Calugaru K, Younten T, Huang S, Lue NF.

records.title: Cap-specific N6-adenosine methyltransferases and applications in m6A Cap-1 mRNA synthesis
records.abstract: In addition to the 5’ Cap-1 structure, the initiating adenosine of mammalian mRNA can be further modified by PCIF1 (Phosphorylated C-terminal domain-interacting factor 1) to form 2’-O,N6-dimethyladenosine (m6A Cap-1). While the biological role is still under investigation, the implications of m6A Cap-1 in mRNA metabolism and viral-host interactions have spurred interest in PCIF1 and m6A Cap-1 as biomarkers, drug targets, and research tools. Here, we identify and characterize two PCIF1-like cap-specific N6-adenosine methyltransferases, PC04 and PC05 and evaluate their applicability in m6A Cap-1 mRNA synthesis  in vitro. We found that both enzymes are highly specific to the m7G cap structure and highly active on Cap-1 RNA oligonucleotides and trinucleotide Cap-1 analogs at nanomolar concentrations. We demonstrate that PC04 or PC05 methylation reactions can be incorporated into established post-transcriptional capping and cap analog-based co-transcriptional  in vitro transcription (IVT) workflows to produce m6A Cap-1 RNAs. Finally, we show that PC05 can be combined with a previously reported FCE::T7 RNA polymerase fusion to synthesize m6A Cap-1 mRNA from DNA templates in a single step, co-transcriptional manner. The robustness of the PCIF1-like cap N6-adenosine methyltransferases can accelerate research into the biological roles of cap m6A modification and development of highly effective mRNA-based therapeutics. records.title: Root gene regulatory network analysis reveals roles for defense hormones and secondary metabolites in establishment of disease-suppressive soil
records.abstract: Summary  Plants recruit beneficial microbiota in their rhizosphere to alleviate stresses. In  Arabidopsis thaliana , foliar infection by  Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (  Hpa ) has been shown to establish a disease-suppressive microbiome that promotes protection against  Hpa infection of the subsequent plant generation grown in this conditioned soil - a phenomenon known as soil-borne legacy (SBL). The root responses involved in SBL establishment have remained largely unclear.  In this study, time-series RNA-seq of roots from  Hpa -infected plants grown in natural soil was conducted over seven days post-inoculation. A gene regulatory network of the responding roots was constructed. The role of predicted key components was verified in follow-up assays.  Root transcriptional reprogramming started within one day after foliar infection. Genes associated with salicylic acid (SA)-mediated defense were upregulated, while those linked to secondary metabolism and jasmonic acid (JA) responsiveness were downregulated. SA accumulation increased at 1 dpi, and JA decreased by 3 dpi. Transcriptional regulation occurred primarily in the tips of the roots. Mutant analyses confirmed that SA, JA, indole glucosinolates, camalexin, and flavonoids contribute to SBL establishment. Our findings reveal rapid systemic transcriptional reprogramming in roots upon foliar pathogen attack, uncovering novel roles of hormone signaling and secondary metabolism in shaping a disease-suppressive soil beyond their known defense functions.
records.authors: Qi R, Glavincheska I, Spooren J, Liu X, Van Laatum M, Verstappen F, Kappers IF, Berendsen RL, Pieterse CM, Van Wees SC.

records.title: NAD metabolism mediates a sex-specific protection against early life infections
records.abstract: Sex influences early-life immunity and infection outcomes, yet how metabolic mechanisms regulate these effects remain unclear. As nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) can support mitochondrial metabolism and immune function, here we explore how NAD metabolism contributes to sex-specific protection against infections in early life. First, in two independent cohorts of 700 and 386 children, we found that females at birth had higher blood NAD levels than males, and strikingly higher birth NAD levels were associated with reduced infection burdens during the first 3 years of life in females, but with tendency of increased burdens in males. At 18 months, plasma nicotinamide associated with sex-specific cytokine responses to antigen challenges and showed a stronger positive association with tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) activity in females. Next, we verified the causal effects of NAD metabolism on infection protection by testing the supplementation of NAD precursor nicotinamide riboside (NR) in infected newborn piglets, used as a translational model of infection-sensitive infants. NR treatment improved survival, bacterial clearance, and disease tolerance only in females, but not in males. Mechanistically, NR increased levels of hepatic TCA cycle metabolites fumarate and malate, and enhanced hepatic inflammatory, hormonal, and mitochondrial-associated transcriptional programs, again only in females. Finally, the sex-specific immune functions mediated by NR were also validated in blood and immune cells  in vitro . Collectively, we identified NAD metabolism as a sex-dependent immunometabolic mediator in early-life infection. Our findings suggest the potential of sex-stratified nutritional interventions in infection-sensitive infants.

records.title: Drp1 deficiency enhances macrophage efferocytosis and partially restores gut microbial dysbiosis in colitis
records.abstract: Abstract    Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) is a key regulator of mitochondrial fission, but its role in intestinal macrophages and gut microbial homeostasis during colitis remains unclear. Herein, Drp1 expression was increased in intestinal macrophages from patients with ulcerative colitis and mice with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, as demonstrated by transcriptomic, single-cell, and immunofluorescence analyses. To determine its functional role, colitis was induced in conditional Drp1 knockout mice and littermate controls. Macrophage Drp1 deficiency reduced disease activity, colon shortening, histopathological injury, and mucus barrier disruption. Colonic transcriptomic profiling further revealed reduced inflammatory signaling and enrichment of pathways related to macrophage differentiation, apoptotic-cell clearance, and efferocytosis. Consistently, Drp1-deficient macrophages exhibited enhanced apoptotic-cell uptake  in vitro  . Furthermore, 16S rRNA sequencing showed that Drp1 deficiency partially reversed colitis-associated alterations in gut microbial community structure, without significantly affecting overall alpha diversity. This microbial remodeling was characterized by increased  Akkermansia  and  Muribaculaceae  , while reduced  Escherichia-Shigella  and  Enterococcus  . Collectively, these findings indicate that Drp1 deficiency attenuates acute colitis by reshaping macrophage functional states and enhancing efferocytosis, while being associated with improved mucosal integrity and partial restoration of gut microbial dysbiosis.
records.authors: Huang C, Liao Y, Zhang Y, Guo X, Xiang L, Zhang L, Ye Z, Zhao Y, Li Y, Zhou Y, Zhou Y.

records.title: Development and Laboratory Evaluation of a Standardized Procedure for Environmental Sampling and Molecular Detection of Human Papillomavirus
records.abstract: Abstract  Background  Environmental surveillance of infectious pathogens is increasingly important for disease prevention and control; however, heterogeneity in sampling, preservation, and transport procedures can substantially affect molecular detection results. Methods  Human papillomavirus (HPV) was used as a non-enveloped DNA virus model to evaluate six determinants of surface sampling performance: swab type, surface material, sampling interval, swab pre-moistening, ambient temperature, and preservation medium. An HPV-positive inoculum was prepared by pooling approximately 150 anonymized male urethral swab specimens, followed by saline elution, genotype confirmation, and quantitative testing. HPV DNA was quantified by real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR). Outcomes were the positive detection rate and a prespecified log-scale recovery index. Results  Polyester and sponge swabs achieved the highest positive detection rates (both 98.04% ± 3.40%), whereas polyester swabs had the highest mean log-scale recovery index. HPV DNA was more readily recovered from smooth, non-porous, non-absorbent surfaces (ceramic tile and polypropylene) than from wood or woven fabric. Dry polyester swabbing yielded a higher positive detection rate than PBS-pre-moistened swabbing (88.75% ± 2.80% vs 80.00% ± 5.23%; P = 0.032), although the log-scale recovery index did not differ significantly. Sampling from 1 to 24 h after inoculation did not significantly affect either outcome. Exposure to 35°C reduced both the positive detection rate and the log-scale recovery index compared with 15°C and 25°C. Dedicated viral transport media maintained HPV DNA detectability throughout 28 days of storage at 2–8°C. PBS first fell below the prespecified 70% detection threshold on day 7, whereas normal saline remained at or above the threshold through 3 h and fell below it at 6 h. Conclusions  Under the tested laboratory conditions, dry polyester swabs combined with dedicated viral transport media provided the most practical overall approach for molecular recovery of HPV from environmental surfaces. Surface properties and ambient temperature were the principal determinants of HPV DNA detectability. These findings support protocol standardization but do not establish viral infectivity or fomite transmission.

records.title: Evidence that the perinatal maternal microbiome mediates metabolite signaling programs that drive sex-specific microglial metabolic alterations and Alzheimer’s disease susceptibility
records.abstract: Abstract  Maternal microbiome-dependent programming of neuroimmune and metabolic pathways during early development may critically shape sex-specific susceptibility to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) later in life. We have documented that in mouse models of Aβ deposition, broad-spectrum antibiotic (ABX)-mediated perturbations of the gut microbiome postnatally (P14-P21) selectively reduces Aβ pathology only in male, but not in female animals. Here, we shift the developmental window upstream to test whether perinatal maternal microbiome perturbations shapes the pathological trajectories of offspring. Dams were treated with the broad-spectrum ABX from preconception through gestation, without direct exposure of the offspring. Strikingly, maternal microbiome disruption selectively reduced cortical Aβ burden in female offspring, with no effect in males, effectively reversing the sex bias observed following postnatal ABX manipulations. To explore the mechanisms underlying this effect, we now report that female offspring exhibited coordinated shifts in microbial composition and amino acid metabolism, that are coupled to cortical transcriptional programs enriched for GPCR signaling and Rho GTPase pathways. As many microbial metabolites and amino acid-derived ligands signal through GPCRs that are expressed by microglia, these transcriptional changes suggest enhanced GPCR-mediated nutrient sensing in microglia of female animals. These systems level changes in microglia drive a metabolically engaged amyloid clearing phenotype, providing a mechanistic link between maternal microbiome disruption and enhanced Aβ clearance in females. Together, these findings demonstrate that maternal microbial inheritance and developmental timing critically shape sex specific AD susceptibility and position temporal microbiome modulation as a potential precision strategy for disease prevention.
records.authors: Saha P, Slimmon N, Nadgauda A, Patel P, Mishra D, Poli PB, Inukai A, Fernandez A, Weigle I, Zhang X, Sisodia SS.

records.title: Co-circulation of H5N1 and H5N6 high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses in migratory birds at a coastal wintering site in China.
records.abstract: Since 2020, H5Nx high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs) belonging to hemagglutinin (HA) clade 2.3.4.4b have undergone widespread dispersal in wild birds, posing substantial threats to global poultry populations and mammals worldwide. In this study, we report the co-circulation of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 and H5N6 HPAIVs associated with mortality events in Anseriformes and Charadriiformes at a coastal wintering site in Fujian Province, China. H5N1 and H5N6 viruses were identified in four species of waterfowl (Bean Goose, Eastern Spot-billed Duck, Eurasian Wigeon, and Eurasian Curlew). Phylogenetic analysis indicated that these H5N1 and H5N6 isolates were clade 2.3.4.4b strains circulating within Eurasia and lacked known mammalian adaptation markers in key proteins. The infected birds exhibited severe systemic multi-organ pathology, with the most pronounced damage observed in the lungs. H5N6 and H5N1 viruses caused lethal injury in BALB/c mice, with H5N1 leading to systemic infection. Environmental sampling also revealed the presence of H5N1 HPAIVs alongside low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (LPAIVs) such as H3N1 and H6N1. Our findings highlight the complex and dynamic transmission patterns of H5 HPAIV in wild bird populations and the substantial threat they pose to mammals, underscoring the critical importance of sustained surveillance for high pathogenicity avian influenza in wild birds.

records.title: The Virome of Rhubarb Consists of Diverse Viruses Belonging to at Least Four Families.
records.abstract: Culinary rhubarb (Rheum spp.) comprises herbaceous perennials that are primarily clonally propagated. Like other asexually reproduced crops, rhubarb is vulnerable to virus transmission, but its virome remains poorly characterized. In April 2024, foliar virus-like symptoms, including chlorotic and necrotic leaf spots, chlorosis, and stunting, were observed on cultivar 'Kerwin' in the rhubarb collection at Cornell AgriTech in Geneva, NY. Symptomatic leaf tissue tested positive for tomato ringspot virus (ToRSV) in a double-antibody sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay using specific antibodies. Subsequently, the virome of 40 rhubarb entries was determined using high-throughput sequencing (HTS) and bioinformatic analyses. Sequence information suggested the presence of ToRSV (genus Nepovirus, family Secoviridae), cherry leafroll virus (genus Nepovirus, family Secoviridae), Arabis mosaic virus (genus Nepovirus, family Secoviridae), broad-leafed dock virus A (BLDVA, genus Macluravirus, family Potyviridae), tobacco streak virus (TSV, genus Ilarvirus, family Bromoviridae), and beet curly top virus (BCTV, genus Curtovirus, family Geminiviridae) in composite leaf samples. The occurrence of these RNA and DNA viruses was confirmed in composite and individual samples after deconvolution by RT-PCR or PCR, respectively, using one or two primer pairs, in combination with bidirectional Sanger sequencing of the amplicons. The symptoms of cultivar 'Kerwin' could not be definitively assigned to ToRSV due to co-infection with BLDVA. This is the first characterization of the rhubarb virome by HTS and the first report of ToRSV, BLDVA, TSV, and BCTV in culinary rhubarb. These findings have implications for the propagation of clean material, distribution of germplasm, and future breeding efforts in rhubarb. [Formula: see text] Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). records.title: SNORD42A serves as an oncogenic biomarker in non-small cell lung cancer.
records.abstract: BackgroundDespite substantial advances in therapeutic strategies, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. The poor prognosis of NSCLC is largely due to the limited efficacy of existing clinical treatments and the lack of reliable and effective molecular therapeutic targets. Studies have shown that small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) play pivotal regulatory roles in multiple pathological processes involved in tumor formation and malignant progression. However, the specific biological functions and underlying molecular mechanisms of individual snoRNAs in the occurrence and development of NSCLC remain largely unclear, highlighting the need for systematic exploration.MethodsA reanalysis of genome-scale clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-Cas9 knockout screening data covering all annotated snoRNAs in NSCLC cell lines was performed. Colony formation assays confirmed the functional role of SNORD42A in NSCLC cells. A combined bioinformatic analysis of our internal sequencing data and public datasets further identified the molecular locus of SNORD42A in the pathogenesis of NSCLC.ResultsGenome-wide screening identified SNORD42A as a key candidate snoRNA regulating NSCLC cell proliferation. Both the in-house snoRNA sequencing data and bioinformatics analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohort demonstrated that SNORD42A was significantly overexpressed in clinical NSCLC tissues compared with paired adjacent normal lung tissues, indicating its potential oncogenic role in NSCLC. Functional validation experiments further demonstrated that SNORD42A knockdown markedly inhibited the clonogenic capacity of NSCLC cells. Moreover, an integrative bioinformatics analysis of TCGA data revealed that SNORD42A expression was closely correlated with cell cycle regulation and cellular senescence signaling pathways, and its expression level was significantly associated with the clinical prognosis of patients with NSCLC.ConclusionsSNORD42A functions as a pro-tumorigenic factor that promotes NSCLC progression, with its effects potentially linked to alterations in cellular protein synthesis. This study revealed the functional importance of SNORD42A in NSCLC malignancy, suggesting that SNORD42A may serve as a novel prognostic biomarker and a promising therapeutic target for the treatment of NSCLC.
records.authors: Cui C, Wang Y, Xia J, Sun T, Chen Y, Wang H, Wu Q.

records.title: Selection of Anti-TIGIT Affibody Molecules Blocking the Interaction between TIGIT and CD155.
records.abstract: T cell immunoglobulin and ITIM domain (TIGIT) is an immune checkpoint receptor expressed on T and NK cells that, upon interaction with its ligand CD155, suppresses immune cell activation. Tumor cells sometimes upregulate CD155 to evade detrimental immune reactions, and TIGIT is therefore an attractive target for the development of novel checkpoint inhibitor therapies. TIGIT has also been shown to be upregulated on tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs), enabling imaging of TILs for patient stratification for immune checkpoint therapy. Here, we have selected so-called affibody molecules targeting TIGIT from a combinatorial affibody library displayed on the surface ofEscherichia coli. The two most promising candidates had equilibrium dissociation constants (K D values) of 2.5 and 6.5 nM, and were found to specifically interact with TIGIT-expressing cells. Furthermore, the affibody candidates were found to successfully block the interaction between TIGIT and CD155, suggesting future application as immune checkpoint inhibitors. Using an ensemble of general language models for in silico evolution, a variant with a 4.4 °C increased melting temperature could be derived, albeit with a 2-fold weaker affinity. The promising results justify further development of the anti-TIGIT affibodies for in vivo TIL-imaging and immune checkpoint therapy.
records.authors: Ehrenborg L, Garousi J, Zhang J, Grönlund H, Gräslund T.

records.title: Phytoremediation of Metals and Nutrients by Aquatic Macrophytes in an Urban Semiarid River (Mossoró, Brazil).
records.abstract: Urban expansion and riverbank anthropogenic pressures have intensified the elemental loading of urban rivers, a problem that is exacerbated in semiarid regions where low flows, long residence times, and evaporation favor solute concentration and changes in aqueous speciation. Here, we quantified nutrients and trace metals and assessed macrophyte bioaccumulation and translocation in the urban reach of the Apodi-Mossoró River. Water and plant tissues of Nymphaea alba and Eichhornia crassipes were collected in eight campaigns across six sites during dry and rainy seasons. The elemental suite comprised N, P, Na, K, Ca, Mg, Cu, Zn, Fe, Mn, Cd, Cr, Ni, and Pb. Descriptive statistics and multivariate analyses evidenced element-specific patterns driven by spatial gradients and climatic seasonality that influence metal mobility and bioavailability. Phytoremediation performance was species dependent: Nymphaea alba displayed higher bioaccumulation and translocation for Pb (16,669.64) and Cu (9.32), whereas Eichhornia crassipes showed greater accumulation and translocation for Cr (11,291.96) and Ni (23.23). Overall, the contrasting uptake and internal partitioning of trace metals, together with seasonal variability in nutrient concentrations, support the use of Nymphaea alba and Eichhornia crassipes as complementary biomonitors and as candidate species for phytoremediation of metal and nutrient contamination in urban semiarid rivers.

records.title: SDHC Gene is a Potential Player in the Pathogenesis of Congenital Heart Disease and Neurodevelopmental Disorder by Promoting eNOS Signaling, Suppressing Inflammation and Improving Angiogenic Endothelial Function.
records.abstract: IntroductionCongenital Heart Disease (CHD) and Neurodevelopmental Disorders (NDD) frequently co-occur due to shared genetic defects in embryonic angiogenesis and mitochondrial metabolism; however, the regulatory mechanisms linking these pathways remain poorly understood.ObjectiveTo identify pathogenic genes underlying CHD-NDD co-development and investigate the regulatory role of Succinate Dehydrogenase Complex Subunit C (SDHC) in endothelial angiogenesis.MethodsBlood samples from 70 children (13 CHD+NDD, 33 CHD, 24 NDD) were analyzed by Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) and Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS). Candidate genes were identified through bidirectional deduplication, multi-library comparison, PPI network analysis, and functional enrichment analysis. SDHC expression was examined by immunofluorescence in the developing mouse heart and brain. In Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) with SDHC overexpression or knockdown, eNOS and TNF-α protein levels were measured by Western blot. Cell migration and tube formation were quantified by scratch and Matrigel assays.ResultsWES identified high-frequency SDHC mutations, including T→TTA (Chr1:161293485, 33.33%) and C→CT (Chr1:161332091, 55.56%) in CHD+NDD. Bioinformatics suggested SDHC involvement in cardiac and neural development. In mice, cardiac SDHC increased age-dependently by 71.83% (P DiscussionThese findings suggest SDHC dysregulation may affect CHD-NDD comorbidity through eNOS modulation and inflammatory responses in HUVECs. The presence of SDHC variants in 7 of 13 patients (53.8%) and functional data indicate SDHC may serve as a candidate angiogenesis regulator linking cardiovascular and neurodevelopmental abnormalities. However, the small cohort (n = 13 CHD + NDD), absence of healthy controls, and lack of patient-derived variant validation limit definitive conclusions. The biological consequences of the identified variants remain unknown because variant-specific functional analyses were not performed. Future studies require expanded cohorts and in vivo SDHC- specific models to investigate potential associations.ConclusionSDHC may play potential roles in eNOS signaling, inflammation suppression, and endothelial angiogenic function. These findings suggest SDHC as a candidate gene associated with CHD-NDD comorbidity.
records.authors: Deng X, Zhao Y, Deng W, Wang Z, Zhou K, Xu Q, Li X, Qin X, Guo L, Tan Y, Qian Y, Xiao Y, Jiang ZS.

records.title: Three new species of Hohenbuehelia (Agaricales, Basidiomycota) from China based on morphological and multi-locus phylogenetic evidence.
records.abstract: The genus Hohenbuehelia, widely distributed in temperate and tropical regions, plays an important role in forest ecosystems. However, the species diversity of Hohenbuehelia in China has been underestimated. This study presents the morphological and molecular characterization of three novel Hohenbuehelia species from China, enhancing the understanding of this genus in the region. Hohenbuehelia albomarginata is characterized by small, gray-brown to brown basidiomata with a frosted, concolorous tomentum on the pileus, often white at the margin, and elongate basidiospores. Hohenbuehelia striata differs in having brown, glabrous basidiomata that are laterally or dorsally attached, lacking a stipe or pseudostipe, with a very faintly translucent-striate pileus margin and ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid basidiospores. Hohenbuehelia guizhouensis has a gray-brown to brown pileus covered with white tomentum, lamellae radiating from the point of attachment, and elongate, ellipsoid to subreniform basidiospores. Phylogenetic analyses based on multigene sequence data further support their taxonomic distinctiveness. All species are comprehensively described, illustrated, and compared with closely related and morphologically similar taxa. This study expands the known diversity of Hohenbuehelia and highlights the need for further exploration of fungal diversity in China.
records.authors: Luo T, Che NJ, Feng WC, Cui YY, Li J.

records.title: Graphene family nanomaterials - atrazine - extracellular polymeric substances: a triangular interplay during short- and long-term exposure of marine microalgae Chlorella sp.
records.abstract: The co-occurrence of graphene family nanomaterials (GFNs) and organic pollutants in aquatic environments raises concerns regarding their individual as well as combined effects on marine primary producers. The present research investigates the toxicity of graphene, graphene oxide (GO), and reduced graphene oxide (rGO), both individually and in combination with atrazine (ATZ), in the marine microalga Chlorella sp. over short-term (72 h) and long-term (360 h) exposure periods, with a particular focus on the protective role of algal extracellular polymeric substances (EPS). For the determination of toxicity, growth, photosynthesis, reactive oxygen species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), and antioxidant enzyme activities were studied. The results show that GFNs in various combinations with ATZ can inhibit growth, hinder photosynthesis, induce oxidative stress and accelerate lipid peroxidation. Among the three GFNs studied, rGO was the most toxic, followed by GO and graphene. Exposure to binary mixtures of GFNs and ATZ resulted in different responses compared to the individual pollutants, indicating the effect of the combination of GFNs and ATZ, as well as the exposure duration. Importantly, EPS markedly alleviated the adverse effects of ATZ, GFNs and their combination by reducing oxidative stresses and improving photosynthesis and biochemical responses. The uptake study revealed decreased accumulation of ATZ in cells in the presence of EPS. Finally, the current work concludes that algal EPS is an important natural defence system that regulates the bioavailability and toxicity of GFNs and other organic contaminants such as ATZ, even when they co-occur in the environment for a long duration.
records.authors: Debroy A, Pulimi M, Mukherjee A.

records.title: A planthopper-secreted miRNA facilitates viral infection by disrupting plant growth-defense balance in rice.
records.abstract: Insect vectors can enhance the pathogenicity of plant arboviruses, yet the molecular mechanisms driving this cross-kingdom manipulation remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that white-backed planthoppers secrete a specific microRNA, miR-133, into rice to facilitate southern rice black-streaked dwarf virus (SRBSDV) infection. Mechanistically, insect-derived miR-133 functions via cross-kingdom RNA interference to directly repress the GOLDEN2-LIKE transcription factor 31 (OsGLK31). OsGLK31 acts as a dual regulator that promotes growth via OsYUCCA-mediated auxin biosynthesis and confers antiviral immunity through OsLOX11-mediated jasmonic acid (JA) biosynthesis. In the absence of infection, the plant repressor OsJAZ10 binds to OsGLK31 to specifically inhibit its immune function, thereby prioritizing growth. However, insect infestation disrupts this balance: insect-secreted miR-133 represses OsGLK31 expression, while OsJAZ10 blocks the transcriptional activity of residual OsGLK31 protein on OsLOX11. This coordinated blockade suppresses both auxin and JA biosynthesis, causing severe dwarfism and dampened viral resistance. Our findings reveal miR-133 as a cross-kingdom effector that disrupts the host plant growth-defense balance to pave the way for viral invasion, offering potential targets for antiviral crop improvement.
records.authors: Zhang B, Jia S, Zhu Y, Gao Q, Ding W, He H, Gao H, Jing D, Li Y, Qiu L.

records.title: The Influence of Nitrogen on Alnus glutinosa Susceptibility to Phytophthora × alni.
records.abstract: Riparian forest ecosystems face multiple anthropogenic pressures, including chronic nitrogen (N) pollution and invasive pathogens. However, the putative synergies among them are poorly understood. In the case of the keystone N-fixing tree Alnus glutinosa attacked by the exotic pathogen Phytophthora × alni, such pressures may act synergistically. N can indirectly promote susceptibility to the pathogen by affecting native soil microbiome composition and disrupting alder's symbiotic partnership with actinobacteria of the genus Frankia. In a greenhouse experiment that involved the manipulation of N through fertilization and Frankia nodulation through soil sterilization, we examined the interactive effects of nodulation, soil microbiota, and P. × alni infection on alder performance. We found that alder survival after infection was strongly influenced by the origin of the substrate in which the plants were grown. Under N-fertilization, mortality due to Phytophthora was higher in plants grown without alder soil amendments. In contrast, in soils amended with alder soil, N-fertilization did not increase alder susceptibility to the pathogen, although it significantly reduced Frankia nodulation. Nodulation was lowest in plants carrying the highest pathogen loads, showing that P. × alni infection not only kills alders but also undermines N-fixation. Our findings show that N-fertilization and P. × alni suppress nodulation and therefore can simultaneously contribute negatively to the N-fixing central function of alders in river ecosystems. Our results also seem to discard any protective role of soil microbiome or Frankia nodulation against P. × alni on alder.
records.authors: Vieites-Blanco C, Caballol M, Oliva J.

records.title: Two-component system VraSR senses host defense peptide PMAP-36 to promote Streptococcus suis pathogenicity through regulating accD expression.
records.abstract: Streptococcus suis (S. suis) is an important zoonotic pathogen that causes severe infections in humans and animals worldwide. Upon infection, the host innate immune system produces host defense peptides (HDPs) to resist S. suis invasion. PMAP-36, a porcine-derived HDP, has been shown to fail to kill S. suis, suggesting that this pathogen has evolved strategies to evade PMAP-36-mediated immune defense. However, the exact mechanism by which S. suis responds to PMAP-36 remains unclear. Here we showed that PMAP-36 significantly enhanced S. suis adhesion, cytotoxicity, and virulence gene expression. The two-component system (TCS) VraSR was essential for PMAP-36 to promote S. suis pathogenicity. We demonstrated that PMAP-36 directly bound to the sensor kinase VraS. Further transcriptomic analysis revealed that VraSR sensed PMAP-36 to regulate fatty acid biosynthesis, in which a key gene accD expression was significantly downregulated in both PMAP-36-treated ΔvraS and ΔvraR mutant strains. Deletion of accD attenuates S. suis in vivo pathogenicity, including reduced bacterial loads, alleviated organ damage, and decreased inflammatory response. Additionally, VraSR-mediated accD expression was critical for S. suis-induced cytotoxicity and inflammatory response, as deletion of vraS or vraR fails to reduce inflammatory cytokines production due to sustained high accD expression. This study reveals VraSR-mediated virulence regulatory mechanism in response to HDP activation, which provides new insight into the development of novel strategies to combat S. suis infection.
records.authors: Pan Y, Lu Y, Zhang T, Hu Z, Liu H, Su B, Lei R, Zhang T, Zhang Y, Cao X, Li Z, Fang R, Peng L.

records.title: Meeting Report of the 6th edition of metabolism and cancer symposium.
records.abstract: The 6th International Meeting "Metabolism and Cancer" was held at the Convention Center in La Grande Motte, France, on October 8-10, 2025. The three-day conference brought together 240 participants from eleven countries and featured 29 scientific presentations, including 15 invited lectures delivered by leading investigators in the field of oncometabolism. The program was structured into four thematic sessions: (i) diet, cachexia, microbiome, and microenvironment; (ii) stem cells and metabolic plasticity; (iii) epigenetics, epitranscriptomics, and metabolism; and (iv) metabolic control of drug resistance, therapy, and biomarkers. This meeting report highlights key conceptual advances and emerging directions discussed during the conference. Future progress in cancer metabolism will depend on elucidating the cross-talk between tumors and peripheral tissues, as organism-level metabolic regulation is likely to critically influence tumor growth, plasticity, and treatment sensitivity. Moving forward, a systems-level integration of metabolic, genomic, and spatial data is poised to redefine cancer metabolism from a descriptive field into a source of actionable vulnerabilities for precision oncology.
records.authors: B Sant'Anna-Silva AC, Del Bove C, Efthymiou G, Henry E, Henry L, Kundnani J, Rossignol R, Zimmermann S.

records.title: First Report of Tenacibaculum maritimum Infection in Grouper (Epinephelus spp.) Aquaculture in Taiwan.
records.abstract: Between April 2024 and 2025, six independent outbreaks of ulcerative skin disease occurred in cultured groupers (Epinephelus spp.) across southern Taiwan and Penghu County during winter-to-spring seasonal transitions at water temperatures ranging from 19°C to 24°C. Affected fish presented with extensive epidermal erosion and deep dermal ulceration on the operculum, lateral trunk and caudal peduncle regions. Histopathology revealed marked integumentary breakdown characterised by epithelial sloughing, deep dermal necrosis and dense basophilic mats of filamentous bacteria tracking along necrotic subcutaneous myofibres. Wet-mount microscopy and Gram-stained lesion smears consistently revealed sheets of long, slender, Gram-negative rods across all cases (n = 18). Eighteen representative isolates exhibiting pale-yellow, flat, adherent colonies with irregular margins were recovered on Marine Agar formulated with natural seawater (salinity 30‰-35‰). Species-specific PCR and near-full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing (1505 bp; > 99.5% identity to the type strain NCIMB 2154T) confirmed the aetiology to be Tenacibaculum maritimum. Physiological profiling revealed a narrow salinity tolerance window (30‰-45‰), in contrast to the broader range of classic temperate strains (10‰-35‰). This study represents the first definitive isolation and molecular/physiological characterisation of T. maritimum in farmed groupers in Taiwan, expanding its host spectrum and geographical range into subtropical mariculture zones.
records.authors: Wu ST, Hsieh CY.

records.title: Substitutions in the yeast Nrd1 RNA-binding domain have distinct effects on NNS terminator recognition.
records.abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) regulate gene expression through combinatorial interactions with RNAs and proteins. The essential S. cerevisiae nuclear RBP Nrd1 serves as a model to investigate the effects of RBPs on transcription and RNA processing. Nrd1 binding to short, noncoding RNAs elicits termination of their synthesis by RNA polymerase (RNAP) II, promotes polyadenylation by the TRAMP complex, and enables 3'-trimming by the nuclear exosome. How Nrd1 discriminates its substrate RNAs and coordinates these processes is not well understood. Here, we made deletions and substitutions in Nrd1 to assess the contributions of different domains to its function. We confirmed the contribution of known protein interaction domains in NNS terminator recognition and identified a region C-terminal to the RNA-binding domain (RBD) required for efficient termination in vivo. We also characterized three RBD substitutions, two of which were obtained in a screen for spindle pole body assembly defects and one of which increases RNAP II terminator recognition by S. pombe Seb1, a Nrd1 ortholog. All three caused NNS terminator readthrough in vivo and decreased RNA-binding affinity of the RBD in vitro. Surprisingly, the substitution with the most severe in vitro RNA-binding defect, G344D, exhibited readthrough of only a minority of snoRNA terminators affected by the original nrd1-5 substitution (V368G), which had the least severe RNA-binding defect. Transcriptome analysis showed that Nrd1-G344D caused dysregulation of mRNAs largely distinct from those affected by Nrd1-5 and identified a role for Nrd1-dependent termination in phosphate regulation similar to that of Seb1 in S. pombe. We conclude that the G344D and V368G substitutions in the RNA recognition motif distinguish between some of the diverse substrates of Nrd1.
records.authors: Zawisza KA, Goguen EC, Brow DA.

records.title: A yeast surface display platform for oral delivery of a SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain dimer inducing mucosal and systemic immunity.
records.abstract: The development of scalable and stable antigen delivery systems remains a central challenge in vaccine biotechnology, particularly for oral immunization targeting mucosal immunity. Here, we report a yeast surface display (YSD)-based platform for the oral delivery of a SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD) dimer. A head-to-tail tandem RBD was genetically fused to the Aga2p subunit and anchored to the cell wall of Saccharomyces cerevisiae via the Aga1p-Aga2p system, generating the YSD-RBD-dimer construct. Flow cytometry confirmed clear surface expression, with 51.1% dual-positive cells recognizing both HA-tag and RBD epitopes. Under simulated gastric conditions (pH 1.2), the antibody-binding signal associated with surface-displayed RBD-dimer showed 97.57% retention after 2 h, indicating preservation of antibody-accessible RBD-associated epitopes. In vivo fluorescence tracking revealed gastrointestinal transit with signals peaking in Peyer's patches at 6 h and mesenteric lymph nodes at 12 h. Oral immunization elicited both systemic and mucosal immune responses, characterized by elevated serum anti-RBD IgG and fecal secretory IgA. Notably, vaccine-induced sera substantially inhibited RBD-ACE2 binding in a cell-based assay, with an inhibition rate of 81.6% ± 6.4%. Antigen-specific lymphocyte proliferation and transcriptional analysis revealed a mixed Th1- and Th2-associated response, with greater induction of IFN-γ and T-bet than of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and GATA-3. No apparent systemic toxicity or histopathological abnormalities were observed, supporting the preliminary safety of the platform. Collectively, this study supports the feasibility of a scalable yeast surface display-based platform for oral delivery of protein antigens and induction of coordinated systemic and mucosal immune responses.

records.title: Standardizing spatial transcriptomic analysis for infectious diseases with STID.
records.abstract: Spatial transcriptomic studies of infectious diseases still rely on fragmented data analysis processes. Here, we developed STID (spatial transcriptomics toolkit for infectious diseases), a standardized framework for spatial transcriptomic analysis of infectious diseases that leverages the Seurat ecosystem and incorporates Python-based modules. STID provides an extensible infection-specific data structure and supports a full suite of analyses, such as pathogen background correction, infection-associated spot and niche identification, single-sample niche characterization, and multi-sample comparative and temporal analyses. STID is broadly applicable to spatial transcriptomic data from infectious diseases caused by bacteria, viruses, and parasites and enables systematic characterization of the structural features, cellular composition, molecular functions, and host-pathogen interactions within pathogen-infected and/or host-responsive niches. Overall, STID provides an accessible, reproducible, and extensible framework for analyzing infection-associated spatial transcriptomic data and for dissecting host-pathogen interactions in their native spatial microenvironments.
records.authors: Qin Y, Peng Y, Chen Q, Chen J, Ren P, Deng H, Wang D, Liu X, Ou Z, Deng Z, Shi X.

records.title: Predictors of HIV reservoir size and decay dynamics in early-treated paediatric infection: a prospective, multicentre longitudinal cohort study.
records.abstract: BackgroundEarly antiretroviral therapy (ART) after perinatal HIV infection can restrict reservoir size and diversity, offering potential for remission. We evaluated HIV-1 DNA dynamics up to four years of age and predictors of reservoir size in early-treated African children.MethodsIn this prospective, multicentre cohort study, infants with perinatal HIV from South Africa, Mozambique, and Mali who initiated ART before 6 months of age and within 3 months of diagnosis were enrolled. Children were followed at 2, 6, 12, and 24 weeks, then biannually for 4 years. Total HIV-1 DNA in PBMCs was quantified longitudinally by droplet digital PCR in 207 children. The main outcomes were HIV-1 DNA reservoir size at year 3 (log10 copies/million PBMC) and longitudinal HIV-1 DNA decay. Multivariable models were developed to identify predictors of reservoir size using generalised additive regression models, and decay dynamics were evaluated using mixed-effects Poisson models including random intercepts and viral load slopes.FindingsOf 207 children, 155 (75%) had >12 months of follow-up. HIV was diagnosed at a median age of 31 days (IQR: 0, 47) and ART started at 33 days (IQR: 23.5, 69.5). Nineteen of 155 (12.3%) had undetectable HIV-1 DNA at year 4. Median decay rate was -0.020 log10 copies/million cells/month (-0.212/year). Smaller reservoirs at year 3 were associated with lower pre-ART viral load (β = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.09, 0.43) and faster first-year HIV-1 DNA decay rate (β = 1.09, 95% CI: 0.02, 2.19), with trends toward smaller reservoirs among females (β = -0.41, 95% CI: -0.87, 0.04) and larger reservoirs among children whose mothers reported social challenges (β = 0.42, 95% CI: -0.04, 0.87). Faster decay correlated with longer time on ART, lower serial viral loads, sustained viral suppression >12 months, earlier ART initiation, and region (Mali). Maternal health issues correlated with slower decay. Eleven "excellent controllers" maintained durable viral suppression, immunological control, and undetectable total HIV-1 DNA at last follow-up.InterpretationEarly virological parameters may help identify children likely to develop smaller HIV reservoirs. Early ART is key to faster reservoir reduction. Maternal health issues influence reservoir decay, reflecting a parental legacy effect. Sex differences should be further explored to understand mechanisms of reservoir control. Children with sustained virological suppression, preserved immune status, and undetectable total HIV-1 DNA may represent candidates with favourable characteristics for HIV remission strategies, as these factors have been associated with a reduced burden of persistent HIV infection and have been observed in rare cases of post-treatment control.FundingEPIICAL consortium through ViiV Healthcare and Penta Foundation.

records.title: Reservoir or Island? Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana) as a Host of 'Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni'-Related Strains.
records.abstract: Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana L.) is a native shrub that is widely found across North America and is a host of 'Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni' associated with X-disease of stone fruits. This pathogen is of major concern to U.S. cherry and peach growers, with the most recent and ongoing outbreak in the Pacific Northwest causing major economic harm. To investigate the role of chokecherry as a potential reservoir and source of orchard-associated strains, we surveyed wild chokecherry trees across 12 U.S. states and compared the strains present with those in commercially cultivated Prunus species. Approximately 47% of chokecherry sampled tested positive for a 'Ca. P. pruni'-related strain and phylogenetic analysis revealed high strain diversity, including six distinct clades and four newly identified lineages. In contrast, 'Ca. P. pruni' strains isolated from cultivated cherry and peach trees exhibited lower diversity and were infected by known disease outbreak-associated strains such as Northwestern-X. These data suggest limited transmission between wild and cultivated hosts in the western United States, with patterns indicating spillover from orchards into nearby chokecherry populations rather than the reverse. However, in states east of the Rocky Mountains, chokecherry likely functions as a reservoir for orchard infections.
records.authors: Hoskins M, Shires M, Thompson A, Molnar C, Cowell S, Harper S.

records.title: Host-virus interactions dominate fitness and conceal additive genetic variation.
records.abstract: Host-parasite coevolution is expected to generate strong selection for resistance and infectivity that has the potential to erode genetic variation. Despite this, natural populations often retain extensive genetic variation in these traits. Genotype-by-genotype interactions on fitness can generate negative frequency-dependent selection, which helps maintain this variation by preventing any host or pathogen genotype from retaining a permanent advantage. Because these interactions place genetic variance in the interaction term rather than in additive differences among hosts or pathogens, that variance is masked from directional selection and can remain 'cryptic'. Here we combine coevolutionary modelling with large‑scale experimental infection assays to quantify how host-pathogen interactions structure fitness variance in a vertically transmitted virus system, Drosophila melanogaster and sigma virus. Simulations show that coevolution typically erodes additive genetic variance in host and pathogen fitness, concentrating variance in host-virus interaction terms. Consistent with these predictions, experiments spanning 90 host-virus genotype combinations reveal that transmission, viral load, and virulence are overwhelmingly governed by host-virus genetic interactions rather than host or virus main effects. As a result, neither host resistance alleles nor viral genotypes confer consistently higher fitness across genetic backgrounds. Interactions tend to be sex‑specific, further limiting heritable fitness variation. Our results demonstrate that coevolution can substantially mask heritable genetic variation from directional selection by rendering fitness context-dependent. This extensive cryptic genetic variation may be revealed either when ecological or evolutionary conditions shift, or when the process of coevolution itself alters the direction of selection. This demonstrates the need to account for genotype-specific interactions when forecasting evolutionary responses.
records.authors: Belyi A, Du Y, Wilson AJ, Longdon B, Jiggins FM.

records.title: Reduction of aflatoxin contamination in maize kernels mediated by host-induced gene silencing.
records.abstract: Aflatoxins produced by some species of Aspergillus pose a significant threat to global food safety, because they contaminate a variety of crops including maize. In this study, we used host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) to reduce aflatoxin accumulation in maize upon infection with Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus. Two RNAi constructs were designed and introduced into maize, one targeting two essential fungal genes involved in ergosterol biosynthesis (CYP51A and CYP51B) and the other targeting three aflatoxin biosynthesis genes (AflC, AflD, and AflR). The presence of RNAi transgenes was confirmed in 17 and 14 independent lines possessing the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi construct and the AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi construct, respectively. Most transgenic lines had single-locus integrations and one or two copies of the transgene. Transgene expression varied considerably among the lines. Small RNA sequencing confirmed the production of siRNAs from the HIGS trigger sequences. Levels of CYP51A, AflC, AflD, and AflR transcripts in Aspergillus spp. were successfully decreased upon infection of transgenic maize. However, significant reduction in the level of CYP51B transcripts was not achieved and the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi transgene had no discernible effect on fungal growth in infected maize. In contrast, we observed significant reductions in aflatoxin accumulation in four AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi transgenic lines infected with A. flavus and in two transgenic lines infected with A. parasiticus. Notably, one AflC/AflD/AflR transgenic line exhibited minimal aflatoxin contamination upon kernel infection with A. parasiticus. These results demonstrate the potential of HIGS to reduce aflatoxin production in mature corn kernels.
records.authors: Ahmed A, Cavanaugh K, Baldrich P, Stergiopoulos I, Michelmore R.

records.title: Virus transmission required for maintenance and host adaptation mirrors neurophysiological differences in rabies-derived peptides.
records.abstract: Pathogen adaptations to new hosts are central to the disease ecology of cross-species transmission and host switching of viruses. The rabies virus is a model for adaptations to different hosts as it induces behavioral changes that facilitate transmission, while being maintained in distinct species-specific cycles of infection. Here, we demonstrate that the rabies virus requires distinct transmission dynamics in two hosts with different ecologies to establish maintenance, using agent-based modeling, analyses of virus glycoprotein-mediated manipulation of neuroreceptor function, and phylogenetic analysis. Epidemiological models suggest that rabies virus variants adapted to arctic foxes, which sustain rabies virus at very low host densities, require a higher probability of transmission than viruses adapted to raccoons. Using in vitro electrophysiology, we demonstrate that the rabies glycoprotein-derived peptides from arctic fox rabies variants are more potent antagonists of alpha7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. These findings suggest a possible functional basis for the behavioral modifications that drive enzootic rabies transmission in the context of host ecology. In addition, a large proportion of residues that may drive rabies virus adaptation to raccoons and arctic foxes are found within this neurotoxin-like region. Furthermore, a residue in the neurotoxin-like region of the mature rabies virus glycoprotein (residue 183) has been associated with pathogenicity, host switching, and disease ecology in previous studies. We propose the hypothesis that rabies virus transmission dynamics adapt to the ecology and physiology of novel hosts through the selection of glycoproteins that elicit specific degrees of behavioral modification and transmission probability.
records.authors: Remal A, Acheson ES, Leighton PA, Rees EE, Rhodes J, O'Brien BCV, Weltzin MM, Hueffer K.

records.title: Structural remodeling and activation of the hdeAB and proVWX operons in response to pH and salt stress.
records.abstract: Escherichia coli is highly sensitive to acid and osmotic stress but adapts by modulating the expression of stress-responsive genes. Nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) play key roles in DNA organization and sensing environmental changes. The histone-like nucleoid structuring protein H-NS is an NAP acting as a global regulator of stress genes. H-NS may alter local chromatin structure to modulate the expression of such genes in response to environmental stress. The H-NS homolog suppressor of td phenotype A (StpA) co-regulates several target genes, but its role is poorly defined. To investigate the regulatory interplay between these two proteins, we examined transcription, DNA binding, and chromatin structure at two regulated operons, hdeAB and proVWX, in E. coli following exposure to acid and salt shock. Our results show that H-NS senses pH and osmotic cues to remodel chromatin and relieve repression, while StpA-in part-compensates for H-NS loss, particularly at proVWX, highlighting a coordinated regulatory network.
records.authors: Ge P, Rashid FM, Gaarthuis LKF, Cajili MKM, Tan M, Pang B, Schnetz K, Dame RT.

records.title: Characterization of Chromone Biosynthetic Pathway Reveals a Noncanonical Mode of Fungal Polyketide Cyclization.
records.abstract: Fungal nonreducing polyketide synthases (NRPKSs) produce therapeutically and ecologically important aromatic polyketides. The product template (PT) domain of fungal NRPKSs catalyzes the regioselective aldol cyclization of the reactive poly-β-ketone chain during polyketide maturation and is essential for product fidelity of the NRPKSs. Herein, we discovered the fungal NRPKS MecA of which the polyketide cyclization steps do not involve a functional PT domain. MecA is encoded in the biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) responsible for the formation of 5-hydroxy-7-methoxy-2,3-dimethylchromone (1) from the biocontrol fungus Trichoderma afroharzianum T22. Heterologous expression and in vitro enzymatic assays fully established a biosynthetic pathway of 1 that involves three enzymes: MecA, dehydratase MecB, and methyltransferase MecC. The PT domain of MecA does not contain the conserved catalytic histidine that is essential for aldol cyclization activity. Consistent with the predicted inactive PT domain, MecA was demonstrated to catalyze a C1-C6 Claisen condensation as the first cyclization step of the pentaketide precursor, instead of the canonical aldol cyclization. Reconstitution of dissected MecA domains further demonstrated that the activity of MecA was not affected when the PT domain was removed. A Claisen Cyclase (CLC) domain that typically catalyzes Claisen cyclization in NRPKSs is also absent in MecA, implying the observed C1-C6 cyclization step is catalyzed by the remaining domains. This work contributes to the diversity of NRPKS cyclization chemistry and enables further genome mining and engineering of NRPKSs that may lead to biosynthesis of new aromatic polyketides.

records.title: From discovery to clinical implementation: a bibliometric analysis of DNA methylation biomarkers in non-small cell lung cancer, 1999-2025.
records.abstract: BackgroundDNA methylation alterations are stable, biologically informative, and detectable in tissue and circulating DNA, making them promising biomarkers for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, few methylation biomarkers have entered routine clinical practice. We aimed to characterize the evolution and translational challenges of this field.MethodsPublications on NSCLC, DNA methylation, and biomarker applications were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection through 31 December 2025. After PRISMA-based screening, bibliometric and knowledge-map analyses were performed.ResultsA total of 1,910 publications were included. Annual output increased after 2010 and peaked in 2022. Lung Cancer was the most productive journal, whereas Cancer Research had the highest citation impact. China contributed the largest publication volume, while the United States had the highest citation impact. Foundational studies focused on promoter hypermethylation, methylation-specific PCR, and methylated DNA detection in accessible biospecimens. Research priorities shifted from candidate-gene studies toward methylation signatures, liquid biopsy, multi-omics integration, immunotherapy-related applications, and computational modeling.ConclusionNSCLC methylation biomarker research has evolved toward integrated translational frameworks. Future progress requires multicenter validation, standardized platforms, clinically defined methylation panels, and AI-assisted integration.Protocol registrationwww.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero identifier is CRD420261426546.
records.authors: Li Y, Wu F, Liu W, He X, Chen C.

records.title: Human astroviruses: molecular virology.
records.abstract: SUMMARYHuman astroviruses (HAstVs) are important etiologic agents of pediatric gastroenteritis and are increasingly recognized as pathogens associated with extraintestinal disease, including encephalitis and meningitis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Despite their clinical relevance, widespread prevalence, and expanding genetic diversity, no approved vaccines or antiviral therapies are available. Progress toward effective interventions requires a comprehensive understanding of HAstV molecular biology, including mechanisms of cell entry, viral replication, and immune recognition. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of HAstV epidemiology, clinical manifestations, evolution, and taxonomy, emphasizing recent advances in molecular and structural virology. We examine the HAstV replication cycle, including emerging insights into receptor usage, double-membrane vesicle biogenesis, protease-driven maturation, the capsid's membrane-lytic activity, and virion uncoating. Recent advances in determining high-resolution structures of the capsid core and spike of classical and non-classical HAstVs are highlighted, providing a framework for understanding virion assembly, maturation, and antibody neutralization. These molecular and structural insights highlight conserved and clade-specific vulnerabilities, refine current models of HAstV biology, and identify key molecular determinants that may serve as targets for antiviral development and vaccine design. We also outline critical unresolved questions that define priorities for future research.
records.authors: Lentz A, López T, Ykema M, Tao YJ, DuBois RM, Arias CF.

records.title: Genomic sequencing of recent rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus 2 strains from diseased European rabbits supports a novel incursion into Washington State, USA.
records.abstract: Five feral European rabbits found dead in Washington state tested positive for rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus 2 (RHDV2) by qPCR. Genomic sequencing revealed a nearly identical RHDV2 strain present in the rabbits. The RHDV2 strain was determined to be divergent from previous United States detections, suggesting a novel RHDV2 incursion.

records.title: Inhibition of Horizontal Gene Transfers under Antibiotic Stress Switches Multi-Drug Resistance to Multi-Drug Hyper-susceptibility in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
records.abstract: AimsTo study the effect of spatial distancing between bacteria on horizontal gene transfers, and on the evolution of multi-drug resistance and multi-drug susceptibility to antibiotics.Methods and resultsWe controlled the plating density of bacteria on agar, and showed that, by repeatedly stressing P. aeruginosa with aztreonam, spatial distancing lowers the rate of minimum inhibitory concentration increase and the number of resistant strains. More importantly, resistant PAO1 that evolved without horizontal gene transfers exhibited 2- to 64-fold increases in susceptibility as that of the wild-type PAO1 to multiple unrelated antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin, imipenem, and tetracycline, with which the bacteria were not treated a priori. While biofilm formation by the wild-type PAO1 is generally promoted by antibiotics, biofilm formation by the hypersusceptible PAO1 was inhibited by the sub-minimum inhibitory concentration of antibiotics.ConclusionsBy spatial distancing, stressing PAO1 with aztreonam caused bacteria to become multi-drug hyper-susceptible rather than the reported multi-drug resistant. The biofilm formation by the hyper-susceptible strain was inhibited, rather than promoted, by sub-lethal concentrations of multiple antibiotics.
records.authors: Iradukunda AM, Sauve NJ, Neogi N, Bender JB, Hall MA, Hess HT, Horzempa J, Luk YY.

records.title: First confirmed outbreak of mud crab reovirus (MCRV) causing mass mortality in orange mud crab Scylla olivacea in India.
records.abstract: Mud crab reovirus (MCRV) has emerged as a major challenge in mud crab farming, often leading to sudden mortality and severe economic losses. This study documents an outbreak of MCRV in a Scylla olivacea fattening facility at Bideipur, Odisha, India. Crabs in poor health condition were collected for analysis. The affected animals were sluggish, showed a grey and unhealthy hepatopancreas with autotomy. Histological examination revealed basophilic inclusion bodies together with necrotic changes in the hepatopancreas, gills, and muscle. Transmission electron microscopy confirmed the presence of non-enveloped, icosahedral viral particles arranged in crystalline arrays predominantly within the cytoplasm, together with nuclear alterations including chromatin condensation and nucleolar displacement. Reverse transcription (RT)-PCR produced a distinct amplification at ~433 bp, verifying MCRV infection. Experimental challenges using oral exposure, waterborne transmission, and cohabitation all resulted in complete mortality, demonstrating both the virulence of the virus and its ease of transmission. This study provides the first evidence of MCRV infecting S. olivacea in India. This outbreak underlines the need for consistent health screening, the use of virus-free seed, and strict biosecurity protocols if mud crab aquaculture is to remain sustainable.
records.authors: Kundu A, Ganesan K, Gopalakrishnan A, Luricson L, Chandrakanthan S, Prabhu NM.

records.title: A mitochondrion-like ribosome in an insect endosymbiont
records.abstract: Understanding how the mitochondrion evolved from a bacterial endosymbiont to an organelle is obscured by time and a lack of comparative examples. It is clear that mitochondrial ribosomes are derived from bacterial ribosomes, but it is unclear whether the baroque and idiosyncratic structural changes seen in mitochondrial ribosomes are specifically driven by mitochondrial evolution or simply reflect the syndrome of being a long-term endosymbiont. Here we show that two of the most characteristic features of mitochondrial ribosomes--the acquisition of host proteins and alterations to specific structural regions--are shared by Hodgkinia, an ancient bacterial endosymbiont of cicadas. These results imply that many of the striking changes observed in mitochondrial ribosomes result from their common ancestry as bacterial endosymbionts rather than their uniqueness as mitochondria.

records.title: Biosynthesis, enzymatic basis, and transcriptional regulation of benzylisoquinoline alkaloids in medicinal plants.
records.abstract: Benzylisoquinoline alkaloids (BIAs) are a class of structurally diverse secondary metabolites, with over 2,500 identified variants classified into seven major categories based on their core skeletons. These compounds exhibit significant pharmacological activities - including antitumor, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory effects - and serve as important sources of clinical drugs such as morphine, berberine, and magnoflorine. Currently, BIAs are primarily obtained through plant cultivation and extraction. However, factors such as low in-planta content, seasonal constraints, and environmental variability contribute to vulnerabilities in the supply chain. In light of these challenges, microbial biosynthesis using engineered strains (e.g., yeast) has emerged as a promising alternative, though it requires complete elucidation and functional expression of all pathway enzymes. Enhancing BIAs production in crops through transcriptional regulation - targeting key enzymes, transcription factors (such as WRKY, bHLH, and AP2/ERF families), and phytohormone signaling - represents a feasible interim strategy. Advanced approaches, including coexpression of enzyme genes and transcription factors, hold promise for accelerating the development of industrial-scale alkaloid-producing cell factories and crop improvement, thereby enabling sustainable drug supply.
records.journal: Zeitschrift fur Naturforschung. C, Journal of biosciences

records.title: Spatial modeling of risk factors for human exposure to West Nile virus in rural Madagascar
records.abstract: Background  West Nile virus (WNV) is an emerging disease transmitted from bird hosts to humans by Culex mosquitoes. Thousands of human cases of WNV infection are reported each year in the United States and Europe, and circulation has been confirmed in Africa and the Indian Ocean, including Madagascar. However, little is known about the current riskscape for people in Madagascar, and what determines its local distribution and human exposure across the population. The goal of this study was to assess WNV seroprevalence and identify associated socio-ecological risk factors in rural Madagascar. Methodology and principal findings  A cross-sectional serological survey was conducted in Ifanadiana District in 2021, nested within a representative longitudinal cohort. We evaluated serological responses to WNV in 3,948 individuals using a multiplex bead assay. We estimated WNV seroprevalence using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and characterized environmental, socioeconomic, and demographic factors that could be associated with exposure to WNV using various data sources, including optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite images, climate variables, and household survey data. Overall seroprevalence was 43%, and populations living in geographically isolated areas and those engaged in agricultural activities were at higher risk, while proximity to dense forests and residential areas were protective against WNV exposure. Conclusions  This study found high rates and local heterogeneity in WNV exposure in a rural district of Madagascar. In addition, environmental, climatic, and socio-demographic data were determinants of WNV transmission, providing a valuable tool for surveillance and decision-making in arbovirus prevention and control. Extending this approach to other orthoflaviviruses could improve understanding of local viral co-circulation and promote the development of more precise and context-specific prevention strategies.
